questions.q: Which laryngeal cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence, the Adam's apple?
options: The epiglottis
The cricoid cartilage
The arytenoid cartilage
The thyroid cartilage
questions.why: The thyroid cartilage is the large, shield-shaped cartilage at the front of the larynx. Its anterior ridge sticks forward as the laryngeal prominence, which can be seen and felt in the neck as the Adam's apple. It is one of the three single cartilages of the larynx and is made of hyaline cartilage.
notes: The epiglottis is the spoon-shaped flap of elastic cartilage that folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It sits behind the tongue, not at the front of the neck, so it does not form the Adam's apple.

The cricoid cartilage is the complete ring just below the thyroid cartilage. It is smaller and lower, so it does not form the Adam's apple. Pick it for a question about the only complete ring in the airway.
The arytenoid cartilages are small paired cartilages at the back of the larynx that anchor and move the vocal folds. Because they sit at the back, they cannot form a ridge at the front of the neck.
Correct. The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence.
questions.answerText: The thyroid cartilage

questions.q: Which term names the vocal folds together with the opening between them?
options: The carina
The epiglottis
The glottis
The vestibular folds
questions.why: The glottis is the part of the larynx made of the true vocal folds and the opening between them. As air passes through this opening, the vocal folds vibrate to produce sound. Food is kept away from the glottis during swallowing when the epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet above it.
notes: The carina is the internal ridge where the trachea forks into the main bronchi, far below the larynx. It has nothing to do with the vocal folds.
The epiglottis is the flap of elastic cartilage above the glottis that covers the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. Its name means above the glottis, which is why students mix the two up.
Correct. The glottis is the vocal folds plus the opening between them.

The vestibular folds are the false vocal cords, the pair just above the true vocal folds. The term asked for names the true vocal folds and the opening between them, so this upper pair is not the answer.
questions.answerText: The glottis

questions.q: Which flexible flap folds down over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing?
options: The soft palate
The epiglottis
The vocal folds
The thyroid cartilage
questions.why: The epiglottis is a spoon-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. During a swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over the laryngeal inlet, sending food back toward the esophagus instead of into the airway. Elastic cartilage lets it bend and spring back with each swallow.
notes: The soft palate lifts to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing, which keeps food from entering the nasal cavity. Pick it if the question asked what blocks food from going up into the nose.
Correct. The epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.
The vocal folds vibrate to produce sound and sit below the laryngeal inlet. They are not the flap that covers the airway during swallowing.
The thyroid cartilage is the large shield that forms the Adam's apple. It is rigid hyaline cartilage and does not fold over the airway.
questions.answerText: The epiglottis

questions.q: Which scroll-shaped projections sit on the lateral walls of the nasal cavity?
options: The vocal folds
The paranasal sinuses
The nasal conchae
The nasal septum
questions.why: The three nasal conchae (superior, middle, and inferior) are scroll-shaped projections on each lateral wall of the nasal cavity. They swirl incoming air so more of it touches the warm, moist mucosa, which warms, moistens, and filters it. The air passages beneath each concha are the meatuses.
notes: The vocal folds are in the larynx and vibrate to produce sound. They are folds of tissue in the airway below the pharynx, not in the nasal cavity.

The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities inside the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones that drain into the nasal cavity. They are spaces inside bone, not projections into the cavity.
Correct. The nasal conchae are scroll-shaped projections on the lateral walls.
The nasal septum is the midline wall that divides the nasal cavity into right and left halves. Pick it if the question asked what separates the two sides.
questions.answerText: The nasal conchae

questions.q: The paranasal sinuses are named for the skull bones that contain them. Which set names those bones?
options: The nasal, lacrimal, zygomatic, and palatine bones
The vomer, mandible, maxillary, and temporal bones
The frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones
The frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal bones
questions.why: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities in the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones, which surround the nasal cavity. They drain into the nasal cavity and share its mucous lining. Each sinus takes its name from the bone that holds it.
notes: The nasal, lacrimal, zygomatic, and palatine bones are small facial bones without named paranasal sinuses. Pick this set for a question listing facial bones of the orbit and nose.

This set mixes one right bone with three wrong ones. The maxilla does hold a sinus, but the vomer, mandible, and temporal bone have no paranasal sinuses. The vomer forms part of the nasal septum, which may be why students link it to the sinuses.
Correct. The frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones hold the paranasal sinuses.
Only the frontal bone in this set holds a paranasal sinus. The parietal, occipital, and temporal bones form the sides, back, and base of the cranium, away from the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText: The frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones

questions.q: Which laryngeal cartilages anchor and move the vocal folds?
options: The cuneiform cartilages
The arytenoid cartilages
The cricoid cartilage
The corniculate cartilages
questions.why: The arytenoid cartilages are a pair of small cartilages at the back of the larynx. The vocal ligaments run from the arytenoids forward to the thyroid cartilage, so when the arytenoids move, they open, close, and tighten the vocal folds. They are the most important of the three pairs of laryngeal cartilages.
notes: The cuneiform cartilages are a small pair in the fold between the arytenoid and the epiglottis. Pick them only if the question asked which paired cartilages sit in that fold.
Correct. The arytenoid cartilages anchor and move the vocal folds.
The cricoid cartilage is the single, complete ring at the bottom of the larynx that the arytenoids rest on. Pick it for a question about the only complete cartilage ring in the airway.
The corniculate cartilages are a small pair that sit on top of the arytenoids. They are neighbors of the arytenoids but do not anchor the vocal folds.
questions.answerText: The arytenoid cartilages

questions.q: The nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx together belong to which division of the respiratory system?
options: The upper respiratory tract
The respiratory zone
The lower respiratory tract
The bronchial tree
questions.why: The respiratory system is grouped by location into upper and lower tracts. The upper respiratory tract is the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx, which take in air and condition it. The lower tract begins at the larynx and includes the trachea, bronchi, and lungs.
notes: Correct. These four structures make up the upper respiratory tract.

The respiratory zone is the group of structures where gas exchange happens: the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. That grouping is by function, and none of these upper structures exchange gases.
The lower respiratory tract is the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs. Pick it if the list started at the larynx and went down into the lungs.
The bronchial tree is the branching airway system below the larynx, from the trachea down. The nose and pharynx are above it.
questions.answerText: The upper respiratory tract

questions.q: The respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli together make up which functional zone?
options: The upper respiratory tract
The pleural cavity
The respiratory zone
The conducting zone
questions.why: The respiratory system is also grouped by function into two zones. The respiratory zone is made of the structures where gas exchange happens: the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. Everything from the nose to the terminal bronchioles only carries air and forms the conducting zone.
notes: The upper respiratory tract is a location grouping: the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx. These structures sit far above the alveoli.
The pleural cavity is the thin, fluid-filled space between the parietal and visceral pleurae. It surrounds the lung but is not part of the airway.
Correct. These structures make up the respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens.
The conducting zone is the passages that only carry air, from the nose down to the terminal bronchioles. Pick it if the list ended at the terminal bronchioles.
questions.answerText: The respiratory zone

questions.q: Which division contains the passages that only carry air, from the nose to the terminal bronchioles?
options: The lower respiratory tract
The respiratory zone
The bronchial tree
The conducting zone
questions.why: The conducting zone includes every passage that carries air without exchanging gases, from the nose to the terminal bronchioles. Along the way it warms, moistens, and filters the incoming air. Gas exchange only begins in the respiratory zone, starting with the respiratory bronchioles.
notes: The lower respiratory tract runs from the larynx to the lungs and includes the alveoli. It starts below the nose and also contains gas exchange structures, so it does not match this description.
The respiratory zone is where gas exchange happens, in the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. It begins just after the terminal bronchioles.
The bronchial tree starts below the larynx at the trachea. It does not include the nose, nasal cavity, or pharynx.
Correct. The conducting zone carries air from the nose to the terminal bronchioles.
questions.answerText: The conducting zone

questions.q: Which region of the pharynx carries air only, and never food?
options: The esophagus
The oropharynx
The nasopharynx
The laryngopharynx
questions.why: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. During swallowing the soft palate lifts to close it off, so food does not enter, and it carries air only. Because it never meets food, it is lined with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium rather than the tougher stratified squamous of the lower regions.
notes: The esophagus is a digestive tube carrying food only, below the laryngopharynx. It is not part of the pharynx and does not carry air.
The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity and carries both air and food. Its stratified squamous lining resists the friction of swallowed food.
Correct. The nasopharynx is the air-only region of the pharynx.
The laryngopharynx carries both air and food, and it is where the air and food paths divide. Pick it for a question about the region opening into both the larynx and the esophagus.
questions.answerText: The nasopharynx

questions.q: Which of these structures belongs to the upper respiratory tract?
options: The larynx
The bronchi
The trachea
The pharynx
questions.why: The upper respiratory tract is the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx. The lower tract begins at the larynx and continues with the trachea, bronchi, and lungs. The pharynx is the last structure of the upper tract, and the larynx is the first of the lower tract.
notes: The larynx is the first structure of the lower respiratory tract, just below the pharynx. Students often place it in the upper tract because it sits in the neck.
The bronchi branch from the trachea in the thorax and belong to the lower respiratory tract. Pick them for a question about the lower tract.
The trachea belongs to the lower respiratory tract, running from the larynx into the thorax. Pick it as part of the lower tract.
Correct. The pharynx is part of the upper respiratory tract.
questions.answerText: The pharynx

questions.q: An emergency airway is placed just above a single, ring-shaped cartilage that lies below the thyroid cartilage. Which cartilage is this ring?
options: A tracheal cartilage
The cricoid cartilage
The epiglottis
The arytenoid cartilage
questions.why: The cricoid cartilage is a single ring of hyaline cartilage at the bottom of the larynx, directly below the thyroid cartilage. It is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. The cricothyroid ligament fills the gap between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, and it is the landmark for an emergency airway.
notes: Tracheal cartilages are C-shaped and open at the back, not complete rings. They lie below the cricoid cartilage, in the trachea.
Correct. The cricoid cartilage is the complete ring below the thyroid cartilage.
The epiglottis is the flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. It sits above the thyroid cartilage, not below it.
The arytenoid cartilages are small paired cartilages that anchor the vocal folds. They are not ring-shaped and are not used as the emergency airway landmark.
questions.answerText: The cricoid cartilage

questions.q: Food and air travel together through one region of the pharynx until it opens into both the larynx and the esophagus. Which region is it?
options: The oropharynx
The laryngopharynx
The nasal vestibule
The nasopharynx
questions.why: The laryngopharynx runs from the epiglottis down to the esophagus. At its lower end, the air path continues forward into the larynx and the food path continues back into the esophagus. It is where the two paths divide.
notes: The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity, from the soft palate to the epiglottis. It carries air and food but does not open directly into the larynx and esophagus.
Correct. The laryngopharynx opens into both the larynx and the esophagus.
The nasal vestibule is the skin-lined area just inside the nostrils. Pick it for a question about the coarse hairs that filter air at the nose.
The nasopharynx sits behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate, and carries air only. Pick it for a question about the air-only region.
questions.answerText: The laryngopharynx

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders the structures a breath travels through from outside the body toward the lungs?
options: Nasal cavity, pharynx, trachea, larynx
Nasal cavity, larynx, pharynx, trachea
Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea
Pharynx, nasal cavity, larynx, trachea
questions.why: Air enters through the nostrils into the nasal cavity, then passes back through the choanae into the pharynx. From the pharynx it moves forward into the larynx, and below the larynx it continues into the trachea. The pharynx is the last part of the upper tract and the larynx is the first part of the lower tract.
notes: This swaps the larynx and trachea. The larynx sits above the trachea and is entered first.
This swaps the pharynx and larynx. Air reaches the pharynx, the shared throat, before it enters the larynx.
Correct. Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, then trachea.
The nasal cavity comes first because air enters through the nostrils. The pharynx lies behind the nasal cavity, so it cannot come before it.
questions.answerText: Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea

questions.q: Moving downward along the front of the neck, which order of airway structures is correct?
options: Thyroid cartilage, trachea, cricoid cartilage
Thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, trachea
Trachea, cricoid cartilage, thyroid cartilage
Cricoid cartilage, thyroid cartilage, trachea
questions.why: The thyroid cartilage forms the Adam's apple near the top of the larynx. Just below it sits the cricoid cartilage, the complete ring at the bottom of the larynx. Below the cricoid, the trachea begins with its C-shaped cartilage rings.
notes: The cricoid cartilage is part of the larynx and sits above the trachea. Placing it below the trachea mixes it up with the tracheal rings.
Correct. The thyroid cartilage is above the cricoid cartilage, which sits above the trachea.
This order runs from bottom to top. It would be correct only if the question asked for the order moving upward.
This swaps the two laryngeal cartilages. The cricoid lies below the thyroid cartilage, not above it.
questions.answerText: Thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, trachea

questions.q: Which structures make up the upper respiratory tract?
options: The nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx
The trachea, carina, and main bronchi
The larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs
The respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
questions.why: The upper respiratory tract is the part of the system above the larynx: the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx. These structures take in air and warm, moisten, and filter it. The lower tract begins at the larynx.
notes: Correct. The nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx form the upper tract.
The trachea, carina, and main bronchi are the top of the bronchial tree in the lower tract. Pick this set for a question about where the trachea divides.
The larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs make up the lower respiratory tract. Pick this set if the question asked about the lower tract.
The respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli form the respiratory zone, a functional grouping where gas exchange happens. Pick this set for a question about the respiratory zone.
questions.answerText: The nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx

questions.q: Besides carrying air, what does the conducting zone do to incoming air?
options: It warms, moistens, and filters the air
It produces sound along its entire length
It secretes surfactant into the air
It exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood
questions.why: The conducting zone runs from the nose to the terminal bronchioles and carries air without exchanging gases. Along the way its mucosa warms and moistens the air, and mucus and cilia trap and sweep away particles. By the time air reaches the alveoli it has been conditioned and cleaned.
notes: Correct. The conducting zone warms, moistens, and filters incoming air.
Sound is produced only at the vocal folds in the larynx. The rest of the conducting zone carries air without making sound.
Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells in the alveoli, which are in the respiratory zone. Pick type II cells for a question about surfactant.
Gas exchange happens only in the respiratory zone, in the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. Pick this job for the respiratory zone.
questions.answerText: It warms, moistens, and filters the air

questions.q: What divides the nasal cavity into right and left halves?
options: The nasal septum
The nasal conchae
The soft palate
The hard palate
questions.why: The nasal septum is the midline wall of the nasal cavity. Its front part is septal cartilage, and its back part is bone, formed by the vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid. It splits the cavity into right and left halves, each opening to the outside through a naris.
notes: Correct. The nasal septum divides the nasal cavity into right and left halves.
The nasal conchae are scroll-shaped projections on the lateral walls of each half. They swirl the air but do not divide the cavity in two.
The soft palate is the muscular posterior part of the palate that lifts to close the nasopharynx during swallowing. Pick it for a question about keeping food out of the nose.
The hard palate is the bony floor of the nasal cavity, separating it from the oral cavity below. Pick it if the question asked what separates the nasal cavity from the mouth.
questions.answerText: The nasal septum

questions.q: Which tubes open into the lateral walls of the nasopharynx, the air-only region behind the nasal cavity?
options: The auditory tubes
The nasolacrimal ducts
The bronchi
The parotid ducts
questions.why: The nasopharynx sits behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate, and it carries air only. The auditory tubes, which connect the middle ear to the throat, open into its lateral walls, and the pharyngeal tonsil sits on its posterior wall. This connection is why throat infections can spread to the middle ear.
notes: Correct. The auditory tubes open into the nasopharynx.
The nasolacrimal ducts drain tears from the eye into the nasal cavity, below the inferior concha. They open into the nasal cavity, in front of the nasopharynx.
The bronchi branch from the trachea in the thorax, far below the pharynx. Pick them for a question about the airways entering the lungs.
The parotid ducts carry saliva from the parotid glands into the oral cavity next to the upper molars. Pick them for a question about salivary drainage.
questions.answerText: The auditory tubes

questions.q: In which structure is the glottis found?
options: The trachea
The pharynx
The nasal cavity
The larynx
questions.why: The glottis is the true vocal folds together with the opening between them, and the vocal folds are inside the larynx, the voice box. The larynx sits between the pharynx above and the trachea below. Air must pass through the glottis to reach the trachea and lungs.
notes: The trachea lies below the larynx and has C-shaped cartilage rings but no vocal folds. Pick it for a question about the windpipe.
The pharynx is the throat above the larynx, shared by air and food. It holds the tonsils but not the vocal folds.
The nasal cavity is at the start of the airway and holds the conchae and meatuses. Pick it for a question about where air is first warmed and filtered.
Correct. The glottis is part of the larynx.
questions.answerText: The larynx

questions.q: What are the paranasal sinuses?
options: Scroll-shaped projections on the lateral walls of the nasal cavity
Air-filled cavities in skull bones that drain into the nasal cavity
Passages beneath the conchae that carry air through the nose
Posterior openings where the nasal cavity becomes the nasopharynx
questions.why: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces in the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones, arranged around the nasal cavity. They are lined with the same mucosa as the nasal cavity and drain into it. Because they connect, a nasal infection can spread into the sinuses.
notes: Scroll-shaped projections on the lateral walls are the nasal conchae. Pick them for a question about the structures that swirl incoming air.
Correct. Paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities in skull bones that drain into the nasal cavity.
The passages beneath each concha are the nasal meatuses, named superior, middle, and inferior. Pick them for a question about the air channels inside the nasal cavity.
The posterior openings into the nasopharynx are the choanae. Pick them for a question about where the nasal cavity ends.
questions.answerText: Air-filled cavities in skull bones that drain into the nasal cavity

questions.q: The thyroid and cricoid cartilages are hyaline cartilage, but the epiglottis has to bend with every swallow. What type of cartilage forms the epiglottis?
options: Hyaline cartilage
Dense irregular connective tissue
Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
questions.why: The epiglottis is made of elastic cartilage, which has many elastic fibers in its matrix. This lets it bend down over the laryngeal inlet with every swallow and then spring back to open the airway. Rigid hyaline cartilage could not bend this way over and over.
notes: Hyaline cartilage forms the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, most of each arytenoid, and the tracheal rings. It is too stiff for a flap that bends with every swallow. Pick it for a question about cartilage that holds the airway open.
Dense irregular connective tissue forms the dermis and organ capsules. It is not cartilage at all.
Correct. The epiglottis is elastic cartilage, so it can bend and spring back.
Fibrocartilage is tough cartilage with thick collagen bundles, found in the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis. Pick it for a question about cartilage that resists compression.
questions.answerText: Elastic cartilage

questions.q: A person laughs while swallowing, food slips into the larynx, and a coughing fit follows. Which structure normally folds over the laryngeal inlet to stop this?
options: The trachealis muscle
The epiglottis
The cricoid cartilage
The soft palate
questions.why: During a normal swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over the laryngeal inlet, so food is directed into the esophagus. If the timing fails, as when someone laughs or talks while swallowing, food can slip into the larynx. The coughing fit is the airway trying to clear it.
notes: The trachealis muscle closes the back of the C-shaped tracheal rings, below the larynx. It does not guard the laryngeal inlet.
Correct. The epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.
The cricoid cartilage is the complete ring at the bottom of the larynx. It holds the airway open but does not move to cover it.
The soft palate lifts to close the nasopharynx, which keeps food from going up into the nose. It does not cover the larynx.
questions.answerText: The epiglottis

questions.q: Which folds of the larynx are the false vocal cords, lying above the true vocal cords and playing no part in sound?
options: The vocal folds
The vestibular folds
The aryepiglottic folds
The vocal ligaments
questions.why: The vestibular folds are the false vocal cords, sitting just above the true vocal folds. They help close the airway during swallowing but do not vibrate to make sound. The true vocal folds below them are the ones that produce the voice.
notes: The vocal folds are the true vocal cords. They are pearly white and vibrate as air passes to produce sound, so they are the opposite of the false cords.
Correct. The vestibular folds are the false vocal cords.
The aryepiglottic folds are folds running from the arytenoid cartilages up to the epiglottis, forming the sides of the laryngeal inlet. They are not called the false vocal cords.
The vocal ligaments are elastic bands inside the true vocal folds, running from the arytenoid cartilages to the thyroid cartilage. Pick them for a question about the bands within the vocal folds.
questions.answerText: The vestibular folds

questions.q: What are the air passages beneath each nasal concha called?
options: The paranasal sinuses
The choanae
The nasal meatuses
The nares
questions.why: Each of the three nasal conchae overhangs a groove-like air passage called a meatus. The passages are named superior, middle, and inferior, matching the concha above each one. Air flowing through the meatuses swirls against the warm, moist mucosa, which helps condition it.
notes: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities inside skull bones that drain into the nasal cavity. They are spaces within bone, not passages beneath the conchae.
The choanae are the posterior openings where the nasal cavity becomes the nasopharynx. Pick them for a question about where air leaves the nasal cavity.
Correct. The nasal meatuses are the passages beneath the conchae.
The nares are the nostrils, the external openings at the front of the nose. Pick them for a question about where air enters the nose.
questions.answerText: The nasal meatuses

questions.q: Air passes from the back of the nasal cavity into the nasopharynx. Through which openings does it pass?
options: The glottis
The choanae
The nares
The auditory tubes
questions.why: The choanae are the paired posterior openings of the nasal cavity. Air that entered through the nostrils crosses the nasal cavity and leaves through the choanae into the nasopharynx. From there it continues down through the oropharynx and laryngopharynx to the larynx.
notes: The glottis is the vocal folds and the opening between them in the larynx. Air reaches it much later, after passing through the pharynx.
Correct. The choanae open from the nasal cavity into the nasopharynx.
The nares are the nostrils at the front of the nose, where air enters the nasal cavity. They are the opposite end of the nasal cavity.
The auditory tubes open into the lateral walls of the nasopharynx and connect it to the middle ear. Air does not pass through them on its way to the lungs.
questions.answerText: The choanae

questions.q: The nasopharynx is lined with ciliated epithelium, but the oropharynx is lined with stratified squamous epithelium. Why does the oropharynx need this tougher lining?
options: It carries air only, so it needs no cilia
It secretes surfactant to keep the throat open
It carries food as well as air and must resist friction
It is where gas exchange begins in the upper tract
questions.why: The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity, so swallowed food passes through it along with air. Stratified squamous epithelium has many layers of cells that can be rubbed away and replaced, which protects against that friction. The nasopharynx carries air only, so it keeps the delicate ciliated lining that sweeps mucus.
notes: Carrying air only describes the nasopharynx, which is why it keeps its ciliated lining. The oropharynx carries both air and food.
Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells in the alveoli, not in the throat. Pick type II cells for a question about surfactant.
Correct. The oropharynx carries food, so it needs a friction-resistant lining.
No part of the pharynx exchanges gases. Gas exchange starts in the respiratory bronchioles, deep in the lungs.
questions.answerText: It carries food as well as air and must resist friction

questions.q: Which statement best describes the overall job of the respiratory system?
options: It breaks down food and absorbs the nutrients into the blood
It pumps blood through the lungs and then out to the body tissues
It returns excess tissue fluid to the bloodstream in vessels
It moves air in and out and brings that air close to the blood
questions.why: The respiratory system is the set of organs that moves air in and out of the body and brings that air very close to the blood so gases can be exchanged. Everything from the nose to the alveoli is either a passage for air or a surface where air meets blood. The actual exchange of gases is a physiology topic, so in anatomy we focus on the structures that make it possible.
notes: Breaking down food and absorbing nutrients is the job of the digestive system. Choose this if the question were about the alimentary canal and its accessory organs.

Pumping blood through the lungs and body is the job of the heart and blood vessels, the cardiovascular system. Pick this if the question asked what the heart does in the pulmonary and systemic circuits.

Returning excess tissue fluid to the blood is the job of the lymphatic system, which collects fluid in lymphatic vessels and empties it into veins near the heart. It would be the answer for a question about lymph.
Correct. The respiratory system moves air and brings it close to the blood for gas exchange.
questions.answerText: It moves air in and out and brings that air close to the blood

questions.q: Which group of structures makes up the upper respiratory tract?
options: Every passage from the nose to the terminal bronchioles
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx
Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, and lungs
questions.why: The upper respiratory tract is the set of structures in the head and neck that take in air and condition it: the nose, the nasal cavity, the paranasal sinuses, and the pharynx (throat). These parts warm, moisten, and filter air before it travels deeper. Everything below them, starting with the larynx in this course's grouping, belongs to the lower respiratory tract.
notes: Every passage from the nose to the terminal bronchioles is the conducting zone, which is a grouping by function rather than by location. Students mix it up with the upper tract because both include the nose.
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli are the respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens. They would be the answer if the question asked which structures form the respiratory zone.
Correct. The nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx make up the upper respiratory tract.
The trachea, bronchi, and lungs sit in the neck and chest and belong to the lower respiratory tract. Pick this group if the question asked about the lower tract.
questions.answerText: Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx

questions.q: The conducting zone is made of passages that only carry air. Which stretch of the airway does it include?
options: From the trachea down to the alveoli
From the respiratory bronchioles to the alveoli
From the nose down to the larynx only
From the nose to the terminal bronchioles
questions.why: The conducting zone is every passage that carries air without exchanging gas, starting at the nose and ending at the terminal bronchioles. Along the way it warms, moistens, and filters the air. The terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways, and the respiratory zone begins right after them.
notes: The trachea to the alveoli starts too low and ends too far. It leaves out the nose and pharynx, which do conduct air, and it includes alveoli, which are gas-exchange structures. This is a mix of the lower tract and both zones.
The respiratory bronchioles to the alveoli is the respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens. Pick this if the question asked which structures form the respiratory zone.

The nose to the larynx is too short. The conducting zone keeps going through the trachea and the whole bronchial tree down to the terminal bronchioles. This range roughly matches the upper airway in the head and neck, which is why it can look right.
Correct. The conducting zone runs from the nose to the terminal bronchioles.
questions.answerText: From the nose to the terminal bronchioles

questions.q: Which group of structures makes up the respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens?
options: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
Bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, and carina
Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, and segmental bronchi
Nasal cavity, pharynx, and larynx
questions.why: The respiratory zone is the part of the airway where the walls are thin enough for gas exchange. It begins with the respiratory bronchioles, which have a few alveoli budding from their walls, continues into alveolar ducts lined with alveoli, and ends in alveolar sacs and alveoli. Everything above the respiratory bronchioles only conducts air.
notes: Correct. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli make up the respiratory zone.

Bronchioles and terminal bronchioles are still conducting airways, and the carina is the ridge where the trachea forks. This group is the end of the conducting zone. Students choose it because bronchioles sound close to the respiratory bronchioles.

The trachea and the main, lobar, and segmental bronchi are large conducting airways with cartilage in their walls. They would be the answer if the question asked for the upper part of the bronchial tree.
The nasal cavity, pharynx, and larynx are conducting passages in the head and neck. Pick them if the question asked for structures that warm, moisten, and filter air early in its path.
questions.answerText: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli

questions.q: Air entering the respiratory system through the nose passes through which openings first?
options: The glottis
The nares
The auditory tube openings
The choanae
questions.why: The nares are the external openings of the nose, the nostrils, so they are the first openings air passes through on its way in. Just inside them is the nasal vestibule, and then the air moves back through the nasal cavity. At the back of the nasal cavity the air leaves through the choanae into the nasopharynx.
notes: The glottis is the vocal folds together with the opening between them, inside the larynx. Air reaches it much later, after the pharynx. Choose it if the question asked for the opening between the vocal folds.
Correct. The nares, or nostrils, are the first openings air passes through.

The auditory tube openings are in the lateral walls of the nasopharynx and connect the throat to the middle ear. They are not part of the air pathway to the lungs. They would be the answer if the question asked what opens into the nasopharynx from the ear.

The choanae are the posterior openings where the nasal cavity becomes the nasopharynx. Air passes through them at the back of the nose, so they come later. Pick the choanae if the question asked where air leaves the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText: The nares

questions.q: What is the name of the skin-lined area just inside the nostrils?
options: The nasopharynx
The nasal meatus
The nasal vestibule
The choanae
questions.why: The nasal vestibule is the entrance area just inside the nostrils. Unlike the rest of the nasal cavity, it is lined with skin, and it holds sebaceous (oil) glands and coarse hairs that catch large particles. It is the first part of the nasal cavity that air enters after passing through the nares.
notes: The nasopharynx is the upper part of the throat behind the nasal cavity. It is reached only after air crosses the whole nasal cavity. Choose it if the question asked where air goes after the choanae.
A nasal meatus is a passage beneath one of the nasal conchae, deeper in the cavity along the lateral wall. Pick a meatus if the question asked about the air channels under the conchae.
Correct. The nasal vestibule is the skin-lined area just inside the nostrils.
The choanae are the posterior openings of the nasal cavity, the opposite end from the nostrils. They would be the answer if the question asked where the nasal cavity opens into the nasopharynx.
questions.answerText: The nasal vestibule

questions.q: What are vibrissae?
options: Coarse hairs in the nasal vestibule that filter particles
Scroll-shaped bones on the lateral nasal wall
Cilia on the nasal respiratory mucosa that sweep mucus back
Mucus-secreting goblet cells of the nasal lining
questions.why: Vibrissae are the coarse hairs in the nasal vestibule, the skin-lined entrance just inside the nostrils. They act as a first, rough filter that catches large particles before air moves deeper into the nasal cavity. Finer particles are trapped later by mucus on the respiratory mucosa.
notes: Correct. Vibrissae are the coarse hairs of the nasal vestibule that filter large particles.

Scroll-shaped projections on the lateral wall are the nasal conchae. They swirl air rather than filter it with hairs. Choose them if the question asked what increases air contact with the warm, moist lining.

Cilia are tiny hairlike projections on the cells of the respiratory mucosa that sweep mucus toward the pharynx. They are microscopic and sit deeper in the cavity. Pick cilia if the question asked what moves trapped mucus toward the throat.

Goblet cells are single-celled glands in the respiratory epithelium that secrete mucus. Their sticky mucus traps fine particles deeper in the airway, while the coarse hairs of the vestibule catch large particles at the entrance. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells make mucus in the airway lining.
questions.answerText: Coarse hairs in the nasal vestibule that filter particles

questions.q: What are the three scroll-shaped projections on each lateral wall of the nasal cavity called?
options: The nasal septa
The paranasal sinuses
The nasal meatuses
The nasal conchae
questions.why: The nasal conchae are three curled projections (superior, middle, and inferior) on the lateral wall of each side of the nasal cavity. Their scroll shape makes incoming air swirl, which increases its contact with the warm, moist lining. That contact lets the air be warmed, moistened, and cleaned before it moves on.
notes: The nasal septum is a single midline wall that divides the cavity into halves, not a set of three lateral projections. Pick the septum if the question asked what separates the right and left sides.

The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities inside the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones, outside the nasal cavity. They drain into it but do not project from its wall. Choose them if the question asked about hollow spaces in the skull bones around the nose.
The nasal meatuses are the air passages beneath each concha, not the projections themselves. Pick the meatuses if the question asked for the channels under the conchae.
Correct. The nasal conchae are the scroll-shaped projections on the lateral wall.
questions.answerText: The nasal conchae

questions.q: What are the nasal meatuses?
options: The external openings of the nose
The air passages beneath each nasal concha
The posterior openings into the nasopharynx
The air-filled cavities inside skull bones
questions.why: A meatus is a passage, and the nasal meatuses are the grooved air channels that run beneath each nasal concha. They are named superior, middle, and inferior to match the concha above each one. Air flowing through these channels is forced against the moist lining, which helps condition it.
notes: The external openings of the nose are the nares, or nostrils. Pick them if the question asked where air first enters the nose.
Correct. The nasal meatuses are the air passages beneath each concha.
The posterior openings into the nasopharynx are the choanae. They would be the answer if the question asked where the nasal cavity ends at the back.

The air-filled cavities inside skull bones are the paranasal sinuses. Most of them drain into the meatuses, which is why students mix the two up, but the sinuses themselves are spaces inside the bones.
questions.answerText: The air passages beneath each nasal concha

questions.q: How do the nasal conchae and meatuses help prepare incoming air?
options: They divide the airflow into right and left streams
They close the nasopharynx during each swallow
They swirl the air over the warm, moist lining
They are the surface where gas exchange takes place
questions.why: The scroll-shaped conchae and the passages beneath them break the airflow into swirling currents. That turbulence pushes more of the air against the warm, moist mucosa, which warms it, adds moisture, and lets mucus trap particles. This is part of how the conducting zone conditions air before it reaches the delicate alveoli.
notes: Dividing the airflow into right and left streams is done by the nasal septum, the midline wall of the nasal cavity. Pick this if the question asked about the septum.
Closing the nasopharynx during swallowing is the job of the soft palate, which lifts up to block food from entering the nose. Choose this if the question were about the soft palate.
Correct. The conchae and meatuses swirl air over the warm, moist lining.
Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli of the respiratory zone, far below the nose. The nasal cavity is entirely conducting zone. This choice confuses conditioning air with exchanging gases.
questions.answerText: They swirl the air over the warm, moist lining

questions.q: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities in which four skull bones?
options: Occipital, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary
Frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary
Frontal, parietal, sphenoid, and maxillary
Frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and mandible
questions.why: The paranasal sinuses are named for the four bones that hold them: the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones. All four sit around the nasal cavity, which is why they are called paranasal (beside the nose). Each one is lined with mucosa and drains into the nasal cavity.
notes: The occipital bone forms the back and base of the skull around the foramen magnum and has no paranasal sinus. This choice swaps out the frontal bone, whose sinus sits just above the eyes.
Correct. The frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones contain the paranasal sinuses.

The parietal bones form the top and sides of the cranium, far from the nasal cavity, and do not contain a paranasal sinus. Students pick this when they remember a four-part list but swap in a cranial bone.
The mandible is the lower jaw and holds the lower teeth, not a sinus. The maxilla, the upper jaw, holds the large maxillary sinus. This choice confuses the two jaw bones.
questions.answerText: Frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary

questions.q: Where do the paranasal sinuses drain?
options: Into the oral cavity
Into the oropharynx
Into the nasal cavity
Into the middle ear
questions.why: Each paranasal sinus is lined with mucosa that makes mucus, and that mucus drains through small openings into the nasal cavity. The sinuses sit in the bones surrounding the nose, so the nasal cavity is the nearest shared space. From there, cilia sweep the mucus back toward the pharynx to be swallowed.
notes: The oral cavity is the mouth, separated from the nasal cavity by the hard and soft palates. The sinuses do not open into it. Pick the oral cavity if the question asked what lies below the hard palate.

The oropharynx is the middle part of the throat behind the mouth. Mucus from the sinuses eventually reaches the pharynx after cilia sweep it back, but the sinuses open directly into the nasal cavity. Pick the oropharynx if the question asked where food and air first share a passage below the soft palate.
Correct. The paranasal sinuses drain into the nasal cavity.
The middle ear connects to the nasopharynx through the auditory tube, not to the paranasal sinuses. Choose it if the question asked where the auditory tube leads.
questions.answerText: Into the nasal cavity

questions.q: Which structure is the throat, a muscular passage shared by air and food?
options: The larynx
The trachea
The pharynx
The esophagus
questions.why: The pharynx is the throat, a muscular tube that runs from behind the nasal cavity down to the level of the larynx and esophagus. It carries both air and food, which is why it belongs to both the respiratory and digestive systems. It has three regions: the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.
notes: The larynx is the voice box below the pharynx. It carries air only and works to keep food out. Pick it if the question asked which structure houses the vocal folds.
The trachea is the windpipe below the larynx, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings. It carries air only. It would be the answer if the question asked which airway leads to the main bronchi.
Correct. The pharynx is the throat, shared by air and food.
The esophagus is the muscular tube behind the trachea that carries food to the stomach. It carries food only. Choose it if the question asked where food goes after the laryngopharynx.
questions.answerText: The pharynx

questions.q: Which region of the pharynx lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate?
options: The nasopharynx
The nasal vestibule
The laryngopharynx
The oropharynx
questions.why: The nasopharynx is the uppermost region of the pharynx, sitting behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. Because the soft palate lifts to seal it off during swallowing, it carries air only. It also holds the pharyngeal tonsil and the openings of the auditory tubes.
notes: Correct. The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate.

The nasal vestibule is the skin-lined entrance just inside the nostrils, at the front of the nasal cavity. It is not part of the pharynx. It would be the answer if the question asked where vibrissae are found.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest region, from the epiglottis down to the esophagus. Choose it if the question asked where the air and food paths divide.
The oropharynx is the middle region, behind the oral cavity, running from the soft palate down to the epiglottis. Pick it if the question asked which region lies behind the mouth.
questions.answerText: The nasopharynx

questions.q: Which region of the pharynx lies behind the oral cavity, from the soft palate to the epiglottis?
options: The larynx
The nasopharynx
The laryngopharynx
The oropharynx
questions.why: The oropharynx is the middle region of the pharynx, directly behind the mouth. It runs from the soft palate down to the epiglottis and carries both air and food. Because food rubs along it, it is lined with stratified squamous epithelium, and it holds the palatine and lingual tonsils.
notes: The larynx is the voice box, a separate airway structure in front of the laryngopharynx, not a region of the pharynx. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure connects the pharynx to the trachea.
The nasopharynx sits above the soft palate, behind the nasal cavity, and carries air only. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the pharyngeal tonsil and auditory tube openings.
The laryngopharynx sits below the oropharynx, from the epiglottis to the esophagus. Choose it if the question asked where the pharynx opens into both the larynx and the esophagus.
Correct. The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity, from the soft palate to the epiglottis.
questions.answerText: The oropharynx

questions.q: In which region of the pharynx do the air and food paths divide, with openings into both the larynx and the esophagus?
options: The oropharynx
The trachea
The laryngopharynx
The nasopharynx
questions.why: The laryngopharynx is the lowest region of the pharynx, running from the epiglottis down to the esophagus. At its lower end, air turns forward into the larynx while food continues back into the esophagus. That is why it is described as the point where the air and food paths divide.
notes: The oropharynx carries both air and food, but it sits higher, behind the mouth. The paths are still shared there. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the palatine tonsils.
The trachea is the windpipe below the larynx and is not part of the pharynx. It carries air only. It would be the answer if the question asked where air goes after the larynx.
Correct. The laryngopharynx opens into both the larynx and the esophagus.
The nasopharynx is the top region behind the nasal cavity and carries air only. Choose it if the question asked which region is sealed off by the soft palate during swallowing.
questions.answerText: The laryngopharynx

questions.q: Which structure is the voice box that connects the pharynx to the trachea?
options: The laryngopharynx
The larynx
The carina
The epiglottis
questions.why: The larynx is the voice box, a framework of nine cartilages that connects the pharynx above to the trachea below. It keeps food out of the airway, holds the airway open, and houses the vocal folds that produce sound. In this course it is the first structure of the lower respiratory tract.
notes: The laryngopharynx is the lowest region of the throat, behind the larynx. Its name sounds similar, but it is part of the pharynx and carries both air and food. Pick it if the question asked where the air and food paths divide.
Correct. The larynx is the voice box between the pharynx and the trachea.
The carina is the internal ridge where the trachea forks into the two main bronchi, well below the larynx. It would be the answer if the question asked where the trachea branches.

The epiglottis is one of the cartilages of the larynx, the flap that folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It is part of the larynx, not the whole voice box. Choose it if the question asked what covers the airway when you swallow.
questions.answerText: The larynx

questions.q: Which pair of jobs belongs to the larynx?
options: Keeping food out of the airway and housing the vocal folds
Exchanging gases and secreting surfactant onto the alveoli
Carrying food down to the stomach and starting the swallow
Swirling incoming air and draining the paranasal sinuses
questions.why: The larynx sits at the top of the airway where food and air paths have just separated, so one of its main jobs is guarding the airway, with the epiglottis folding over the inlet during swallowing. It also houses the vocal folds, which vibrate to produce sound, which is why it is called the voice box. Its cartilage framework also holds the airway open.
notes: Correct. The larynx keeps food out of the airway and houses the vocal folds.
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, and surfactant is secreted by Type II alveolar cells. Choose this pair if the question were about the alveolus.
Carrying food to the stomach is the job of the esophagus, and swallowing is driven by the muscles of the mouth and pharynx. This pair describes the digestive path, not the larynx.
Swirling incoming air is the job of the nasal conchae and meatuses, and the sinuses drain into the nasal cavity. Pick this pair if the question were about the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText: Keeping food out of the airway and housing the vocal folds

questions.q: Which laryngeal cartilage is the large shield-shaped one that forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple)?
options: The epiglottis
The thyroid cartilage
The cricoid cartilage
The arytenoid cartilage
questions.why: The thyroid cartilage is the largest cartilage of the larynx, a shield-shaped plate at the front of the neck. Its anterior ridge forms the laryngeal prominence, which you can feel as the Adam's apple. Like the cricoid and arytenoid cartilages, it is made of hyaline cartilage.
notes: The epiglottis is the spoon-shaped flap of elastic cartilage that folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It would be the answer if the question asked which cartilage protects the airway when you swallow.
Correct. The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence.
The cricoid cartilage is the ring-shaped cartilage just below the thyroid cartilage. Pick it if the question asked which cartilage is the only complete ring in the airway.
The arytenoid cartilages are small paired cartilages at the back of the larynx that anchor and move the vocal folds. Choose them if the question asked what controls the position of the vocal folds.
questions.answerText: The thyroid cartilage

questions.q: Which laryngeal cartilage sits just below the thyroid cartilage and is the only complete ring in the airway?
options: The cuneiform cartilage
A tracheal cartilage
The cricoid cartilage
The corniculate cartilage
questions.why: The cricoid cartilage is a ring-shaped cartilage directly below the thyroid cartilage, at the base of the larynx. It is the only cartilage in the airway that forms a complete ring all the way around. The tracheal cartilages below it are C-shaped, open at the back where the trachealis muscle closes the gap.
notes: The cuneiform cartilages are small paired cartilages in the fold between the arytenoid and the epiglottis. They would be the answer if the question asked which paired cartilages lie in that fold.

The tracheal cartilages are C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, open in the back. They are incomplete rings, which is the exact contrast with the cricoid. Choose them if the question asked what holds the trachea open.
Correct. The cricoid cartilage is the complete ring just below the thyroid cartilage.

The corniculate cartilages are small paired cartilages that sit on top of the arytenoids. They are tiny horn-like pieces, not rings. Pick them if the question asked which cartilages perch on the arytenoids.
questions.answerText: The cricoid cartilage

questions.q: Which laryngeal cartilage is the flexible flap that folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing?
options: The thyroid cartilage
The epiglottis
The soft palate
The vestibular fold
questions.why: The epiglottis is a spoon-shaped flap at the top of the larynx. During swallowing it folds back over the laryngeal inlet, the opening into the larynx, so food and drink slide past into the esophagus. It is made of elastic cartilage, unlike the stiff hyaline thyroid and cricoid cartilages, because it has to bend and spring back with every swallow.
notes: The thyroid cartilage is the large, rigid shield at the front of the larynx that forms the Adam's apple. It does not fold over anything. Pick it if the question asked which cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence.
Correct. The epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

The soft palate is a muscular flap at the back of the roof of the mouth, not a laryngeal cartilage. It lifts to close the nasopharynx during swallowing. Choose it if the question asked what keeps food out of the nasal cavity.

The vestibular folds are the false vocal cords, mucosal folds above the true vocal folds. They help close the airway but are folds of tissue, not a cartilage flap. They would be the answer if the question asked which folds sit above the true vocal cords.
questions.answerText: The epiglottis

questions.q: Which paired laryngeal cartilages anchor the vocal folds and move them?
options: The cuneiform cartilages
The corniculate cartilages
The arytenoid cartilages
The cricoid cartilages
questions.why: The arytenoid cartilages are a pair of small cartilages at the back of the larynx, resting on the cricoid cartilage. The vocal ligaments attach to them, so when the arytenoids shift and pivot, the vocal folds open, close, and tighten. They are considered the most important of the three pairs of laryngeal cartilages.
notes: The cuneiform cartilages are small paired cartilages in the fold between the arytenoid and the epiglottis. Choose them if the question asked which paired cartilages lie in that fold.

The corniculate cartilages are tiny paired cartilages that sit on top of the arytenoids. Being so close to the arytenoids is why students pick them. They would be the answer if the question asked which cartilages perch on the arytenoids.
Correct. The arytenoid cartilages anchor and move the vocal folds.
The cricoid is a single ring-shaped cartilage, not a pair, and the vocal folds do not attach to it. Pick the cricoid if the question asked for the only complete ring in the airway.
questions.answerText: The arytenoid cartilages

questions.q: The true vocal cords are also known by which name?
options: The vocal folds
The laryngeal prominence
The vestibular folds
The glottis
questions.why: The true vocal cords are called the vocal folds. They are folds of mucous membrane that hold the vocal ligaments, and they look pearly white because their lining has very few blood vessels. They vibrate as air passes between them, and that vibration makes sound.
notes: Correct. The true vocal cords are the vocal folds.

The laryngeal prominence is the Adam's apple, the ridge of the thyroid cartilage at the front of the neck. It would be the answer if the question asked which feature you can feel on the front of the larynx.

The vestibular folds are the false vocal cords, sitting just above the true folds. They help close the airway during swallowing and play no part in sound. Pick them if the question asked for the false vocal cords.
The glottis is the vocal folds together with the opening between them. It includes the folds but is a larger term. Choose it if the question asked for the folds plus the space between them.
questions.answerText: The vocal folds

questions.q: What do the true vocal folds do?
options: They close the airway when swallowing but make no sound
They form the ridge of the Adam's apple on the neck
They vibrate as air passes over them to produce sound
They fold over the laryngeal inlet during each swallow
questions.why: The true vocal folds are the paired shelves of tissue inside the larynx that contain the vocal ligaments. When air pushed up from the lungs passes between them, they vibrate and produce sound. The arytenoid cartilages change their position and tension, which changes the sound.
notes: Closing the airway during swallowing while playing no part in sound describes the vestibular folds, the false vocal cords above the true folds. Pick this if the question asked about the false vocal cords.
The ridge of the Adam's apple is the laryngeal prominence of the thyroid cartilage. It would be the answer if the question asked what the thyroid cartilage forms.
Correct. The true vocal folds vibrate as air passes to produce sound.
Folding over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing is the job of the epiglottis. Choose this if the question asked how the epiglottis protects the airway.
questions.answerText: They vibrate as air passes over them to produce sound

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the conducting zone and the respiratory zone?
options: The conducting zone carries and conditions air, and the respiratory zone exchanges gases
Both zones exchange gases, but the respiratory zone has more cartilage
The conducting zone ends at the larynx, and the respiratory zone begins at the trachea
The conducting zone exchanges gases, and the respiratory zone only carries and conditions air
questions.why: The conducting zone is every passage from the nose to the terminal bronchioles, and its job is to carry air while warming, moistening, and filtering it. The respiratory zone starts at the respiratory bronchioles and includes the alveolar ducts and alveoli, where the walls are thin enough for gas exchange. The two zones are a grouping by function, which is different from the upper and lower tract grouping by location.
notes: Correct. The conducting zone carries and conditions air, and the respiratory zone exchanges gases.

Only the respiratory zone exchanges gases, and it has no cartilage at all. Cartilage is found in the larger conducting airways and disappears at the bronchioles. Pick a cartilage-based contrast only if the question compared bronchi with bronchioles.

This describes the upper and lower respiratory tracts, which split near the larynx, not the two zones. The conducting zone continues all the way to the terminal bronchioles. Choose a larynx boundary only if the question were about the upper and lower tracts.
This statement reverses the two zones. Students fall for it because the word respiratory sounds like it should mean breathing air in, but the respiratory zone is where gas exchange happens.
questions.answerText: The conducting zone carries and conditions air, and the respiratory zone exchanges gases

questions.q: What does the upper respiratory tract do to incoming air before it reaches the lungs?
options: It exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide
It secretes surfactant onto the airway lining
It warms, moistens, and filters the air
It cools and dries the air to protect the alveoli
questions.why: The upper respiratory tract conditions air before it travels deeper. The nasal conchae swirl air over a warm, moist mucosa, which warms and humidifies it, while vibrissae, mucus, and cilia trap and remove particles. Conditioned air protects the delicate alveoli, which are easily damaged by cold, dry, or dirty air.
notes: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide happens in the respiratory zone, at the alveoli. The upper tract is entirely conducting. Pick this if the question asked what happens in the alveoli.
Surfactant is secreted by Type II alveolar cells deep in the lungs, not by the upper tract. Choose it if the question asked what keeps alveoli from collapsing.
Correct. The upper respiratory tract warms, moistens, and filters incoming air.
This is the reverse of what happens. The upper tract warms and moistens air, because cold, dry air is harder on the lower airways. This choice comes from mixing up the direction of the change.
questions.answerText: It warms, moistens, and filters the air

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the three regions of the pharynx by what they carry?
options: The nasopharynx carries air only, and the other two carry air and food
The laryngopharynx carries air only, and the other two carry air and food
All three regions carry both air and food the entire time
The nasopharynx and oropharynx carry air only, and the laryngopharynx carries food
questions.why: The nasopharynx sits above the soft palate, and the soft palate lifts during swallowing to seal it off, so it carries air only. The oropharynx (behind the mouth) and the laryngopharynx (from the epiglottis to the esophagus) carry both air and food. Their lining reflects this: the nasopharynx has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, while the two lower regions have tougher stratified squamous epithelium.
notes: Correct. The nasopharynx carries air only, and the oropharynx and laryngopharynx carry air and food.

The laryngopharynx carries both air and food, since it is where the two paths divide into the larynx and esophagus. This choice flips the top and bottom regions. The air-only region is the one at the top, the nasopharynx.
The nasopharynx does not carry food, because the soft palate closes it off during swallowing. This choice ignores the job of the soft palate. Pick a both-paths answer only for the two lower regions.

The oropharynx sits right behind the mouth, so food passes through it with every swallow. Students pick this because the oropharynx is near the nose, but only the region above the soft palate is air-only.
questions.answerText: The nasopharynx carries air only, and the other two carry air and food

questions.q: Why is the epiglottis important during swallowing?
options: It closes the gap at the back of each tracheal cartilage ring
It tightens the vocal folds so food cannot pass into the trachea
It folds over the laryngeal inlet so food stays out of the airway
It lifts to close off the nasopharynx so food stays out of the nose
questions.why: During a swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds back over the laryngeal inlet, the opening into the larynx. That directs food and drink back into the esophagus instead of down into the trachea. It is made of flexible elastic cartilage so it can bend and spring back every time you swallow.
notes: The gap at the back of each tracheal ring is closed by the trachealis muscle, not the epiglottis. It would be the answer if the question asked what lies between the trachea and the esophagus.

The vocal folds are moved by the arytenoid cartilages, and their main job is producing sound. This choice gives the epiglottis a job it does not have. Choose arytenoid movement if the question asked how the vocal folds are positioned.
Correct. The epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet to keep food out of the airway.
Lifting to close off the nasopharynx is the job of the soft palate. Pick this if the question asked what keeps food from going up into the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText: It folds over the laryngeal inlet so food stays out of the airway

questions.q: The vocal ligaments inside the vocal folds run between which two cartilages?
options: The corniculate and cuneiform cartilages
The cricoid cartilage and the epiglottis
The thyroid cartilage and the epiglottis
The arytenoids and the thyroid cartilage
questions.why: The vocal ligaments are elastic bands inside the vocal folds that stretch from the arytenoid cartilages at the back of the larynx to the thyroid cartilage at the front. Because they are anchored this way, movement of the arytenoids opens, closes, and tightens the vocal folds. That is how the arytenoids control voice production.
notes: The corniculate cartilages sit on the arytenoids, and the cuneiform cartilages lie in the fold between the arytenoid and epiglottis. They are small supporting pieces. This choice confuses them with the arytenoids because all three are paired.

The cricoid is the complete ring at the base of the larynx, and the epiglottis is the flap at the top. The vocal ligaments do not stretch between them. Pick this pair only if the question asked for the lowest and highest laryngeal cartilages.

The thyroid cartilage is the front anchor of the vocal ligaments, but the epiglottis is not involved in sound. Choose the epiglottis if the question asked what covers the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.
Correct. The vocal ligaments run from the arytenoid cartilages to the thyroid cartilage.
questions.answerText: The arytenoids and the thyroid cartilage

questions.q: A patient coughs violently after a sip of water goes down the wrong way and enters the laryngeal inlet. Which structure failed to seal the airway during that swallow?
options: The epiglottis
The soft palate
The thyroid cartilage
The trachealis muscle
questions.why: During a normal swallow, the epiglottis folds back over the laryngeal inlet so food and liquid slide past into the esophagus. When something slips past it into the larynx, the airway responds with a coughing fit to clear it. So liquid entering the laryngeal inlet means the epiglottis did not seal the opening in time.
notes: Correct. The epiglottis normally folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

The soft palate lifts to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing. If it failed, liquid would go up into the nose instead. Pick the soft palate if the question described water coming out of the nose.

The thyroid cartilage is the rigid shield that forms the Adam's apple. It protects the larynx from the front but does not move to cover the inlet. Choose it if the question asked which cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence.

The trachealis muscle closes the gap at the back of the tracheal rings, below the larynx. It plays no part in sealing the inlet. It would be the answer if the question asked what lies between the trachea and the esophagus.
questions.answerText: The epiglottis

questions.q: Air breathed in through the nose passes through the three regions of the pharynx in which order?
options: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx
Oropharynx, nasopharynx, laryngopharynx
Nasopharynx, laryngopharynx, oropharynx
Laryngopharynx, oropharynx, nasopharynx
questions.why: The pharynx is the throat, and its three regions are stacked from top to bottom. The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity above the soft palate, the oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity, and the laryngopharynx runs from the epiglottis down to where the airway and esophagus divide. Air from the nose meets them in that top-to-bottom order.
notes: Correct. Air from the nose passes the nasopharynx, then the oropharynx, then the laryngopharynx.

This order starts at the oropharynx, behind the mouth, and then climbs back up to the nasopharynx. Air from the nose meets the nasopharynx first because it lies directly behind the nasal cavity, while air breathed through the mouth enters at the oropharynx and never passes the nasopharynx.
This order skips past the oropharynx and comes back to it. The laryngopharynx is the lowest region, so it must come last.
This is the order from bottom to top, the reverse of the path of inhaled air. It would fit air moving upward, such as during exhalation through the nose.
questions.answerText: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx

questions.q: As air moves down through the larynx toward the trachea, it passes between the true vocal cords. What is the name for the vocal folds together with the opening between them?
options: Epiglottis
Glottis
Vestibular folds
Carina
questions.why: The glottis is the vocal folds together with the opening between them. The vocal folds, the true vocal cords, vibrate as air passes through the glottis to produce sound. Below the glottis the larynx continues into the trachea.
notes: The epiglottis is the flexible flap of elastic cartilage that folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It would be the answer if the question asked what keeps food out of the airway.
Correct. The glottis is the vocal folds and the opening between them.

The vestibular folds are the false vocal cords above the true folds. They close the airway during swallowing and play no part in sound, so they would be the answer if the question asked about the folds above the true vocal cords.
The carina is the internal ridge at the bottom of the trachea where it forks into the main bronchi. It would be the answer if the question asked where the trachea divides.
questions.answerText: Glottis

questions.q: Which list names the parts of the upper respiratory tract?
options: Nose, pharynx, trachea, and main bronchi
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
Larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs
Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx
questions.why: The upper respiratory tract is the set of passages above the larynx that take in air and condition it, warming, moistening, and filtering it on the way down. It is made up of the nose, the nasal cavity, the paranasal sinuses that drain into the nasal cavity, and the pharynx. Everything from the larynx down belongs to the lower respiratory tract.
notes: This list mixes the two tracts, since the trachea and main bronchi lie below the larynx in the lower tract. Students pick it when they forget that the larynx is the dividing line between the upper and lower tracts.

The respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli are the respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens deep in the lungs. Choose this list if the question asked for the structures of the respiratory zone.
The larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs make up the lower respiratory tract. Pick this list if the question asked for the parts of the lower tract.
Correct. The upper tract is the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx.
questions.answerText: Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx

questions.q: Which part of the respiratory system includes all the passages that only carry air, from the nose down to the terminal bronchioles?
options: Upper respiratory tract
Lower respiratory tract
Respiratory zone
Conducting zone
questions.why: The conducting zone is every passage that moves air without exchanging gases with the blood, from the nose through the pharynx, larynx, trachea, and bronchi down to the terminal bronchioles. Along the way it warms, moistens, and filters the air. The zones and the tracts are two separate ways of grouping the same parts, so the conducting zone crosses from the upper tract into the lower tract.
notes: The upper respiratory tract stops at the pharynx, so it does not reach the terminal bronchioles. It would be the answer if the question asked for the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx as a group.

The lower respiratory tract runs from the larynx through the lungs, including the alveoli where gases are exchanged, and it leaves out the nose. Choose it if the question asked for the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs as a group.
The respiratory zone is where gas exchange happens: the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. Pick it if the question asked which structures exchange gases with the blood.
Correct. The conducting zone carries air from the nose to the terminal bronchioles.
questions.answerText: Conducting zone

questions.q: Gas exchange happens in the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. What is this group of structures called?
options: Conducting zone
Upper respiratory tract
Respiratory zone
Respiratory mucosa
questions.why: The respiratory zone is the part of the system where air comes close enough to the blood for gases to cross. It begins at the respiratory bronchioles, which have a few alveoli budding from their walls, and continues through the alveolar ducts to the alveoli. Everything above it, down to the terminal bronchioles, is the conducting zone.
notes: The conducting zone is the set of passages that only carry air, from the nose to the terminal bronchioles. Pick it if the question asked which passages warm, moisten, and filter air without exchanging gases.
The upper respiratory tract is the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx, far from the alveoli. It would be the answer if the question asked which structures lie above the larynx.
Correct. The respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli form the respiratory zone.

The respiratory mucosa is the lining of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells found in the nasal cavity and airways. Choose it if the question asked which lining traps particles in mucus and sweeps them toward the pharynx.
questions.answerText: Respiratory zone

questions.q: Which scroll-shaped projections on the lateral walls of the nasal cavity swirl incoming air so it contacts the warm, moist lining?
options: Nasal septum
Choanae
Nasal meatuses
Nasal conchae
questions.why: The nasal conchae are three scroll-shaped projections, superior, middle, and inferior, on each lateral wall of the nasal cavity. They make air tumble as it passes, which increases its contact with the warm, moist mucosa. That contact warms and moistens the air and lets mucus trap particles before the air moves on.
notes: The nasal septum is the midline wall that divides the nasal cavity into right and left halves. It would be the answer if the question asked what separates the two sides of the nasal cavity.
The choanae are the posterior openings where the nasal cavity becomes the nasopharynx. Choose them if the question asked where air leaves the back of the nasal cavity.
The nasal meatuses are the air passages beneath each concha, not the projections themselves. Pick them if the question asked about the grooves that air flows through under the conchae.
Correct. The nasal conchae swirl the air against the nasal lining.
questions.answerText: Nasal conchae

questions.q: Which region of the pharynx carries air only and lies behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate?
options: Laryngopharynx
Larynx
Oropharynx
Nasopharynx
questions.why: The nasopharynx is the uppermost region of the pharynx, sitting behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. Because food does not normally enter it, it carries air only and is lined with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. It holds the pharyngeal tonsil and the openings of the auditory tubes, and the soft palate lifts to close it during swallowing.
notes: The laryngopharynx is the lowest region, from the epiglottis to the esophagus, where the air and food paths divide. It would be the answer if the question asked for the region just above the larynx and esophagus.
The larynx is the voice box below the pharynx, not a region of the pharynx. Choose it if the question asked which structure connects the pharynx to the trachea.
The oropharynx lies behind the oral cavity, from the soft palate to the epiglottis, and carries both air and food. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the palatine tonsils.
Correct. The nasopharynx carries air only and lies above the soft palate.
questions.answerText: Nasopharynx

questions.q: Which region of the pharynx lies behind the oral cavity, from the soft palate to the epiglottis, and carries both air and food?
options: Esophagus
Oropharynx
Nasopharynx
Laryngopharynx
questions.why: The oropharynx is the middle region of the pharynx, directly behind the mouth. Because both air and swallowed food pass through it, it is lined with stratified squamous epithelium, which stands up to friction. It holds the palatine and lingual tonsils.
notes: The esophagus is the muscular tube that carries food from the laryngopharynx to the stomach, not part of the pharynx. Choose it if the question asked which tube food enters after leaving the pharynx.
Correct. The oropharynx is the middle region, shared by air and food.
The nasopharynx lies above the soft palate, behind the nasal cavity, and carries air only. Pick it if the question asked which region holds the pharyngeal tonsil and the auditory tube openings.

The laryngopharynx is the lowest region, below the epiglottis, where the air and food paths divide. It would be the answer if the question asked for the region that leads into both the larynx and the esophagus.
