questions.answerText: Oropharynx

questions.q: Which region of the pharynx runs from the epiglottis down to the esophagus and is where the air and food paths divide?
options: Laryngopharynx
Oropharynx
Nasopharynx
Larynx
questions.why: The laryngopharynx is the lowest region of the pharynx, lying behind the larynx from the level of the epiglottis down to the esophagus. Air turns forward into the larynx here while food continues back into the esophagus. Like the oropharynx, it carries both air and food and is lined with stratified squamous epithelium.
notes: Correct. The laryngopharynx is where the air and food paths split.
The oropharynx is the middle region behind the mouth, from the soft palate to the epiglottis. It would be the answer if the question asked which region holds the palatine tonsils.
The nasopharynx is the uppermost region, above the soft palate, and carries air only. Pick it if the question asked which region lies behind the nasal cavity.
The larynx is the voice box that air enters after the laryngopharynx, not a region of the pharynx itself. Choose it if the question asked which structure houses the vocal folds.
questions.answerText: Laryngopharynx

questions.q: Which structure connects the pharynx to the trachea, keeps food out of the airway, and houses the vocal folds?
options: Laryngopharynx
Larynx
Trachea
Epiglottis
questions.why: The larynx, or voice box, sits between the pharynx and the trachea. It is built from nine cartilages that hold the airway open, it closes off the airway during swallowing, and it houses the vocal folds that vibrate to produce sound. Its largest cartilage, the thyroid cartilage, forms the laryngeal prominence or Adam's apple.
notes: The laryngopharynx is the lowest region of the pharynx, lying behind the larynx and shared by air and food. It would be the answer if the question asked where the air and food paths divide.
Correct. The larynx is the voice box between the pharynx and trachea.
The trachea is the windpipe below the larynx, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings. Pick it if the question asked which airway runs from the larynx to the carina.

The epiglottis is one cartilage of the larynx, the flap that folds over the inlet during swallowing, not the whole voice box. Choose it if the question asked which elastic cartilage keeps food out of the airway.
questions.answerText: Larynx

questions.q: Which flexible flap of elastic cartilage folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing to keep food out of the airway?
options: Cricoid cartilage
Epiglottis
Soft palate
Thyroid cartilage
questions.why: The epiglottis is a spoon-shaped flap at the top of the larynx. During a swallow it folds down over the laryngeal inlet so food and liquid slide past into the esophagus instead of the airway. It is the one unpaired laryngeal cartilage made of elastic cartilage, because it has to bend and spring back with every swallow.
notes: The cricoid cartilage is the ring-shaped cartilage just below the thyroid cartilage, the only complete ring in the airway. It would be the answer if the question asked which laryngeal cartilage forms a full circle.
Correct. The epiglottis covers the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

The soft palate is the muscular back part of the roof of the mouth, and it lifts to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing. Choose it if the question asked what keeps food from entering the nasal cavity.
The thyroid cartilage is the large shield-shaped cartilage at the front of the larynx that forms the Adam's apple. Pick it if the question asked which cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence.
questions.answerText: Epiglottis

questions.q: What is the name for the vocal folds together with the opening between them?
options: Glottis
Vestibular folds
Epiglottis
Laryngeal prominence
questions.why: The glottis is the sound-producing part of the larynx: the true vocal folds plus the opening between them. As air passes through that opening, the vocal folds vibrate to make sound. The epiglottis is named for sitting above (epi) the glottis.
notes: Correct. The glottis is the vocal folds and the opening between them.

The vestibular folds are the false vocal cords above the true folds, which help close the airway during swallowing but play no part in sound. They would be the answer if the question asked for the folds that sit just above the vocal folds.
The epiglottis is the elastic cartilage flap above the glottis that covers the airway during swallowing. Pick it if the question asked which structure keeps food out of the larynx.
The laryngeal prominence is the Adam's apple, the bump formed by the thyroid cartilage on the front of the neck. Choose it if the question asked about the visible landmark of the larynx.
questions.answerText: Glottis

questions.q: During a swallow, a bit of food slips into the laryngeal opening and triggers coughing. Which structure normally folds over the opening to prevent this?
options: The epiglottis
The thyroid cartilage
The soft palate
The cricoid cartilage
questions.why: The epiglottis is a flexible, spoon-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. During swallowing it folds back over the laryngeal inlet, so food and liquid slide past into the esophagus instead of into the airway. When food slips past it, coughing is the airway's attempt to clear it.
notes: Correct. The epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

The thyroid cartilage is the large shield-shaped cartilage that forms the Adam's apple. It protects the larynx from the front but does not cover the opening, so choose it for a question about the laryngeal prominence.
The soft palate also moves during swallowing, but it lifts to close off the nasopharynx so food does not go up into the nose. Pick it for a question about food or liquid coming out of the nose.

The cricoid cartilage is the ring below the thyroid cartilage and the only complete cartilage ring in the airway. It would be the answer for a question about the base of the larynx or the landmark for an emergency airway.
questions.answerText: The epiglottis

questions.q: Besides producing the voice, what other major job does the larynx perform?
options: It guards the airway during swallowing
It exchanges gases with the blood
It drains the paranasal sinuses
It warms and moistens incoming air
questions.why: The larynx connects the pharynx to the trachea, and it does more than house the vocal folds. During swallowing, the epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet and the vestibular folds close the airway, so food and liquid are sent into the esophagus instead of the trachea. Its cartilages also hold the airway open, keeping a clear path for air.
notes: Correct. The epiglottis and vestibular folds close off the airway when you swallow.
Gas exchange happens in the respiratory zone, in the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. The larynx is part of the conducting zone and only carries air.
The paranasal sinuses drain into the nasal cavity, not the larynx. Choose the nasal cavity for a question about where the sinuses empty.
Warming and moistening air is mainly the job of the nasal cavity, with its conchae and moist mucosa. Pick the nasal cavity for a question about conditioning incoming air.
questions.answerText: It guards the airway during swallowing

questions.q: How do the nasal conchae help condition incoming air?
options: They close the nasopharynx during swallowing
They swirl air over warm, moist mucosa
They filter large particles with coarse hairs
They exchange gases with the blood
questions.why: The nasal conchae are three scroll-shaped projections on the lateral wall of each side of the nasal cavity. They make the air tumble and swirl as it passes, which increases its contact with the warm, moist mucosa covering them. More contact means the air is warmed and moistened, and more particles are trapped in mucus, before it moves on toward the lungs.
notes: Closing the nasopharynx during swallowing is the job of the soft palate, which lifts up. Choose the soft palate for a question about keeping food out of the nose.
Correct. The conchae swirl air across a large area of warm, moist lining.
Coarse hairs that filter large particles are found in the nasal vestibule, just inside the nostrils. Pick the vestibule for a question about the first filter in the nose.
Gas exchange happens only in the respiratory zone of the lungs. The conchae are in the conducting zone and only condition the air.
questions.answerText: They swirl air over warm, moist mucosa

questions.q: Why is the nasal vestibule good at filtering out large particles?
options: It is lined with olfactory epithelium
It has skin with coarse hairs
It is lined with alveolar macrophages
It has scroll-shaped conchae
questions.why: The nasal vestibule is the area just inside the nostrils. It is lined with skin that has sebaceous glands and coarse hairs, sometimes called vibrissae. These hairs act as a first screen, catching large particles like dust before the air moves deeper into the nasal cavity.
notes: Olfactory epithelium is a small patch in the roof of the nasal cavity that houses the receptors for smell. Pick it for a question about where smell is detected.
Correct. The coarse hairs of the vestibule catch large particles at the entrance of the nose.
Alveolar macrophages patrol the alveoli deep in the lungs and engulf small particles that get past every earlier filter. Choose them for a question about the last line of defense in the alveoli.
The conchae are on the lateral walls of the nasal cavity, deeper than the vestibule. They swirl air over moist mucosa, so choose them for a question about warming and moistening air.
questions.answerText: It has skin with coarse hairs

questions.q: Which list names the parts of the upper respiratory tract, as grouped in this course?
options: Nose, nasal cavity, trachea, and bronchi
Larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx
questions.why: The upper respiratory tract is the part of the airway in the head and upper neck: the nose, the nasal cavity, the paranasal sinuses, and the pharynx. These structures take in air and condition it by warming, moistening, and filtering it. In this course the larynx begins the lower respiratory tract.
notes: The nose and nasal cavity are upper tract structures, but the trachea and bronchi lie in the neck and thorax and belong to the lower tract. This list mixes the two groups.
This is the lower respiratory tract, from the larynx down into the lungs. Pick this list if the question asked for the lower tract.
These are respiratory zone structures deep in the lungs, where gas exchange happens. Choose this list for a question about the respiratory zone, not the upper tract.
Correct. The upper tract runs from the nose through the pharynx.
questions.answerText: Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx

questions.q: Which structures make up the respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens?
options: Nasal cavity, pharynx, and larynx
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
Segmental bronchi, bronchioles, and terminal bronchioles
Trachea, main bronchi, and lobar bronchi
questions.why: The respiratory zone is the part of the airway where gas exchange actually happens. It begins just past the terminal bronchioles with the respiratory bronchioles, which have a few alveoli budding from their walls, then continues into the alveolar ducts and alveoli. Everything before that point, from the nose to the terminal bronchioles, is the conducting zone, which only carries air.
notes: These are upper airway structures that warm, moisten, and filter air. Choose them for a question about the upper respiratory tract.
Correct. These are the airways with alveoli, where gases cross into the blood.

These are the last airways of the conducting zone, ending at the terminal bronchioles. Students choose this list because it sits so close to the exchange surface, but these walls have no alveoli; it would be the answer for the end of the conducting zone.
These are large conducting airways supported by cartilage. Pick them if the question asked which airways carry air into the lungs without exchanging gas.
questions.answerText: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli

questions.q: A segment of airway carries air but has no alveoli in its walls. Which of these could it be?
options: An alveolar sac
An alveolar duct
A terminal bronchiole
A respiratory bronchiole
questions.why: An airway with no alveoli belongs to the conducting zone, which only carries air from the nose down to the terminal bronchioles. The terminal bronchiole is the last airway of that zone. Past it, every structure has alveoli in or along its walls: respiratory bronchioles have a few budding from their walls, alveolar ducts are lined entirely with them, and alveolar sacs are clusters of them.
notes: An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli sharing a common space, so it is all exchange surface. Choose it for the grape-like cluster at the very end of the airway.
An alveolar duct is a passage whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli. It would be the answer for the airway that leads from a respiratory bronchiole into the alveolar sacs.
Correct. The terminal bronchiole is the last conducting airway, with no alveoli.
A respiratory bronchiole has a few alveoli budding from its walls, so it is the first airway of the respiratory zone. Pick it if the question asked where gas exchange begins.
questions.answerText: A terminal bronchiole

questions.q: Which laryngeal cartilage forms the Adam's apple?
options: Arytenoid cartilage
Epiglottis
Thyroid cartilage
Cricoid cartilage
questions.why: The thyroid cartilage is the largest cartilage of the larynx, a shield-shaped piece that forms the front of the voice box. Its anterior ridge is the laryngeal prominence, known as the Adam's apple, which is usually larger in males. It sits just above the cricoid cartilage, the ring at the bottom of the larynx.
notes: The arytenoid cartilages are small paired cartilages at the back of the larynx that anchor and move the vocal folds. They would be the answer for a question about which cartilages control the vocal cords.
The epiglottis is the flexible flap of elastic cartilage that folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. Choose it for the cartilage that keeps food out of the airway.
Correct. The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence.

The cricoid cartilage is the ring just below the thyroid cartilage, the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. Pick it if the question asked which laryngeal cartilage fully encircles the airway.
questions.answerText: Thyroid cartilage

questions.q: What does the epiglottis do?
options: It vibrates as air passes to produce sound
It forms a complete ring that holds the airway open
It lifts to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing
It folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing
questions.why: The epiglottis is a flexible, spoon-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. During swallowing, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over the laryngeal inlet, so food and drink slide past into the esophagus instead of entering the airway. Elastic cartilage lets it bend and spring back with every swallow, which the stiff hyaline thyroid and cricoid cartilages could not do.
notes: Vibrating to produce sound is the job of the vocal folds, the true vocal cords stretched across the larynx. Pick this if the question asked what makes the voice.
A complete ring holding the airway open describes the cricoid cartilage, just below the thyroid cartilage. It would be the answer for the only complete cartilage ring in the airway.

Lifting to close off the nasopharynx is the job of the soft palate, which keeps food from going up into the nasal cavity. Choose this for a question about why food does not come out of the nose when you swallow.
Correct. The epiglottis is the lid that covers the airway during a swallow.
questions.answerText: It folds over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing

questions.q: A student laughs while eating, and a bit of food slips into the larynx instead of the esophagus, setting off a coughing fit. Which structure normally covers the laryngeal inlet during a swallow to prevent this?
options: Soft palate
Epiglottis
Thyroid cartilage
Trachealis muscle
questions.why: During a swallow the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over the laryngeal inlet like a lid, steering food back toward the esophagus. If someone laughs or talks while swallowing, the airway may be open at the wrong moment and food can slip past the epiglottis. The coughing fit is the airway's attempt to push the food back out.
notes: The soft palate rises to close off the nasopharynx during a swallow, keeping food out of the nasal cavity. Pick it if the food had come up into the nose instead of entering the larynx.
Correct. The epiglottis covers the laryngeal inlet so food goes down the esophagus.

The thyroid cartilage is the large shield-shaped cartilage forming the front of the larynx (the Adam's apple). It protects the larynx but does not cover its opening; choose it for a question about the laryngeal prominence.

The trachealis muscle is the smooth muscle that closes the open back of each C-shaped tracheal ring, next to the esophagus. It would be the answer for a question about the posterior wall of the trachea.
questions.answerText: Epiglottis

questions.q: Which list gives the three regions of the pharynx from top to bottom?
options: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx
Oropharynx, nasopharynx, laryngopharynx
Nasopharynx, laryngopharynx, oropharynx
Laryngopharynx, oropharynx, nasopharynx
questions.why: The pharynx is the throat, a muscular tube running from behind the nasal cavity down to the larynx and esophagus. The nasopharynx sits behind the nasal cavity, above the soft palate; the oropharynx sits behind the oral cavity, from the soft palate to the epiglottis; and the laryngopharynx runs from the epiglottis down to the esophagus. Each region is named for the structure it sits behind.
notes: Correct. Nose, then mouth, then larynx, from top to bottom.
This swaps the top two regions. The nasal cavity sits above the oral cavity, so the nasopharynx behind it is the highest region.
This puts the laryngopharynx in the middle, but it is the lowest region, leading down to the larynx and esophagus. The oropharynx, behind the mouth, sits between the other two.
These are the right three regions listed from bottom to top. Pick this order if the question asked for the regions from inferior to superior.
questions.answerText: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx

questions.q: Which part of the pharynx carries air only, and which parts carry both air and food?
options: The laryngopharynx carries air only; the nasopharynx and oropharynx carry both
The oropharynx carries air only; the nasopharynx and laryngopharynx carry both
All three regions of the pharynx carry both air and food
The nasopharynx carries air only; the oropharynx and laryngopharynx carry both
questions.why: The nasopharynx lies above the soft palate, and during a swallow the soft palate lifts to seal it off, so it carries air only. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx lie below that point, where food from the mouth and air from the nose share the same passage. Their linings match: the nasopharynx has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium like the rest of the airway, while the shared regions have tougher stratified squamous epithelium to resist friction from food.
notes: The laryngopharynx is where the air and food paths finally divide into the larynx and the esophagus, so food passes through it. Students choose this because its name sounds like part of the airway.
The oropharynx sits directly behind the mouth, so food passes through it with every swallow. Pick the oropharynx for a question about which region holds the palatine tonsils.
Food normally never enters the nasopharynx, because the soft palate lifts to close it off during swallowing. Students choose this when they picture the whole pharynx as one shared tube.
Correct. Only the nasopharynx is closed off from food.
questions.answerText: The nasopharynx carries air only; the oropharynx and laryngopharynx carry both

questions.q: What do the nasal conchae and meatuses do to inhaled air?
options: They vibrate as the air passes through to produce sound
They bring the air close to the blood so oxygen can cross into it
They swirl air against the moist lining to warm and filter it
They close off the nasal cavity from the pharynx during swallowing
questions.why: The nasal conchae are three scroll-shaped projections on the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, and the meatuses are the narrow passages beneath them. They turn the airflow into swirls, bringing more air into contact with the warm, moist, mucus-covered lining. That contact warms and moistens the air and traps dust and particles in the mucus before the air reaches the lungs.
notes: Sound is produced by the vocal folds in the larynx, not by the nasal conchae. Choose this description for a question about the true vocal cords.
Gas exchange happens in the alveoli deep in the lungs, not in the nasal cavity. Pick this for a question about the job of the alveoli and the respiratory membrane.
Correct. The conchae increase contact between the air and the lining so the air is conditioned.
Closing off the nasal route during swallowing is the job of the soft palate, which lifts to seal the nasopharynx. It would be the answer for a question about why food does not enter the nose.
questions.answerText: They swirl air against the moist lining to warm and filter it

questions.q: Which structure is inflamed in rhinitis?
options: The lining of the paranasal sinuses
The vocal folds of the larynx
The lining of the bronchi
The nasal mucosa
questions.why: Rhinitis is inflammation of the nasal mucosa, the lining of the nasal cavity. The lining swells and makes extra mucus. Allergies or infections cause it.
notes: Inflamed linings of the paranasal sinuses are sinusitis, which often starts when the sinus openings into the nasal cavity are blocked.
Inflamed, swollen vocal folds are laryngitis, which turns the voice hoarse.
A bronchial lining that stays inflamed and makes too much mucus is chronic bronchitis, a problem much lower in the airway.
Correct. Rhinitis inflames the nasal mucosa, the lining of the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText: The nasal mucosa

questions.q: The openings that drain a patient's paranasal sinuses into the nasal cavity become blocked, and the lining of the sinuses becomes inflamed. Which disorder fits?
options: Rhinitis
Sinusitis
Laryngitis
Pleurisy
questions.why: Sinusitis is inflammation of the lining of the paranasal sinuses. It often starts when the sinus openings into the nasal cavity are blocked. Rhinitis is the related problem in the nasal cavity itself, the nasal mucosa.
notes: Rhinitis inflames the nasal mucosa, the lining of the nasal cavity itself, not the sinuses that drain into it.
Correct. Sinusitis is inflammation of the lining of the paranasal sinuses, often after their openings are blocked.
Laryngitis inflames the vocal folds of the larynx and turns the voice hoarse. It does not involve the sinuses.
Pleurisy is inflammation of the pleurae around the lungs, which causes sharp pain with each breath. It does not involve the sinuses or their openings.
questions.answerText: Sinusitis

questions.q: Why does laryngitis make the voice hoarse?
options: The nasal mucosa swells and makes extra mucus that muffles the voice
The epiglottis stays open and lets air slip past the vocal folds
The vocal folds are inflamed and swollen, so they cannot vibrate normally
The cricoid cartilage softens, so the larynx cannot hold its shape
questions.why: Laryngitis affects the larynx and its vocal folds. The folds become inflamed and swollen, so they cannot vibrate normally, and the voice turns hoarse. The problem is in the folds themselves, not in the cartilage frame of the larynx or in the nasal cavity.
notes: A swollen nasal mucosa with extra mucus is rhinitis. It affects the nasal cavity, not the vocal folds that make the voice.
The epiglottis covers the laryngeal inlet during a swallow. Laryngitis is inflammation of the vocal folds, not a problem with the epiglottis.
Correct. In laryngitis the inflamed, swollen vocal folds cannot vibrate normally.
The cricoid cartilage is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway. Laryngitis inflames the vocal folds and does not change the cartilage.
questions.answerText: The vocal folds are inflamed and swollen, so they cannot vibrate normally

questions.q: A patient with a sinus infection has pus draining from the space above the superior nasal concha, called the sphenoethmoidal recess. Which sinus is most likely infected, and which bone holds it?
options: The maxillary sinus, in the maxilla.
The back ethmoidal air cells, in the ethmoid bone.
The frontal sinus, in the frontal bone.
The sphenoidal sinus, in the sphenoid bone.
questions.why: Each paranasal sinus is named for the bone it sits in, and each drains through a small opening into the nasal cavity. Most drain into the middle meatus, and the back ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus. Only the sphenoidal sinus, deep in the skull behind the nasal cavity, drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. So pus at that spot points to the sphenoidal sinus in the sphenoid bone.
notes: The maxillary sinus is the largest sinus, in the cheek below each orbit, but it drains into the middle meatus, not the space above the superior concha.
The back ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus, the groove under the superior concha. The recess is the space above that concha.
The frontal sinus sits in the forehead above the orbits and drains into the middle meatus, so it would not send pus into the sphenoethmoidal recess.
Correct. The sphenoidal sinus is the only sinus that drains into the space above the superior concha.
questions.answerText: The sphenoidal sinus, in the sphenoid bone.

questions.q: A child has enlarged adenoids that crowd the openings on the side walls of the pharyngeal region where the adenoids sit. Which region is it, and what are those openings?
options: The oropharynx; the auditory tubes, which lead to the middle ears.
The nasopharynx; the auditory tubes, which lead to the middle ears.
The nasopharynx; the choanae, which lead from the nasal cavity.
The laryngopharynx; the openings of the larynx and the esophagus.
questions.why: The adenoids are the pharyngeal tonsil when it is enlarged, and it sits on the back wall of the nasopharynx, the air-only region behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. The same region has the openings of the auditory tubes on its side walls, and those tubes connect the nasopharynx to the middle ears. That is why swollen adenoids can crowd the auditory tube openings.
notes: The oropharynx sits behind the mouth and holds the palatine and lingual tonsils. The adenoids and the auditory tube openings are higher, in the nasopharynx.
Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) sits on the back wall of the nasopharynx, and the auditory tubes open on its side walls.
The region is right, but the choanae open into the nasopharynx from the front, from the nasal cavity. The openings on its side walls are the auditory tubes.
The laryngopharynx is where the air and food paths split into the larynx and esophagus. The adenoids and the auditory tube openings sit higher, in the nasopharynx.
questions.answerText: The nasopharynx; the auditory tubes, which lead to the middle ears.

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. Beyond dividing the trunk, what role does it play in breathing?
options: It separates the two pleural cavities so each lung can inflate
Its contraction enlarges the thoracic cavity, drawing air into the lungs
It closes off the trachea during swallowing
It squeezes the lungs from below to push air into them
questions.why: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle and the main muscle of breathing. When it contracts, it flattens and moves down, making the thoracic cavity larger, and air flows into the lungs. So the same partition that divides the trunk also drives each breath in.
notes: The two pleural cavities are separated by the mediastinum, the central compartment holding the heart. The diaphragm lies beneath both lungs, not between them.
Correct. Contraction enlarges the chest and draws air in.
Closing off the airway during swallowing is the job of the epiglottis in the larynx. The diaphragm is far below, at the floor of the thorax.
Squeezing the lungs would push air out, not in. Contraction of the diaphragm makes the chest larger, which is the opposite of squeezing.
questions.answerText: Its contraction enlarges the thoracic cavity, drawing air into the lungs

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structure is the windpipe, held permanently open by C-shaped rings of cartilage?
options: The trachea
A main bronchus
The larynx
The pharynx
questions.why: The trachea, or windpipe, runs from the larynx down into the thorax, where it forks into the two main bronchi. C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage keep it permanently open so air can pass at all times. The open back of each C is closed by the trachealis muscle, which lies against the esophagus.
notes: Correct. The trachea is the windpipe held open by C-shaped cartilage rings.
A main bronchus is one of the two branches the trachea divides into at the carina. Its cartilage changes from rings to plates inside the lung, and it is not called the windpipe.
The larynx is the voice box above the trachea, built from nine cartilages including the thyroid and cricoid. Pick it if the question asked which structure houses the vocal folds.
The pharynx is the throat, a muscular tube shared by air and food. It has no cartilage rings holding it open.
questions.answerText: The trachea

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which serous membrane covers the outer surface of the lung itself?
options: The parietal peritoneum
The parietal pleura
The visceral pleura
The visceral pericardium
questions.why: Each lung is wrapped by a double-layered serous membrane called the pleura. The visceral pleura clings directly to the outer surface of the lung, while the parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall. Visceral always means the layer on the organ, and parietal means the layer on the body wall.
notes: The parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominopelvic cavity. Pick it for a question about the membrane lining the abdominal wall.
The parietal pleura lines the inside of the thoracic wall, not the lung surface. Pick it if the question asked which pleura a surgeon meets first when cutting through the chest wall.
Correct. The visceral pleura covers the surface of the lung.
The visceral pericardium, also called the epicardium, covers the surface of the heart. It follows the same visceral pattern but belongs to the heart.
questions.answerText: The visceral pleura

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: How many lobes does the right lung have?
options: Five lobes
Two lobes
Three lobes
Four lobes
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes: superior, middle, and inferior. A horizontal fissure separates the superior lobe from the middle lobe, and an oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from the middle and superior lobes above it. The right lung is the larger of the two because the heart takes up room on the left.
notes: Five is the total number of lobes in both lungs together, three on the right plus two on the left. Pick five only if the question asked how many lobes there are in all.
Two lobes is the count for the left lung, which has only a superior and an inferior lobe. Pick two if the question asked about the left lung.
Correct. The right lung has superior, middle, and inferior lobes.
Four lobes is not the count for either lung. Students sometimes add a lobe for the lingula, but the lingula is part of the left superior lobe, not a separate lobe.
questions.answerText: Three lobes

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which alveolar cells secrete surfactant?
options: Alveolar macrophages
Type II alveolar cells
Pulmonary capillary endothelial cells
Type I alveolar cells
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells scattered in the alveolar wall that secrete surfactant. Surfactant is a fluid that lowers surface tension and keeps the alveoli from collapsing. Type I cells, by contrast, are the thin, flat cells where gases cross.
notes: Alveolar macrophages, also called dust cells, patrol the alveolar surface and engulf debris. Pick them for a question about cleaning the alveoli.
Correct. Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant.
Pulmonary capillary endothelial cells line the capillaries that wrap each alveolus. They form the blood side of the respiratory membrane, not the surfactant-secreting cells.
Type I alveolar cells are thin, flat simple squamous cells that form most of the alveolar wall, where gases cross. Pick them for a question about the gas exchange surface.
questions.answerText: Type II alveolar cells

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the narrow superior tip of a lung called?
options: The base
The lingula
The apex
The hilum
questions.why: The apex is the narrow top of each lung. It rises just above the clavicle, into the root of the neck. The opposite end, the broad inferior surface resting on the diaphragm, is the base.
notes: The base is the broad inferior surface of the lung that rests on the diaphragm. Pick it if the question asked for the bottom of the lung.
The lingula is the tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe, below the cardiac notch. Pick it for a question about the left lung's tongue-like extension.
Correct. The apex is the narrow superior tip of the lung.
The hilum is the indentation on the medial surface where the bronchus and vessels enter and leave. Pick it for a question about where structures pass into the lung.
questions.answerText: The apex

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structure is the indentation on the medial surface of a lung where the bronchus and vessels enter and leave?
options: The hilum
The base
The apex
The cardiac notch
questions.why: The hilum is the indented region on the medial, mediastinal surface of each lung. The main bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, and lymphatics pass through it, and that bundle is called the root of the lung. The same word hilum is used for the indented side of the kidney and lymph node, where vessels enter and leave.
notes: Correct. The hilum is where the bronchus and vessels enter and leave the lung.
The base is the broad inferior surface resting on the diaphragm. Pick it for a question about the bottom surface of the lung.
The apex is the narrow superior tip of the lung, rising just above the clavicle. Pick it for a question about the top of the lung.
The cardiac notch is the indentation in the left lung that makes room for the heart. It is on the anterior border of the left lung, not the entry point for the bronchus and vessels.
questions.answerText: The hilum

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the branching system of airways that runs from the trachea down to the terminal bronchioles called?
options: The alveolar sac
The bronchial tree
The root of the lung
The respiratory membrane
questions.why: Below the larynx the airway branches again and again, like an upside-down tree, from the trachea to the main, lobar, and segmental bronchi and then the bronchioles. This branching system is called the bronchial tree. With each division the airways get narrower and more numerous.
notes: An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli sharing a common space at the very end of the airways. Pick it for a question about the clusters at the ends of the alveolar ducts.
Correct. The bronchial tree is the branching system of airways below the larynx.
The root of the lung is the bundle of the main bronchus, pulmonary vessels, nerves, and lymphatics at the hilum. Pick it for a question about what passes into the lung at the hilum.
The respiratory membrane is the thin barrier between alveolar air and blood. Pick it for a question about where gases cross.
questions.answerText: The bronchial tree

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Air leaving the trachea passes the carina. Which airways does it enter next?
options: The alveolar ducts
The lobar bronchi
The main bronchi
The terminal bronchioles
questions.why: The carina is the internal ridge at the bottom of the trachea where it forks in two. Each fork is a main (primary) bronchus, one entering each lung at the hilum. From there the main bronchi divide into lobar, then segmental, bronchi.
notes: Alveolar ducts are respiratory zone passages lined entirely with alveoli, near the very end of the tree. Pick them for a question about the airway between the respiratory bronchioles and the alveolar sacs.
The lobar bronchi are the secondary bronchi, one to each lobe. They branch from the main bronchi, one step later than the carina.
Correct. The trachea forks at the carina into the two main bronchi.
Terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone, many divisions further down the tree. Pick them if the question asked for the airway just before the respiratory zone.
questions.answerText: The main bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The lobar bronchi are also called the secondary bronchi. What does one lobar bronchus supply?
options: One bronchopulmonary segment
One whole lung
One alveolar sac
One lobe of a lung
questions.why: Each main bronchus divides into lobar bronchi, one for each lobe. The right lung has three lobes and so receives three lobar bronchi, while the left lung has two lobes and two lobar bronchi. The name lobar comes from the lobe each one supplies.
notes: A bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a segmental (tertiary) bronchus, the next branch after the lobar bronchi. Pick this if the question asked about segmental bronchi.
One whole lung is supplied by a main (primary) bronchus. Pick the main bronchus if the question asked which airway enters each lung.
An alveolar sac lies at the very end of the tree, after the alveolar duct. It is reached only after many more divisions.
Correct. Each lobar bronchus supplies one lobe.
questions.answerText: One lobe of a lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The left lung has a cardiac notch along its anterior border. What is the structural reason for it?
options: It anchors the visceral pleura
It marks where the apex begins
It makes room for the heart
It allows the trachea to fork
questions.why: The heart sits in the mediastinum and tilts toward the left side of the thorax. The left lung gives up room for it, and the indentation along its anterior border is called the cardiac notch. This is also why the left lung is smaller and has only two lobes.
notes: The visceral pleura clings to the whole surface of the lung and needs no notch to anchor it. Pick the visceral pleura for a question about the membrane on the lung surface.
The apex is the narrow superior tip of the lung, above the clavicle. The cardiac notch is lower, along the anterior border near the heart.
Correct. The cardiac notch is where the left lung makes room for the heart.
The trachea forks at the carina, in the mediastinum, before the airways enter either lung. The cardiac notch has nothing to do with that split.
questions.answerText: It makes room for the heart

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The trachea has C-shaped cartilage rings, but bronchioles have no cartilage. What tissue makes up much of a bronchiole wall instead?
options: Elastic cartilage
Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
questions.why: As the bronchial tree branches, cartilage shrinks and smooth muscle takes over. By the level of the bronchioles the cartilage is gone, and a complete layer of smooth muscle makes up much of the wall. Without cartilage to hold them open, bronchioles narrow a great deal when that muscle contracts, as they do in asthma.
notes: Elastic cartilage forms the epiglottis, which has to bend and spring back. Bronchioles have no cartilage of any kind.
Correct. Bronchioles have no cartilage, and smooth muscle makes up much of their wall.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary muscle attached to bones, such as the diaphragm and intercostals that move the chest wall. It is not found in the walls of the bronchioles.
Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments. Pick it for a question about what attaches muscle to bone.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A surgeon cuts inward through the thoracic wall toward a lung. Which pleura is reached first?
options: The visceral pleura
The pleural fluid
The parietal pleura
The pericardium
questions.why: The parietal pleura lines the inner surface of the thoracic wall, so it is the first serous layer reached from outside. Beneath it is the pleural cavity with its thin film of fluid, and then the visceral pleura on the surface of the lung. Parietal means wall and visceral means organ.
notes: The visceral pleura covers the lung surface, so it is reached last, after the parietal pleura and the pleural cavity. Pick it if the question asked which pleura clings to the lung.
Pleural fluid is the thin film in the pleural cavity between the two layers. It lies deep to the parietal pleura, and it is a fluid rather than a membrane.
Correct. The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall and is reached first.
The pericardium surrounds the heart in the mediastinum. A cut through the lateral chest wall toward a lung does not pass through it.
questions.answerText: The parietal pleura

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The right lung has both a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure. Which fissure pattern does the left lung have?
options: An oblique fissure only
A horizontal fissure only
No fissures at all
A horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure
questions.why: The left lung has two lobes, superior and inferior, separated by a single oblique fissure. The right lung needs two fissures to separate three lobes, and its horizontal fissure sets off the middle lobe. Since the left lung has no middle lobe, it has no horizontal fissure.
notes: Correct. The left lung has only an oblique fissure.
The horizontal fissure separates the superior and middle lobes of the right lung. The left lung has no middle lobe, so it has no horizontal fissure.
The left lung still has two lobes, so it needs one fissure to divide them. A lung with no fissures would be a single lobe.
Both fissures are found in the right lung, where they separate the superior, middle, and inferior lobes. Pick this pattern for a question about the right lung.
questions.answerText: An oblique fissure only

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which airway is the last airway of the conducting zone, just before gas exchange begins?
options: The segmental bronchus
The terminal bronchiole
The alveolar duct
The respiratory bronchiole
questions.why: Terminal bronchioles are the final airways of the conducting zone. They still only carry air, since no alveoli bud from their walls. The next airway, the respiratory bronchiole, starts the respiratory zone because a few alveoli open from its walls.
notes: The segmental bronchus is the tertiary bronchus supplying one bronchopulmonary segment. It is several divisions above the end of the conducting zone.
Correct. The terminal bronchiole is the last conducting airway.
The alveolar duct is a respiratory zone passage lined entirely with alveoli. It comes after the respiratory bronchiole, deeper into the gas exchange region.
The respiratory bronchiole is the first airway of the respiratory zone, with a few alveoli budding from its walls. Pick it if the question asked where gas exchange first begins.
questions.answerText: The terminal bronchiole

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description fits an alveolar sac?
options: The thin barrier between alveolar air and blood
A cluster of alveoli that share a common space
A single tiny air sac where gases cross
A passage whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli
questions.why: An alveolar sac sits at the end of an alveolar duct and looks like a bunch of grapes. Several alveoli open into one shared central space, the sac. Air reaches the sac through the alveolar duct, and gas exchange happens across the walls of the individual alveoli.
notes: The thin barrier between alveolar air and blood is the respiratory membrane. Pick it for a question about the layers that gases cross.
Correct. An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli sharing a common space.
A single tiny air sac where gases cross is one alveolus. Pick alveolus if the question asked about the individual site of gas exchange.
A passage lined entirely with alveoli is an alveolar duct, which leads into the alveolar sacs. Pick it for the airway just before the sacs.
questions.answerText: A cluster of alveoli that share a common space

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory disorder is defined by air entering the pleural cavity and breaking its seal?
options: Pneumothorax
Pneumonia
Asthma
Emphysema
questions.why: A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, the sealed space between the parietal and visceral pleurae. Normally that space holds only a thin film of fluid. When air gets in through a puncture of the chest wall or lung, the seal is lost and the lung collapses.
notes: Correct. A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, which lets the lung collapse.
Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid. The problem is inside the lung, not air in the pleural cavity.
Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, which causes wheezing. Pick it for a question about the small airways.
Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and reduces the surface for gas exchange. Pick it for a question about permanent loss of alveolar surface.
questions.answerText: Pneumothorax

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory disorder is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, causing wheezing?
options: Pneumothorax
Asthma
Pneumonia
Emphysema
questions.why: Asthma affects the bronchi and bronchioles. The airway lining is inflamed, the smooth muscle tightens, and extra mucus collects, so the airways narrow and air whistles through them as a wheeze. The narrowing is worst in the bronchioles because they have no cartilage to hold them open.
notes: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse. It involves the space around the lung, not the airways.
Correct. Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles.
Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid. Pick it for a question about inflamed, fluid-filled air sacs.
Emphysema destroys the alveolar walls rather than narrowing the bronchioles. Pick it for a question about lost surface area for gas exchange.
questions.answerText: Asthma

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structures form the dense net that wraps each alveolus?
options: The pulmonary capillaries
The alveolar ducts
The terminal bronchioles
The bronchial arteries
questions.why: Each alveolus is wrapped in a dense net of pulmonary capillaries. The walls of the alveolus and the capillary lie so close together that they form the respiratory membrane, where gases cross between air and blood. These capillaries come from branches of the pulmonary arteries and drain into the pulmonary veins.
notes: Correct. Pulmonary capillaries wrap each alveolus.
Alveolar ducts are air passages lined with alveoli. They lead air to the alveoli but are airways, not a net of blood vessels.
Terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone. They carry air toward the alveoli but do not wrap around them.
The bronchial arteries supply oxygen-rich blood to the walls of the bronchi and lung tissue. They nourish the lung itself rather than forming the gas exchange net around the alveoli.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary capillaries

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: On a slide, a student finds a small conducting airway with a wall of smooth muscle, no cartilage, and no alveoli. Which structure is it?
options: An alveolar duct
A segmental bronchus
A bronchiole
A respiratory bronchiole
questions.why: Bronchioles are the smallest conducting airways. As the bronchial tree branches, cartilage disappears and smooth muscle takes over, so a bronchiole wall has smooth muscle and no cartilage. Because no alveoli open from its wall, it still only carries air.
notes: An alveolar duct has walls lined entirely with alveoli. Pick it if the slide showed a passage made of alveoli.
A segmental bronchus is a tertiary bronchus that still has plates of cartilage in its wall. Pick it if the airway had cartilage and supplied one bronchopulmonary segment.
Correct. A bronchiole has smooth muscle, no cartilage, and no alveoli.
A respiratory bronchiole has a few alveoli budding from its wall. The absence of alveoli rules it out.
questions.answerText: A bronchiole

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: On a slide, an airway has a few alveoli budding from its walls. It is the first airway of the respiratory zone. Which structure is it?
options: A respiratory bronchiole
An alveolar sac
A terminal bronchiole
An alveolar duct
questions.why: The respiratory bronchiole comes right after the terminal bronchiole. A few alveoli bud from its walls, so some gas exchange can happen there, which makes it the first part of the respiratory zone. Farther down, the alveolar ducts are lined entirely with alveoli.
notes: Correct. A respiratory bronchiole has a few alveoli budding from its walls.
An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli sharing a common space at the end of the tree. It is a dead-end cluster rather than an airway with a few buds.
A terminal bronchiole has no alveoli in its wall and is the last airway of the conducting zone. Pick it for the airway just before the respiratory zone.
An alveolar duct is lined entirely with alveoli, not just a few. Pick it if the walls were made completely of alveoli.
questions.answerText: A respiratory bronchiole

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which part of the lung is the broad inferior surface that rests on the diaphragm?
options: The cardiac notch
The base of the lung
The hilum of the lung
The apex of the lung
questions.why: The base of each lung is its broad, concave lower surface, shaped to sit on the dome of the diaphragm. The opposite end is the narrow apex, which rises above the clavicle. The heart uses the same two words the other way around, with its apex pointing down and its base at the top.
notes: The cardiac notch is the indentation on the anterior border of the left lung that makes room for the heart. It is not the surface on the diaphragm.
Correct. The base is the broad inferior surface resting on the diaphragm.
The hilum is the indentation on the medial surface where the bronchus and vessels enter and leave. Pick it for a question about the entry point of the root of the lung.
The apex is the narrow superior tip of the lung, above the clavicle. Pick it for a question about the top of the lung.
questions.answerText: The base of the lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory passage has walls lined entirely with alveoli?
options: A respiratory bronchiole
A terminal bronchiole
A segmental bronchus
An alveolar duct
questions.why: Alveolar ducts come after the respiratory bronchioles in the respiratory zone. Their walls are made entirely of alveoli opening one after another, and they lead into the alveolar sacs. Moving from respiratory bronchiole to alveolar duct, the number of alveoli increases from a few to complete coverage.
notes: A respiratory bronchiole has only a few alveoli budding from its walls. Pick it if the airway showed scattered alveoli rather than complete coverage.
A terminal bronchiole has no alveoli at all and is the last conducting airway. Pick it for the airway just before gas exchange begins.
A segmental bronchus is a tertiary bronchus with cartilage in its wall and no alveoli. It belongs to the conducting zone, well above the alveolar ducts.
Correct. An alveolar duct is lined entirely with alveoli.
questions.answerText: An alveolar duct

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which thin, sealed, fluid-filled space between two membranes lets the lung glide as it expands?
options: The pleural cavity
The mediastinum
The alveolar sac
The hilum
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin space between the parietal pleura on the thoracic wall and the visceral pleura on the lung. It holds only a film of serous fluid, which lets the two layers slide smoothly as the lung expands and recoils. Because it is sealed, letting air in causes the lung to collapse.
notes: Correct. The pleural cavity is the thin fluid-filled space that lets the lung glide.
The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thorax between the lungs, holding the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus. It is not the space around each lung.
An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli that holds air for gas exchange. It is inside the lung, not between two membranes.
The hilum is the indentation on the medial lung surface where the bronchus and vessels enter. It is a region of the lung, not a fluid-filled space.
questions.answerText: The pleural cavity

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which cell type is thin and flat and forms most of the alveolar wall, where gases cross?
options: Type I alveolar cells
Alveolar macrophages
Type II alveolar cells
Goblet cells
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are simple squamous cells, meaning thin and flat. They cover most of the alveolar surface and form the air side of the respiratory membrane. Their thinness gives gases a very short distance to cross between alveolar air and the blood in the capillaries.
notes: Correct. Type I alveolar cells form most of the alveolar wall.
Alveolar macrophages, or dust cells, wander over the alveolar surface and engulf debris. Pick them for a question about cleaning the alveoli.
Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant. Pick them for a question about the cells that keep alveoli from collapsing.
Goblet cells secrete mucus in the respiratory mucosa of the airways, not in the alveolar wall. Pick them for a question about where airway mucus comes from.
questions.answerText: Type I alveolar cells

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structure is the internal ridge where the trachea forks into the two main bronchi?
options: The laryngeal prominence
The carina
The hilum
The glottis
questions.why: The carina is a ridge of cartilage inside the lower end of the trachea, at the point where it splits into the right and left main bronchi. Its lining is very sensitive, so anything touching it triggers strong coughing. It marks the end of the trachea and the start of the bronchi.
notes: The laryngeal prominence is the Adam's apple, formed by the thyroid cartilage. It is an external landmark on the larynx, not an internal ridge in the trachea.
Correct. The carina is the ridge where the trachea forks.
The hilum is the indentation on the medial lung surface where the main bronchus enters the lung. It is where the bronchus enters, not where the trachea splits.
The glottis is the vocal folds and the opening between them, in the larynx above the trachea. Pick it for a question about voice production.
questions.answerText: The carina

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which bronchus is a tertiary bronchus supplying a single bronchopulmonary segment?
options: A main bronchus
A lobar bronchus
A segmental bronchus
A terminal bronchiole
questions.why: The bronchial tree branches in order: main (primary) bronchi to each lung, lobar (secondary) bronchi to each lobe, and segmental (tertiary) bronchi to each bronchopulmonary segment. A bronchopulmonary segment is a smaller section of a lobe with its own airway and blood supply. The segmental bronchi then branch further into bronchioles.
notes: A main bronchus is a primary bronchus that supplies a whole lung. Pick it for a question about the first branch after the carina.
A lobar bronchus is a secondary bronchus that supplies one lobe. Pick it for a question about one lobe.
Correct. A segmental bronchus is a tertiary bronchus that supplies one bronchopulmonary segment.
A terminal bronchiole is the last conducting airway, far smaller than a bronchus and without cartilage. Pick it for the airway just before the respiratory zone.
questions.answerText: A segmental bronchus

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory disorder is the destruction of the alveolar walls, reducing the surface available for gas exchange?
options: Pneumothorax
Asthma
Emphysema
Lung cancer
questions.why: In emphysema the walls between alveoli break down, and many small sacs merge into a few large ones. Large sacs have far less total surface than many small ones, so the area available for gas exchange shrinks. The change is structural and permanent.
notes: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that collapses the lung. Pick it for a question about a puncture that breaks the pleural seal.
Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, causing wheezing. The alveolar walls stay intact.
Correct. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and reduces the gas exchange surface.
Lung cancer is a malignant tumor of the lung tissue, strongly linked to smoking. Pick it for a question about a tumor rather than a breakdown of alveolar walls.
questions.answerText: Emphysema

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory disorder is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid?
options: Asthma
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
Emphysema
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection of the lung in which the alveoli become inflamed and fill with fluid. Fluid-filled alveoli cannot hold air, so less surface is available for gas exchange. Unlike emphysema, the alveolar walls are not destroyed.
notes: Asthma narrows the bronchioles, not the alveoli. Pick it for a question about wheezing from small airway narrowing.
Correct. Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, outside the lung. Pick it for a question about a collapsed lung after a chest wound.
Emphysema destroys the alveolar walls rather than filling the alveoli with fluid. Pick it for a question about permanent loss of alveolar surface.
questions.answerText: Pneumonia

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which thin barrier lies between the alveolar air and the blood, and is the structure that gases cross?
options: The bronchiole wall
The respiratory membrane
The parietal pleura
The visceral pleura
questions.why: The respiratory membrane is the extremely thin barrier between alveolar air and the blood in a pulmonary capillary. It is made of the alveolar epithelium, the fused basement membranes, and the capillary endothelium. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross it during gas exchange.
notes: The bronchiole wall has smooth muscle and no cartilage, and it is far too thick for gases to cross, so it only carries air. Pick it for a question about the airways narrowed in asthma.
Correct. The respiratory membrane is the barrier that gases cross between air and blood.
The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall. Pick it for a question about the outer layer of the pleural membranes.
The visceral pleura covers the outside of the whole lung. It faces the pleural cavity, not the air inside the alveoli.
questions.answerText: The respiratory membrane

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: How does the right main bronchus differ in shape from the left main bronchus?
options: It is narrower and more horizontal
It has no cartilage, like a bronchiole
It is wider and more vertical
It is held open by complete cartilage rings
questions.why: The right main bronchus is wider and runs more vertically than the left, which is narrower and angles out more horizontally to pass under the aortic arch. This shape makes the right main bronchus the more direct continuation of the trachea. That is why inhaled objects most often lodge in the right lung.
notes: Narrower and more horizontal describes the left main bronchus, the mirror image of the correct answer. Pick it if the question asked about the left side.
Both main bronchi contain cartilage. Losing all cartilage happens much farther down the tree, at the bronchioles.
Correct. The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.
The cricoid cartilage is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway. The main bronchi are supported by incomplete cartilage, so this is not what sets the right side apart.
questions.answerText: It is wider and more vertical

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory disorder is a long-term blockage of airflow that includes both emphysema and chronic bronchitis?
options: COPD
Asthma
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
questions.why: COPD stands for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is a long-term blockage of airflow that groups together emphysema and chronic bronchitis, and it affects both the airways and the alveoli. Chronic means long-lasting and obstructive means airflow is blocked.
notes: Correct. COPD includes both emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
Asthma narrows the bronchioles and causes wheezing, but it is a separate disorder from the COPD group. Pick it for a question about inflammation of the small airways.
Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid. It is usually a short-term illness rather than a long-term blockage.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that collapses the lung. Pick it for a question about a punctured chest wall.
questions.answerText: COPD

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders the airways a breath passes through after the larynx?
options: Main bronchi, trachea, segmental bronchi, lobar bronchi
Trachea, lobar bronchi, main bronchi, segmental bronchi
Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi
Trachea, segmental bronchi, lobar bronchi, main bronchi
questions.why: Below the larynx, air enters the trachea, which forks at the carina into the main (primary) bronchi, one per lung. Each main bronchus splits into lobar (secondary) bronchi, one per lobe, and each lobar bronchus splits into segmental (tertiary) bronchi, one per bronchopulmonary segment. The airways get narrower and more numerous at each step.
notes: The trachea comes before the main bronchi, since the main bronchi are formed by the trachea splitting. This order also puts segmental before lobar, which reverses that step.
This swaps the main and lobar bronchi. The trachea forks into the main bronchi first, and only then do they divide into lobar bronchi.
Correct. Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, then segmental bronchi.
This keeps the trachea first but then lists the bronchi from smallest to largest. The branches get smaller at every division after the trachea, so the main bronchi must come next.
questions.answerText: Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders the deepest airways as a breath reaches gas exchange?
options: Alveolar duct, terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolus
Respiratory bronchiole, terminal bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolus
Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolus
Terminal bronchiole, alveolar duct, respiratory bronchiole, alveolus
questions.why: The terminal bronchiole is the last airway of the conducting zone. Next comes the respiratory bronchiole, with a few alveoli budding from its walls, followed by the alveolar duct, lined entirely with alveoli. The duct ends in alveolar sacs made of individual alveoli, where gas exchange happens.
notes: The alveolar duct is in the respiratory zone, so it cannot come before the terminal bronchiole, which is still in the conducting zone.
This swaps the two bronchioles. The terminal bronchiole has no alveoli and comes first, before the respiratory bronchiole that begins the respiratory zone.
Correct. Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, then alveolus.
This puts the alveolar duct before the respiratory bronchiole. The number of alveoli increases along the path, so the airway with a few alveoli comes before the one lined entirely with them.
questions.answerText: Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolus

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which set of features correctly describes the left lung?
options: Three lobes, an oblique fissure only, and no notch
Two lobes, an oblique fissure only, and a cardiac notch
Three lobes, two fissures, and a cardiac notch
Two lobes, two fissures, and no notch
questions.why: The left lung is the smaller lung because the heart takes up room on the left. It has two lobes, superior and inferior, divided by a single oblique fissure. The cardiac notch on its anterior border makes room for the heart, and the lingula projects below that notch.
notes: Three lobes need two fissures to separate them, so this combination does not exist in either lung. The right lung has three lobes and two fissures.
Correct. The left lung has two lobes, one oblique fissure, and a cardiac notch.
Three lobes and two fissures describe the right lung, and the right lung has no cardiac notch. This set mixes features of both lungs.
Two lobes are right for the left lung, but it has only one fissure, and it does have a cardiac notch. The second fissure, the horizontal fissure, belongs to the right lung.
questions.answerText: Two lobes, an oblique fissure only, and a cardiac notch

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which set correctly names the last airway of the conducting zone, the first airway of the respiratory zone, and the tiny air sac where gas exchange happens?
options: Respiratory bronchiole, terminal bronchiole, alveolar sac
Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolus
Segmental bronchus, terminal bronchiole, alveolus
Bronchiole, terminal bronchiole, alveolar duct
questions.why: The terminal bronchiole has no alveoli and ends the conducting zone. The respiratory bronchiole has a few alveoli budding from its walls, so it begins the respiratory zone. The alveolus is the tiny air sac where gas exchange happens across the respiratory membrane.
notes: This swaps the two bronchioles. The respiratory bronchiole is the first respiratory zone airway, not the last conducting one.
Correct. Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, and alveolus mark the boundary and the endpoint.
The segmental bronchus is far above the end of the conducting zone, and the terminal bronchiole has no alveoli, so it does not start the respiratory zone.
The terminal bronchiole still belongs to the conducting zone, so it cannot be the first airway of the respiratory zone. The alveolar duct is also a passage, not the air sac where gases cross.
questions.answerText: Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolus

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structures make up the lower respiratory tract?
options: The nose, nasal cavity, and paranasal sinuses
The pharynx and the paranasal sinuses
The nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx
The larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs
questions.why: The lower respiratory tract starts at the larynx and continues down through the trachea and bronchi into the lungs. It includes both conducting airways and the alveoli of the respiratory zone. The location grouping (upper and lower tract) does not line up with the functional grouping (conducting and respiratory zones), which is why both are tested.
notes: The nose, nasal cavity, and paranasal sinuses are upper tract structures. Pick this set for a question about where air is first warmed and filtered.
The pharynx and paranasal sinuses both belong to the upper respiratory tract. Pick them for a question about the upper tract.
These are the three regions of the pharynx, which belongs to the upper tract. Pick this set for a question about how the pharynx is divided.
Correct. The larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs form the lower tract.
questions.answerText: The larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What holds the trachea permanently open?
options: Complete rings of hyaline cartilage
The trachealis muscle
Plates of elastic cartilage
C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage
questions.why: The trachea is held open by a stack of C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, so the airway never collapses. The open part of each C faces backward, toward the esophagus. That gap is closed by the trachealis muscle, a band of smooth muscle.
notes: The cricoid cartilage of the larynx is the only complete cartilage ring in the airway. Tracheal rings are open at the back, so they are C-shaped rather than complete.
The trachealis muscle is smooth muscle that closes the gap at the back of each C-shaped ring. It spans the gap but is not what holds the airway open.
Elastic cartilage forms the epiglottis, which must bend and spring back. The trachea uses rigid hyaline cartilage to stay open.
Correct. C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage keep the trachea open.
questions.answerText: C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structures pass through the hilum of a lung as part of the root of the lung?
options: The coronary arteries and the cardiac veins
The trachea and the aortic arch
The inferior vena cava and the thoracic duct
The main bronchus and the pulmonary vessels
questions.why: The hilum is the indentation on the medial surface of each lung. The bundle passing through it is the root of the lung: the main bronchus, the pulmonary artery, the pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, and lymphatics. These structures connect the lung to the trachea and heart in the mediastinum.
notes: The coronary arteries and cardiac veins supply and drain the heart wall. Pick them for a question about the blood supply of the heart.

The trachea and aortic arch stay in the mediastinum. The trachea divides into the main bronchi before reaching either lung, and the aortic arch curves over the left main bronchus without entering the lung.
The inferior vena cava returns blood from the lower body to the right atrium, and the thoracic duct runs up through the posterior thorax. Neither enters the lung.
Correct. The main bronchus and the pulmonary vessels form the root of the lung at the hilum.
questions.answerText: The main bronchus and the pulmonary vessels

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Where in the lungs does gas exchange take place?
options: In the trachea
In the alveoli
In the terminal bronchioles
In the main bronchi
questions.why: Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, the tiny air sacs at the ends of the airways. Their walls are thin type I cells wrapped in pulmonary capillaries, forming the respiratory membrane that oxygen and carbon dioxide cross. The lungs hold hundreds of millions of alveoli, giving a huge exchange surface.
notes: The trachea is a conducting airway held open by cartilage. Its walls are far too thick for gases to cross into the blood.
Correct. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli.
Terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone. They carry air to the respiratory zone but have no alveoli, so no gas exchange happens there.
The main bronchi carry air into each lung through the hilum. They are conducting airways, not exchange surfaces.
questions.answerText: In the alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which layers make up the respiratory membrane?
options: Type II cells, a surfactant film, and alveolar macrophages
Alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium
Ciliated epithelium, hyaline cartilage plates, and smooth muscle
Visceral pleura, pleural fluid, and parietal pleura
questions.why: The respiratory membrane is the thin barrier between the air in an alveolus and the blood in a pulmonary capillary. It has three layers: the alveolar epithelium (mostly type I cells), the fused basement membranes of the alveolus and capillary, and the capillary endothelium. Keeping it this thin gives gases a very short distance to cross.
notes: Type II cells, surfactant, and alveolar macrophages are all found in or on the alveolus, but they are not the layers that gases cross. Pick them for a question about what keeps alveoli open and clean.
Correct. The respiratory membrane is alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium.
Ciliated epithelium, hyaline cartilage, and smooth muscle describe the wall of a bronchus. Pick this set for a question about the layers of a large conducting airway.
The visceral pleura, pleural fluid, and parietal pleura make up the pleural membranes around the lung. Pick this set for a question about the layers a surgeon meets around the lung.
questions.answerText: Alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Where is the carina located?
options: At the upper end of the trachea, just below the cricoid cartilage
At the hilum of each lung, where the bronchus enters
At the lower end of the trachea, where it forks into the main bronchi
Inside the larynx, between the true vocal folds
questions.why: The carina is an internal ridge at the inferior end of the trachea, inside the thorax. It marks the exact point where the trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi. The lining over the carina is very sensitive, so contact there sets off coughing.
notes: The upper end of the trachea, just below the cricoid cartilage, is where the trachea begins. Students mix the two ends up, but the carina is at the bottom where the trachea forks.
The hilum is the indentation on each lung where the main bronchus enters. The carina is in the mediastinum before the bronchi reach either lung.
Correct. The carina is at the lower end of the trachea, where it splits.
The space between the true vocal folds is part of the glottis in the larynx. Pick the glottis for a question about the opening between the vocal folds.
questions.answerText: At the lower end of the trachea, where it forks into the main bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: After the main bronchi, which airways branch next, one to each lobe of a lung?
options: The terminal bronchioles
The segmental bronchi
The alveolar ducts
The lobar bronchi
questions.why: Each main bronchus divides into lobar (secondary) bronchi, one for each lobe. The right main bronchus gives off three lobar bronchi for its three lobes, and the left gives off two. The lobar bronchi then divide into segmental bronchi.
notes: Terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways, many divisions below the main bronchi. Pick them for the airway just before the respiratory zone.
The segmental bronchi are tertiary bronchi that branch from the lobar bronchi, one to each bronchopulmonary segment. They come one step later.
Alveolar ducts are respiratory zone passages lined with alveoli, near the very end of the tree. Pick them for the airway after the respiratory bronchiole.
Correct. The lobar bronchi come next, one to each lobe.
questions.answerText: The lobar bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe lies just below the cardiac notch?
options: The lingula
The apex
The hilum
The middle lobe
questions.why: The lingula is a small, tongue-shaped extension of the left superior lobe, just below the cardiac notch. Its name means little tongue. It sits in roughly the same position on the left that the middle lobe occupies on the right, but it is part of the superior lobe rather than a separate lobe.
notes: Correct. The lingula is the tongue-shaped part of the left superior lobe.
The apex is the narrow superior tip of the lung, above the clavicle. Pick it for a question about the top of the lung.
The hilum is the indentation on the medial surface where the bronchus and vessels enter. Pick it for a question about the root of the lung.
The middle lobe belongs only to the right lung, between its horizontal and oblique fissures. The left lung has no middle lobe.
questions.answerText: The lingula

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A terminal bronchiole and a respiratory bronchiole sit next to each other in the bronchial tree. Which feature is found in the respiratory bronchiole but not the terminal bronchiole?
options: Plates of hyaline cartilage
C-shaped cartilage rings
A lining of stratified squamous epithelium
Alveoli budding from its walls
questions.why: The terminal bronchiole is the last conducting airway and has no alveoli. The respiratory bronchiole that follows has a few alveoli budding from its walls, so a little gas exchange happens there, and that is why it begins the respiratory zone. Neither airway has cartilage.
notes: Plates of hyaline cartilage support the bronchi inside the lung. Cartilage is gone by the bronchiole level, so neither of these airways has it.
C-shaped cartilage rings are found in the trachea. Bronchioles of every kind have no cartilage.
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, where food causes friction. Bronchioles are lined by much thinner epithelium.
Correct. A few alveoli bud from the walls of a respiratory bronchiole.
questions.answerText: Alveoli budding from its walls

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: As the bronchial tree branches into smaller and smaller airways, how do cartilage and smooth muscle change?
options: Cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases
Both cartilage and smooth muscle increase
Cartilage increases and smooth muscle decreases
Both stay the same at every level
questions.why: The large airways need cartilage to stay open, so the trachea has C-shaped rings and the bronchi have plates. As the airways get smaller, the cartilage fades out and smooth muscle takes over.
