By the bronchioles there is no cartilage at all, so when their smooth muscle contracts they narrow a great deal, while cartilage keeps the larger bronchi open.
notes: Correct. Cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases down the tree.
Cartilage does not increase as airways shrink. By the bronchioles it has disappeared completely.
This is the reverse of the real pattern. The trachea has the most cartilage, and the bronchioles have none.

The airway wall changes a lot along the tree, from cartilage rings in the trachea to no cartilage in the bronchioles. If the wall stayed the same, the bronchioles would have cartilage holding them open and could not narrow so much in asthma.
questions.answerText: Cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What normally fills the pleural cavity?
options: A thin film of serous pleural fluid
Lymph draining from the lung
Blood from the pulmonary capillaries
Air drawn in with each breath
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin, sealed space between the parietal and visceral pleurae. It holds only a thin film of serous fluid, which lets the two layers glide smoothly as the lung expands. Anything else in this space, such as air or blood, breaks the seal and can collapse the lung.
notes: Correct. A thin film of serous fluid fills the pleural cavity.
Lymph from the lung drains through lymphatic vessels to nodes at the hilum and in the mediastinum. It travels inside vessels, not loose in the pleural cavity.
Blood from the pulmonary capillaries stays inside vessels and returns through the pulmonary veins. Blood in the pleural cavity would be a sign of injury.
Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax, which makes the lung collapse. Inhaled air belongs inside the airways and alveoli, not between the pleurae.
questions.answerText: A thin film of serous pleural fluid

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structures does emphysema destroy?
options: The alveolar walls
The bronchiole walls
The pleural membranes
The tracheal cartilage
questions.why: Emphysema destroys the walls of the alveoli. As the walls break down, many small alveoli merge into a few large spaces, and the total surface for gas exchange drops. Emphysema is one of the two conditions grouped under COPD.
notes: Correct. Emphysema destroys the alveolar walls.
The bronchioles are the target of asthma, which inflames and narrows them. Pick the bronchioles for a question about asthma.
The pleural membranes are involved in a pneumothorax, when air enters the space between them. Emphysema damages the lung tissue itself.
The tracheal cartilage is not damaged in emphysema. Pick the trachea for a question about the C-shaped rings that hold the windpipe open.
questions.answerText: The alveolar walls

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: During an asthma attack, the bronchioles narrow but the trachea and main bronchi stay open. Which structural difference explains this?
options: The trachea and main bronchi have no smooth muscle at all
Bronchioles have complete cartilage rings that squeeze shut
Bronchioles lack cartilage, while larger airways are held open by it
The main bronchi are lined with alveoli that hold them open
questions.why: Asthma inflames and narrows the airways, and the narrowing is worst in the bronchioles. A bronchiole has no cartilage, and smooth muscle makes up much of its wall, so when that muscle tightens and the lining swells, nothing holds the airway open. The trachea and bronchi have cartilage rings and plates that keep them open even when their walls are irritated.
notes: The trachea does have smooth muscle, the trachealis, across the back of its C-shaped rings. What keeps it open is the cartilage, not a lack of muscle.
Bronchioles have no cartilage at all. The only complete cartilage ring in the airway is the cricoid cartilage of the larynx.
Correct. Without cartilage, bronchioles can narrow, while cartilage keeps larger airways open.
The main bronchi are conducting airways with no alveoli. Alveoli first appear in the respiratory bronchioles.
questions.answerText: Bronchioles lack cartilage, while larger airways are held open by it

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A child inhales a small bead that slips past the epiglottis into the lower airway. Which lung does it most often land in, and why?
options: The left lung, because the left main bronchus is wider and more vertical
The left lung, because it has only two lobes
The right lung, because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical
The right lung, because it has a cardiac notch that traps objects
questions.why: The right main bronchus is wider and runs more vertically than the left, so it lines up more directly with the trachea. An inhaled object falling down the trachea tends to follow this straighter path. That is why aspirated objects most often lodge in the right lung.
notes: This assigns the right bronchus's shape to the left. The left main bronchus is narrower and more horizontal, which makes objects less likely to enter it.
The number of lobes does not decide where an object lands. The angle and width of the main bronchus does.
Correct. The wider, more vertical right main bronchus lines up with the trachea.
The cardiac notch is on the left lung, not the right. It makes room for the heart and does not trap inhaled objects.
questions.answerText: The right lung, because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A stab wound punctures the chest wall, and the lung on that side collapses. Into which space has air entered?
options: The alveoli
The mediastinum
The pericardial cavity
The pleural cavity
questions.why: The pleural cavity is a sealed space between the parietal and visceral pleurae that normally holds only a thin film of fluid. A wound through the chest wall lets air into this space, breaking the seal, and the lung collapses. This is called a pneumothorax.
notes: Air belongs in the alveoli, and air there does not collapse the lung. The problem in a pneumothorax is air outside the lung.
The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thorax holding the heart, trachea, and esophagus. Pick it for a question about the space between the two lungs.
The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart. Air or fluid there would press on the heart, not collapse a lung.
Correct. Air in the pleural cavity breaks the seal and collapses the lung.
questions.answerText: The pleural cavity

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: An infection inflames the air sacs of the lung and fills them with fluid. Which structure is affected, and which disorder is this?
options: The trachea, in COPD
The bronchioles, in asthma
The pleural cavity, in pneumothorax
The alveoli, in pneumonia
questions.why: The air sacs of the lung are the alveoli. In pneumonia, an infection inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid, so they cannot hold air for gas exchange. Naming both the structure and the disorder links the problem to the exact place it happens.
notes: COPD involves the airways and alveoli and includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis. It is a long-term blockage, not an infection of the trachea.
Asthma inflames and narrows the bronchioles, the small airways, not the air sacs. It causes wheezing rather than fluid-filled alveoli.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that collapses the lung. It is not an infection of the air sacs.
Correct. Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid.
questions.answerText: The alveoli, in pneumonia

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In emphysema, many small alveoli merge into a few large ones. Which structural feature of the lung is lost?
options: The seal of the pleural cavity
The C-shaped tracheal rings
The large surface area for gas exchange
The cartilage of the bronchi
questions.why: Many tiny alveoli together have far more wall surface than a few large sacs holding the same volume. When emphysema destroys the walls between alveoli, the small sacs merge and much of that surface disappears. Less surface means less area where gases can cross, and the change is permanent.
notes: Losing the pleural seal is a pneumothorax, caused by air entering the pleural cavity. Emphysema damages the alveoli, not the pleura.
The tracheal rings are cartilage in the windpipe and are not affected by emphysema. Pick them for a question about what holds the trachea open.
Correct. Merging alveoli lose much of the surface area for gas exchange.
Bronchial cartilage is in the larger airways, not the alveoli. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, which have no cartilage.
questions.answerText: The large surface area for gas exchange

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which two conditions are grouped together under COPD?
options: Asthma and pneumonia
Asthma and pneumothorax
Pneumothorax and lung cancer
Emphysema and chronic bronchitis
questions.why: COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is a long-term blockage of airflow. It groups emphysema, which destroys alveolar walls, with chronic bronchitis, a long-lasting inflammation of the bronchi. Together they affect both the airways and the alveoli.
notes: Asthma narrows the bronchi and bronchioles, and pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid. Both are lung disorders, but this pair is not what COPD groups together.
Asthma and pneumothorax affect the bronchioles and the pleural cavity. Asthma also blocks airflow, which may cause the mix-up, but it is classified separately from COPD.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity and lung cancer is a malignant tumor. Neither is a long-term blockage of airflow grouped under COPD.
Correct. COPD includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
questions.answerText: Emphysema and chronic bronchitis

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A patient is told a malignant tumor has formed in the tissue of the lung. Which disorder does this describe?
options: Lung cancer
Asthma
Pneumonia
Emphysema
questions.why: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor in the lung tissue. It usually starts in the epithelium lining the airways or alveoli, and it is strongly linked to smoking. Unlike the other choices here, it is defined by abnormal tissue growth rather than by destroyed walls, fluid in the air sacs, or narrowed airways.
notes: Correct. A malignant tumor of the lung is lung cancer.
Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles. Pick it for a question about wheezing from the small airways.
Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid. Pick it for a question about inflamed, fluid-filled air sacs.
Emphysema destroys the alveolar walls but does not form a tumor. Pick it for a question about lost surface area for gas exchange.
questions.answerText: Lung cancer

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The lungs hold hundreds of millions of tiny alveoli, each wrapped in capillaries. Why does this design suit gas exchange?
options: Each alveolus has its own cartilage ring that keeps the lungs from collapsing
Together the tiny sacs create a huge, thin surface in close contact with the blood
The tiny sacs keep blood far from the air to protect the lung
Each alveolus connects directly to its own main bronchus so air arrives faster
questions.why: Dividing the lung into hundreds of millions of tiny sacs gives it an enormous total wall surface. Each alveolus is wrapped in pulmonary capillaries, and the wall between air and blood is extremely thin. A huge surface plus a short distance is what allows oxygen and carbon dioxide to cross quickly.
notes: Alveoli have no cartilage. Their walls are thin type I cells, and surfactant from type II cells is what helps keep them from collapsing.
Correct. Many tiny alveoli give a huge, thin surface next to the blood.
The design does the opposite, bringing blood as close to the air as possible. The respiratory membrane is extremely thin so gases can cross easily.
There are only two main bronchi, one for each lung. Air reaches the alveoli through many branching airways, not through a private bronchus for each sac.
questions.answerText: Together the tiny sacs create a huge, thin surface in close contact with the blood

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Type I alveolar cells are thin, flat, simple squamous cells. Why is this shape well suited to their job?
options: A thin wall gives gases a very short distance to cross between air and blood
A flat shape lets them contract and push air out of the alveolus
A thin wall lets them secrete surfactant more easily
A flat shape lets them wander over the alveolar surface and engulf dust
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells form most of the alveolar wall and the air side of the respiratory membrane. Because they are simple squamous, a single layer of flat cells, gases only have to cross a very thin barrier to move between alveolar air and capillary blood. A thicker wall would slow that crossing.
notes: Correct. Thin, flat cells keep the distance for gases short.
Alveolar cells do not contract. Air moves in and out because the diaphragm and chest wall change the size of the thoracic cavity and the lungs recoil, not because the alveolar wall squeezes.
Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells, which are cuboidal, not flat. Pick type II cells for a question about surfactant.
Wandering and engulfing debris is the job of alveolar macrophages, the dust cells. Pick them for a question about cleaning the alveoli.
questions.answerText: A thin wall gives gases a very short distance to cross between air and blood

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The C-shaped cartilage rings of the trachea are open at the back, where the trachea lies against the esophagus. Why is this arrangement useful?
options: The open back faces forward to make room for the thyroid cartilage
The open back lets air pass from the trachea into the esophagus
The esophagus can expand forward during swallowing while the airway stays open
The open back lets the trachea collapse fully during each exhalation
questions.why: The trachea sits directly in front of the esophagus. The back of each C-shaped ring is open and closed only by the trachealis, a band of smooth muscle, so the soft back wall can give way when a swallowed mass of food stretches the esophagus. The cartilage in front and on the sides still keeps the airway open.
notes: The open part of the C faces backward toward the esophagus, not forward. The thyroid cartilage is part of the larynx, above the trachea.
The trachea and esophagus are separate tubes, and the trachealis muscle closes the gap so air cannot cross between them. Air and food share only the pharynx.
Correct. The open back lets the esophagus expand while the cartilage keeps the airway open.
The cartilage rings exist to keep the trachea from collapsing. A trachea that collapsed with each breath would block airflow.
questions.answerText: The esophagus can expand forward during swallowing while the airway stays open

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The right lung has three lobes, while the left lung is smaller and has only two. Which explanation fits the anatomy of the thorax?
options: The heart sits toward the left and takes up that space
The liver pushes up under the left lung and takes its space
The stomach fills the lower part of the left thoracic cavity
The left main bronchus is too narrow to supply three lobes
questions.why: The heart sits in the mediastinum but tilts toward the left, with its apex pointing down and to the left. The left lung gives up room for it, which is why the left lung is smaller, has only two lobes, and carries a cardiac notch along its anterior border. The right lung has more room and three lobes.
notes: Correct. The heart takes up space on the left side of the thorax.
The liver lies mostly on the right, under the right dome of the diaphragm. This mirrors the real arrangement and would not explain a smaller left lung.
The stomach lies in the abdominal cavity, below the diaphragm. It does not sit in the thoracic cavity.
The number of lobar bronchi follows the number of lobes, not the other way around. A narrower bronchus does not determine lobe count.
questions.answerText: The heart sits toward the left and takes up that space

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Airways branch again and again, getting narrower and more numerous from the trachea to the bronchioles. Why does this branching pattern serve breathing well?
options: Repeated branching carries air to hundreds of millions of alveoli throughout both lungs
Branching lets each airway exchange gases along its full length
Each branch adds more cartilage, making the lungs stiffer
Branching keeps air in the conducting zone so it never reaches the alveoli
questions.why: The alveoli are spread through every part of both lungs, so air has to be delivered to all of them. The bronchial tree divides from the trachea into main, lobar, and segmental bronchi and then bronchioles, reaching every region of the lung. The more branches there are, the more alveoli can be reached.
notes: Correct. Branching delivers air to alveoli throughout both lungs.
The conducting airways have walls too thick for gas exchange. Exchange only happens in the respiratory zone, starting at the respiratory bronchioles.
Cartilage actually decreases as the airways branch and gets replaced by smooth muscle. The bronchioles have no cartilage.
The conducting zone's job is to lead air to the respiratory zone, not to keep it out. Air must reach the alveoli for gas exchange.
questions.answerText: Repeated branching carries air to hundreds of millions of alveoli throughout both lungs

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The airways are lined with ciliated epithelium and mucus-secreting goblet cells. How does this lining protect the delicate alveoli?
options: Cilia sweep particles down into the alveoli, where macrophages digest them
Goblet cells secrete surfactant that dissolves inhaled dust
Mucus traps inhaled particles and cilia sweep them up toward the pharynx
Cartilage in the lining filters particles out of the air
questions.why: The conducting airways are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. The goblet cells secrete sticky mucus that traps dust and microbes, and the cilia beat to move the mucus up toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed. This keeps most particles from ever reaching the thin-walled alveoli.
notes: This reverses the direction the cilia beat. They move mucus up and out, away from the alveoli, so fewer particles reach them.
Surfactant comes from type II alveolar cells and keeps alveoli from collapsing. Goblet cells secrete mucus, not surfactant.
Correct. Mucus traps particles and cilia move them up toward the pharynx.
Cartilage supports the wall of the larger airways but sits beneath the lining, not in it. It holds the airway open but does not filter air.
questions.answerText: Mucus traps inhaled particles and cilia sweep them up toward the pharynx

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: When the diaphragm contracts, it flattens and air flows into the lungs. Why does this contraction cause inhalation?
options: It enlarges the thoracic cavity, so the lungs expand and air flows in
Contracting the diaphragm squeezes the lungs, forcing air inward
The diaphragm blows air into the lungs the way a bellows does
Contracting the diaphragm opens the glottis, which pulls air down
questions.why: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped skeletal muscle forming the floor of the thoracic cavity, and the base of each lung rests on it. When it contracts, the dome flattens and moves down, making the thoracic cavity taller. The lungs, held against the chest wall by the pleurae, expand with it, and air flows in to fill the larger space.
notes: Correct. A flatter diaphragm enlarges the thoracic cavity, so the lungs expand and fill with air.
Squeezing the lungs would push air out, not in. That is closer to what happens when the diaphragm relaxes and the cavity gets smaller.
The diaphragm is not connected to the airways and does not push air. It changes the size of the thoracic cavity, and air flows in on its own.
The glottis opens and closes with the vocal folds in the larynx, controlled by the arytenoid cartilages. The diaphragm is far below in the thorax and does not move the glottis.
questions.answerText: It enlarges the thoracic cavity, so the lungs expand and air flows in

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which cells, sometimes called dust cells, patrol the alveolar surface and engulf debris?
options: Type II alveolar cells
Goblet cells
Type I alveolar cells
Alveolar macrophages
questions.why: Alveolar macrophages are wandering immune cells on the inner surface of the alveoli. They engulf dust, microbes, and other debris that got past the mucus and cilia of the conducting airways. Their nickname, dust cells, comes from this cleanup job.
notes: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant to keep the alveoli from collapsing. Pick them for a question about surfactant.
Goblet cells secrete mucus in the lining of the conducting airways, where the mucus traps particles. They are not found on the alveolar surface.
Type I alveolar cells are thin, flat cells that form most of the alveolar wall, where gases cross. They stay in place and do not engulf debris.
Correct. Alveolar macrophages are the dust cells that engulf debris.
questions.answerText: Alveolar macrophages

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which lobe is found only in the right lung?
options: The lingula
The superior lobe
The middle lobe
The inferior lobe
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior), while the left lung has only superior and inferior lobes. The middle lobe is set off by the horizontal fissure above and the oblique fissure below. The left lung has the lingula in a similar position, but the lingula is part of its superior lobe.
notes: The lingula is the tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe, not a lobe of its own. It belongs to the left lung, not the right.
Both lungs have a superior lobe, so it is not unique to the right lung.
Correct. Only the right lung has a middle lobe.
Both lungs have an inferior lobe, below the oblique fissure. It is shared by both sides.
questions.answerText: The middle lobe

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In this course's grouping, which structures make up the lower respiratory tract?
options: Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx
Larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs
Nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx
Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli only
questions.why: The lower respiratory tract begins at the larynx (voice box) and continues through the trachea, the branching bronchi, and the lungs themselves. It is a grouping by location, separating the airway in the neck and chest from the nose and throat above it. Notice that the lower tract includes both conducting airways and the gas-exchange structures inside the lungs.
notes: The nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx make up the upper respiratory tract. Pick this group if the question asked about the upper tract.
Correct. The larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs make up the lower respiratory tract.
The nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx are the three regions of the pharynx, which belongs to the upper tract. They would be the answer if the question asked for the parts of the throat.

Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli are the respiratory zone. They sit inside the lungs, so they are part of the lower tract, but they are only a small piece of it. Choose this if the question asked for the respiratory zone.
questions.answerText: Larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the carina?
options: The muscle that closes the back of each tracheal ring
The indentation on the medial lung where the bronchus enters
The only complete ring of cartilage in the airway
The internal ridge where the trachea forks into the bronchi
questions.why: The carina is a ridge of cartilage inside the lower end of the trachea, right where it splits into the right and left main bronchi. It marks the point where the single windpipe becomes two airways, one for each lung. On a model, you find it by looking down into the trachea at the fork.
notes: The muscle that closes the back of each C-shaped tracheal ring is the trachealis muscle. It would be the answer if the question asked what lies against the esophagus in the tracheal wall.
The indentation on the medial surface of a lung where the bronchus and vessels enter and leave is the hilum. Pick it if the question asked where the root of the lung attaches.
The only complete ring of cartilage in the airway is the cricoid cartilage at the bottom of the larynx. Choose it if the question asked which cartilage forms a full ring.
Correct. The carina is the internal ridge where the trachea forks into the main bronchi.
questions.answerText: The internal ridge where the trachea forks into the bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which bronchi are the primary bronchi, with one entering each lung?
options: The main bronchi
The lobar bronchi
The segmental bronchi
The terminal bronchioles
questions.why: The main bronchi, also called primary bronchi, are the first two branches of the trachea at the carina. One enters the right lung and one enters the left lung, each passing in at the hilum. The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left.
notes: Correct. The main bronchi are the primary bronchi, one entering each lung.
The lobar bronchi are the secondary bronchi, one to each lobe of a lung. They branch off the main bronchi, one step later. Pick them if the question asked which bronchi supply each lobe.
The segmental bronchi are the tertiary bronchi, one to each bronchopulmonary segment. They are two steps below the main bronchi. Choose them if the question asked about the third level of branching.
Terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone, deep inside the lung. They would be the answer if the question asked where the conducting zone ends.
questions.answerText: The main bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Lobar bronchi are also called secondary bronchi. What does each one supply?
options: One lobe of a lung
One alveolar sac
One bronchopulmonary segment
One whole lung
questions.why: Each main bronchus divides into lobar bronchi, the secondary bronchi, and each lobar bronchus serves one lobe. That means the right lung, with three lobes, has three lobar bronchi, and the left lung, with two lobes, has two. The name lobar is the clue, since it matches the lobe it supplies.
notes: Correct. Each lobar bronchus supplies one lobe of a lung.
An alveolar sac is fed by an alveolar duct deep in the respiratory zone. It would be the answer if the question asked what an alveolar duct leads into.
One bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a segmental (tertiary) bronchus, the next level down. Choose this if the question asked what the tertiary bronchi supply.
One whole lung is supplied by a main (primary) bronchus. Pick this if the question asked about the main bronchi.
questions.answerText: One lobe of a lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which bronchi are the tertiary bronchi, one to each bronchopulmonary segment?
options: The lobar bronchi
The respiratory bronchioles
The segmental bronchi
The main bronchi
questions.why: The segmental bronchi are the tertiary bronchi, the third level of branching in the bronchial tree. Each one supplies a bronchopulmonary segment, a wedge-shaped section of a lobe with its own airway and blood supply. They branch from the lobar bronchi and go on to divide into bronchioles.
notes: The lobar bronchi are the secondary bronchi, one to each lobe. They come just before the segmental bronchi. Choose them if the question asked which bronchi supply each lobe.

Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways of the respiratory zone, with a few alveoli budding from their walls. They would be the answer if the question asked where gas exchange first becomes possible.
Correct. The segmental bronchi are the tertiary bronchi.
The main bronchi are the primary bronchi, one entering each lung. Pick them if the question asked for the first branches of the trachea.
questions.answerText: The segmental bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which airways are the smallest conducting airways, with smooth muscle in their walls and no cartilage?
options: The bronchioles
The alveolar ducts
The segmental bronchi
The lobar bronchi
questions.why: Bronchioles are the small airways that branch from the segmental bronchi. As the bronchial tree gets smaller, cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases, and the bronchioles are where the cartilage disappears. With smooth muscle and no cartilage, bronchioles can change their diameter, which is why they can constrict.
notes: Correct. Bronchioles are the smallest conducting airways, with smooth muscle and no cartilage.
Alveolar ducts are respiratory zone passages whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli. They do not just conduct air. Choose them if the question asked for passages lined with alveoli.
The segmental bronchi still have cartilage plates in their walls. They are one level above the bronchioles. Pick them if the question asked for the tertiary bronchi.
The lobar bronchi are large secondary bronchi supported by cartilage. They would be the answer if the question asked which bronchi supply each lobe.
questions.answerText: The bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which airways are the last airways of the conducting zone, just before gas exchange begins?
options: The segmental bronchi
The terminal bronchioles
The respiratory bronchioles
The alveolar ducts
questions.why: Terminal means end, and the terminal bronchioles are the end of the conducting zone. Air in them is still only being carried, not exchanged. The very next airways, the respiratory bronchioles, have alveoli budding from their walls and begin the respiratory zone.
notes: The segmental bronchi are much higher in the tree, the tertiary bronchi that supply bronchopulmonary segments. Choose them if the question asked about the third level of branching.
Correct. The terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways.
The respiratory bronchioles come right after the terminal bronchioles and are the first airways of the respiratory zone. Pick them if the question asked where gas exchange first begins.
Alveolar ducts are in the respiratory zone, with walls lined entirely by alveoli. They would be the answer if the question asked which passages lead into the alveolar sacs.
questions.answerText: The terminal bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which airways are the first airways of the respiratory zone, with a few alveoli budding from their walls?
options: The terminal bronchioles
The respiratory bronchioles
The alveolar sacs
The alveolar ducts
questions.why: Respiratory bronchioles branch from the terminal bronchioles and are the first airways where gas exchange can occur. Scattered alveoli bud out from their walls, so they are partly airway and partly exchange surface. Further along, the alveolar ducts are lined completely with alveoli.
notes: The terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone, just before the respiratory bronchioles. They have no alveoli. Pick them if the question asked where the conducting zone ends.
Correct. Respiratory bronchioles are the first respiratory zone airways, with a few alveoli on their walls.
Alveolar sacs are clusters of alveoli sharing a common space at the very end of the airway. They would be the answer if the question asked what an alveolar duct opens into.

Alveolar ducts come after the respiratory bronchioles, and their walls are lined entirely with alveoli rather than having just a few. Choose them if the question asked for passages fully lined with alveoli.
questions.answerText: The respiratory bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces air from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles?
options: Trachea, carina, lobar bronchi, main bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Trachea, carina, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Trachea, carina, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, terminal bronchioles, bronchioles
Trachea, carina, main bronchi, segmental bronchi, lobar bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
questions.why: The bronchial tree branches from largest to smallest. The trachea forks at the carina into the main (primary) bronchi, one per lung, which divide into lobar (secondary) bronchi, one per lobe, and then segmental (tertiary) bronchi, one per segment. These branch into bronchioles, and the last of the bronchioles are the terminal bronchioles.
notes: This sequence puts the lobar bronchi before the main bronchi. The main bronchi come first because there is one per lung, and each then splits into lobar bronchi, one per lobe.
Correct. Air passes from the trachea through the carina, main, lobar, and segmental bronchi, then bronchioles and terminal bronchioles.
This sequence puts terminal bronchioles before ordinary bronchioles. Terminal means end, so the terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways, after the other bronchioles.
This sequence swaps the lobar and segmental bronchi. Remember primary, secondary, tertiary: main, lobar, segmental. A lobe is bigger than a segment, so the lobar branch comes first.
questions.answerText: Trachea, carina, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Bronchioles have smooth muscle in their walls but no cartilage. What does that structure allow them to do?
options: Exchange gases directly with the capillary blood
Secrete surfactant into the airway
Change their diameter to regulate airflow
Stay rigidly open no matter what
questions.why: As the bronchial tree branches, cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases, and at the bronchioles the cartilage is gone. Without stiff cartilage holding them open, the smooth muscle can contract to narrow the bronchioles or relax to widen them. This lets them regulate airflow, and it is also why bronchioles can constrict too much, as in asthma.
notes: Bronchioles are still conducting airways and are too thick-walled for gas exchange. Exchange begins at the respiratory bronchioles and alveoli. Pick gas exchange if the question asked about the alveoli.
Surfactant is secreted by Type II alveolar cells, not by bronchiole smooth muscle. It would be the answer if the question asked what keeps alveoli from collapsing.
Correct. Smooth muscle without cartilage lets bronchioles change diameter and regulate airflow.

Staying rigidly open is what cartilage does, as in the trachea and bronchi. Bronchioles lack cartilage, so this is the opposite of their design. Choose it if the question asked why the trachea does not collapse.
questions.answerText: Change their diameter to regulate airflow

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces air from a terminal bronchiole to the alveoli?
options: Terminal bronchiole, alveolar duct, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar sac
Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolar sac
Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar sac, alveolar duct
Respiratory bronchiole, terminal bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolar sac
questions.why: The terminal bronchiole is the last conducting airway. It leads into a respiratory bronchiole, the first respiratory zone airway with a few alveoli on its walls. That opens into an alveolar duct, lined entirely with alveoli, which ends in an alveolar sac, a cluster of alveoli sharing a common space.
notes: This sequence puts the alveolar duct before the respiratory bronchiole. The respiratory bronchiole has only a few alveoli, so it comes first, and the duct, lined completely with alveoli, comes after it.
Correct. Air goes from the terminal bronchiole to the respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, and alveolar sac.
This sequence puts the alveolar sac before the alveolar duct. The duct is a passage that leads into the sac, so the sac is the dead end at the finish of the path.
This sequence starts with the respiratory bronchiole. The terminal bronchiole is the end of the conducting zone, so air reaches it before the respiratory bronchiole, not after.
questions.answerText: Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolar sac

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A child inhales a small bead, and an X-ray shows it lodged in the right lung. Which feature of the airway best explains why it went right?
options: The left main bronchus has no cartilage
The right lung has three lobes and the left has two
The left lung has a cardiac notch for the heart
The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical
questions.why: At the carina the trachea splits into the two main bronchi, and they are not mirror images. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, nearly in line with the trachea, while the left is narrower and angles off more sharply. An inhaled object falling down the trachea follows the straighter, wider path, so it most often lands in the right lung.
notes: Both main bronchi are supported by cartilage, which is lost only at the level of the bronchioles. This choice describes a bronchiole, so pick a cartilage-free wall if the question asked which airways can constrict in asthma.

The right lung does have three lobes, but the number of lobes does not steer an object entering the airway. The object is directed at the carina, before any lobes are reached. Pick this if the question compared the lobes of the two lungs.

The left lung does have a cardiac notch for the heart, but the notch is on the lung, past the point where the object chose a side at the carina. The shape of the right main bronchus is the explanation. Choose the cardiac notch if the question asked why the left lung is smaller.
Correct. The wider, more vertical right main bronchus directs inhaled objects into the right lung.
questions.answerText: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: During an asthma attack the bronchioles constrict. Which statement best describes where the problem is and how it affects the alveoli?
options: The narrowing is in the pleural cavity, so the lung collapses
The narrowing is in the conducting zone, so less air reaches the alveoli
The narrowing is in the larynx, so air stops before the trachea
The narrowing is in the respiratory zone, so the alveolar walls are destroyed
questions.why: Bronchioles are conducting airways, with smooth muscle and no cartilage, so they can constrict. When they narrow, air has a harder time moving through them, and less of it reaches the alveoli in the respiratory zone downstream. The alveoli themselves are not damaged, but they receive less fresh air while the bronchioles stay narrow.
notes: A problem in the pleural cavity that collapses the lung is a pneumothorax, caused by air entering that space. Choose this if the question described a chest puncture.
Correct. Constricted bronchioles are a conducting zone problem that reduces airflow to the alveoli.

The larynx is above the trachea and is not where asthma acts. Asthma is a disease of the small airways. This choice would fit only an obstruction high in the airway, such as a blocked laryngeal inlet.
Destruction of alveolar walls in the respiratory zone is emphysema, a permanent structural change. Pick this if the question described a permanent loss of exchange surface.
questions.answerText: The narrowing is in the conducting zone, so less air reaches the alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: How many lobes does the left lung have?
options: One lobe
Three lobes
Two lobes
Four lobes
questions.why: The left lung has two lobes, a superior lobe and an inferior lobe, separated by a single oblique fissure. It gives up space to the heart, which sits slightly to the left, and it is the smaller of the two lungs. The lingula is a tongue-shaped part of the left superior lobe, not a separate lobe.
notes: One lobe would mean the left lung had no fissure at all, but it has an oblique fissure dividing it in two. This is a guess from thinking the smaller lung must be undivided.
Three lobes is the right lung, with superior, middle, and inferior lobes. Pick three if the question asked about the right lung.
Correct. The left lung has two lobes, superior and inferior.
Neither lung has four lobes. Students sometimes count the lingula as an extra lobe, but it is part of the left superior lobe.
questions.answerText: Two lobes

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which fissures divide the right lung into its lobes?
options: A horizontal fissure only
Two oblique fissures, upper and lower
An oblique fissure only
Horizontal and oblique fissures
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes, so it needs two fissures to separate them. The horizontal fissure separates the superior lobe from the middle lobe, and the oblique fissure separates the middle lobe (and part of the superior lobe) from the inferior lobe. The left lung, with only two lobes, has just the oblique fissure.
notes: A horizontal fissure only would create just two lobes. The right lung needs a second fissure, the oblique fissure, to form its inferior lobe. This choice forgets the fissure the two lungs share.
The right lung has one oblique fissure, not two. Its second fissure runs horizontally, which is how the middle lobe is set apart. This is a made-up combination.
An oblique fissure only is the left lung, which has two lobes. Pick this if the question asked about the left lung.
Correct. The right lung has a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure.
questions.answerText: Horizontal and oblique fissures

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which fissure does the left lung have?
options: A cardiac fissure only
A horizontal fissure only
A horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure
An oblique fissure only
questions.why: The left lung has two lobes, superior and inferior, so it needs only one fissure between them, the oblique fissure. It has no horizontal fissure because it has no middle lobe. Where the right lung would have a middle lobe, the left lung instead has the cardiac notch and the lingula.
notes: There is no cardiac fissure. The left lung has a cardiac notch, an indentation for the heart, which is not a fissure between lobes. This choice confuses the notch with a fissure.
A horizontal fissure is found only in the right lung, where it separates the superior and middle lobes. Pick it if the question asked which fissure is unique to the right lung.
A horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure together belong to the right lung, which has three lobes. Choose this pair if the question asked about the right lung.
Correct. The left lung has only an oblique fissure.
questions.answerText: An oblique fissure only

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which lung is larger?
options: They are exactly equal
The right lung
The left lung
It varies with body position
questions.why: The right lung is the larger of the two. It has three lobes, while the left lung has two lobes and gives up room for the heart, which sits slightly to the left in the mediastinum. That missing space shows up as the cardiac notch on the left lung.
notes: The two lungs are not identical. The left lung gives up room for the heart, so the lungs differ in size and in number of lobes. This choice assumes the body is perfectly symmetrical.
Correct. The right lung is larger.
The left lung is the smaller one, with two lobes and a cardiac notch where the heart takes up space. Pick it if the question asked which lung has a cardiac notch.
Lung size is a fixed anatomical difference, not something that changes with posture. This choice is a guess that avoids committing to either side.
questions.answerText: The right lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the cardiac notch?
options: An indentation in the left lung for the heart
The tongue-shaped part of the left lung
The ridge where the trachea forks in two
The indentation on the medial lung where vessels enter
questions.why: The cardiac notch is an indentation along the anterior border of the left lung that makes room for the heart. Because the heart sits slightly to the left in the mediastinum, the left lung curves around it. This is one reason the left lung is smaller than the right.
notes: Correct. The cardiac notch is the indentation in the left lung that accommodates the heart.
The tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe is the lingula, which sits just below the cardiac notch. It would be the answer if the question asked for the part shaped like a tongue.
The ridge where the trachea forks into the main bronchi is the carina. Choose it if the question asked about the branching point of the trachea.
The indentation on the medial surface where the bronchus and vessels enter and leave is the hilum. Pick it if the question asked where the root of the lung attaches.
questions.answerText: An indentation in the left lung for the heart

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which part of a lung is the narrow superior tip that rises just above the clavicle?
options: The lingula
The apex
The base
The hilum
questions.why: The apex of a lung is its narrow, rounded top. It rises slightly above the clavicle into the root of the neck. The opposite end, the broad base, sits on the diaphragm.
notes: The lingula is the tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe, below the cardiac notch. It would be the answer if the question asked about the tongue-shaped part of the left lung.
Correct. The apex is the narrow superior tip that rises above the clavicle.
The base is the broad inferior surface of the lung that rests on the diaphragm, the opposite end from the apex. Pick it if the question asked which surface sits on the diaphragm.
The hilum is the indentation on the medial surface where the bronchus and vessels enter and leave. Choose it if the question asked where the root of the lung attaches.
questions.answerText: The apex

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What does the base of a lung rest on?
options: The heart
The clavicle
The sternum
The diaphragm
questions.why: The base of a lung is its broad inferior surface, and it rests on the dome of the diaphragm. The diaphragm is the muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. The opposite end of the lung, the apex, rises just above the clavicle.
notes: The heart sits medial to the lungs in the mediastinum and fits into the cardiac notch of the left lung. Choose it if the question asked what the cardiac notch accommodates.
The clavicle is the landmark for the apex, the narrow top of the lung that rises just above it. Pick the clavicle if the question asked about the apex.

The sternum is the breastbone at the front of the thoracic cage, anterior to the heart and the medial edges of the lungs. The lungs do not rest on it. It would be the answer if the question asked which bone the costal cartilages join in front.
Correct. The base of a lung rests on the diaphragm.
questions.answerText: The diaphragm

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which serous membrane lines the inside of the thoracic wall?
options: The visceral pleura
The parietal pericardium
The parietal peritoneum
The parietal pleura
questions.why: The pleura is the serous membrane of the lungs, and it has two layers. The parietal pleura lines the inner surface of the thoracic wall (parietal means wall), and it also covers the top of the diaphragm and the sides of the mediastinum. The visceral pleura covers the lung itself.
notes: The visceral pleura is the layer stuck directly to the outer surface of the lung. Pick it if the question asked which membrane covers the lung.
The parietal pericardium is part of the sac around the heart, in the mediastinum. Choose it if the question asked about the membrane lining the pericardial cavity.
The parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominopelvic cavity, below the diaphragm. It would be the answer if the question asked which membrane lines the abdominal wall.
Correct. The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall.
questions.answerText: The parietal pleura

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which serous membrane covers the outer surface of each lung?
options: The parietal pleura
The visceral pericardium
The visceral pleura
The mediastinum
questions.why: The visceral pleura is the inner layer of the pleura, attached directly to the outer surface of the lung and dipping into its fissures. Visceral refers to an organ, so the visceral layer is the one on the organ itself. It faces the parietal pleura across the thin, fluid-filled pleural cavity.
notes: The parietal pleura is the outer layer, lining the thoracic wall rather than the lung. Pick it if the question asked which membrane lines the inside of the chest wall.
The visceral pericardium, also called the epicardium, covers the surface of the heart. Choose it if the question asked which serous layer is on the heart.
Correct. The visceral pleura covers the outer surface of the lung.

The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, holding the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus. It is a region, not a membrane. It would be the answer if the question asked where the heart sits.
questions.answerText: The visceral pleura

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the pleural cavity?
options: The central chest region that holds the heart
The space inside the lungs that holds all of the alveoli
The fluid-filled space between the two pleural layers
The space between the heart and the pericardial sac
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin space between the parietal pleura on the thoracic wall and the visceral pleura on the lung. It holds only a thin film of serous fluid. That fluid lets the lung glide smoothly against the chest wall as it expands, and the sealed space helps keep the lung expanded.
notes: The central chest region holding the heart is the mediastinum. Pick it if the question asked about the compartment between the two lungs.

The air spaces inside the lungs are the alveoli and the airways that lead to them. The pleural cavity is outside the lung, not inside it. Students mix these up because both are described as spaces in the chest.
Correct. The pleural cavity is the fluid-filled space between the parietal and visceral pleurae.
The space between the heart and its sac is the pericardial cavity. It is the heart's version of the same serous arrangement. Choose it if the question were about the heart.
questions.answerText: The fluid-filled space between the two pleural layers

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory zone passages have walls lined entirely with alveoli?
options: The terminal bronchioles
The alveolar ducts
The segmental bronchi
The respiratory bronchioles
questions.why: Alveolar ducts are passages in the respiratory zone whose walls are made almost completely of alveoli opening off them. They branch from the respiratory bronchioles and lead into alveolar sacs. Compared with a respiratory bronchiole, which has only a few alveoli, an alveolar duct is lined with them all the way around.
notes: Terminal bronchioles have no alveoli at all. They are the last airways of the conducting zone. Choose them if the question asked where the conducting zone ends.
Correct. Alveolar ducts have walls lined entirely with alveoli.
Segmental bronchi are large conducting airways with cartilage in their walls, far from the alveoli. They would be the answer if the question asked for the tertiary bronchi.
Respiratory bronchioles have only a few alveoli budding from their walls, not walls lined entirely with them. Pick them if the question asked for the first airways of the respiratory zone.
questions.answerText: The alveolar ducts

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structures are the tiny air sacs that serve as the site of gas exchange?
options: The pleural cavities
The paranasal sinuses
The bronchioles
The alveoli
questions.why: Alveoli are tiny, thin-walled air sacs at the end of the respiratory tree, and the lungs hold hundreds of millions of them. Each one is wrapped in pulmonary capillaries, so air and blood are separated by only a very thin barrier. That makes the alveoli the main site of gas exchange.
notes: The pleural cavities are thin, fluid-filled spaces between the pleural layers around each lung. They hold fluid, not air. They would be the answer if the question asked where air collects in a pneumothorax.

The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities in the skull bones around the nose. They are lined with mucosa that drains into the nasal cavity and play no part in gas exchange. Choose them if the question asked about spaces in the frontal or maxillary bones.
Bronchioles are small conducting airways with smooth muscle walls. They carry air but do not exchange gases. Pick them if the question asked which airways lack cartilage.
Correct. The alveoli are the air sacs where gas exchange happens.
questions.answerText: The alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is an alveolar sac?
options: A fluid-filled space surrounding the lung
A passage whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli
A cluster of alveoli that share a common space
A single alveolus wrapped in capillaries
questions.why: An alveolar sac is a grape-like cluster of alveoli that open into a shared central space. It sits at the very end of an alveolar duct, so it is the dead end of the airway. Grouping alveoli this way packs a huge amount of exchange surface into a small volume.
notes: A fluid-filled space surrounding the lung is the pleural cavity. It would be the answer if the question asked about the space between the parietal and visceral pleurae.
A passage lined with alveoli is an alveolar duct, which leads into the alveolar sacs. Choose it if the question asked for the passage before the sac.
Correct. An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli sharing a common space.
A single alveolus wrapped in capillaries is one alveolus, the individual unit within the sac. Pick this if the question asked about one alveolus and its pulmonary capillaries.
questions.answerText: A cluster of alveoli that share a common space

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which cells are the thin, flat simple squamous cells that form most of the alveolar wall?
options: Goblet cells
Type II alveolar cells
Type I alveolar cells
Alveolar macrophages
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are simple squamous cells, meaning a single layer of very thin, flat cells. They form most of the alveolar wall, and gases cross through them. Their thinness keeps the distance between air and blood as short as possible.
notes: Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells in the pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium of the larger airways. They are not found in the alveolar wall. They would be the answer if the question asked what makes mucus in the trachea.
Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal, not flat, and are scattered among the Type I cells. Their job is to secrete surfactant. Pick them if the question asked which cells make surfactant.
Correct. Type I alveolar cells are the thin, flat cells that form most of the alveolar wall.

Alveolar macrophages are the dust cells that wander over the alveolar surface and engulf debris. They are not part of the wall itself. Choose them if the question asked which cells clear inhaled particles.
questions.answerText: Type I alveolar cells

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which cells in the alveolar wall secrete surfactant?
options: Type II alveolar cells
Type I alveolar cells
Capillary endothelial cells
Alveolar macrophages
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells are rounder, cuboidal cells scattered among the flat type I cells of the alveolar wall. Their job is to secrete surfactant, a fluid that lowers surface tension and keeps the alveoli from collapsing. They cover only a small part of the wall, while the type I cells cover nearly all of it.
notes: Correct. Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant.
Type I alveolar cells are the thin, flat cells that form most of the wall where gases cross. They do not secrete surfactant. Pick them if the question asked which cells form the gas-exchange surface.

Capillary endothelial cells line the pulmonary capillaries on the blood side of the respiratory membrane. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells form the inner lining of the capillaries around an alveolus.

Alveolar macrophages are the dust cells that patrol the alveolar surface and engulf debris. They clean rather than secrete surfactant. Choose them if the question asked which cells remove inhaled particles.
questions.answerText: Type II alveolar cells

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What does surfactant do in the alveoli?
options: It lets the lungs glide against the thoracic wall
It fills the alveoli to fight infection by microbes
It traps dust so cilia can sweep it up toward the pharynx
It lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse
questions.why: The inside of each alveolus is coated with a thin layer of water, and water molecules pull on each other, creating surface tension that tends to squeeze the tiny sacs shut. Surfactant, secreted by Type II alveolar cells, lowers that surface tension. That keeps the alveoli from collapsing, especially at the end of each breath out.
notes: Letting the lungs glide against the thoracic wall is the job of the fluid in the pleural cavity, outside the lung. It would be the answer if the question asked about pleural fluid.
Alveoli filling with fluid is what happens in pneumonia, an infection, and it interferes with gas exchange. Choose this if the question described pneumonia.
Trapping dust and sweeping it toward the pharynx is the job of mucus and cilia in the conducting airways. Pick this if the question asked about the respiratory mucosa.
Correct. Surfactant lowers surface tension and helps keep alveoli from collapsing.
questions.answerText: It lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which cells, nicknamed dust cells, patrol the alveolar surface and engulf debris and microbes?
options: Goblet cells
Type II alveolar cells
Alveolar macrophages
Type I alveolar cells
questions.why: Alveolar macrophages are immune cells that move across the alveolar surface and engulf (swallow up) inhaled dust, debris, and microbes. They are called dust cells because the particles they collect can be seen inside them. They are the last line of cleaning, since the mucus and cilia of the conducting airways do not reach the alveoli.
notes: Goblet cells secrete mucus in the larger conducting airways, where mucus traps particles before they reach the alveoli. Choose them if the question asked which cells produce mucus in the trachea.
Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant. They do not engulf debris. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells keep alveoli from collapsing.
Correct. Alveolar macrophages are the dust cells.
Type I alveolar cells are thin, flat cells that form the gas-exchange surface. They stay in place as part of the wall. Pick them if the question asked which cells form most of the alveolar wall.
questions.answerText: Alveolar macrophages

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What wraps around each alveolus?
options: A band of smooth muscle
A supporting ring of hyaline cartilage
A dense net of pulmonary capillaries
A layer of visceral pericardium
questions.why: Each alveolus is wrapped in a dense web of pulmonary capillaries, the smallest blood vessels of the pulmonary circuit. The capillary wall and the alveolar wall are pressed together, so air and blood are separated by only the thin respiratory membrane. That close contact is what makes gas exchange possible.
notes: Smooth muscle bands are found in the walls of bronchioles, where they can narrow the airway. Choose smooth muscle if the question asked what lets bronchioles constrict.
Hyaline cartilage supports the trachea and bronchi but is gone by the bronchioles, long before the alveoli. Pick cartilage if the question asked what holds the trachea open.
Correct. A dense net of pulmonary capillaries wraps each alveolus.

The visceral pericardium covers the heart, not the alveoli. The lung surface is covered by visceral pleura, and the alveoli inside are surrounded by capillaries. This choice mixes up the serous membrane of the heart with the structures inside the lung.
questions.answerText: A dense net of pulmonary capillaries

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the right and left lungs by their lobes?
options: The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two
Both lungs have three lobes, but the left ones are smaller
Both lungs have two lobes separated by an oblique fissure
The right lung has two lobes and the left lung has three
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior), separated by a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure. The left lung has two lobes (superior and inferior), separated by an oblique fissure only. The left lung gives up room to the heart, which is why it is the smaller of the two.
notes: Correct. The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two.
The left lung does not have a middle lobe. It has two lobes, and where a middle lobe would be, it has the cardiac notch and the lingula. This choice assumes the lungs are mirror images.

Only the left lung is limited to two lobes and a single oblique fissure. The right lung adds a horizontal fissure and a middle lobe. Pick this description if the question asked only about the left lung.
This reverses the two lungs. The extra lobe belongs to the right lung, the larger one, and the left lung has fewer because it shares space with the heart.
questions.answerText: The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why is the left lung smaller than the right lung?
options: It sits higher because the liver pushes up on the left side
Its main bronchus is narrower, so less lung tissue develops
It is compressed by the esophagus running down its surface
It gives up room for the heart, shown by its cardiac notch
questions.why: The heart sits in the mediastinum but tips toward the left side of the chest. The left lung makes room for it, which shows up as the cardiac notch, an indentation along its anterior border. With less room, the left lung ends up the smaller of the two.
notes: The liver sits mostly on the right side, under the right dome of the diaphragm, not the left. This choice puts the liver on the wrong side, so it cannot explain a smaller left lung.

The left main bronchus is narrower and angles more sharply than the right, but that does not set the size of the lung. The left lung is smaller because of the space it shares with the heart. This choice mixes up a bronchus fact with a lung fact.
The esophagus runs down the mediastinum behind the trachea and heart, not along the surface of the left lung. Choose the esophagus if the question asked what lies directly behind the trachea.
Correct. The left lung gives up room for the heart, which forms the cardiac notch.
questions.answerText: It gives up room for the heart, shown by its cardiac notch

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the parietal pleura and the visceral pleura?
options: Both layers cover the lung, with the parietal layer outside the visceral layer
The parietal pleura covers the lung, and the visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall
The parietal pleura covers the heart, and the visceral pleura covers the lung
The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, and the visceral pleura covers the lung
questions.why: The pleura is a double-layered serous membrane. The parietal layer (parietal means wall) lines the inside of the thoracic wall, and the visceral layer (visceral means organ) is attached directly to the surface of the lung. Between them is the pleural cavity, a thin space with a film of fluid.
notes: Only the visceral pleura is attached to the lung. The parietal pleura is on the chest wall, with the pleural cavity between them. This choice forgets that the two layers are separated by a space.
This reverses the two layers. Remember that parietal refers to a wall and visceral refers to an organ, so the visceral layer is the one on the lung.
The heart is covered by the pericardium, not the pleura. Pick a heart covering if the question asked about the visceral or parietal pericardium.
Correct. The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, and the visceral pleura covers the lung.
questions.answerText: The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, and the visceral pleura covers the lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does the pleural cavity hold a thin film of fluid?
options: It supplies the alveoli with surfactant
It lets the lung glide as it expands
It drains mucus out of the bronchi
It carries oxygen to the lung tissue
questions.why: The pleural cavity is a sealed, thin space between the parietal and visceral pleurae, and it holds only a small amount of serous fluid. The fluid acts as a lubricant, letting the lung surface glide smoothly against the thoracic wall as the lung expands and recoils with each breath. The sealed space also helps keep the lung expanded, which is why letting air into it causes collapse.
notes: Surfactant is made by Type II alveolar cells inside the alveoli, not by the pleural fluid outside the lung. Pick surfactant if the question asked what prevents alveolar collapse.
Correct. Pleural fluid lets the lung glide against the thoracic wall as it expands.

Mucus in the bronchi is moved upward by cilia toward the pharynx, inside the airway. Pleural fluid is outside the lung and never touches the bronchi. Choose cilia if the question asked how mucus leaves the airways.
Oxygen reaches the lung tissue through the air in the airways and the blood in the vessels, not through pleural fluid. This choice gives the fluid a job it does not have.
questions.answerText: It lets the lung glide as it expands

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why are Type I alveolar cells so thin and flat?
options: To let them move freely across the alveolar surface
To make room for surfactant in the alveolar wall
To give gases a very short distance to cross
To make the alveolar wall strong and stiff
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are simple squamous cells, the thinnest kind of epithelium. Gases cross the alveolar wall by diffusion (moving from where they are more concentrated to where they are less), and diffusion is fastest across a short distance. Keeping these cells flat means air and blood are separated by only a very thin barrier, the respiratory membrane.
notes: Moving freely over the alveolar surface describes alveolar macrophages, the dust cells. Type I cells stay in place as part of the wall. Choose this if the question asked about macrophages.
Surfactant is secreted by the separate Type II alveolar cells, which are cuboidal. The flatness of Type I cells is not about surfactant. Pick surfactant if the question asked about Type II cells.
Correct. Thin, flat Type I cells give gases a very short distance to cross.

Thin, flat cells make a delicate wall, not a stiff one. Strength comes from structures like cartilage in the larger airways. This choice confuses thinness with toughness, which is the opposite of how alveoli are built.
questions.answerText: To give gases a very short distance to cross

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes Type II alveolar cells?
options: They are flat cells that form most of the wall where the gases cross
They are cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant to prevent collapse
They are wandering cells that engulf inhaled debris and microbes
They are ciliated cells that sweep mucus out of the alveoli
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells scattered among the flat Type I cells. They secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension in the thin layer of water lining each alveolus. Without enough surfactant, alveoli tend to collapse, which is why these cells are essential even though they make up a small part of the wall.
notes: Flat cells that form most of the gas-exchange wall are the Type I alveolar cells. Pick this if the question asked about Type I cells.
Correct. Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal and secrete surfactant.
Wandering cells that engulf debris are the alveolar macrophages, or dust cells. Choose this if the question asked which cells clean the alveolar surface.

Ciliated cells are found in the pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium of the conducting airways, not in the alveoli. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells sweep mucus up the trachea.
questions.answerText: They are cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant to prevent collapse

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The mucus and cilia of the conducting airways do not reach the alveoli. What clears debris and microbes that make it all the way to the alveolar surface?
options: Goblet cells trap them in mucus
Surfactant dissolves them away
Type I cells absorb them into the blood
Alveolar macrophages engulf them
questions.why: The conducting airways clean air with mucus from goblet cells and cilia that sweep it toward the pharynx, but the alveoli have no cilia or goblet cells. Instead, alveolar macrophages, the dust cells, patrol the alveolar surface and engulf any debris and microbes that arrive. Their location on the exchange surface puts them exactly where the airway's other defenses end.
notes: Goblet cells make mucus in the conducting airways, such as the trachea and bronchi. They are not present in the alveoli. Pick goblet cells if the question asked what traps particles in the larger airways.
Surfactant lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse. It does not dissolve debris. Choose surfactant if the question asked what keeps alveoli open.
Type I alveolar cells form the thin exchange wall and do not absorb debris. This choice confuses the path of gases across the wall with the clearing of particles.
Correct. Alveolar macrophages engulf debris and microbes on the alveolar surface.
questions.answerText: Alveolar macrophages engulf them

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why are pulmonary capillaries wrapped so tightly around each alveolus?
options: To carry lymph away from the lung tissue
To hold the alveolus open like a stiff supporting ring
To deliver surfactant into the alveolar space
To bring blood very close to the air for exchange
questions.why: Gas exchange needs air and blood to be as close together as possible. Wrapping each alveolus in a dense net of capillaries means blood flows right against the alveolar wall, separated from the air by only the thin respiratory membrane (alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium). This arrangement packs a huge exchange surface into the lungs.
notes: Carrying lymph is the job of lymphatic vessels, not blood capillaries. Choose lymphatic vessels if the question asked how excess tissue fluid leaves the lung.
Capillaries are thin, soft vessels and do not hold anything open. Support rings of cartilage are found only in the larger airways. This choice confuses a blood vessel with a supporting structure.
Surfactant is secreted by Type II alveolar cells in the alveolar wall, not delivered by the capillaries. Pick Type II cells if the question asked where surfactant comes from.
Correct. Capillaries wrap the alveoli to bring blood close to the air for gas exchange.
questions.answerText: To bring blood very close to the air for exchange

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A premature newborn's Type II alveolar cells are not yet making enough surfactant. What is most likely to happen to the baby's alveoli?
options: Their walls are permanently destroyed
They leak air out into the pleural cavity
They fill with fluid from an infection
They collapse because surface tension stays high
questions.why: Surfactant lowers the surface tension of the thin layer of water lining each alveolus. Without enough of it, that surface tension stays high and tends to pull the tiny sacs closed, especially at the end of each breath out. So a newborn without enough surfactant has alveoli that collapse easily, which makes breathing hard work.
notes: Permanent destruction of alveolar walls is emphysema, a long-term disease, usually linked to smoking. Choose this if the question described a permanent loss of exchange surface.
Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax, caused by a puncture of the chest wall or lung. It would be the answer if the question described a chest injury.
Alveoli filling with fluid from an infection describes pneumonia. A lack of surfactant is not an infection. Pick this if the question described an infection that inflames the alveoli.
Correct. Without enough surfactant, high surface tension makes alveoli collapse.
questions.answerText: They collapse because surface tension stays high

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Inhaling a toxic gas damages a patient's Type I alveolar cells. Which process is most directly impaired?
options: Mucus clearance by cilia in the trachea
Removal of debris from the alveolar surface
Surfactant secretion by the alveolar wall
Gas diffusion across the alveolar wall
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are the thin, flat cells that form most of the alveolar wall, and they are the cells that gases cross. If they are damaged, the barrier between air and blood is disrupted, and gas diffusion (movement of gases from high to low concentration across the wall) is impaired. The other jobs listed belong to other cells.
notes: Mucus clearance by cilia happens in the pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium of the conducting airways, far from the alveoli. Choose this if the question described damage to the tracheal lining.
Removing debris from the alveolar surface is the job of the alveolar macrophages, or dust cells. It would be the answer if the question said the macrophages were damaged.
Surfactant secretion is the job of Type II alveolar cells. Damage to Type II cells would impair it most directly. Pick this if the question said Type II cells were damaged.
Correct. Type I cells form the gas-exchange surface, so damage to them impairs gas diffusion.
questions.answerText: Gas diffusion across the alveolar wall

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement best explains why the alveoli are ideal for gas exchange but also easy to damage?
options: Their walls are lined with thick cartilage, which protects them but slows the exchange of gases
Their thin, capillary-wrapped walls make exchange fast, but damage or fluid quickly cuts it
They have few capillaries, so exchange is slow but the walls rarely suffer any injury
They are covered in cilia, which clean them well but break easily when air is cold
questions.why: Alveoli have extremely thin walls made of flat Type I cells, and each one is wrapped in pulmonary capillaries, so the distance between air and blood is tiny and the total surface is enormous. That design makes gas exchange very efficient. But a wall that thin is fragile, so anything that destroys it (as in emphysema) or fills the space with fluid (as in pneumonia) quickly reduces exchange.
notes: Alveoli have no cartilage. Cartilage supports the trachea and bronchi and disappears by the bronchioles. This choice describes the larger airways, not the exchange surface.
Correct. The thin, capillary-wrapped wall is efficient for exchange but easily damaged or flooded.
Alveoli are wrapped in a dense net of capillaries, not a few. This statement reverses the actual design. Students might pick it by thinking delicate tissue must be poorly supplied.
Cilia line the conducting airways, not the alveoli. The alveoli are cleaned by macrophages instead. Pick cilia if the question asked how mucus is moved out of the trachea.
questions.answerText: Their thin, capillary-wrapped walls make exchange fast, but damage or fluid quickly cuts it

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Structurally, what do most common respiratory disorders do?
options: They cause the trachea to grow extra rings
They permanently enlarge the paranasal sinuses of the skull
They narrow the airways, damage the alveoli, or affect the pleurae
They destroy the cartilage of the larynx
questions.why: Most respiratory disorders do one of three things to a structure. Some narrow or block the airways, as in asthma and chronic bronchitis. Some damage or fill the alveoli, as in emphysema and pneumonia, and some affect the pleurae and pleural cavity, as in pleurisy and pneumothorax.
notes: The trachea does not grow extra rings in any common disorder. This change sounds structural, but it is not something any disorder in this unit does.
Sinusitis inflames the lining of the sinuses, but no common disorder enlarges the sinus spaces in the bone. This choice does not describe what most respiratory disorders do.
Correct. Most disorders narrow or block the airways, damage or fill the alveoli, or affect the pleurae.

Laryngitis inflames the vocal folds, but no common disorder destroys the laryngeal cartilages. This choice picks one structure and a change that does not happen, so it does not describe most disorders.
questions.answerText: They narrow the airways, damage the alveoli, or affect the pleurae

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
