questions.q: Which structure is affected in asthma?
options: The larynx
The alveoli
The bronchioles
The pleural cavity
questions.why: Asthma affects the bronchi and bronchioles, and the narrowing is worst in the bronchioles. Bronchioles have smooth muscle and no cartilage, so when the lining is inflamed and the muscle tightens, nothing holds them open and they narrow. That narrowing causes the wheezing and breathlessness of an asthma attack.
notes: The larynx is the voice box in the upper part of the lower tract. It is not the site of asthma. It would be the answer if the question asked where the vocal folds are housed.
The alveoli are affected in emphysema and pneumonia, where walls are destroyed or sacs fill with fluid. Pick the alveoli if the question asked about either of those disorders.
Correct. Asthma affects the bronchioles.
The pleural cavity is affected in pneumothorax, when air enters the space between the pleurae. Choose it if the question asked about a collapsed lung after a chest puncture.
questions.answerText: The bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description best defines asthma?
options: Inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles with wheezing
An infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid
Destruction of alveolar walls that reduces exchange surface
Air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse
questions.why: Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, the small airways with smooth muscle walls and no cartilage. When they narrow, air moving through them makes a whistling sound called wheezing, and the person feels short of breath. The problem is in the airways, not the alveoli themselves.
notes: Correct. Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, causing wheezing.
An infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid is pneumonia. Choose this if the question asked to define pneumonia.
Destruction of alveolar walls is emphysema, a permanent loss of exchange surface. Pick this if the question asked to define emphysema.
Air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse is a pneumothorax. It would be the answer if the question asked to define pneumothorax.
questions.answerText: Inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles with wheezing

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structures are affected in COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)?
options: The pleurae and pleural cavity
The airways and the alveoli
The nasal cavity and sinuses
The larynx and vocal folds
questions.why: COPD is a long-term blockage of airflow that includes two conditions: chronic bronchitis, which affects the airways, and emphysema, which destroys the alveolar walls. Because it combines both, COPD affects the airways and the alveoli. This makes it broader than asthma, which centers on the bronchioles, or pneumonia, which centers on the alveoli.
notes: The pleurae and pleural cavity are affected in pneumothorax, when air breaks the pleural seal. Pick this if the question asked about a collapsed lung.
Correct. COPD affects both the airways and the alveoli.
The nasal cavity and sinuses are in the upper respiratory tract and are not where COPD acts. Choose them if the question asked which structures warm and filter incoming air.
The larynx and vocal folds produce sound and guard the airway, and they are not the site of COPD. They would be the answer if the question asked which structures are involved in speaking.
questions.answerText: The airways and the alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: COPD is a long-term blockage of airflow. Which two conditions does it include?
options: Emphysema and chronic bronchitis
Asthma and pneumonia
Pneumothorax and emphysema
Pneumonia and lung cancer
questions.why: COPD, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is an umbrella term for long-term airflow blockage. It includes emphysema, in which alveolar walls are destroyed, and chronic bronchitis, in which the airways are inflamed over a long period. Both are lasting conditions, which is what the word chronic means.
notes: Correct. COPD includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

Asthma narrows the bronchioles in attacks, and pneumonia is an infection of the alveoli. Neither is one of the two conditions grouped under COPD. Pick asthma if the question asked which disorder narrows the bronchioles.

Emphysema is part of COPD, but pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, a separate problem outside the airways. This pair is half right. Pick pneumothorax if the question asked about a collapsed lung after a puncture.

Pneumonia is an infection that fills alveoli with fluid, and lung cancer is a malignant tumor. They are separate disorders, not parts of COPD. Choose lung cancer if the question asked which disorder is a malignant tumor.
questions.answerText: Emphysema and chronic bronchitis

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structure is damaged in emphysema?
options: The bronchioles
The alveoli
The pleural cavity
The trachea
questions.why: Emphysema destroys the walls of the alveoli, the tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens. As the walls break down, many small sacs merge into a few large ones, so the total exchange surface shrinks. The change is structural and permanent.
notes: The bronchioles are the site of asthma, where the small airways narrow. Pick them if the question asked about asthma.
Correct. Emphysema damages the alveoli.
The pleural cavity is the site of pneumothorax, when air enters the space between the pleurae. Choose it if the question asked about a collapsed lung.
The trachea is a large airway held open by C-shaped cartilage rings, and it is not the site of emphysema. It would be the answer if the question asked which airway forks at the carina.
questions.answerText: The alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What happens to the lung in emphysema?
options: Air leaks into the pleural cavity, and the lung then collapses
The alveoli fill with fluid from an infection
The alveolar walls are destroyed and exchange surface shrinks
The bronchioles narrow during attacks and then reopen
questions.why: In emphysema the thin walls between alveoli break down. Many small air sacs merge into fewer, larger ones, which leaves much less total surface where air and blood meet. Because the walls do not grow back, the loss of exchange surface is permanent.
notes: Air leaking into the pleural cavity and collapsing the lung is a pneumothorax. It would be the answer if the question described a chest puncture.
Alveoli filling with fluid from an infection is pneumonia. The alveoli are still intact, just flooded. Choose this if the question asked about pneumonia.
Correct. In emphysema the alveolar walls are destroyed and the exchange surface shrinks.
Bronchioles narrowing in attacks and then reopening describes asthma, which affects the small airways. Pick this if the question asked about asthma.
questions.answerText: The alveolar walls are destroyed and exchange surface shrinks

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structures are inflamed in pneumonia?
options: The alveoli
The bronchioles
The pleural cavities
The nasal conchae
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid. Because the alveoli are the air sacs where gas exchange happens, flooding them leaves less space for air to reach the blood. The alveolar walls are not destroyed as in emphysema, but they cannot work well while they are full of fluid.
notes: Correct. Pneumonia inflames the alveoli.
The bronchioles are the site of asthma, where the small airways narrow. They would be the answer if the question asked about wheezing from narrowed airways.
The pleural cavities are the site of pneumothorax, where air enters the space between the pleurae. Pick them if the question asked about a collapsed lung after a puncture.
The nasal conchae are scroll-shaped projections in the nasal cavity that swirl incoming air. They are not the site of pneumonia. Choose them if the question asked how the nose conditions air.
questions.answerText: The alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description best defines pneumonia?
options: A malignant tumor of the lung tissue strongly linked to smoking
Destruction of alveolar walls that merges small sacs into large ones
Long-term narrowing of the airways that includes chronic bronchitis
An infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection of the lung in which the alveoli become inflamed and fill with fluid. The fluid takes up the space where air should be, so less air reaches the exchange surface. Unlike emphysema, the alveolar walls are not destroyed, so the alveoli can recover once the infection clears.
notes: A malignant tumor of lung tissue strongly linked to smoking is lung cancer. Choose this if the question asked to define lung cancer.
Destruction of alveolar walls that merges small sacs into large ones is emphysema. Pick this if the question asked to define emphysema.
Long-term airway obstruction that includes chronic bronchitis is COPD. It would be the answer if the question asked to define COPD.
Correct. Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid.
questions.answerText: An infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which space is affected in a pneumothorax?
options: The mediastinum
The pleural cavity
The pericardial cavity
The alveolar sacs
questions.why: Pneumothorax means air in the thorax, and specifically it means air in the pleural cavity, the thin space between the parietal and visceral pleurae. Normally that space is sealed and holds only a film of fluid. When air gets in, the seal is lost and the lung can collapse.
notes: The mediastinum is the central compartment of the chest holding the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus. It would be the answer if the question asked which region lies between the two pleural cavities.
Correct. A pneumothorax affects the pleural cavity.
The pericardial cavity is the space around the heart, between the layers of the pericardium. Pick it if the question asked about fluid around the heart.
The alveolar sacs are supposed to hold air, so air in them is normal. They are affected in pneumonia and emphysema. Choose them if the question asked where pneumonia fluid collects.
questions.answerText: The pleural cavity

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description best defines a pneumothorax?
options: Fluid filling the alveoli during an infection of the lung
Air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse
Narrowing of the bronchioles that causes wheezing
Fluid collecting in the sac around the heart
questions.why: A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, usually after a puncture of the chest wall or the lung. The pleural cavity is normally a sealed space with only a thin film of fluid, and that seal helps hold the lung against the chest wall. When air gets in, the seal is lost and the lung collapses.
notes: Fluid filling the alveoli during infection is pneumonia. Pick this if the question asked to define pneumonia.
Correct. A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse.
Narrowing of the bronchioles with wheezing is asthma. Choose this if the question asked to define asthma.
Fluid collecting in the sac around the heart affects the pericardial cavity, not the pleural cavity. It would be the answer if the question were about the pericardium.
questions.answerText: Air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which respiratory disorder is a malignant tumor of the lung tissue?
options: Lung cancer
Asthma
Emphysema
Pneumonia
questions.why: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor, a growth of abnormal cells that can invade nearby tissue and spread. It usually starts in the epithelium lining the airways or alveoli, and it is strongly linked to smoking. It is the only choice here defined by a tumor rather than narrowing, destruction, or fluid.
notes: Correct. Lung cancer is a malignant tumor of the lung.
Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles. It would be the answer if the question described wheezing from narrowed small airways.

Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, but it is not a tumor. It is also strongly linked to smoking, which is why students mix it up with lung cancer. Pick emphysema if the question described a permanent loss of exchange surface.
Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid. It is not a tumor. Choose it if the question described fluid-filled, inflamed alveoli.
questions.answerText: Lung cancer

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description best defines lung cancer?
options: Destruction of the alveolar walls, also strongly linked to smoking
Air in the pleural cavity after a chest puncture
A malignant tumor of lung tissue, strongly linked to smoking
Inflammation and narrowing of the small airways
questions.why: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor of the lung tissue, a growth of abnormal cells that can invade and spread. Smoking is the risk factor most strongly linked to it. What sets it apart from the other disorders in this unit is that it is a tumor, not a blockage, an infection, or a leak.
notes: Destruction of alveolar walls is emphysema. Smoking is linked to both emphysema and lung cancer, so the smoking link alone does not tell them apart. Pick this if the question asked to define emphysema.
Air in the pleural cavity after a puncture is a pneumothorax. It would be the answer if the question asked to define pneumothorax.
Correct. Lung cancer is a malignant tumor of lung tissue, strongly linked to smoking.
Inflammation and narrowing of the small airways is asthma. Choose this if the question asked to define asthma.
questions.answerText: A malignant tumor of lung tissue, strongly linked to smoking

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares asthma and emphysema by the structure each one affects?
options: Asthma narrows the bronchioles, and emphysema destroys alveolar walls
Both narrow the bronchioles, but emphysema is permanent
Asthma destroys alveolar walls, and emphysema narrows the bronchioles
Asthma affects the pleural cavity, and emphysema affects the alveoli
questions.why: Asthma is a disease of the small airways: the bronchioles become inflamed and narrow, which blocks airflow. Emphysema is a disease of the exchange surface: the alveolar walls are destroyed, which shrinks the area where gases cross. So one disorder narrows the passages leading to the alveoli, and the other damages the alveoli themselves.
notes: Correct. Asthma narrows the bronchioles, and emphysema destroys alveolar walls.
Emphysema does not act by narrowing the bronchioles. Its damage is to the alveolar walls. It is true that emphysema is permanent, which is what makes this choice tempting.
This reverses the two disorders. Asthma acts on the airways, which can tighten because they have smooth muscle, and emphysema acts on the alveoli.
The pleural cavity is affected in pneumothorax, not asthma. Pick the pleural cavity if the question compared pneumothorax with another disorder.
questions.answerText: Asthma narrows the bronchioles, and emphysema destroys alveolar walls

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Pneumonia and emphysema both affect the alveoli. Which statement correctly compares what goes wrong in each?
options: Both fill the alveoli with fluid, but only pneumonia is caused by smoking
Pneumonia lets air into the pleural cavity, and emphysema narrows the bronchioles
Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid, and emphysema destroys the alveolar walls
Pneumonia destroys the alveolar walls, and emphysema fills the alveoli with fluid
questions.why: In pneumonia, an infection inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid, so air cannot reach the exchange surface even though the walls are intact. In emphysema, the alveolar walls themselves are destroyed, merging small sacs into large ones and permanently reducing the exchange surface. Both hurt gas exchange at the alveoli, but one floods them and the other breaks them down.
notes: Emphysema does not fill alveoli with fluid, and pneumonia is an infection rather than a smoking disease. Smoking is linked to emphysema and lung cancer. This choice mixes up the cause and the damage.
Air in the pleural cavity is pneumothorax, and narrowed bronchioles are asthma. This statement describes two other disorders. Pick it only if the question compared pneumothorax and asthma.
Correct. Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid, and emphysema destroys the alveolar walls.
This reverses the two disorders. Pneumonia is the infection that floods alveoli, and emphysema is the structural, permanent destruction of their walls.
questions.answerText: Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid, and emphysema destroys the alveolar walls

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares pneumothorax and pneumonia by the space each one affects?
options: Pneumothorax affects the alveoli, and pneumonia affects the pleural cavity
Pneumothorax affects the pleural cavity, and pneumonia affects the alveoli
Pneumothorax affects the bronchioles, and pneumonia affects the trachea
Both affect the pleural cavity, but pneumonia adds fluid instead of air
questions.why: A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, the sealed space outside the lung between the parietal and visceral pleurae, and it can let the lung collapse. Pneumonia is an infection inside the lung that fills the alveoli with fluid. So pneumothorax is a problem around the lung, while pneumonia is a problem inside the air sacs.
notes: This reverses the two spaces. Students mix them up because both names start with pneumo, which refers to air or the lungs. Pneumothorax is the one in the thorax outside the lung.
Correct. Pneumothorax affects the pleural cavity, and pneumonia affects the alveoli.
Neither disorder is defined by the bronchioles or the trachea. Narrowed bronchioles are asthma. Pick bronchioles if the question asked which structure asthma affects.
Pneumonia does not affect the pleural cavity. Its fluid collects inside the alveoli. This choice moves pneumonia to the wrong side of the visceral pleura.
questions.answerText: Pneumothorax affects the pleural cavity, and pneumonia affects the alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In emphysema, many small alveoli merge into a few large air sacs. Why does that reduce gas exchange?
options: A few large sacs have much less total wall surface
Large sacs fill with fluid more easily than small ones
A few large sacs narrow the bronchioles that feed them
Large sacs push air back into the pleural cavity
questions.why: Gas exchange happens across the alveolar walls, so the amount of wall surface sets how much exchange can occur. Many small sacs have far more total wall area than the same volume divided into a few large sacs. When emphysema destroys the walls between alveoli, the lung trades a huge exchange surface for a small one, and the change is permanent.
notes: Correct. Merging into a few large sacs leaves much less wall surface for gas exchange.
Filling with fluid is what happens in pneumonia, an infection. Emphysema is a loss of wall, not a flooding of the sacs. Pick fluid-filled alveoli if the question asked about pneumonia.
Narrowing of the bronchioles is asthma, which affects the airways before the alveoli. This choice blames the wrong structure. Pick bronchiole narrowing if the question asked about wheezing.
Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax, caused by a puncture. Emphysema does not move air into the pleural cavity by itself. Choose this if the question asked about a collapsed lung.
questions.answerText: A few large sacs have much less total wall surface

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does air entering the pleural cavity cause a lung to collapse?
options: It breaks the pleural seal that holds the lung expanded
It washes the surfactant out of the alveoli so they shut
It narrows the bronchioles so no air can reach the lung
It tears the visceral pericardium away from the heart
questions.why: The pleural cavity is a sealed space between the parietal pleura on the chest wall and the visceral pleura on the lung, holding only a thin film of fluid. That sealed space keeps the lung held out against the chest wall. When a puncture lets air in, the seal is lost, the lung is no longer held out, and it collapses.
notes: Correct. Air breaks the seal of the pleural space, so the lung is no longer held expanded.

Surfactant is inside the alveoli, on the other side of the visceral pleura and the lung tissue. Air in the pleural cavity does not reach it. Pick lost surfactant if the question asked why a premature newborn's alveoli collapse.
Narrowing of the bronchioles is asthma, an airway problem. Pneumothorax acts outside the lung, not inside the airways. Choose this if the question asked about asthma.
The visceral pericardium covers the heart, not the lung, and it is a different serous membrane. This choice mixes up the pleura and the pericardium.
questions.answerText: It breaks the pleural seal that holds the lung expanded

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A patient has episodes of wheezing and breathlessness, and testing shows her bronchioles are inflamed and narrowed. Which disorder best matches?
options: Asthma
Emphysema
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
questions.why: Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, the small airways with smooth muscle and no cartilage. Narrowed bronchioles make air whistle as it moves through, which is wheezing, and they limit how much air gets in and out. The episodes and the bronchiole findings point to asthma.
notes: Correct. Inflamed, narrowed bronchioles with wheezing match asthma.

Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and permanently reduces exchange surface. It affects the alveoli, not mainly the bronchioles. Choose it if the scenario described a permanent loss of alveolar surface.
Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid. It would be the answer if the scenario described inflamed, fluid-filled alveoli.

Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that lets a lung collapse, usually after a puncture. It does not narrow the bronchioles. Pick it if the scenario described a chest wound and a collapsed lung.
questions.answerText: Asthma

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A longtime smoker's lung tissue shows that many small alveoli have merged into a few large sacs, a permanent loss of exchange surface. Which disorder best matches?
options: Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
Emphysema
Asthma
questions.why: Emphysema destroys the walls between alveoli, so many small air sacs merge into a few large ones. That leaves much less surface for gas exchange, and because the walls do not regrow, the loss is permanent. A permanent, structural loss of alveolar surface is the hallmark of emphysema.
notes: Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid during an infection, but the walls stay intact and can recover. Choose it if the scenario described inflamed, fluid-filled alveoli.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that collapses the lung. It does not change the alveoli themselves. It would be the answer if the scenario described a chest puncture.
Correct. A permanent loss of alveolar surface from merged sacs is emphysema.
Asthma narrows the bronchioles in episodes and does not destroy alveoli. Pick asthma if the scenario described wheezing from narrowed small airways.
questions.answerText: Emphysema

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A patient with a fever and cough is found to have inflamed alveoli filled with fluid in one region of the lung. Which disorder best matches?
options: Emphysema
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
Asthma
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid. The fever points to an infection, and the fluid-filled alveoli show where it is. Because fluid takes up the space where air should be, less air reaches the exchange surface in that part of the lung.
notes: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls but does not fill them with fluid, and it is not an infection. Pick it if the scenario described a permanent loss of alveolar surface.
Correct. Inflamed, fluid-filled alveoli from an infection match pneumonia.
Pneumothorax puts air in the pleural cavity, outside the lung, not fluid in the alveoli. Choose it if the scenario described a puncture and a collapsed lung.
Asthma narrows the bronchioles and does not fill the alveoli. It would be the answer if the scenario described wheezing from narrowed small airways.
questions.answerText: Pneumonia

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A stab wound to the chest wall lets air enter the space between the parietal and visceral pleurae. What condition can result?
options: Asthma, with narrowed bronchioles
Pneumothorax, with a collapsed lung
Pneumonia, with fluid in the alveoli
Emphysema, with merging of alveoli
questions.why: The space between the parietal and visceral pleurae is the pleural cavity, which is normally sealed and holds only a thin film of fluid. A wound that lets air into it breaks the seal, so the lung is no longer held against the chest wall and can collapse. Air in the pleural cavity is called a pneumothorax.
notes: Asthma narrows the bronchioles and is not caused by a chest wound. It would be the answer if the scenario described wheezing from narrowed small airways.
Correct. Air entering the pleural cavity causes a pneumothorax, which can collapse the lung.
Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid. A stab wound puts air outside the lung, not fluid inside it. Choose it if the scenario described fever and fluid-filled alveoli.
Emphysema is a slow, permanent destruction of alveolar walls, usually linked to smoking, not the result of a wound. Pick it if the scenario described a long-term loss of exchange surface.
questions.answerText: Pneumothorax, with a collapsed lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In asthma the bronchioles narrow, but the trachea does not. Which structural difference explains this?
options: The trachea is held open by cartilage, which bronchioles lack
The trachea is lined by visceral pleura that resists narrowing
The trachea has more smooth muscle than the bronchioles
The bronchioles are wrapped in capillaries that squeeze them
questions.why: Moving down the bronchial tree, cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases, and the bronchioles are where the cartilage disappears. The trachea is held permanently open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, so it cannot be squeezed shut. Bronchioles have no cartilage, and smooth muscle makes up much of their wall, so when the lining is inflamed and the muscle tightens, they narrow.
notes: Correct. Cartilage holds the trachea open, while bronchioles lack cartilage and can constrict.
The visceral pleura covers the outer surface of the lungs, not the trachea, and it does not hold airways open. Pick visceral pleura if the question asked which membrane covers the lung.

This reverses the pattern. Smooth muscle increases as the airways get smaller, so the bronchioles have relatively more of it, not less. Students pick this by thinking a bigger airway must have more of everything.
Pulmonary capillaries wrap the alveoli, not the bronchioles, and they do not squeeze airways. Choose capillaries if the question asked what surrounds each alveolus.
questions.answerText: The trachea is held open by cartilage, which bronchioles lack

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces inhaled air from the nasal cavity to the terminal bronchioles?
options: Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, main bronchi, segmental bronchi, lobar bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Nasal cavity, larynx, pharynx, trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Nasal cavity, pharynx, trachea, larynx, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
questions.why: Air passes from the nasal cavity into the pharynx (the throat), then through the larynx (the voice box) into the trachea. The trachea forks into the main bronchi, which divide into lobar bronchi for each lobe, then segmental bronchi for each segment, then bronchioles. The terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone, the part that only carries air.
notes: This sequence swaps the lobar and segmental bronchi. Lobar bronchi supply whole lobes and come first, and each one divides into smaller segmental bronchi for the bronchopulmonary segments.
Correct. This is the conducting path from the nasal cavity to the terminal bronchioles.
This sequence puts the larynx before the pharynx. The pharynx lies directly behind the nasal cavity and leads down to the larynx, so the larynx comes second.
This sequence puts the trachea above the larynx. The larynx sits on top of the trachea and connects the pharynx to it, so air reaches the larynx first.
questions.answerText: Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces air from a terminal bronchiole into the alveoli?
options: Terminal bronchiole, segmental bronchi, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, alveoli
Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar sacs, alveolar ducts, alveoli
Terminal bronchiole, alveolar ducts, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar sacs, alveoli
Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, alveoli
questions.why: Past the terminal bronchiole the airway enters the respiratory zone, where gas exchange can happen. Respiratory bronchioles come first, with a few alveoli budding from their walls. They lead into alveolar ducts, whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli, and the ducts end in alveolar sacs, which are clusters of alveoli sharing a common space.
notes: Segmental bronchi are much larger conducting airways that come well before the bronchioles. They would fit a trace from the main bronchi downward, not one that starts at a terminal bronchiole.
This sequence swaps the alveolar sacs and alveolar ducts. The ducts are the passages, and the sacs are the dead-end clusters at their ends, so the sacs come last before the individual alveoli.

This sequence puts the alveolar ducts before the respiratory bronchioles. The respiratory bronchioles still look like small airways with only a few alveoli, so they come first, and the ducts lined with alveoli come next.
Correct. This is the respiratory zone in order.
questions.answerText: Terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Inhaled air has just reached a terminal bronchiole. Has gas exchange with the blood started yet?
options: Yes, because gas exchange begins as soon as air enters the trachea
Yes, because terminal bronchioles are the first part of the respiratory zone
No, because gas exchange begins only in the alveolar sacs
No, because terminal bronchioles are the last part of the conducting zone
questions.why: The airway is divided into a conducting zone, which only carries air, and a respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens. The terminal bronchioles are the final airways of the conducting zone. Gas exchange becomes possible one step later, in the respiratory bronchioles, which have a few alveoli budding from their walls.
notes: The trachea is part of the conducting zone, which warms, moistens, and filters air but does not exchange gases. Its thick wall with cartilage rings is far too thick for gases to cross.
The first part of the respiratory zone is the respiratory bronchiole, not the terminal bronchiole. That statement would be true if the air had reached a respiratory bronchiole.
Gas exchange actually begins earlier, in the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts, which have alveoli in their walls. This choice treats only the very end of the tree as the respiratory zone.
Correct. The terminal bronchiole still belongs to the conducting zone, so exchange has not begun.
questions.answerText: No, because terminal bronchioles are the last part of the conducting zone

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Inhaled air has just reached a respiratory bronchiole. Has gas exchange become possible?
options: Yes, because a few alveoli bud from its walls, starting the respiratory zone
No, because gas exchange happens only in the alveolar sacs
No, because respiratory bronchioles are the last part of the conducting zone
Yes, because its walls are lined with cartilage rings like the trachea
questions.why: The respiratory bronchioles are the first airways of the respiratory zone. A few alveoli bud from their walls, and alveoli are where gases cross between air and blood. So once air reaches a respiratory bronchiole, gas exchange has become possible.
notes: Correct. The alveoli in its walls make the respiratory bronchiole the start of the respiratory zone.

Gas exchange happens wherever alveoli are present, which includes the respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts, not just the sacs. This choice treats only the end of the tree as the respiratory zone.
The last part of the conducting zone is the terminal bronchiole, one step earlier. This statement would be true if the air had only reached a terminal bronchiole.
Bronchioles have no cartilage at all, and cartilage would not allow gas exchange anyway. Cartilage rings describe the trachea, which is part of the conducting zone.
questions.answerText: Yes, because a few alveoli bud from its walls, starting the respiratory zone

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: An inhaled peanut reaches the carina. Which airways could it enter next?
options: The right or left lobar bronchus
The right or left segmental bronchus
The right or left main bronchus
The larynx or the trachea
questions.why: The carina is the internal ridge at the bottom of the trachea where it forks into the two main bronchi, also called the primary bronchi. Anything that reaches the carina must go into either the right or the left main bronchus. Each main bronchus then enters a lung and divides into lobar bronchi.
notes: The lobar bronchi come one level later, after a main bronchus divides inside the lung. They would be the answer if the object had already entered a main bronchus.
The segmental bronchi are two levels past the carina, branching from the lobar bronchi. They would be the answer if the object had reached a lobar bronchus.
Correct. The carina splits the trachea into the right and left main bronchi.
The larynx and trachea are above the carina, so the object has already passed through them. They would be the answer if the question asked what it passed through after the pharynx.
questions.answerText: The right or left main bronchus

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Inhaled objects land in the right lung more often than the left. What structural difference explains this?
options: The left main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the right
The right main bronchus has no cartilage, so it stays open wider
The right lung has more lobes, so it pulls in more air
The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left
questions.why: At the carina the trachea splits into two main bronchi that are not identical. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, almost in line with the trachea, while the left is narrower and angles off more sharply. An object falling down the trachea therefore tends to drop straight into the right main bronchus.
notes: This is the mirror image of the truth. The left main bronchus is the narrower, more horizontal one, so objects are less likely to enter it. Pick wider and more vertical only for the right side.
Both main bronchi are supported by cartilage, which holds them open. Cartilage is lost only at the level of the bronchioles, so this choice confuses the main bronchi with much smaller airways.

The right lung does have three lobes and the left has two, but the number of lobes does not steer an object. Students pick this because the right lung is larger, but the angle and width of the bronchus decide where an object goes.
Correct. The wider, more vertical right main bronchus lines up with the trachea.
questions.answerText: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In the bronchial tree, which airways come immediately after the main (primary) bronchi?
options: Bronchioles
Lobar bronchi
Trachea
Segmental bronchi
questions.why: Each main bronchus enters a lung and divides into lobar bronchi, also called secondary bronchi, one for each lobe. The right lung has three lobes and so three lobar bronchi, and the left lung has two. Each lobar bronchus then divides into segmental bronchi for the bronchopulmonary segments.
notes: Bronchioles are much smaller airways with smooth muscle and no cartilage, reached only after the segmental bronchi. They would be the answer if the question started at the segmental bronchi.
Correct. The main bronchi divide into lobar bronchi.
The trachea is above the main bronchi, splitting into them at the carina. It would be the answer if the question asked which airway leads into the main bronchi.
Segmental bronchi, or tertiary bronchi, come one level after the lobar bronchi. They would be the answer if the question started at the lobar bronchi.
questions.answerText: Lobar bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In the lower respiratory tract, which airway comes immediately before the alveolar ducts?
options: Alveolar sacs
Terminal bronchioles
Segmental bronchi
Respiratory bronchioles
questions.why: The respiratory bronchioles connect the terminal bronchioles to the alveolar ducts. They are the first airways of the respiratory zone, with only a few alveoli budding from their walls. They lead into alveolar ducts, whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli.
notes: Alveolar sacs come after the alveolar ducts, as the clusters of alveoli at the ends of the ducts. They would be the answer if the question asked what the alveolar ducts lead into.
Terminal bronchioles come one step earlier, at the end of the conducting zone. They would be the answer if the question asked which airway comes just before the respiratory bronchioles.
Segmental bronchi are larger conducting airways several branchings earlier. They would be the answer if the question asked what the lobar bronchi divide into.
Correct. Respiratory bronchioles lead into the alveolar ducts.
questions.answerText: Respiratory bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A stab wound punctures the chest wall. Which sequence explains how this can collapse the lung (pneumothorax)?
options: Bronchioles narrow, airflow is blocked, and breathing becomes wheezy
Fluid fills the alveoli, air cannot reach the blood, and exchange drops
Alveolar walls break down, air spaces enlarge, and surface area shrinks
Air enters the pleural cavity, the pleural seal breaks, and the lung collapses
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin, sealed, fluid-filled space between the parietal pleura on the chest wall and the visceral pleura on the lung. That seal keeps the lung expanded against the chest wall. When a wound lets air into the pleural cavity, the seal is lost and the lung can collapse, which is a pneumothorax.
notes: Narrowing of the bronchioles with wheezing describes asthma. It would be the answer if the question asked how asthma reduces airflow.
Fluid filling the alveoli describes pneumonia, an infection of the alveoli. It would be the answer if the question asked how pneumonia reduces gas exchange.
Breakdown of alveolar walls into fewer, larger air spaces describes emphysema. It would be the answer if the question asked how emphysema reduces the exchange surface.
Correct. Air in the pleural cavity breaks the seal and lets the lung collapse.
questions.answerText: Air enters the pleural cavity, the pleural seal breaks, and the lung collapses

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A long-time smoker has emphysema. Why does this disease reduce gas exchange?
options: The bronchioles narrow from inflammation, slowing air on its way in
Alveolar walls are destroyed, merging small sacs into fewer large ones with less surface area
The alveoli fill with fluid from an infection, blocking air from the blood
Air leaks into the pleural cavity, letting part of the lung collapse
questions.why: Gas exchange depends on the huge surface area of hundreds of millions of tiny alveoli. Emphysema destroys the thin walls between alveoli, so many small sacs merge into a few large ones. The total surface where gases cross shrinks, and the change is structural and permanent.
notes: Inflamed, narrowed bronchioles describe asthma, a disease of the small airways. It would be the answer if the question asked why asthma causes wheezing.
Correct. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and shrinks the exchange surface.
Fluid filling inflamed alveoli describes pneumonia. It would be the answer if the patient had a lung infection rather than emphysema.
Air leaking into the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax. It would be the answer if the question described a collapsed lung after a chest injury.
questions.answerText: Alveolar walls are destroyed, merging small sacs into fewer large ones with less surface area

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A patient with pneumonia has trouble getting oxygen into the blood. Which structures fill with fluid in pneumonia?
options: Paranasal sinuses
Pleural cavity
Bronchioles
Alveoli
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli, the tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens, and fills them with fluid. Oxygen must cross from the air in the alveoli through the respiratory membrane into the blood. When the alveoli are filled with fluid instead of air, that exchange is impaired.
notes: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces in the skull bones that drain into the nasal cavity. They would be the answer if the question were about sinus congestion, not a lung infection.
The pleural cavity is the space between the two pleurae, outside the lung. It would be the answer if the question asked where air collects in a pneumothorax.
The bronchioles are small airways that narrow in asthma. They would be the answer if the question asked which airways constrict during an asthma attack.
Correct. Pneumonia fills the alveoli with fluid.
questions.answerText: Alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: During an asthma attack, a patient wheezes and struggles to move air. Which airways narrow the most, because they have no cartilage to hold them open?
options: Alveolar ducts
Bronchioles
Trachea
Main bronchi
questions.why: Asthma inflames the bronchi and bronchioles, and the narrowing is worst in the bronchioles. Bronchioles have smooth muscle in their walls and no cartilage, so when the lining swells and the muscle tightens, nothing holds them open. The trachea and main bronchi keep their cartilage, so they stay open while the bronchioles narrow, and the restricted airflow produces wheezing and breathlessness.
notes: Alveolar ducts belong to the respiratory zone and are lined with alveoli, not with the smooth muscle that narrows in asthma. They would be the answer if the question asked which passages lead into the alveolar sacs.
Correct. Bronchioles have no cartilage, so they narrow the most in asthma.

The trachea is held permanently open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, so it does not narrow the way bronchioles do. It would be the answer if the question asked which airway leads from the larynx to the main bronchi.

The main bronchi can be inflamed in asthma too, but their cartilage holds them open, so they do not narrow nearly as much as the bronchioles. They would be the answer if the question asked which airways branch from the trachea at the carina.
questions.answerText: Bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A premature infant's type II alveolar cells are not yet producing enough surfactant. What structural problem is most likely?
options: The alveoli are more likely to collapse
The bronchioles narrow and wheeze
The alveolar walls are destroyed
Air leaks into the pleural cavity
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells in the alveolar wall that secrete surfactant. Surfactant lowers surface tension, the inward pull of the thin film of water lining each alveolus. With too little surfactant that pull is stronger, so the alveoli are more likely to collapse.
notes: Correct. Without enough surfactant, the alveoli tend to collapse.
Narrowed, wheezing bronchioles describe asthma, a disease of the small airways rather than the alveoli. It would be the answer if the question described an asthma attack.
Destruction of the alveolar walls is emphysema, usually caused by years of smoking. It would be the answer if the question described a long-time smoker losing exchange surface.
Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax, caused by a puncture of the chest wall or lung. It would be the answer if the question described a chest wound.
questions.answerText: The alveoli are more likely to collapse

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Moving from the inside of the thoracic wall inward to the surface of the lung, in which order do you meet the pleural layers?
options: Parietal pleura, pleural cavity, visceral pleura
Pleural cavity, parietal pleura, visceral pleura
Visceral pleura, pleural cavity, parietal pleura
Parietal pleura, visceral pleura, pleural cavity
questions.why: The pleurae are serous membranes. The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, and the visceral pleura covers the outer surface of the lung. Between them is the pleural cavity, a thin, fluid-filled space that lets the lung glide as it expands.
notes: Correct. The parietal pleura is on the wall, the visceral pleura is on the lung, and the cavity lies between them.
This puts the pleural cavity against the thoracic wall. The parietal pleura is the layer that lines the wall, so it must come first, with the cavity just inside it.
This is the order from the lung outward to the chest wall, the reverse of the path asked. It would be correct if the question started at the lung surface.
This puts the pleural cavity outside both membranes. The cavity is the space between the two layers, so it cannot come after the visceral pleura on the lung.
questions.answerText: Parietal pleura, pleural cavity, visceral pleura

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Oxygen moves from the air in an alveolus into a pulmonary capillary. Which list names the layers of the respiratory membrane it crosses, in order?
options: Alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, capillary endothelium
Visceral pleura, pleural cavity, parietal pleura
Alveolar epithelium, smooth muscle, hyaline cartilage
Capillary endothelium, fused basement membranes, alveolar epithelium
questions.why: The respiratory membrane is the thin barrier between alveolar air and blood. Oxygen first crosses the alveolar epithelium (mostly flat type I cells), then the fused basement membranes of the alveolus and the capillary, and finally the capillary endothelium. Because each layer is so thin, gases cross quickly.
notes: Correct. Oxygen crosses the alveolar epithelium, the fused basement membranes, and the capillary endothelium.
The pleurae surround the whole lung and line the chest wall. They have nothing to do with gas exchange, so this list would fit a question about the coverings of the lung.

Smooth muscle and cartilage are found in the walls of the conducting airways, such as the bronchi. They would make the barrier far too thick for gas exchange, so this list describes an airway wall, not the respiratory membrane.
These are the right layers in the reverse order. This order would fit carbon dioxide moving from the blood into the alveolus.
questions.answerText: Alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, capillary endothelium

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which list names the parts of the lower respiratory tract?
options: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
Pharynx, larynx, trachea, and esophagus
Nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx
Larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs
questions.why: In this course the lower respiratory tract begins at the larynx and includes the trachea, the bronchi, and the lungs. These structures lie below the pharynx and carry air down into the chest, ending in the alveoli inside the lungs. The upper tract, by contrast, is the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx.
notes: The respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli are only the deepest part of the lungs, the respiratory zone. Choose this list if the question asked which structures carry out gas exchange.
This list mixes in the esophagus, which is a digestive organ, and the pharynx, which belongs to the upper tract. Students pick it because the esophagus runs right behind the trachea.
The nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx form the upper respiratory tract. Pick this list if the question asked for the parts of the upper tract.
Correct. The lower tract is the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs.
questions.answerText: Larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which airway, the windpipe, runs from the larynx to the carina and is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage?
options: Esophagus
Main bronchus
Trachea
Larynx
questions.why: The trachea is the windpipe, running from the bottom of the larynx down into the chest, where it forks at the carina. C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage keep it permanently open. The open part of each ring faces backward, where the trachealis muscle closes the gap against the esophagus.
notes: The esophagus is the food tube that lies just behind the trachea, against the trachealis muscle, with no cartilage rings. Choose it if the question asked which digestive tube runs behind the windpipe.
A main bronchus is one of the two branches the trachea splits into at the carina, each entering a lung. It would be the answer if the question asked which airway begins below the carina.
Correct. The trachea is the windpipe held open by C-shaped cartilage rings.
The larynx is the voice box above the trachea, built of nine separate cartilages rather than a stack of C-shaped rings. Pick it if the question asked which structure houses the vocal folds.
questions.answerText: Trachea

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which internal ridge marks the point where the trachea divides into the two main bronchi?
options: Cricoid cartilage
Cardiac notch
Hilum
Carina
questions.why: The carina is a ridge of cartilage inside the lower end of the trachea, right at the fork where the right and left main bronchi split off. It sits at the base of the trachea in the mediastinum. It marks the end of the trachea and the start of the bronchial tree.
notes: The cricoid cartilage is the complete ring of cartilage at the bottom of the larynx, above the trachea. It would be the answer if the question asked which cartilage is the only complete ring in the airway.
The cardiac notch is the indentation in the left lung that makes room for the heart. Choose it if the question asked which feature of the left lung accommodates the heart.
The hilum is the indentation on the medial surface of each lung where the bronchus and vessels enter. Pick it if the question asked where a main bronchus enters a lung.
Correct. The carina is the ridge where the trachea forks.
questions.answerText: Carina

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which bronchi, also called primary bronchi, branch from the trachea with one entering each lung?
options: Segmental bronchi
Main bronchi
Terminal bronchioles
Lobar bronchi
questions.why: The trachea splits at the carina into the right and left main bronchi, the first branches of the bronchial tree. Each one enters a lung at its hilum. The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left, which is why an inhaled object most often lands in the right lung.
notes: Segmental bronchi, or tertiary bronchi, branch from the lobar bronchi to supply each bronchopulmonary segment. They would be the answer if the question asked about the third level of branching.
Correct. The main (primary) bronchi branch from the trachea, one to each lung.

Terminal bronchioles are tiny airways at the very end of the conducting zone, many branchings after the main bronchi. Choose them if the question asked for the last conducting airways before gas exchange.
Lobar bronchi, or secondary bronchi, are the next branches, one for each lobe of a lung. Pick them if the question asked which bronchi supply individual lobes.
questions.answerText: Main bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which bronchi, also called secondary bronchi, each supply one lobe of a lung?
options: Segmental bronchi
Lobar bronchi
Respiratory bronchioles
Main bronchi
questions.why: Each main bronchus divides into lobar bronchi, one for each lobe. The right lung has three lobes, so it has three lobar bronchi, and the left lung has two lobes and two lobar bronchi. These are the second level of the bronchial tree, after the main bronchi and before the segmental bronchi.
notes: Segmental bronchi are the next level down, each supplying one bronchopulmonary segment within a lobe. They would be the answer if the question asked about the tertiary bronchi.
Correct. Lobar (secondary) bronchi supply one lobe each.
Respiratory bronchioles are tiny airways in the respiratory zone with alveoli budding from their walls. Choose them if the question asked which airways are the first to take part in gas exchange.
The main bronchi are the first branches off the trachea, one for each whole lung rather than each lobe. Pick them if the question asked which bronchi enter the lungs at the hilum.
questions.answerText: Lobar bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which bronchi, also called tertiary bronchi, each supply one bronchopulmonary segment?
options: Segmental bronchi
Bronchioles
Main bronchi
Lobar bronchi
questions.why: Segmental bronchi branch from the lobar bronchi, and each one supplies a bronchopulmonary segment, a wedge-shaped section of a lobe with its own air and blood supply. They are the third level of the bronchial tree. Below them the airways keep dividing until cartilage disappears and they become bronchioles.
notes: Correct. Segmental (tertiary) bronchi supply one bronchopulmonary segment each.
Bronchioles are smaller airways further down the tree, with smooth muscle and no cartilage. Choose them if the question asked which airways have lost their cartilage.
The main bronchi are the primary bronchi, the first branches off the trachea, one to each lung. They would be the answer if the question asked which bronchi begin at the carina.
Lobar bronchi are the secondary bronchi, one level higher, supplying a whole lobe. Pick them if the question asked which bronchi go to each lobe.
questions.answerText: Segmental bronchi

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which small conducting airways have smooth muscle in their walls but no cartilage?
options: Bronchioles
Segmental bronchi
Alveolar ducts
Trachea
questions.why: As the bronchial tree branches, cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases. By the bronchioles the cartilage is gone, and smooth muscle makes up much of the wall, so the muscle can narrow or widen the airway. Cartilage keeps the larger bronchi open, but bronchioles can narrow a great deal, which is why the narrowing in asthma is worst in the bronchioles.
notes: Correct. Bronchioles have smooth muscle and no cartilage.
Segmental bronchi still have cartilage plates in their walls, which keep them from collapsing. Pick them if the question asked which bronchi supply the bronchopulmonary segments.

Alveolar ducts are passages lined with alveoli in the respiratory zone, so they take part in gas exchange rather than just conducting air. Choose them if the question asked which passages are lined entirely with alveoli.

The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, the opposite of a cartilage-free wall. It would be the answer if the question asked which airway has the trachealis muscle across the back of its rings.
questions.answerText: Bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which airways are the last passages of the conducting zone, just before gas exchange begins?
options: Alveolar ducts
Segmental bronchi
Respiratory bronchioles
Terminal bronchioles
questions.why: Terminal bronchioles are the final branches of the conducting zone, the airways that carry air but do not exchange gases. Each one leads into respiratory bronchioles, where the first alveoli appear and the respiratory zone begins. Terminal means end, which points to their place at the end of the conducting airways.
notes: Alveolar ducts are passages lined entirely with alveoli, well inside the respiratory zone. Choose them if the question asked which passages lead into the alveolar sacs.
Segmental bronchi are much higher in the tree, still carrying cartilage and supplying whole bronchopulmonary segments. They would be the answer if the question asked for the tertiary bronchi.
Respiratory bronchioles are the next step, the first airways of the respiratory zone with a few alveoli on their walls. Pick them if the question asked where gas exchange begins.
Correct. Terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways.
questions.answerText: Terminal bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which airways are the first of the respiratory zone, with a few alveoli budding from their walls?
options: Alveolar sacs
Respiratory bronchioles
Alveolar ducts
Terminal bronchioles
questions.why: Respiratory bronchioles branch from the terminal bronchioles and mark the start of the respiratory zone. A few alveoli bud from their walls, so some gas exchange can happen there. Further along, the walls become lined entirely with alveoli in the alveolar ducts, which end in alveolar sacs.
notes: Alveolar sacs are clusters of alveoli sharing a common space at the very end of the airway. Choose them if the question asked which structure is a cluster of alveoli at the end of an alveolar duct.
Correct. Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways of the respiratory zone.

Alveolar ducts come after the respiratory bronchioles and are lined entirely with alveoli rather than having just a few. They would be the answer if the question asked which passages have walls made completely of alveoli.
Terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone, with no alveoli on their walls. Pick them if the question asked for the final conducting airways.
questions.answerText: Respiratory bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description matches the right lung?
options: Three lobes, with a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure
Three lobes, with an oblique fissure and a cardiac notch
Two lobes, with an oblique fissure and a cardiac notch
Two lobes, with a horizontal fissure only
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes, superior, middle, and inferior, separated by two fissures. The horizontal fissure separates the superior lobe from the middle lobe, and the oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from the lobes above it. The right lung is larger than the left because it does not have to make room for the heart, so it has no cardiac notch.
notes: Correct. The right lung has three lobes separated by horizontal and oblique fissures.

This mixes the two lungs: three lobes belong to the right lung, but the cardiac notch belongs to the left. Students choose it when they remember the lobe count but forget which side the heart pushes into.
Two lobes, an oblique fissure, and a cardiac notch describe the left lung. Pick this description if the question asked about the left lung.

No lung has two lobes with only a horizontal fissure, since the horizontal fissure is found only in the right lung, which has three lobes. Students choose it when they mix up which fissure each lung keeps.
questions.answerText: Three lobes, with a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description matches the left lung?
options: Two lobes, with a horizontal fissure and a cardiac notch
Two lobes, with an oblique fissure and a cardiac notch
Three lobes, with an oblique fissure and a cardiac notch
Three lobes, with a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure
questions.why: The left lung has two lobes, superior and inferior, separated by a single oblique fissure. It is smaller than the right lung because the heart tilts to the left, and its anterior border has a cardiac notch that makes room for the heart. Below the notch, a tongue-shaped piece of the superior lobe called the lingula curves around the heart.
notes: This gives the left lung the wrong fissure, since the horizontal fissure is found only in the right lung. Students choose it when they remember the cardiac notch but mix up which fissure each lung keeps.
Correct. The left lung has two lobes, an oblique fissure, and a cardiac notch.

This mixes the two lungs: the cardiac notch belongs to the left lung, but three lobes belong to the right. Students choose it when they remember the notch but forget that the left lung gives up a lobe to make room for the heart.
Three lobes with horizontal and oblique fissures describe the right lung. Pick this description if the question asked about the right lung.
questions.answerText: Two lobes, with an oblique fissure and a cardiac notch

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which indentation on the medial surface of each lung is where the main bronchus, blood vessels, and nerves enter and leave?
options: Lingula
Hilum
Apex
Cardiac notch
questions.why: The hilum is a depression on the medial surface of each lung, facing the mediastinum. The main bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, and lymphatics all pass through it. Bundled together at the hilum, these structures are called the root of the lung.
notes: The lingula is the tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe below the cardiac notch. Choose it if the question asked about the small extension of the left lung that curves around the heart.
Correct. The hilum is where the bronchus, vessels, and nerves enter and leave the lung.
The apex is the narrow superior tip of the lung, rising just above the clavicle. It would be the answer if the question asked for the top of the lung.

The cardiac notch is an indentation in the anterior border of the left lung that makes room for the heart, and nothing enters the lung there. Pick it if the question asked which feature accommodates the heart.
questions.answerText: Hilum

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which serous membrane lines the inner surface of the thoracic wall around each lung?
options: Parietal peritoneum
Parietal pericardium
Parietal pleura
Visceral pleura
questions.why: The pleura is the serous membrane around each lung, and like other serous membranes it has two layers. The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall, while the visceral pleura covers the lung itself. Parietal always refers to the layer on the body wall and visceral to the layer on the organ.
notes: The parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominopelvic cavity, below the diaphragm. Choose it if the question asked which membrane lines the abdominal wall.
The parietal pericardium is the serous layer lining the fibrous pericardium around the heart. It would be the answer if the question asked about the outer serous layer of the heart's sac.
Correct. The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall.
The visceral pleura covers the outer surface of the lung itself rather than the chest wall. Pick it if the question asked which membrane is attached directly to the lung.
questions.answerText: Parietal pleura

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the thin, fluid-filled space between the parietal and visceral pleurae called?
options: Pericardial cavity
Thoracic cavity
Pleural cavity
Mediastinum
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the narrow, sealed space between the parietal pleura on the chest wall and the visceral pleura on the lung. It holds only a thin film of serous fluid, which lets the lung glide as it expands and keeps the two layers stuck together. If air gets into this space, the seal is lost and the lung can collapse.
notes: The pericardial cavity is the fluid space between the layers of the serous pericardium around the heart. It would be the answer if the question asked about the space around the heart rather than the lungs.

The thoracic cavity is the whole chest cavity, which contains both pleural cavities and the mediastinum. Choose it if the question asked for the large cavity above the diaphragm, not the thin space between two membranes.
Correct. The pleural cavity is the fluid-filled space between the pleurae.
The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thorax between the two lungs, holding the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus. Pick it if the question asked where the heart sits.
questions.answerText: Pleural cavity

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which alveolar cells are thin and flat (simple squamous) and form most of the alveolar wall where gases cross?
options: Alveolar macrophages
Type I alveolar cells
Type II alveolar cells
Goblet cells
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are extremely thin, flat cells that make up most of the alveolar wall. Being so thin keeps the distance between the air and the blood very short, which is exactly what gas exchange needs. They form the epithelial part of the respiratory membrane.
notes: Alveolar macrophages are wandering immune cells, the dust cells, that engulf debris on the alveolar surface. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells clean the alveoli.
Correct. Type I alveolar cells form the thin wall where gases cross.
Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells scattered among the type I cells, and they secrete surfactant. Pick them if the question asked which cells keep the alveoli from collapsing.

Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells in the respiratory mucosa of the larger airways, not in the alveolar wall. Choose them if the question asked which cells produce the mucus that traps particles in the conducting passages.
questions.answerText: Type I alveolar cells

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which alveolar cells are cuboidal and secrete surfactant, which keeps the alveoli from collapsing?
options: Type I alveolar cells
Goblet cells
Type II alveolar cells
Alveolar macrophages
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells scattered among the flat type I cells of the alveolar wall. They secrete surfactant, a fluid that lowers surface tension, meaning the pull of water molecules on each other that would otherwise make the tiny sacs stick shut. Without enough surfactant the alveoli tend to collapse.
notes: Type I alveolar cells are the thin, flat cells that form most of the alveolar wall and do not secrete surfactant. Pick them if the question asked which cells form the surface where gases cross.
Goblet cells secrete mucus in the conducting airways, not surfactant in the alveoli. Choose them if the question asked which cells add mucus to the respiratory mucosa.
Correct. Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant.
Alveolar macrophages are immune cells that engulf dust and debris in the alveoli. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells are called dust cells.
questions.answerText: Type II alveolar cells

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which cells, often called dust cells, patrol the alveolar surface and engulf debris?
options: Goblet cells
Type I alveolar cells
Alveolar macrophages
Type II alveolar cells
questions.why: Alveolar macrophages are immune cells that move over the inner surface of the alveoli and engulf dust, microbes, and other debris that reach that far. They are needed because the alveoli are beyond the reach of the mucus and cilia that clean the conducting airways. Their nickname, dust cells, comes from this cleanup job.
notes: Goblet cells secrete mucus in the larger airways, where mucus and cilia trap and sweep away particles. Choose them if the question asked which cells help clean the conducting zone rather than the alveoli.
Type I alveolar cells are the flat cells forming most of the alveolar wall, built for gas exchange rather than cleanup. Pick them if the question asked which cells form the surface gases cross.
Correct. Alveolar macrophages are the dust cells of the alveoli.
Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells keep the alveoli from collapsing.
questions.answerText: Alveolar macrophages

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which disorder is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, causing wheezing and breathlessness?
options: Pneumothorax
Emphysema
Asthma
Pneumonia
questions.why: Asthma is a disorder of the small airways. The bronchioles have smooth muscle and no cartilage, so when they are inflamed and their smooth muscle tightens, they narrow and air has trouble moving through. The narrowed airways produce the wheezing and breathlessness of an asthma attack.
notes: A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that lets a lung collapse. Choose it if the question described a chest wound or a collapsed lung.
Emphysema destroys the alveolar walls rather than narrowing the bronchioles. Pick it if the question asked about the disorder that reduces the surface for gas exchange.
Correct. Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles.
Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid. It would be the answer if the question described inflamed, fluid-filled air sacs.
questions.answerText: Asthma

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which disorder destroys the alveolar walls, merging many small air sacs into fewer large ones and reducing the surface for gas exchange?
options: Emphysema
Pneumonia
Asthma
Lung cancer
questions.why: In emphysema the walls between neighboring alveoli break down, so many small sacs merge into a few large ones. Many small sacs have far more total surface than a few large ones, so the area available for gas exchange shrinks. The change is structural and permanent, and emphysema is one of the conditions grouped as COPD.
notes: Correct. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and shrinks the exchange surface.
Pneumonia inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid from infection, without permanently destroying their walls. It would be the answer if the question described infected, fluid-filled alveoli.
Asthma narrows the bronchioles through inflammation and smooth muscle tightening, leaving the alveolar walls intact. Pick it if the question asked about wheezing from narrowed small airways.
Lung cancer is a malignant tumor of lung tissue. Choose it if the question asked about a tumor strongly linked to smoking.
questions.answerText: Emphysema

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which disorder is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid?
options: Asthma
Pneumonia
Emphysema
Pneumothorax
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection of the lung in which the alveoli become inflamed and fill with fluid. Fluid in the air sacs blocks air from reaching the thin alveolar wall, so less gas can cross into the blood. The structure affected is the alveolus, the same site where gas exchange normally happens.
notes: Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, not an infection of the alveoli. Pick it if the question described wheezing from tightened small airways.
Correct. Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid.
Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, enlarging the air sacs rather than filling them with fluid. Choose it if the question asked about the permanent loss of exchange surface.
A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, outside the lung, that lets the lung collapse. It would be the answer if the question described a punctured chest wall.
questions.answerText: Pneumonia

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which disorder is air in the pleural cavity, which breaks the seal and lets the lung collapse?
options: Pneumonia
Emphysema
Pneumothorax
Pulmonary embolism
questions.why: Normally the pleural cavity is a sealed space holding only a thin film of fluid, which keeps the lung pressed against the chest wall. If the chest wall or the lung is punctured, air enters this space and the seal is lost. The lung then pulls away from the wall and collapses, which is a pneumothorax (pneumo means air, thorax means chest).
notes: Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid, inside the lung rather than in the pleural cavity. Pick it if the question described infected, fluid-filled air sacs.
Emphysema is destruction of the alveolar walls, which happens inside the lung tissue. Choose it if the question asked about the permanent loss of exchange surface.
Correct. Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax.

A pulmonary embolism is a clot lodged in an artery of the lung, a vessel problem rather than air in the pleural cavity. It would be the answer if the question described a leg clot that traveled to the lungs.
questions.answerText: Pneumothorax

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which disorder is a malignant tumor of the lung tissue, strongly linked to smoking?
options: Pneumonia
Emphysema
Lung cancer
COPD
questions.why: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor, meaning a growth of abnormal cells that can invade nearby tissue and spread. It arises in the lung tissue and is strongly linked to smoking. Smoking is also linked to COPD and emphysema, so the word tumor is what points to lung cancer here.
notes: Pneumonia is an infection that fills the alveoli with fluid. Choose it if the question described inflamed, infected air sacs.
Emphysema is the destruction of alveolar walls, which is also linked to smoking but involves no tumor. It would be the answer if the question described enlarged air sacs and lost exchange surface.
Correct. Lung cancer is a malignant tumor of the lung.
COPD is a long-term blockage of airflow that includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis, not a tumor. Pick it if the question asked for the umbrella term for chronic obstructive airway disease.
questions.answerText: Lung cancer

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Oxygen moving from the air in an alveolus into the blood must cross which thin barrier?
options: Visceral pleura
Respiratory membrane
Respiratory mucosa
Bronchiole wall
questions.why: The respiratory membrane is the very thin barrier between alveolar air and the blood in the pulmonary capillaries. It has three parts: the alveolar epithelium (mostly flat type I cells), the fused basement membranes of the alveolus and the capillary, and the capillary endothelium. Its thinness is what makes gas exchange possible.
notes: The visceral pleura is the serous membrane covering the outside of the lung, not the barrier inside each alveolus. Pick it if the question asked which membrane covers the lung surface.
Correct. Oxygen crosses the respiratory membrane to reach the blood.

The respiratory mucosa is the ciliated, mucus-producing lining of the nasal cavity and conducting airways, which filters air rather than exchanging gases. It would be the answer if the question asked which lining traps particles and sweeps them toward the pharynx.
The bronchiole wall belongs to the conducting zone, so air passes along it without gases crossing into the blood. Choose it if the question asked which airway wall has smooth muscle and no cartilage.
questions.answerText: Respiratory membrane

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces air from the trachea to the sites of gas exchange?
options: Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli
Trachea, lobar bronchi, main bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli
Trachea, main bronchi, segmental bronchi, lobar bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli
Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli
questions.why: The bronchial tree branches from large to small. The trachea splits into main bronchi (one per lung), then lobar bronchi (one per lobe), then segmental bronchi (one per bronchopulmonary segment), then bronchioles that lose their cartilage. The terminal bronchioles end the conducting zone, and the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli form the respiratory zone where gases are exchanged.
notes: This sequence swaps the terminal and respiratory bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways, so they come before the respiratory bronchioles, where the first alveoli appear.
This sequence puts the lobar bronchi before the main bronchi. The trachea first splits into the two main bronchi, and only then does each main bronchus divide into lobar bronchi.
This sequence swaps the lobar and segmental bronchi. Lobar bronchi supply whole lobes and must come first, before the segmental bronchi divide each lobe into segments.
Correct. Air passes through each level of the bronchial tree in this order, from largest to smallest.
