questions.answerText: Trachea, main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A child inhales a small bead, and it lodges in the right lung. Which feature of the airway best explains why?
options: The left lung has a cardiac notch
The right bronchus is wider and more vertical
The right main bronchus is longer and narrower
The right lung has three lobes
questions.why: The trachea forks at the carina into the right and left main bronchi. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, almost in line with the trachea, while the left is narrower and angles off more sharply. An inhaled object falling down the trachea follows the straighter, wider path, so it most often lands in the right lung.
notes: The cardiac notch is the indentation in the left lung that makes room for the heart. It answers a question about why the left lung is smaller, but it does not steer objects into the right bronchus.
Correct. The wider, more vertical right main bronchus is the easier path for an inhaled object.
This reverses the real anatomy. The left main bronchus is the longer, narrower, more horizontal one, which is why objects are less likely to enter it.

The right lung does have three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior), but lobes are divisions of lung tissue beyond the main bronchus. Pick this for a question about how many lobes or fissures the right lung has, not about where an object enters.
questions.answerText: The right bronchus is wider and more vertical

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A patient's bronchioles become inflamed and narrowed, causing wheezing and breathlessness. Which disorder fits?
options: Emphysema
Asthma
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
questions.why: Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles, the small conducting airways. Bronchioles have smooth muscle in their walls and no cartilage, so they can constrict. When they narrow, air has to squeeze through, which produces the whistling sound of wheezing and makes breathing hard.
notes: Emphysema is permanent destruction of the alveolar walls, which shrinks the surface for gas exchange. Choose it when the damage is in the alveoli rather than the airways leading to them.
Correct. Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles.
Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid. Pick it for fluid-filled air sacs, not tightened bronchioles.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that breaks the seal and lets the lung collapse. It would be the answer for a collapsed lung after a chest wall puncture, not narrowed airways.
questions.answerText: Asthma

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In a long-term smoker, many alveolar walls are destroyed and small air sacs merge into a few large ones. Which disorder fits?
options: Asthma
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
Emphysema
questions.why: Emphysema is destruction of the alveolar walls. As the thin walls between neighboring alveoli break down, many small sacs merge into fewer large ones, which greatly reduces the surface area available for gas exchange. The damage is structural and permanent, and emphysema is one of the conditions grouped under COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).
notes: Asthma narrows the bronchioles through inflammation, and the airways can open again with treatment. Choose it for wheezing from narrowed small airways, not for destroyed alveoli.
Pneumonia is an infection that fills alveoli with fluid. The alveoli are inflamed but not merged into larger sacs, so pick it for an infection with fluid-filled air spaces.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse. It affects the space around the lung, so choose it for a punctured chest wall rather than damaged alveolar walls.
Correct. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and merges small sacs into larger ones.
questions.answerText: Emphysema

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: An infection inflames a patient's alveoli and fills them with fluid. Which disorder fits?
options: Emphysema
Lung cancer
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection of the lung that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid. Alveoli are meant to hold air pressed against a very thin wall, so fluid inside them gets in the way of gas exchange. Unlike in emphysema, the air sacs are still structurally present, but they are flooded.
notes: Emphysema is permanent destruction of alveolar walls, not an infection. Choose it when the alveoli have broken down and merged, usually after years of smoking.
Lung cancer is a malignant tumor of the lung tissue, strongly linked to smoking. It would be the answer for an abnormal growth, not for infected, fluid-filled air sacs.
Correct. Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid.
Pneumothorax is air, not fluid, in the pleural cavity around the lung, which makes the lung collapse. Pick it for a punctured chest wall or lung.
questions.answerText: Pneumonia

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A stab wound lets air into the space between the parietal and visceral pleurae. Which disorder fits?
options: Pneumothorax
Emphysema
Pneumonia
Cardiac tamponade
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin space between the parietal pleura on the chest wall and the visceral pleura on the lung, and it normally holds only a sealed film of fluid. When air enters this space, the seal is broken, the lung is no longer held out against the chest wall, and it collapses. Air in the pleural cavity is called a pneumothorax (pneumo means air, thorax means chest).
notes: Correct. Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax, and it lets the lung collapse.
Emphysema is destruction of the alveolar walls over many years. It is not caused by a wound and does not involve air entering the pleural cavity.
Pneumonia is infection inside the alveoli, which fill with fluid. It is inside the lung, so pick it when the problem is in the air sacs rather than the space around the lung.

Cardiac tamponade is fluid building up in the pericardial cavity around the heart. It is the matching problem for the heart's serous sac, so choose it when the heart rather than the lung is being compressed.
questions.answerText: Pneumothorax

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A premature infant's lungs do not yet make enough surfactant. What problem with the alveoli becomes likely?
options: The alveoli fill with infected fluid
The alveolar walls are destroyed
Air leaks into the pleural cavity
The alveoli tend to collapse
questions.why: Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells and lowers the surface tension of the thin fluid film lining each alveolus. Without enough of it, that surface tension pulls the tiny alveolar walls inward and the air sacs tend to collapse. Premature infants, whose lungs have not yet made enough surfactant, can have serious trouble keeping their alveoli open for this reason.
notes: Infected fluid in the alveoli describes pneumonia. Pick it for an infection, not for missing surfactant.
Destruction of alveolar walls describes emphysema, usually from years of smoking. It is permanent damage to the walls, not a failure to keep them open.
Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax, which collapses the whole lung from outside. Surfactant works inside each alveolus, so its absence does not let air into the pleural space.
Correct. Without enough surfactant, the alveoli tend to collapse.
questions.answerText: The alveoli tend to collapse

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Type I alveolar cells are damaged. Which alveolar job is most directly impaired?
options: Warming and moistening incoming air
Secretion of surfactant
Gas diffusion across the wall
Engulfing inhaled debris
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are thin, flat simple squamous cells that form most of the alveolar wall. Their thinness keeps the distance between air and blood very short, and they are part of the respiratory membrane that gases cross. When they are damaged, that barrier is disrupted and gases cannot move across the wall as easily.
notes: Warming and moistening air happens in the conducting zone, especially the nasal cavity with its conchae and moist mucosa. It is not an alveolar job, so pick it for a question about the upper airway.
Secreting surfactant is the job of type II alveolar cells, the cuboidal cells scattered among the type I cells. Pick it for a question about type II cell damage.
Correct. Type I cells form the thin wall that gases cross.
Engulfing debris is the job of alveolar macrophages, the dust cells that patrol the alveolar surface. Choose it when those immune cells fail.
questions.answerText: Gas diffusion across the wall

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Type II alveolar cells are damaged. What is most directly reduced?
options: Surfactant secretion
Pleural fluid production
Mucus secretion
Gas diffusion across the wall
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells scattered among the flat type I cells of the alveolar wall. Their job is to secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension and keeps the alveoli from collapsing. Damage to them most directly reduces surfactant, which in turn makes alveolar collapse more likely.
notes: Correct. Type II alveolar cells are the cells that secrete surfactant.

Pleural fluid is the thin film of serous fluid between the parietal and visceral pleurae, made by those serous membranes. Choose it for a question about what lets the lung glide against the chest wall.

Mucus is secreted by goblet cells in the pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium of the conducting airways, such as the nasal cavity and trachea. Pick it for a question about trapping particles in the upper airways.
Gas diffusion depends mainly on the thin type I cells that form most of the alveolar wall. It would be the answer if the question said type I cells were damaged.
questions.answerText: Surfactant secretion

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A patient's alveolar macrophages stop working. Which defense in the alveoli is weakened?
options: Removal of inhaled debris and microbes
Prevention of alveolar collapse
Sweeping of mucus toward the pharynx
Filtering of large particles by nasal hairs
questions.why: Alveolar macrophages, often called dust cells, are immune cells that patrol the alveolar surface and engulf debris and microbes. The alveoli lie beyond the mucus and cilia of the conducting airways, so whatever reaches them must be cleared by these cells. If the macrophages fail, inhaled particles and germs that make it this deep are not removed.
notes: Correct. Alveolar macrophages engulf debris and microbes that reach the alveoli.
Preventing alveolar collapse is the job of surfactant from type II alveolar cells. It would be the answer if type II cells failed, not macrophages.

Sweeping mucus toward the pharynx is done by the cilia of the respiratory mucosa lining the conducting airways. Pick it for damage to the ciliated lining of the nasal cavity, trachea, or bronchi, not the alveoli.
Coarse hairs in the nasal vestibule, just inside the nostrils, filter the largest particles. Choose it for a question about the first filter at the entrance of the nose.
questions.answerText: Removal of inhaled debris and microbes

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A lesion is found along the edge of the cardiac notch. Which lobe of which lung contains it?
options: Right middle lobe
Right superior lobe
Left superior lobe
Left inferior lobe
questions.why: The cardiac notch is the indentation in the anterior border of the left lung that makes room for the heart. Only the left lung has one, and it is cut into the superior lobe, with the tongue-shaped lingula hanging just below it. A lesion along the edge of the notch is therefore in the left superior lobe.
notes: The right middle lobe sits against the right side of the heart and has no notch, because the heart lies mostly to the left. Pick it for a question about the lobe that only the right lung has, between the horizontal and oblique fissures.
The right superior lobe lies above the horizontal fissure of the right lung, and the right lung has no cardiac notch. Choose it for a lesion near the apex of the right lung.
Correct. The cardiac notch is cut into the anterior border of the left superior lobe.
The left inferior lobe lies below the oblique fissure and rests on the diaphragm. It would be the answer for a lesion at the base of the left lung, not along the cardiac notch.
questions.answerText: Left superior lobe

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A lesion is found in the middle lobe of a lung. Which lung must it be, and why?
options: The left lung, because its middle lobe sits beside the heart
The right lung, because it has the cardiac notch
Either lung, because both have three lobes
The right lung, because only it has three lobes
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes, superior, middle, and inferior, separated by a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure. The left lung has only two lobes, superior and inferior, separated by a single oblique fissure, because it gives up room for the heart. A middle lobe therefore exists only in the right lung.
notes: The left lung has only a superior and an inferior lobe. The tongue-shaped lingula of its superior lobe sits roughly where a middle lobe would be, which is why students sometimes mistake it for one.
The right lung does contain the middle lobe, but the cardiac notch is on the left lung. Pick the cardiac notch for a question about which lung makes room for the heart.
Only the right lung has three lobes; the left has two. This choice comes from assuming the lungs are mirror images, when the left lung is smaller to make room for the heart.
Correct. Only the right lung has a middle lobe.
questions.answerText: The right lung, because only it has three lobes

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: An airway is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, with smooth muscle closing the gap at the back. Which airway is it?
options: Bronchiole
Alveolar duct
Larynx
Trachea
questions.why: The trachea, or windpipe, is held permanently open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage. The open part of each C faces posteriorly, where the trachealis muscle closes the gap against the esophagus. The rings keep the airway from collapsing, while the soft back wall lets the esophagus expand when food passes.
notes: Bronchioles are small airways with smooth muscle walls and no cartilage at all. Choose them when the question describes an airway that can constrict because cartilage is absent.
Alveolar ducts are passages in the respiratory zone whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli. They have no cartilage rings and would be the answer for an airway made almost entirely of air sacs.

The larynx is built of nine separate cartilages, including the shield-shaped thyroid cartilage and the complete ring of the cricoid cartilage. Pick it for an airway with vocal folds rather than a stack of repeating C-shaped rings.
Correct. C-shaped cartilage rings closed posteriorly by the trachealis muscle mark the trachea.
questions.answerText: Trachea

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A small airway has a wall of smooth muscle with no cartilage, and no alveoli bud from it. Which airway is it?
options: Bronchiole
Respiratory bronchiole
Segmental bronchus
Trachea
questions.why: Moving down the bronchial tree, cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases. The bronchioles are where cartilage disappears entirely, and smooth muscle makes up much of their wall. Because no alveoli bud from its wall, this airway is still a conducting passage rather than part of the respiratory zone.
notes: Correct. Bronchioles have smooth muscle walls with no cartilage and no alveoli.
Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways of the respiratory zone, with a few alveoli budding from their walls. They would be the answer if the question mentioned alveoli on the wall.
Segmental bronchi, the tertiary bronchi, still have plates of cartilage in their walls. Pick them for the airway that supplies one bronchopulmonary segment.
The trachea is the large airway held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage. Choose it for an airway with cartilage rings, the opposite of this description.
questions.answerText: Bronchiole

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: An airway has a few alveoli budding from its wall, but its wall is not yet lined entirely with alveoli. Which airway is it?
options: Alveolar sac
Terminal bronchiole
Respiratory bronchiole
Alveolar duct
questions.why: Respiratory bronchioles are the first airways of the respiratory zone, the part of the lungs where gas exchange happens. They branch from the terminal bronchioles and have scattered alveoli budding from their walls. Farther along, the alveolar ducts are lined entirely with alveoli, so a few scattered alveoli mark the respiratory bronchiole.
notes: An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli that share a common space at the end of an alveolar duct. It would be the answer for a grapelike cluster at the very end of the airway.
Terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone and have no alveoli on their walls. Pick them for the final airway before gas exchange begins.
Correct. A few scattered alveoli on the wall mark a respiratory bronchiole.
Alveolar ducts are passages whose walls are lined entirely with alveoli. Choose them when the wall is made of air sacs all the way around, not just a few scattered ones.
questions.answerText: Respiratory bronchiole

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A student says gas exchange begins in the terminal bronchioles. Where does it actually begin?
options: In the respiratory bronchioles
In the terminal bronchioles
In the segmental bronchi
Only in the alveolar sacs
questions.why: The airways are divided into a conducting zone, which only carries air, and a respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens. The terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone. Gas exchange begins in the next airways, the respiratory bronchioles, because they are the first to have alveoli budding from their walls.
notes: Correct. The respiratory bronchioles are the first airways with alveoli, so exchange begins there.
This is the student's mistake. Terminal bronchioles are the last conducting airways and have no alveoli, so choose them for a question about where the conducting zone ends.
Segmental bronchi are well up in the conducting zone and are still supported by cartilage. Pick them for a question about the airway that supplies one bronchopulmonary segment.

Alveolar sacs are a major site of exchange, but they are not the first. Exchange starts wherever alveoli first appear, beginning with the respiratory bronchioles and continuing through the alveolar ducts.
questions.answerText: In the respiratory bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A student says the pleural cavity normally contains air. What does it actually contain?
options: Mucus from goblet cells
A thin film of serous fluid
Nothing at all, like a vacuum
Air that has passed through the alveoli
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin space between the parietal pleura, which lines the chest wall, and the visceral pleura, which covers the lung. It is sealed and normally holds only a thin film of serous fluid, which lets the lung glide against the chest wall as it expands. Air belongs inside the airways and alveoli, and air in the pleural cavity is a disorder called a pneumothorax.
notes: Mucus is made by goblet cells in the lining of the conducting airways to trap particles. Choose it for a question about the respiratory mucosa of the nasal cavity or trachea, not a serous space.
Correct. The pleural cavity normally holds only a thin film of serous fluid.
The pleural cavity is a very narrow space, but it is not empty. Its thin fluid film is what lets the two pleural layers slide smoothly against each other.
Air belongs inside the lung, in the airways and alveoli. If air gets into the pleural cavity, the seal is lost and the lung collapses, which is a pneumothorax.
questions.answerText: A thin film of serous fluid

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does emphysema reduce how much oxygen reaches the blood?
options: Lost alveolar walls leave less exchange surface
Narrowed bronchioles block air from reaching the alveoli
Air in the pleural cavity collapses the lung
Fluid fills the alveoli and blocks diffusion
questions.why: Emphysema destroys the thin walls between alveoli, so many small air sacs merge into a few large ones. Gas exchange happens across the alveolar walls, and many small sacs provide far more wall surface than a few large ones. Losing that surface leaves less area for oxygen to cross into the blood, and the loss is permanent.
notes: Correct. Emphysema shrinks the exchange surface by destroying alveolar walls.
Narrowed bronchioles describe asthma, a problem of the conducting airways. Pick it for wheezing from tightened small airways, not destroyed alveoli.
Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax, which collapses the lung from outside. It would be the answer for a punctured chest wall, not damage to the alveolar walls.
Fluid-filled alveoli describe pneumonia, an infection. Choose it when the air sacs are flooded rather than destroyed.
questions.answerText: Lost alveolar walls leave less exchange surface

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does pneumonia reduce how much oxygen reaches the blood?
options: The alveolar walls are permanently destroyed
The bronchioles constrict and narrow
Fluid and inflammation fill the alveoli
The pleural seal breaks and the lung collapses
questions.why: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid. Normally the alveoli hold air right against a very thin wall wrapped in capillaries, so oxygen has only a short distance to travel. Fluid and inflammation keep air from reaching much of that surface, so less oxygen crosses into the blood.
notes: Permanent destruction of alveolar walls describes emphysema. Choose it when the exchange surface itself has been lost, usually after years of smoking.
Constricted bronchioles describe asthma, which narrows the conducting airways. Pick it for wheezing and difficulty moving air, not fluid-filled alveoli.
Correct. Fluid in inflamed alveoli keeps air away from the exchange surface.
A broken pleural seal is a pneumothorax, which collapses the lung from outside. It would be the answer for air entering the pleural cavity.
questions.answerText: Fluid and inflammation fill the alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does asthma mainly affect airflow rather than the gas exchange surface itself?
options: It narrows bronchioles, which only conduct air
It collapses the lung from the outside
It fills the alveoli with fluid
It destroys the alveoli, which only conduct air
questions.why: Asthma is inflammation and narrowing of the bronchioles. Bronchioles belong to the conducting zone, the airways that carry air to the alveoli but do not exchange gases themselves. Narrowing them makes it hard to move air in and out, while the alveoli, the actual exchange surface, are left structurally intact.
notes: Correct. Asthma targets conducting airways, so it limits airflow while the alveoli stay intact.
Collapsing the lung from outside describes a pneumothorax, air in the pleural cavity. Choose it when the pleural seal is broken, not when the airways narrow.
Fluid in the alveoli describes pneumonia, which affects the exchange surface directly. Pick it for an infection that floods the air sacs.
This mixes up two things. Destroying alveoli describes emphysema, and alveoli are the exchange surface of the respiratory zone, not conducting airways.
questions.answerText: It narrows bronchioles, which only conduct air

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does air entering the pleural cavity make the lung collapse?
options: It fills the alveoli and pushes them apart
It breaks the pleural seal that holds the lung out
It narrows the bronchioles so air cannot enter
It destroys the type II cells that make surfactant
questions.why: The pleural cavity is a sealed space between the parietal pleura on the chest wall and the visceral pleura on the lung, and it holds only a thin film of fluid. That sealed film keeps the lung surface held against the chest wall, so the lung expands when the chest expands. When air gets in, the seal is broken, the lung is no longer held out, and it collapses. This is a pneumothorax.
notes: Air in the pleural cavity is outside the lung, not inside the alveoli. Air belongs in the alveoli normally, so this choice mixes up the pleural cavity with the air spaces.
Correct. Air breaks the pleural seal, so the lung is no longer held out and collapses.
Narrowed bronchioles describe asthma, which limits airflow but leaves the pleural seal intact. Choose it for wheezing, not a collapsed lung.
Loss of type II cells reduces surfactant and lets individual alveoli collapse. Pick it for a question about premature infants or surfactant, not for air in the pleural space.
questions.answerText: It breaks the pleural seal that holds the lung out

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does the respiratory membrane need to be extremely thin?
options: To keep the path for diffusing gases short
To warm and moisten the incoming air
To trap dust before it reaches the blood
To keep the alveoli from collapsing
questions.why: The respiratory membrane is the barrier between the air in an alveolus and the blood in a pulmonary capillary. It is made of the alveolar epithelium (mostly thin type I cells), fused basement membranes, and the capillary endothelium. Gases cross it by diffusion, which is fast only over very short distances, so the thinner the membrane, the more easily oxygen and carbon dioxide can pass.
notes: Correct. A thin membrane keeps the path for diffusing gases very short.
Warming and moistening air happens in the conducting zone, especially the nasal cavity with its conchae and moist mucosa. It is the answer for a question about conditioning air in the nose.

Trapping dust is the job of mucus in the conducting airways and of alveolar macrophages in the alveoli. A thin membrane does nothing to trap particles, so choose those defenses for a question about cleaning the air.
Keeping alveoli from collapsing is the job of surfactant from type II alveolar cells. Pick surfactant for a question about what keeps the air sacs open.
questions.answerText: To keep the path for diffusing gases short

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the job of the thin film of fluid in the pleural cavity?
options: It cushions the heart as it beats
It lets the lungs glide smoothly as they expand
It traps inhaled particles before they reach the alveoli
It carries oxygen from the alveoli to the blood
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin space between the parietal pleura, which lines the chest wall, and the visceral pleura, which covers the lung. Its film of serous fluid reduces friction, so the two layers slide smoothly past each other each time the lungs expand and recoil. The sealed film also keeps the lung surface held against the chest wall, which is why air entering this space lets the lung collapse.
notes: The fluid that lets the heart beat with little friction is in the pericardial cavity, the matching serous space around the heart. Pick the pericardial cavity for a question about the heart.
Correct. The pleural fluid reduces friction so the lung glides against the chest wall.
Trapping inhaled particles is done by mucus and cilia in the conducting airways. Choose the respiratory mucosa for a question about filtering air.
Oxygen moves from the alveoli into the blood across the respiratory membrane, not through the pleural fluid. Pick the respiratory membrane for a question about where gases cross.
questions.answerText: It lets the lungs glide smoothly as they expand

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why are the bronchioles the airways that regulate airflow?
options: Their alveoli can expand to pull in air
Their smooth muscle can change their diameter
Their cilia can push air toward the lungs
Their C-shaped cartilage rings can open and close
questions.why: As the bronchial tree branches, cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases, and at the bronchioles the cartilage disappears entirely. With no cartilage and smooth muscle making up much of the wall, bronchioles can constrict to narrow the airway or relax to widen it. Cartilage keeps the larger bronchi open, so they cannot narrow nearly as much, which is why the narrowing in asthma is worst in the bronchioles.
notes: Alveoli are the air sacs of the respiratory zone, where gas exchange happens. Bronchioles of the conducting zone have no alveoli, so choose alveoli for a question about the exchange surface.
Correct. Smooth muscle without cartilage lets bronchioles narrow or widen.
Cilia sweep mucus and trapped particles toward the pharynx; they do not move air or change airway size. Pick them for a question about clearing debris from the conducting airways.
C-shaped cartilage rings are found in the trachea, and their job is to hold the airway permanently open, not to adjust it. Pick them for a question about what keeps the trachea from collapsing.
questions.answerText: Their smooth muscle can change their diameter

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why don't the terminal bronchioles exchange gases with the blood?
options: They are conducting airways with no alveoli
They lie beyond the respiratory zone
They are lined only by alveolar macrophages
Their walls are reinforced with cartilage rings
questions.why: The terminal bronchioles are the last airways of the conducting zone, the passages that only carry air. Gas exchange needs alveoli, the thin-walled air sacs wrapped in capillaries, and the terminal bronchioles have none in their walls. Exchange begins in the next airways, the respiratory bronchioles, which have the first alveoli budding from them.
notes: Correct. Without alveoli, the terminal bronchioles only carry air.
This reverses the order. Terminal bronchioles come just before the respiratory zone, which starts with the respiratory bronchioles and continues through the alveolar ducts and alveoli.
Alveolar macrophages are dust cells that patrol the alveoli, not a lining of the terminal bronchioles. Pick them for a question about clearing debris from the alveolar surface.
Cartilage has already disappeared by the bronchiole level, so terminal bronchioles have smooth muscle walls, not cartilage rings. C-shaped rings belong to the trachea.
questions.answerText: They are conducting airways with no alveoli

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why is each alveolus wrapped in a dense net of pulmonary capillaries?
options: To supply the bronchi with oxygen-rich blood
To produce surfactant for the alveolar wall
To hold the lung against the chest wall
To bring blood close to alveolar air
questions.why: Gas exchange happens by diffusion, which works only across very short distances. Wrapping each alveolus in pulmonary capillaries brings the blood extremely close to the air, separated only by the thin respiratory membrane. With hundreds of millions of alveoli, this arrangement gives the blood an enormous surface over which to pick up oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
notes: The walls of the bronchi and other lung tissue get their own blood from the bronchial vessels, part of the root of the lung. Pick the bronchial vessels for a question about feeding the lung tissue itself.
Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells in the alveolar wall, not by capillaries. Choose type II cells for a question about what keeps alveoli from collapsing.
The lung is held against the chest wall by the sealed pleural cavity and its thin film of fluid. Pick the pleurae for a question about how the lung follows the chest wall as it expands.
Correct. The capillary net puts blood right against the alveolar air.
questions.answerText: To bring blood close to alveolar air

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Respiratory disorders can narrow the airways, damage the alveoli, or affect the pleurae. Which disorder mainly affects the alveoli?
options: Asthma
Chronic bronchitis
Pneumonia
Pneumothorax
questions.why: Most respiratory disorders can be sorted by the structure they hit: the airways, the alveoli, or the pleurae. Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid, so it damages the exchange surface itself. Asthma and chronic bronchitis narrow or block the airways, and a pneumothorax affects the pleural cavity.
notes: Asthma narrows the bronchioles, which are conducting airways, so it is a problem of blocked airflow. Pick it as the example of an airway disorder.
Chronic bronchitis is long-term inflammation of the bronchi, the larger conducting airways, and it is grouped with emphysema under COPD. It blocks airflow rather than mainly damaging the alveoli.
Correct. Pneumonia inflames and floods the alveoli, the exchange surface.
Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, which collapses the lung from outside. It affects the space around the lung rather than the airways or the alveolar walls.
questions.answerText: Pneumonia

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which group lists only structures of the lower respiratory tract?
options: Nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx
Trachea, bronchi, and lungs
Nasal conchae, nasal meatuses, and choanae
Nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx
questions.why: The lower respiratory tract runs from the larynx down through the trachea and bronchi into the lungs. These structures carry air into the thorax and, deep in the lungs, bring it close to the blood for gas exchange. Everything above the larynx, from the nose through the pharynx, belongs to the upper tract.
notes: These are the three regions of the pharynx, all part of the upper tract. Choose this group for a question about the pharynx from top to bottom.
Correct. The trachea, bronchi, and lungs are all part of the lower tract.

These are features of the nasal cavity in the upper tract: the conchae and meatuses on its lateral wall and the choanae opening into the nasopharynx. They would be the answer for a question about how the nasal cavity is shaped to condition air.
These are upper respiratory tract structures in the head and throat. Pick this group if the question asked for the upper tract.
questions.answerText: Trachea, bronchi, and lungs

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which sequence follows the bronchial tree from the main bronchi to the end of the conducting zone?
options: Lobar bronchi, main bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Main bronchi, segmental bronchi, lobar bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles
Main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, terminal bronchioles, bronchioles
questions.why: The trachea splits at the carina into two main (primary) bronchi, one to each lung. Each main bronchus splits into lobar (secondary) bronchi, one per lobe, and those split into segmental (tertiary) bronchi, one per bronchopulmonary segment. The segmental bronchi branch into bronchioles, which end as terminal bronchioles, the last airways of the conducting zone.
notes: This puts the lobar bronchi first, but the main bronchi come straight off the trachea and only then divide into lobar bronchi. Students pick this when they forget that each lung gets a single main bronchus before any lobe is served.
Correct. The tree narrows from lung to lobe to segment, then into bronchioles.
This swaps lobar and segmental bronchi. Lobes are the larger units, so the lobar (secondary) bronchi come before the segmental (tertiary) bronchi that serve the smaller segments.
This puts terminal bronchioles before bronchioles. Terminal means last, so terminal bronchioles are the final branches of the conducting zone.
questions.answerText: Main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: How do the walls of bronchioles differ from the walls of bronchi?
options: Bronchioles have smooth muscle walls and no cartilage; bronchi are supported by cartilage
Bronchioles have C-shaped cartilage rings closed by the trachealis muscle
Bronchioles are lined by stratified squamous epithelium to resist friction
Bronchioles are supported by cartilage; bronchi have smooth muscle walls and no cartilage
questions.why: As the bronchial tree branches, cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases. Bronchi are still held open by cartilage, but bronchioles have lost their cartilage entirely and have walls of smooth muscle. That is why bronchioles can constrict, and why asthma, which narrows the bronchioles, is a disease of the small airways.
notes: Correct. Bronchioles trade cartilage for smooth muscle.
C-shaped cartilage rings with the trachealis muscle closing the gap describe the trachea. Pick this description for a question about what holds the windpipe open.

Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, where food rubs past. Choose it for a question about the lining of the parts of the pharynx shared with food, not the small airways.
This reverses the pattern. Cartilage is greatest in the large airways and disappears by the bronchiole, where smooth muscle takes over.
questions.answerText: Bronchioles have smooth muscle walls and no cartilage; bronchi are supported by cartilage

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A tumor blocks one segmental (tertiary) bronchus. Which part of the lung loses its air supply?
options: One bronchopulmonary segment
One entire lung
One single alveolus
One entire lobe
questions.why: Each segmental (tertiary) bronchus supplies one bronchopulmonary segment, a distinct section of a lobe with its own airway. Blocking that bronchus cuts off air to that one segment while the neighboring segments keep working. This is why each segment is treated as a separate functional unit of the lung.
notes: Correct. One segmental bronchus serves one bronchopulmonary segment.
A whole lung would lose air if a main (primary) bronchus were blocked, since each main bronchus enters one lung. Choose this for a blockage just past the carina.
A single alveolus sits at the very end of the airway tree, far beyond a segmental bronchus. A blocked segmental bronchus affects a huge number of alveoli at once, not just one.
A whole lobe would lose air if a lobar (secondary) bronchus were blocked, since each lobar bronchus supplies one lobe. Pick this if the tumor were in a lobar bronchus.
questions.answerText: One bronchopulmonary segment

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: How many lobes does each lung have?
options: Right lung three, left lung two
Both lungs have two
Both lungs have three
Right lung two, left lung three
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior), separated by a horizontal fissure and an oblique fissure. The left lung has only two lobes (superior and inferior), separated by an oblique fissure. The left lung is smaller because it shares the left side of the thorax with the heart.
notes: Correct. Three lobes on the right and two on the left.
Two lobes is right only for the left lung. The right lung also has a middle lobe, set off by its horizontal fissure.
Three lobes is right for the right lung, but the left lung has only two because it gives up room for the heart. Students choose this when they assume the lungs are mirror images.
This swaps the two lungs. The heart sits mostly to the left of the midline, so the left lung is the smaller one with fewer lobes.
questions.answerText: Right lung three, left lung two

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the cardiac notch, and which lung has it?
options: An indentation in the right lung that makes room for the heart
The medial indentation where the bronchus and vessels enter a lung
The tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe
An indentation in the left lung that makes room for the heart
questions.why: The cardiac notch is an indentation in the anterior border of the left lung that makes room for the heart. About two thirds of the heart's mass lies to the left of the midline, so the left lung is shaped around it. Just below the notch, the left superior lobe forms a small tongue-shaped projection called the lingula.
notes: The heart lies mostly to the left of the midline, so it is the left lung, not the right, that is notched around it. Students choose this when they forget which way the heart tilts.

That describes the hilum, the indentation on the medial surface of each lung where the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and nerves enter and leave. Pick it if the question asked where the root of the lung attaches.
That describes the lingula, which sits just below the cardiac notch on the left superior lobe. Choose it for a question about the tongue-shaped part of the left lung.
Correct. The cardiac notch is the space in the left lung where the heart fits.
questions.answerText: An indentation in the left lung that makes room for the heart

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the parietal and visceral pleura?
options: The parietal pleura lines the abdominal wall; the visceral pleura covers the abdominal organs
The visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall; the parietal pleura covers the lung
The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the visceral pleura covers the lung
The parietal pleura surrounds the heart; the visceral pleura covers the lung
questions.why: The pleura is a serous membrane with two layers. The parietal pleura lines the inner thoracic wall (parietal refers to a body wall), and the visceral pleura clings to the outer surface of the lung (visceral refers to an organ). The thin, fluid-filled pleural cavity between them lets the lung glide against the chest wall as it expands.
notes: Those are the parietal and visceral peritoneum, the serous membranes of the abdominopelvic cavity. They would be the answer for a question about the membranes lining the abdomen and covering its organs.
This swaps the two layers. Parietal always means the layer on the body wall and visceral always means the layer on the organ, in the pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum alike.
Correct. Parietal is on the wall and visceral is on the lung.
The membrane around the heart is the pericardium, not the pleura. Pick the pericardium for a question about the serous sac that encloses the heart.
questions.answerText: The parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the visceral pleura covers the lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does the left lung have only two lobes and a cardiac notch, while the right lung has three lobes?
options: The heart sits mostly to the left of the midline, so the left lung gives up room for it
The aorta passes through the left lung and divides it into fewer lobes
The left main bronchus is wider, so it supplies fewer and larger lobes
The liver sits beneath the left lung and pushes it upward into a smaller space
questions.why: About two thirds of the heart's mass lies to the left of the midline. The left lung shares that side of the thorax with the heart, so it is smaller, has only two lobes, and carries a cardiac notch along its anterior border where the heart sits. The right lung has more room, so it is larger and has three lobes.
notes: Correct. The left lung is smaller because the heart takes up part of the left side of the thorax.
The aorta arches over the heart and descends in the mediastinum, between the lungs, not through either lung. The number of lobes reflects the room left by the heart, not a vessel passing through.

It is the right main bronchus that is wider and more vertical, which is why inhaled objects usually lodge in the right lung. Pick this bronchus fact for a question about where an inhaled object is most likely to go.

The liver lies on the right side, under the right dome of the diaphragm, not under the left lung. Students choose this when they misplace the liver; it would fit a question about which abdominal organ lies beneath the right lung.
questions.answerText: The heart sits mostly to the left of the midline, so the left lung gives up room for it

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares type I and type II alveolar cells?
options: Type I cells are thin and form most of the wall; type II cells secrete surfactant
Type I cells secrete surfactant; type II cells are thin and form most of the wall
Type I cells secrete mucus; type II cells sweep it away with cilia
Type I cells engulf debris on the surface; type II cells form most of the wall
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are thin, flat, simple squamous cells that form most of the alveolar wall, so gases have only a short distance to cross. Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells scattered among them that secrete surfactant, a fluid that lowers surface tension and keeps the alveoli from collapsing. A third cell, the alveolar macrophage, patrols the surface and engulfs debris.
notes: Correct. Type I cells form the thin exchange wall, and type II cells make surfactant.
This swaps the two jobs. The thin type I cells are built for gas exchange, while the plumper cuboidal type II cells make and secrete surfactant.

Mucus secretion and ciliary sweeping belong to the goblet cells and ciliated cells of the conducting airways, such as the trachea. Choose this for a question about how the respiratory mucosa traps and clears particles.
Engulfing debris is the job of alveolar macrophages, also called dust cells, which are not type I cells. Pick macrophages for a question about which cells clean the alveolar surface.
questions.answerText: Type I cells are thin and form most of the wall; type II cells secrete surfactant

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What is the apex of a lung?
options: The medial indentation where the bronchus and vessels enter
The tongue-shaped projection of the left superior lobe
The broad inferior surface, resting on the diaphragm
The narrow superior tip, rising just above the clavicle
questions.why: The apex of each lung is its narrow superior tip, which rises just above the clavicle into the root of the neck. The broad base sits at the opposite end, resting on the diaphragm. Knowing that the apex reaches above the clavicle explains why a deep wound at the base of the neck can reach the top of the lung.
notes: That describes the hilum, on the medial surface of each lung, where the root of the lung enters. Choose it for a question about where the main bronchus and pulmonary vessels join the lung.
That describes the lingula of the left lung, which sits below the cardiac notch. It would be the answer for a question about the tongue-shaped part of the left superior lobe.
That describes the base of the lung, the end opposite the apex. Pick it if the question asked which surface rests on the diaphragm.
Correct. The apex is the top of the lung, reaching just above the clavicle.
questions.answerText: The narrow superior tip, rising just above the clavicle

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: The base of each lung is its broad inferior surface. What does it rest on?
options: The clavicle
The diaphragm
The heart
The first rib
questions.why: The base of each lung is its broad, concave inferior surface, and it rests on the dome of the diaphragm. Because the diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity, the lung bases sit just above the abdominal organs. The apex, at the opposite end, rises just above the clavicle.
notes: The clavicle is at the top of the thorax, and the apex of the lung rises just above it. Pick the clavicle if the question asked about the apex rather than the base.
Correct. Each lung base sits on the dome of the diaphragm.

The heart sits between the lungs in the mediastinum, pressing into their medial surfaces and making the cardiac notch in the left lung. Choose it for a question about what the medial surface of the left lung is shaped around.
The first rib curves around the top of the thoracic cavity, near the apex of each lung. It would be a reasonable landmark for a question about the apex, not the base.
questions.answerText: The diaphragm

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: What does the pleural cavity contain, and what does that allow?
options: A thin film of serous fluid that lets the lung glide
Loose fat that cushions the lung against the ribs
The main bronchus and pulmonary vessels entering the lung
Air that holds the lung open between breaths
questions.why: The pleural cavity is the thin, sealed space between the parietal pleura on the thoracic wall and the visceral pleura on the lung. It holds only a thin film of serous fluid, which lets the lung slide smoothly against the chest wall as it expands and recoils with each breath. If air gets into this space, the seal is lost and the lung can collapse, a condition called pneumothorax.
notes: Correct. The fluid film lets the two pleural layers slide over each other.
The pleural cavity holds no fat or cushioning tissue, only a thin fluid film. Students choose this when they picture the space as padding rather than a lubricated gap between two membranes.
The main bronchus and pulmonary vessels enter at the hilum as the root of the lung, not within the pleural cavity. Choose them for a question about what passes through the hilum.
Air in the pleural cavity is not normal; it is a pneumothorax, which breaks the seal and lets the lung collapse. Pick air for a question about what enters the pleural cavity after a chest wound.
questions.answerText: A thin film of serous fluid that lets the lung glide

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why does the right dome of the diaphragm sit a little higher than the left?
options: The liver lies under the right dome
The heart rests on top of the right dome
Only the right side has a central tendon
The right phrenic nerve comes from more spinal nerves
questions.why: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle that forms the floor of the thoracic cavity. The liver sits just under its right side, so the right dome sits a little higher than the left. Both sides share one central tendon, and both are supplied by phrenic nerves from C3, C4, and C5.
notes: Correct. The liver lies under the right dome, so that side sits a little higher.
Weight resting on top of a dome would press it down, not lift it. The right dome sits higher because the liver lies under it.

There is one central tendon, the flat sheet of tendon at the top of the whole dome that all the muscle fibers pull toward. It is not a right-side feature, so it does not explain the difference in height.
Both phrenic nerves come from the same spinal nerves, C3, C4, and C5, so the two sides are supplied the same way. The difference in height comes from the liver underneath.
questions.answerText: The liver lies under the right dome

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which pair of structures both pass through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm?
options: The esophagus and the vagus nerves
The inferior vena cava and the aorta
The esophagus and the thoracic duct
The aorta and the thoracic duct
questions.why: The aortic hiatus lies behind the diaphragm at T12, between its two crura. The aorta passes through it, and the thoracic duct passes with it. Above the diaphragm the vessel is the thoracic aorta, and below it the vessel is called the abdominal aorta.
notes: The esophagus and the vagus nerves pass together through the esophageal hiatus at T10. That pair answers a question about the T10 opening.
The inferior vena cava has its own opening, the caval opening in the central tendon at T8, so it does not travel with the aorta.
The thoracic duct does pass with the aorta, but the esophagus goes through a separate opening, the esophageal hiatus at T10.
Correct. The aorta and the thoracic duct pass together through the aortic hiatus at T12.
questions.answerText: The aorta and the thoracic duct

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: In the cadaver, you follow the vagus nerves down from the thorax into the abdomen. Through which diaphragm opening do they pass?
options: The caval opening at T8
The esophageal hiatus at T10
The aortic hiatus at T12
The esophageal hiatus at T12
questions.why: The vagus nerves pass through the esophageal hiatus along with the esophagus. This opening is in the muscle of the diaphragm at the level of T10. So when you follow the esophagus through the diaphragm, you are following the path of the vagus nerves too.
notes: The caval opening at T8 carries the inferior vena cava through the central tendon. The vagus nerves do not use it.
Correct. The vagus nerves pass with the esophagus through the esophageal hiatus at T10.
The aortic hiatus at T12 carries the aorta and the thoracic duct, not the vagus nerves.
The esophageal hiatus is the right opening, but it sits at T10. T12 is the level of the aortic hiatus.
questions.answerText: The esophageal hiatus at T10

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: You trace the inferior vena cava down from the heart toward the abdomen. Where does it pass through the diaphragm?
options: Through the muscle at T10
Behind the diaphragm, between the crura, at T12
Through the muscle at T8
Through the central tendon at T8
questions.why: The inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening, which sits in the central tendon at the level of T8. The central tendon is the flat sheet of tendon at the top of the dome that all the muscle fibers pull toward. The other two openings sit lower: the esophageal hiatus in the muscle at T10 and the aortic hiatus behind the diaphragm at T12.
notes: The opening in the muscle at T10 is the esophageal hiatus, which carries the esophagus and the vagus nerves.
The opening behind the diaphragm between the crura at T12 is the aortic hiatus, which carries the aorta and the thoracic duct.
T8 is the right level, but the caval opening sits in the central tendon, not in the muscle. The opening in the muscle is the esophageal hiatus at T10.
Correct. The caval opening for the inferior vena cava is in the central tendon at T8.
questions.answerText: Through the central tendon at T8

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which muscle has fibers that run downward and forward, the same direction as your fingers with your hands in your front pockets?
options: Internal intercostals
External intercostals
Diaphragm
Scalenes
questions.why: The external intercostals are the outer layer of muscle between the ribs, and their fibers run downward and forward. They lift the ribs during inspiration. The internal intercostals lie just deep to them, with fibers at right angles that run downward and backward.
notes: The internal intercostals run at right angles to the external layer, downward and backward. Pick them for a question about the deeper layer.
Correct. The external intercostal fibers run downward and forward, like hands in front pockets.
The diaphragm is a dome whose fibers rise toward the central tendon. It closes the bottom of the thoracic cavity rather than filling the spaces between the ribs.
The scalenes are accessory muscles that help lift the rib cage when you breathe in harder than normal. They are not one of the layers between the ribs.
questions.answerText: External intercostals

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: When you need to breathe in harder than normal, which accessory muscles help lift the rib cage?
options: The internal intercostals and the abdominal muscles
The scalenes, sternocleidomastoid, and pectoralis minor
The two crura of the diaphragm
None, because a harder breath in comes from recoil alone
questions.why: The diaphragm and the external intercostals do the work of normal breathing in. When you need to breathe in harder than normal, accessory muscles help lift the rib cage: the scalenes, the sternocleidomastoid, and the pectoralis minor. Forced breathing out uses a different set, the internal intercostals and the abdominal muscles.
notes: The internal intercostals and the abdominal muscles work in forced expiration, the hard breath out. They are the answer for blowing out candles, not for a harder breath in.
Correct. The scalenes, sternocleidomastoid, and pectoralis minor help lift the rib cage when you breathe in harder than normal.
The crura are the muscular legs that anchor the diaphragm to the lumbar vertebrae. They are part of the diaphragm itself, not accessory muscles that lift the ribs.
Recoil of the lungs and chest wall moves air out during quiet expiration. It does not pull air in, so a harder breath in needs extra muscles.
questions.answerText: The scalenes, sternocleidomastoid, and pectoralis minor

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A classmate says the internal intercostals must contract every time you breathe out. Why is this wrong for quiet breathing at rest?
options: The external intercostals contract to pull the ribs down in every quiet breath out
The diaphragm contracts and pushes upward to force the air out of the lungs
Quiet expiration needs no muscle effort, because the lungs and chest wall recoil
The scalenes lower the rib cage a little during each quiet breath out at rest
questions.why: Quiet expiration needs no muscle effort. The lungs and chest wall recoil on their own, and that recoil moves air out at rest. The internal intercostals and the abdominal muscles join in only for forced expiration, such as a hard cough.
notes: The external intercostals lift the ribs during inspiration. They are not the muscles that pull the ribs down.
When the diaphragm contracts, it flattens and moves down, which is inspiration. It does not contract to push air out.
Correct. At rest, breathing out needs no muscle effort because the lungs and chest wall recoil on their own.
The scalenes are accessory muscles that help lift the rib cage in a harder than normal breath in. They do not lower the ribs.
questions.answerText: Quiet expiration needs no muscle effort, because the lungs and chest wall recoil

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Moving from the highest diaphragm opening to the lowest, which list gives where each opening sits?
options: Muscle, then central tendon, then between the crura
Between the crura, then muscle, then central tendon
Central tendon, then between the crura, then muscle
Central tendon, then muscle, then between the crura
questions.why: The highest opening is the caval opening for the inferior vena cava, in the central tendon at T8. Next is the esophageal hiatus, in the muscle at T10. Lowest is the aortic hiatus at T12, which lies behind the diaphragm between its two crura.
notes: This swaps the top two. The highest opening, at T8, is in the central tendon, and the esophageal hiatus in the muscle comes next at T10.
This is the order from lowest to highest. The opening between the crura is the lowest, at T12, not the highest.
This swaps the bottom two. The esophageal hiatus in the muscle at T10 comes before the aortic hiatus between the crura at T12.
Correct. The order is the caval opening (central tendon, T8), the esophageal hiatus (muscle, T10), then the aortic hiatus (between the crura, T12).
questions.answerText: Central tendon, then muscle, then between the crura

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which structure does chronic bronchitis affect, and what happens to it?
options: The alveoli, whose walls break down and merge into larger spaces
The alveoli, which an infection inflames and fills with fluid
The bronchi, whose lining stays inflamed and makes too much mucus
The pleurae, whose layers become rough and rub with each breath
questions.why: Chronic bronchitis affects the bronchi. Their lining stays inflamed and makes too much mucus, and the mucus blocks the airways. It is one of the two main parts of COPD, along with emphysema.
notes: Alveolar walls that break down and merge into fewer, larger spaces describe emphysema, the other main part of COPD.
Alveoli inflamed by an infection and filled with fluid describe pneumonia, an alveolar problem rather than a bronchial one.
Correct. In chronic bronchitis the bronchial lining stays inflamed and makes too much mucus, which blocks the airways.
Rough, inflamed pleural layers that rub with each breath describe pleurisy, a problem of the pleurae, not the airways.
questions.answerText: The bronchi, whose lining stays inflamed and makes too much mucus

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Why do the bronchi and bronchioles clog in cystic fibrosis?
options: The airway smooth muscle tightens and squeezes the bronchioles narrow
The alveolar walls break down and merge into a few large spaces
Air enters the pleural cavity, and the lung on that side collapses
An inherited disorder makes the mucus so thick and sticky that the cilia cannot clear it
questions.why: Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disorder that affects the bronchi and bronchioles. Its mucus is thick and sticky, so the cilia lining the airways cannot sweep it away. The mucus builds up and clogs the airways.
notes: Tightening airway smooth muscle, with an inflamed lining and extra mucus, is asthma. In cystic fibrosis the problem is the thick mucus itself.
Alveolar walls that break down and merge describe emphysema, which affects the alveoli rather than clogging the bronchi and bronchioles.
Air in the pleural cavity that collapses the lung is a pneumothorax, a pleural problem rather than an airway one.
Correct. In cystic fibrosis, an inherited disorder, the mucus is so thick and sticky that the cilia cannot clear it, so it clogs the airways.
questions.answerText: An inherited disorder makes the mucus so thick and sticky that the cilia cannot clear it

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: Which description matches tuberculosis?
options: An infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid
A bacterial infection that forms tubercles and scar tissue in the lung
A malignant tumor that usually starts in the epithelium of the airways
Extra fluid in the pleural cavity that presses on the lung
questions.why: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection of the lung tissue. It forms small nodules called tubercles, along with scar tissue. Pneumonia is also an infection, but it inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid instead.
notes: An infection that inflames the alveoli and fills them with fluid is pneumonia. Fluid in the air sacs, not nodules and scarring, is its sign.
Correct. Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that forms small nodules (tubercles) and scar tissue in the lung tissue.
A malignant tumor that usually starts in the epithelium lining the airways or alveoli is lung cancer, which is strongly linked to smoking.
Extra fluid in the pleural cavity that presses on the lung is a pleural effusion, a problem of the pleural cavity rather than the lung tissue.
questions.answerText: A bacterial infection that forms tubercles and scar tissue in the lung

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: A patient sitting upright has a pleural effusion. Which space holds the extra fluid, and where in that space does it pool?
options: The pleural cavity, in the costodiaphragmatic recess
The pleural cavity, at the top near the apex of the lung
The alveoli, inside the air sacs of the lung
The bronchi, inside the lumen of the airways
questions.why: A pleural effusion is extra fluid in the pleural cavity, and the fluid presses on the lung. In a person sitting or standing, it pools in the costodiaphragmatic recess. This recess is the low pocket where the parietal pleura turns from the ribs onto the diaphragm.
notes: Correct. The fluid is in the pleural cavity, and in an upright person it pools in the costodiaphragmatic recess.
The fluid is in the pleural cavity, but it does not collect at the top. In a person sitting or standing, it pools in the costodiaphragmatic recess at the bottom edge.
Fluid filling the alveoli is pneumonia, where an infection inflames the air sacs. A pleural effusion collects outside the lung, in the pleural cavity.
Mucus in the lumen of the bronchi is the problem in chronic bronchitis and cystic fibrosis. A pleural effusion is fluid outside the lung, in the pleural cavity.
questions.answerText: The pleural cavity, in the costodiaphragmatic recess

questions.topic: Trachea, bronchial tree, lungs and pleurae
questions.q: On the cadaver, you study a removed lung. At its hilum the pulmonary artery is the highest structure and the pulmonary veins are the lowest, and its front edge has a deep notch. Which lung is it, and how many lobes should you find?
options: The right lung, with two lobes separated by an oblique fissure.
The right lung, with three lobes separated by two fissures.
The left lung, with three lobes separated by two fissures.
The left lung, with two lobes separated by an oblique fissure.
questions.why: Two clues work together here. In the left hilum the pulmonary artery is the highest structure, while in the right hilum a bronchus sits at or above the artery, and the veins are lowest in both. The cardiac notch in the front edge makes room for the heart, which tilts to the left. Both clues point to the left lung, which has a superior and an inferior lobe separated by an oblique fissure.
notes: Two lobes and an oblique fissure only describe the left lung. The right lung has three lobes, and the cardiac notch is found only on the left.
The right lung has three lobes and both a horizontal and an oblique fissure, but in its hilum a bronchus sits at or above the artery, and it has no cardiac notch.
The side is right but the lobe count is wrong. The left lung gave up its middle lobe to the heart, so it has only two lobes and one fissure.
Correct. The artery on top at the hilum and the cardiac notch both mark the left lung, which has two lobes and an oblique fissure only.
questions.answerText: The left lung, with two lobes separated by an oblique fissure.

questions.q: Which structure is the first part of the respiratory zone?
options: The respiratory bronchiole
The terminal bronchiole
The segmental bronchus
The trachea
questions.why: The respiratory zone begins where alveoli first appear in the airway wall, and that is the respiratory bronchiole, so gas exchange can start there. The terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway, with no alveoli in its wall. The segmental bronchus and the trachea are larger conducting airways that only move air.
questions.answerText: The respiratory bronchiole

questions.q: Across which structure does gas move between air and blood in the lung?
options: The wall of the terminal bronchiole and its smooth muscle
The alveolar wall and the capillary wall together
The cartilage rings of the bronchi
The pleural membrane covering the lung
questions.why: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the respiratory membrane, which is the thin alveolar epithelium plus fused basement membranes plus capillary endothelium, a barrier under one micrometer thick. The terminal bronchiole wall and its smooth muscle are too thick and has no capillary bed dedicated to exchange. Cartilage rings hold airways open, and the pleural membrane sits outside the lung entirely.
questions.answerText: The alveolar wall and the capillary wall together

questions.q: What is the approximate volume of the anatomic dead space in a healthy adult?
options: About 50 mL
About 500 mL
About 150 mL
About 1200 mL
questions.why: The conducting airways hold roughly 150 mL of air, close to 1 mL per pound of ideal body weight, and that air never reaches an exchange surface. About 500 mL is a normal tidal volume, not the dead space inside it. About 50 mL is far too small for the whole airway tree, and 1200 mL is closer to residual volume.
questions.answerText: About 150 mL

questions.q: Besides gas exchange, which of these is a normal function of the respiratory system?
options: Producing red blood cells in the alveolar wall
Absorbing nutrients from inspired air
Storing calcium for release during exercise
Regulating blood pH by adjusting carbon dioxide removal
questions.why: Because CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid, changing how much CO2 the lungs blow off changes blood H+ directly, which makes ventilation one of the two main pH control systems. Red blood cells are made in bone marrow, not in alveoli. Nutrients are absorbed in the gut, and calcium storage belongs to bone.
questions.answerText: Regulating blood pH by adjusting carbon dioxide removal

questions.q: Which airway is the last structure of the conducting zone?
options: The alveolar duct
The terminal bronchiole
The respiratory bronchiole
The alveolar sac
questions.why: The terminal bronchiole is the smallest airway with no alveoli in its wall, so it is the last place that only conducts air. Respiratory bronchioles already carry scattered alveoli and belong to the respiratory zone. Alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs are further downstream and are almost entirely exchange surface.
questions.answerText: The terminal bronchiole

questions.q: Which cell type forms most of the alveolar surface where gas diffuses?
options: The alveolar macrophage
The type II alveolar cell
The type I alveolar cell
The ciliated columnar cell
questions.why: Type I alveolar cells are extremely flat simple squamous cells, and that thinness is exactly what makes the diffusion distance short enough for rapid gas exchange. Type II cells are cuboidal and secrete surfactant, covering only a small fraction of the surface. Macrophages patrol the alveolus for debris, and ciliated columnar cells line conducting airways, not alveoli.
questions.answerText: The type I alveolar cell

questions.q: What structural feature of conducting zone airways is absent from alveoli?
options: A layer of surfactant on the inner surface
A blood supply from pulmonary capillaries
A moist inner surface
Cartilage or smooth muscle in the wall
questions.why: Conducting airways need cartilage and smooth muscle to stay open and to change their diameter, while the alveolar wall is a single squamous layer with no such support, which is what keeps the diffusion barrier thin. Surfactant is found in alveoli, not in conducting airways. Both zones are moist, and the alveolus is the site with the densest capillary supply.
questions.answerText: Cartilage or smooth muscle in the wall

questions.q: What does the conducting zone do to inspired air before it reaches the alveoli?
options: Warms it, humidifies it, and filters out particles
Cools it and removes water vapor from it
Adds oxygen to it from bronchial capillaries
Removes carbon dioxide from it before exchange
questions.why: Mucus and the rich submucosal blood supply bring air to body temperature and full saturation with water vapor, and the mucociliary escalator traps particles, so the alveoli receive clean conditioned air. Cooling and drying is the opposite of what happens. Oxygen is not added along the way, and carbon dioxide is removed at the alveolus, not in the conducting airways.
questions.answerText: Warms it, humidifies it, and filters out particles

questions.q: A person breathes cold dry air at 5 C. What is the condition of that air by the time it reaches the alveoli?
options: Still near 5 C but fully saturated with water vapor
Warmed to about 37 C and fully saturated with water vapor
Warmed to about 37 C but still dry
Unchanged in temperature and in water content
questions.why: The conducting zone is built to condition air, so by the carina and certainly by the alveolus the air is at body temperature and 100 percent humidified, which protects the delicate exchange surface. Air that stayed at 5 C would injure the alveoli and would also be unable to hold much water. Warm but dry air would dehydrate the surface, and truly unchanged air would do both kinds of damage.
questions.answerText: Warmed to about 37 C and fully saturated with water vapor

questions.q: Tidal volume is 500 mL and anatomic dead space is 150 mL. How much of one breath actually reaches the respiratory zone?
options: 150 mL
500 mL
650 mL
350 mL
questions.why: Fresh air reaching exchange surface is tidal volume minus dead space, so 500 minus 150 gives 350 mL per breath. The 150 mL figure is the part that stays in the conducting airways and never exchanges. The full 500 mL ignores dead space entirely, and 650 mL adds the two numbers instead of subtracting.
questions.answerText: 350 mL

questions.q: A tracheostomy tube bypasses the nose, mouth, and pharynx. What is the immediate effect on the anatomic dead space?
options: It decreases, because part of the conducting zone is bypassed
It increases, because a new airway is added in series
It is unchanged, because dead space is fixed by lung size
It falls to zero, because air enters the trachea directly
questions.why: Anatomic dead space is the volume of all conducting airways, so removing the upper airway from the path takes roughly half of it away. Adding tubing outside the body would increase dead space, but a tracheostomy shortens the path rather than lengthening it. Dead space is not fixed, and it cannot reach zero because the trachea and bronchi still conduct air.
questions.answerText: It decreases, because part of the conducting zone is bypassed

questions.q: Which change would most directly slow oxygen diffusion into the blood?
options: Loss of cartilage from a large bronchus
Thickening of the alveolar and capillary walls
Increased mucus production in the trachea
Weakness of the external intercostal muscles
questions.why: Diffusion rate falls as the barrier gets thicker, so any process that adds tissue between alveolar air and capillary blood directly slows gas transfer. Loss of bronchial cartilage and extra tracheal mucus both affect conduction of air, not the exchange barrier itself. Weak intercostals reduce how much air arrives but do not change how fast gas crosses the membrane.
questions.answerText: Thickening of the alveolar and capillary walls

questions.q: A mucus plug completely blocks one terminal bronchiole. What happens to the alveoli downstream of the plug?
options: They stop being perfused but remain ventilated
They continue to exchange gas normally
They stop being ventilated but remain perfused
They immediately fill with fluid from the capillaries
questions.why: A terminal bronchiole is the sole air supply to its cluster of alveoli, so blocking it cuts off ventilation while pulmonary capillary blood keeps flowing past, creating blood that leaves the lung without picking up oxygen. Perfusion is set by the pulmonary arteries, not by the airway. Normal exchange is impossible without fresh air, and capillary fluid does not pour into a blocked alveolus.
questions.answerText: They stop being ventilated but remain perfused

questions.q: Why does the respiratory zone have a total surface area of roughly 70 square meters?
options: It provides room to store extra oxygen between breaths
It slows airflow so that air can be warmed
It increases the pressure of gas in the alveoli
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to surface area
questions.why: Fick's law makes the amount of gas crossing a membrane proportional to the area available, so hundreds of millions of small alveoli move far more oxygen per second than a few large sacs would. Oxygen is not stored in air spaces in any useful quantity. Warming happens in the conducting zone, and surface area does not change alveolar gas pressure.
questions.answerText: Diffusion rate is directly proportional to surface area

questions.q: A patient hypoventilates for several minutes. What happens to arterial pH?
options: It falls, because retained carbon dioxide generates H+
It rises, because retained carbon dioxide generates HCO3-
It rises, because less oxygen is delivered to tissues
It does not change, because the kidneys fix it within minutes
questions.why: CO2 that is not blown off combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates to H+ and HCO3-, so a rising PCO2 always drives pH down. The reaction does yield HCO3-, but it yields H+ at the same time, and it is the H+ that sets pH. Reduced oxygen delivery causes lactate production, which would also lower pH, and renal compensation takes days rather than minutes.
questions.answerText: It falls, because retained carbon dioxide generates H+

questions.q: A long term smoker has paralyzed airway cilia. Trace the consequence for the conducting zone and for gas exchange.
options: Surfactant production falls, so alveoli collapse at the end of every expiration
Mucus and trapped particles accumulate in the airways, narrowing them and raising infection risk
The alveolar membrane thins, so gas exchange temporarily improves
Anatomic dead space falls, so alveolar ventilation rises
questions.why: The mucociliary escalator normally sweeps trapped debris upward to be swallowed, so losing ciliary motion leaves mucus sitting in the conducting airways, which narrows the lumen and gives bacteria a place to grow. Surfactant comes from type II alveolar cells and is not made by ciliated cells. The alveolar membrane thickens rather than thins in chronic injury, and a mucus filled airway does not reduce dead space in any helpful way.
questions.answerText: Mucus and trapped particles accumulate in the airways, narrowing them and raising infection risk

questions.q: A disease destroys alveolar walls but leaves every conducting airway wide open. Predict the effect on airflow into the lung and on arterial PO2.
options: Both airflow and arterial PO2 are preserved
Airflow into the lung falls but arterial PO2 is preserved
Airflow into the lung is preserved but arterial PO2 falls
Both airflow and arterial PO2 fall in proportion
questions.why: The two zones do different jobs, so intact conducting airways still deliver air normally while destroyed alveoli remove the surface where oxygen crosses into blood, and arterial PO2 drops. Saying both are preserved ignores the lost exchange area. Saying airflow falls confuses the conducting zone with the respiratory zone, and a proportional fall in both would require damage to airways as well.
