questions.answerText: Airflow into the lung is preserved but arterial PO2 falls

questions.q: A patient shifts from breathing 500 mL twelve times a minute to breathing 250 mL twenty four times a minute. Minute ventilation is unchanged. Why does gas exchange worsen?
options: A larger fraction of each small breath stays in the fixed 150 mL dead space
The dead space volume doubles when breathing frequency doubles
Faster breathing shortens the time available for diffusion across the membrane
Smaller breaths reduce the surface area of the alveoli by half
questions.why: Dead space is an anatomic volume that does not shrink with the breath, so a 250 mL breath wastes 150 mL and delivers only 100 mL of fresh air, while a 500 mL breath delivers 350 mL. Dead space does not change with rate, since the airways are the same size. Diffusion across the membrane is complete in about a third of the capillary transit time, so it is not the limiting step here, and alveolar surface area does not change with tidal volume.
questions.answerText: A larger fraction of each small breath stays in the fixed 150 mL dead space

questions.q: An inhaled particle 15 micrometers across and one 0.5 micrometers across enter the airway together. Where does each most likely end up?
options: Both are trapped in the nasal mucosa before reaching the trachea
The small particle is trapped in the upper conducting airways and the large one reaches the alveoli
Both reach the alveoli because airflow is fast in the bronchi
The large particle is trapped in the upper conducting airways and the small one reaches the alveoli
questions.why: Large particles have too much inertia to follow the sharp turns of the nose and pharynx, so they strike mucus and are cleared, while particles under about one micrometer travel with the airstream all the way to the respiratory zone where only macrophages can remove them. Reversing the two ignores how inertial impaction works. Not everything is trapped in the nose, and airflow velocity actually falls sharply in the small airways because total cross sectional area is so large.
questions.answerText: The large particle is trapped in the upper conducting airways and the small one reaches the alveoli

questions.q: What does Boyle's law state about a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature?
options: Pressure varies inversely with volume
Pressure varies directly with volume
Volume varies inversely with temperature
Pressure is independent of container volume
questions.why: Boyle's law says P times V is constant, so squeezing a gas into a smaller space raises its pressure and letting it expand lowers its pressure, which is exactly how the thorax moves air. A direct relationship would mean a bigger chest raises alveolar pressure, which would make inspiration impossible. Volume and temperature are related by Charles's law, and pressure certainly does depend on container volume.
questions.answerText: Pressure varies inversely with volume

questions.q: What is alveolar pressure at the end of a quiet expiration, before the next breath begins?
options: About 4 mmHg below atmospheric pressure, or negative 4 mmHg
Equal to atmospheric pressure, or 0 mmHg relative
About 1 mmHg above atmospheric pressure, or positive 1 mmHg
About 1 mmHg below atmospheric pressure, or negative 1 mmHg
questions.why: Between breaths the airway is open and no air is moving, and airflow stops precisely when the pressure difference is zero, so alveolar pressure has equalized with atmospheric. The value 4 mmHg below atmospheric is intrapleural pressure, not alveolar. The values 1 mmHg above and 1 mmHg below atmospheric occur during expiration and inspiration respectively, when air is actually flowing.
questions.answerText: Equal to atmospheric pressure, or 0 mmHg relative

questions.q: What is alveolar pressure during quiet inspiration?
options: About 1 mmHg above atmospheric
About 10 mmHg below atmospheric
About 1 mmHg below atmospheric
Exactly equal to atmospheric
questions.why: Thoracic expansion drops alveolar pressure only about 1 mmHg below atmospheric, and that small gradient is enough to move 500 mL of air because airway resistance is low. A pressure above atmospheric would push air out, which is expiration. Ten mmHg below is far larger than a quiet breath requires, and an equal pressure would produce no flow at all.
questions.answerText: About 1 mmHg below atmospheric

questions.q: What is alveolar pressure during quiet expiration?
options: About 1 mmHg below atmospheric
About 4 mmHg below atmospheric
About 30 mmHg above atmospheric
About 1 mmHg above atmospheric
questions.why: As the lung recoils, its volume falls, so by Boyle's law alveolar pressure rises just above atmospheric and air flows out. A pressure below atmospheric would draw air in. The negative 4 mmHg value belongs to the intrapleural space, and pressures near 30 mmHg above atmospheric occur only during forced expiration such as a cough.
questions.answerText: About 1 mmHg above atmospheric

questions.q: Which muscle does most of the work of quiet inspiration?
options: The diaphragm
The rectus abdominis
The internal intercostals
The sternocleidomastoid
questions.why: Diaphragm contraction accounts for roughly two thirds of the volume change in a quiet breath, because flattening the dome lengthens the thoracic cavity from top to bottom. The rectus abdominis and internal intercostals are expiratory muscles used during forced breathing. The sternocleidomastoid is an accessory inspiratory muscle recruited only when breathing becomes labored.
questions.answerText: The diaphragm

questions.q: What drives quiet expiration in a healthy person at rest?
options: Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles
Passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
Contraction of the abdominal muscles
Relaxation of airway smooth muscle
questions.why: Inspiration stretches elastic tissue, and when the inspiratory muscles relax that stored energy pulls the lung back down in volume with no muscular work required. Internal intercostals and abdominal muscles do drive expiration, but only during forced expiration such as exercise or coughing. Airway smooth muscle tone changes resistance, not the volume change that empties the lung.
questions.answerText: Passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall

questions.q: What determines the direction of airflow between the atmosphere and the alveoli?
options: The oxygen concentration difference between air and alveoli
The difference between intrapleural and atmospheric pressure
The pressure difference between atmospheric air and alveolar air
The compliance of the chest wall alone
questions.why: Bulk flow follows a total pressure gradient, so air moves toward whichever side has the lower pressure, and the relevant two points are the mouth and the alveolus. Oxygen concentration gradients drive diffusion across the membrane, not bulk flow through airways. Intrapleural pressure matters for keeping the lung inflated, and compliance affects how much pressure is needed rather than which way air goes.
questions.answerText: The pressure difference between atmospheric air and alveolar air

questions.q: What happens to thoracic cavity volume when the diaphragm contracts?
options: It decreases as the dome flattens and moves downward
It stays the same while the ribs move outward
It decreases as the dome rises into the thorax
It increases as the dome flattens and moves downward
questions.why: A relaxed diaphragm bulges upward into the thorax, so contraction pulls it flat and down, adding vertical height to the cavity and increasing its volume. Volume cannot decrease while the floor of the cavity descends. The dome rising is what happens during expiration when the diaphragm relaxes.
questions.answerText: It increases as the dome flattens and moves downward

questions.q: The diaphragm contracts and thoracic volume increases. What happens to alveolar pressure and why?
options: It rises, because the lungs are stretched outward by the expanding chest wall
It falls, because the same amount of gas now occupies a larger volume
It stays constant, because air enters immediately
It falls, because oxygen is consumed by the alveolar cells
questions.why: Boyle's law applies directly, so expanding the alveoli spreads the same gas molecules over more space and pressure drops below atmospheric, which is what pulls air in. Stretching a gas container outward lowers pressure rather than raising it. Air entry follows the pressure drop rather than preventing it, and alveolar oxygen consumption is far too slow to explain a change within one breath.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the same amount of gas now occupies a larger volume

questions.q: At the exact instant airflow stops at the end of inspiration, what is alveolar pressure?
options: Below atmospheric pressure
Above atmospheric pressure
Equal to atmospheric pressure
Equal to intrapleural pressure
questions.why: Airflow is driven by a pressure difference, so flow reaches zero exactly when that difference reaches zero, which means alveolar pressure has climbed back to atmospheric as air filled the lung. A pressure still below atmospheric would keep pulling air in. A pressure above atmospheric would start expiration, and alveolar pressure never equals the much lower intrapleural pressure in a lung that is still inflated.
questions.answerText: Equal to atmospheric pressure

questions.q: How do the external intercostal muscles contribute to inspiration?
options: They lift the ribs upward and outward, widening the thorax
They pull the ribs downward and inward, narrowing the thorax
They pull the diaphragm downward from above
They compress the abdominal contents against the diaphragm
questions.why: Their fibers run downward and forward, so contraction swings each rib up and out in a bucket handle motion that increases the side to side and front to back dimensions of the chest. Pulling ribs down and in is the action of the internal intercostals during forced expiration. The intercostals do not attach to the diaphragm, and abdominal compression pushes the diaphragm up, which empties the lung.
questions.answerText: They lift the ribs upward and outward, widening the thorax

questions.q: Which muscles are recruited during forced expiration?
options: The diaphragm and the external intercostals
The abdominal muscles and the internal intercostals
The scalenes and the sternocleidomastoid
The diaphragm and the abdominal muscles together
questions.why: Abdominal contraction drives the viscera and the diaphragm upward while internal intercostals pull the ribs down, and together they shrink the thorax faster than recoil alone could. The diaphragm and external intercostals are the inspiratory pair. Scalenes and sternocleidomastoid are accessory inspiratory muscles, and the diaphragm never helps empty the lung because its contraction always enlarges the cavity.
questions.answerText: The abdominal muscles and the internal intercostals

questions.q: Atmospheric pressure is 760 mmHg and alveolar pressure is 759 mmHg. Which way is air moving?
options: Out of the lungs, because alveolar pressure is lower
No air moves, because the difference is too small
Into the lungs, because alveolar pressure is lower
Into the lungs, because alveolar pressure is higher
questions.why: Gas flows from higher to lower pressure, so a 1 mmHg deficit inside the alveolus pulls air inward, which is precisely the gradient of a normal quiet inspiration. Air would leave the lung only if alveolar pressure exceeded atmospheric. A 1 mmHg difference is small but entirely sufficient because airway resistance is low, and describing 759 as higher than 760 misreads the numbers.
questions.answerText: Into the lungs, because alveolar pressure is lower

questions.q: A sealed 2.0 L container of gas at 760 mmHg is compressed to 1.0 L at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
options: 380 mmHg
760 mmHg
1140 mmHg
1520 mmHg
questions.why: Boyle's law gives P1V1 equal to P2V2, so 760 times 2.0 divided by 1.0 equals 1520 mmHg, a doubling of pressure for a halving of volume. The value 380 mmHg comes from dividing instead of multiplying, which is what would happen if the container expanded to 4.0 L. Pressure cannot stay at 760 when volume changes, and 1140 mmHg does not satisfy the equation.
questions.answerText: 1520 mmHg

questions.q: Which change would increase the pressure gradient that drives air into the lungs during inspiration?
options: A stronger diaphragm contraction that expands the thorax further
A slower relaxation of the abdominal muscles
An increase in alveolar pressure above atmospheric
A reduction in the elastic recoil of the chest wall during inspiration
questions.why: More thoracic expansion means a larger volume increase, which by Boyle's law drops alveolar pressure further below atmospheric and widens the driving gradient. Abdominal relaxation speed does not set the inspiratory gradient. Raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric would reverse flow, and chest wall recoil is not what generates the inspiratory pressure drop.
questions.answerText: A stronger diaphragm contraction that expands the thorax further

questions.q: A spinal cord injury silences both phrenic nerves but leaves the intercostal nerves intact. Trace what happens during an attempted quiet breath.
options: The thorax widens only slightly, so alveolar pressure falls less and tidal volume is greatly reduced
The thorax cannot change volume at all, so no air moves in or out
Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric, so air is pushed out instead of in
Tidal volume stays completely normal, because the intercostal muscles fully replace the work of the diaphragm
questions.why: Losing the diaphragm removes about two thirds of the volume change of a quiet breath, so the intercostals can still widen the ribcage a little and generate a smaller pressure drop, giving a small but nonzero tidal volume. Complete failure would require losing the intercostals as well. Alveolar pressure cannot rise during an attempted inspiration, and the intercostals alone cannot match diaphragmatic descent.
questions.answerText: The thorax widens only slightly, so alveolar pressure falls less and tidal volume is greatly reduced

questions.q: A climber breathes at an altitude where atmospheric pressure is 500 mmHg. What must alveolar pressure be for air to flow into the lungs?
options: Slightly below 760 mmHg, for example 759 mmHg
Exactly 500 mmHg, since flow depends on volume not pressure
Slightly above 500 mmHg, for example 501 mmHg
Slightly below 500 mmHg, for example 499 mmHg
questions.why: What matters is the difference between alveolar and ambient pressure, so at altitude the alveolus must simply be a little below the local 500 mmHg for air to move in. Using 759 mmHg applies sea level numbers to a place where they no longer hold, and that alveolar pressure would push air out at altitude. Equal pressures give zero flow, and a pressure above ambient drives expiration.
questions.answerText: Slightly below 500 mmHg, for example 499 mmHg

questions.q: During a forceful cough, alveolar pressure reaches about 100 mmHg above atmospheric. Compared with quiet expiration, predict the pressure gradient and the airflow rate.
options: The gradient is much larger but airflow rate is unchanged
Both the gradient and the airflow rate are much larger
The gradient is larger but airflow reverses direction
Both the gradient and the airflow rate are smaller
questions.why: Forced expiratory muscles compress the thorax hard, so by Boyle's law alveolar pressure climbs far above atmospheric, and since flow equals the pressure difference divided by resistance, flow rises with it, which is what makes a cough able to expel mucus. Airflow cannot stay unchanged when the driving pressure rises a hundredfold. Flow direction is still outward because the alveolus is the high pressure side, and nothing here makes the gradient smaller.
questions.answerText: Both the gradient and the airflow rate are much larger

questions.q: A drug completely paralyzes all respiratory muscles while the airway remains open to room air. Predict thoracic volume change, alveolar pressure, and airflow.
options: Volume rises steadily, alveolar pressure falls, and air flows in continuously
Volume falls steadily, alveolar pressure rises, and air flows out continuously
Volume settles and stops changing, alveolar pressure equals atmospheric, and airflow is zero
Volume is unchanged, alveolar pressure falls steadily, and air continues to flow into the lung
questions.why: Without muscle contraction the chest cannot change volume, so after the lung recoils to its resting point there is no further Boyle's law effect, alveolar pressure equilibrates with atmospheric, and bulk flow ceases. Continuous inflow or outflow would require a sustained volume change that no muscle is producing. Alveolar pressure cannot stay below atmospheric while the airway is open and volume is fixed.
questions.answerText: Volume settles and stops changing, alveolar pressure equals atmospheric, and airflow is zero

questions.q: What is intrapleural pressure in a healthy person at the end of a quiet expiration?
options: About 4 mmHg below atmospheric
Equal to atmospheric
About 4 mmHg above atmospheric
About 1 mmHg above atmospheric
questions.why: The pleural space sits between two structures pulling away from each other, and that traction holds it at roughly 4 mmHg subatmospheric at rest, with values near negative 6 mmHg at the height of inspiration. A pressure equal to atmospheric means the seal has been lost and the lung collapses. Positive intrapleural pressures are abnormal and occur only with forced expiration or trapped air.
questions.answerText: About 4 mmHg below atmospheric

questions.q: How is transpulmonary pressure defined?
options: Atmospheric pressure minus alveolar pressure
Alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure
Intrapleural pressure minus atmospheric pressure
Alveolar pressure minus atmospheric pressure
questions.why: Transpulmonary pressure is the distending pressure across the lung wall, so it compares the pressure inside the alveolus with the pressure just outside the lung in the pleural space, and it is always positive in an inflated lung. Atmospheric minus alveolar is the gradient that drives airflow, not the one that holds the lung open. The other two subtractions do not describe any pressure across the lung tissue.
questions.answerText: Alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure

questions.q: Which two opposing forces create the subatmospheric intrapleural pressure?
options: Inward recoil of the chest wall and outward recoil of the lung
Contraction of the diaphragm and relaxation of the intercostals
Inward elastic recoil of the lung and outward recoil of the chest wall
Surface tension of the alveoli and pressure of the pulmonary capillaries
questions.why: The lung always tries to shrink and the chest wall always tries to spring outward, and because the pleural fluid holds them together these opposite pulls stretch the pleural space and lower its pressure. Reversing which structure pulls which way describes a situation that would compress the pleural space and raise its pressure. Muscle activity changes the pressure during a breath but does not create the resting negativity, and capillary pressure plays no role here.
questions.answerText: Inward elastic recoil of the lung and outward recoil of the chest wall

questions.q: What is the main function of the thin layer of pleural fluid?
options: It lowers the surface tension inside the alveoli so that they stay open at end expiration
It supplies oxygen to the outer surface of the lung
It cushions the lung against the pressure of the heart
It couples the lung to the chest wall by surface tension while allowing them to slide
questions.why: The fluid behaves like water between two glass slides, letting the layers glide during a breath while making them nearly impossible to pull apart, which is how chest wall expansion is transmitted to the lung. Lowering the surface tension inside the alveolus is the job of surfactant, which is a different secretion. Oxygen reaches lung tissue through bronchial and pulmonary circulations, and cushioning is not the physiological point of the coupling.
questions.answerText: It couples the lung to the chest wall by surface tension while allowing them to slide

questions.q: What happens to intrapleural pressure during inspiration?
options: It becomes more negative, falling to about 6 mmHg below atmospheric
It becomes less negative, rising toward atmospheric
It becomes positive, rising to about 6 mmHg above atmospheric
It stays fixed at about 4 mmHg below atmospheric
questions.why: Chest wall expansion pulls the pleural surfaces further apart and stretches the lung more, so the pressure in that sealed space drops further below atmospheric during every inspiration. Rising toward atmospheric happens during expiration as the lung recoils. Positive intrapleural pressure during inspiration would collapse the lung, and the pressure is not fixed since it cycles with each breath.
questions.answerText: It becomes more negative, falling to about 6 mmHg below atmospheric

questions.q: What is a pneumothorax?
options: Fluid in the alveolar air spaces
Air in the pleural cavity
Blood in the pulmonary capillaries
Collapse of a bronchus from outside pressure
questions.why: The prefix pneumo means air and thorax names the chest cavity, so a pneumothorax is air that has entered the normally airtight pleural space, destroying the pressure gradient that holds the lung open. Fluid in the alveoli describes pulmonary edema. Blood in the pulmonary capillaries is normal, and external compression of a bronchus is a separate airway problem.
questions.answerText: Air in the pleural cavity

questions.q: What does the term atelectasis mean?
options: Overinflation of alveoli beyond their normal volume
Inflammation of the pleural membranes
Collapse of lung tissue so that alveoli contain no air
Thickening of the alveolar capillary membrane
questions.why: Atelectasis is airless collapsed lung, which happens when transpulmonary pressure falls to zero or when an obstructed region absorbs its trapped gas. Overinflation is the opposite problem and is seen in emphysema. Pleural inflammation is pleurisy, and a thickened exchange membrane is a diffusion problem rather than a collapse.
questions.answerText: Collapse of lung tissue so that alveoli contain no air

questions.q: Which pressure directly holds the alveoli open against their tendency to recoil?
options: Atmospheric pressure
Intrapleural pressure alone
Pulmonary capillary pressure
Transpulmonary pressure
questions.why: The lung is distended by the difference between the pressure inside it and the pressure around it, and that difference is transpulmonary pressure, so as long as it stays positive the lung stays inflated. Atmospheric pressure by itself is just a reference point. Intrapleural pressure matters only in comparison with alveolar pressure, and capillary pressure acts on blood vessels rather than on the air spaces.
questions.answerText: Transpulmonary pressure

questions.q: Alveolar pressure is 0 mmHg and intrapleural pressure is 4 mmHg below atmospheric. What is transpulmonary pressure?
options: 4 mmHg
0 mmHg
Negative 4 mmHg
8 mmHg
questions.why: Subtracting negative 4 from 0 gives positive 4 mmHg, a distending pressure that keeps the lung inflated at the resting volume. A value of 0 would mean no distending force and the lung would collapse. Negative 4 comes from reversing the subtraction, and 8 mmHg would require an intrapleural pressure of negative 8.
questions.answerText: 4 mmHg

questions.q: At the peak of inspiration alveolar pressure is 1 mmHg below atmospheric and intrapleural pressure is 6 mmHg below atmospheric. What is transpulmonary pressure?
options: 7 mmHg
5 mmHg
Negative 5 mmHg
1 mmHg
questions.why: Negative 1 minus negative 6 equals positive 5 mmHg, larger than the resting value of 4, which is exactly why the lung is more inflated at this moment. Adding the two magnitudes gives 7 and ignores that both numbers are negative. Negative 5 reverses the subtraction, and 1 mmHg is just the alveolar value on its own.
questions.answerText: 5 mmHg

questions.q: A knife wound opens the chest wall into the pleural cavity on one side. What happens to that chest wall immediately?
options: It collapses inward, following the collapsing lung
It springs outward, because its own outward recoil is no longer opposed
It stays exactly where it was, because ribs are rigid
It moves outward, but only during the next inspiratory effort by the muscles
questions.why: The chest wall is normally held in, compressed slightly by the lung pulling inward through the pleural coupling, so breaking the seal lets it expand toward its own larger resting position while the lung recoils away from it. The chest wall and lung move in opposite directions, not together. The ribcage is springy rather than rigid, and the movement is immediate rather than waiting for the next inspiratory effort.
questions.answerText: It springs outward, because its own outward recoil is no longer opposed

questions.q: Why does a pneumothorax on the right side usually leave the left lung inflated?
options: The left lung is supported by the heart
The left lung has stronger elastic recoil
Each lung sits in its own separate pleural cavity
The mediastinum seals the airways on the left
questions.why: The two pleural sacs do not communicate, so air entering one leaves the pressure in the other untouched and that lung keeps its normal transpulmonary pressure. The heart does not hold the lung open. Stronger recoil would make a lung collapse more readily, not less, and the mediastinum does not seal off airways.
questions.answerText: Each lung sits in its own separate pleural cavity

questions.q: A large volume of fluid accumulates in one pleural cavity. What is the effect on the lung on that side?
options: The lung expands because the fluid improves pleural coupling
The lung is compressed because the fluid raises pleural pressure toward atmospheric
The lung is unaffected because fluid cannot transmit pressure
The lung stiffens because the pleural fluid dilutes the surfactant lining the alveoli
questions.why: Extra fluid takes up space in the sealed cavity and pushes pleural pressure up, which shrinks transpulmonary pressure and lets the lung recoil to a smaller volume. A thin film couples the layers, but a large collection separates them and pushes them apart. Fluid transmits pressure very effectively, and pleural fluid does not reach the surfactant lining inside the alveoli.
questions.answerText: The lung is compressed because the fluid raises pleural pressure toward atmospheric

questions.q: What normally prevents the lungs from collapsing to their own resting volume inside the chest?
options: Cartilage rings that hold the alveoli open
Continuous low level contraction of the diaphragm muscle between breaths
The positive pressure of the pulmonary arteries
The subatmospheric intrapleural pressure created by the pleural seal
questions.why: Because pleural pressure is lower than alveolar pressure, there is a net outward distending force on the lung at all times, and that is why an excised lung shrinks but an intact one does not. Cartilage supports conducting airways and never reaches alveoli. The diaphragm relaxes between breaths, and pulmonary arterial pressure acts inside vessels rather than distending air spaces.
questions.answerText: The subatmospheric intrapleural pressure created by the pleural seal

questions.q: During a maximal forced inspiration against a closed airway, what happens to intrapleural pressure?
options: It becomes far more negative, reaching values such as 20 mmHg below atmospheric
It becomes positive, reaching values such as 20 mmHg above atmospheric
It stays near 4 mmHg below atmospheric because the airway is closed
It equalizes with atmospheric because no air can enter
questions.why: Powerful inspiratory effort expands the chest wall strongly, and with no air able to enter, the pleural space is stretched much further than in a normal breath, driving its pressure sharply down. Positive values occur with forced expiration against a closed airway, which is the opposite maneuver. The pressure does change even without airflow because the volume of the sealed space changes.
questions.answerText: It becomes far more negative, reaching values such as 20 mmHg below atmospheric

questions.q: A needle punctures the chest wall and air rushes into one pleural cavity. Trace the change in intrapleural pressure, transpulmonary pressure, and lung volume.
options: Intrapleural pressure falls further, transpulmonary pressure rises, and the lung overinflates
Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric, transpulmonary pressure falls to zero, and the lung collapses
Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric, transpulmonary pressure rises, and the lung stays inflated
Intrapleural pressure is unchanged, transpulmonary pressure falls, and the lung partly deflates
questions.why: Once the sealed space is open to the outside, its pressure can only equal atmospheric, so alveolar minus intrapleural becomes zero and nothing opposes the lung's elastic recoil. A further fall in pleural pressure would require the space to stay sealed. Transpulmonary pressure cannot rise when the pressure outside the lung goes up, and intrapleural pressure certainly does change once the cavity is open.
questions.answerText: Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric, transpulmonary pressure falls to zero, and the lung collapses

questions.q: A chest injury creates a flap that lets air enter the pleural space on inspiration but not leave on expiration. Predict what happens to intrapleural pressure over several breaths and to venous return.
options: Intrapleural pressure becomes progressively more negative and venous return rises
Intrapleural pressure stays near zero and venous return is unchanged
Intrapleural pressure becomes progressively positive and venous return falls
Intrapleural pressure oscillates normally and only the injured lung is affected
questions.why: A one way valve traps a little more air with every breath, so pressure in that cavity climbs above atmospheric and pushes on the mediastinum, compressing the great veins so that less blood returns to the heart. More negative pressure would require air to be removed rather than added. Pressure cannot stay at zero when volume keeps increasing in a closed space, and the rising pressure spreads beyond the injured side.
questions.answerText: Intrapleural pressure becomes progressively positive and venous return falls

questions.q: After a pneumothorax is treated, a drain removes the trapped air and restores a subatmospheric pleural pressure. Explain in order why the lung reinflates.
options: Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, which pushes the lung outward until it meets the chest wall again
Pleural pressure falls below alveolar pressure, so transpulmonary pressure turns positive and the lung is distended
Elastic recoil of the lung increases, which pulls the alveoli open from within
Surfactant is redistributed, which raises surface tension and reopens the alveoli
questions.why: Reinflation is a pressure story: removing pleural air restores the negative pressure outside the lung, so the inside minus outside difference turns positive and stretches the tissue back open. Alveolar pressure only briefly exceeds atmospheric during expiration and is not what holds the lung open. Elastic recoil always acts to collapse the lung, and raising surface tension would promote collapse rather than reopening.
questions.answerText: Pleural pressure falls below alveolar pressure, so transpulmonary pressure turns positive and the lung is distended

questions.q: An isolated lung is removed from the chest and an isolated chest wall is studied separately. Predict the resting volume of each compared with their volumes in the intact thorax.
options: Both are smaller than in the intact thorax
The lung is larger than in the thorax and the chest wall is smaller
Both are larger than in the intact thorax
The lung is smaller than in the thorax and the chest wall is larger
questions.why: In the intact chest each structure is held away from its own resting position, the lung stretched open and the chest wall held in, so freeing them lets the lung shrink and the chest wall spring out. Both shrinking would mean the chest wall recoils inward, which contradicts why pleural pressure is negative. Both enlarging would mean the lung is compressed in the thorax, and reversing the two describes the opposite of the resting forces.
questions.answerText: The lung is smaller than in the thorax and the chest wall is larger

questions.q: What does lung compliance measure?
options: The change in lung volume produced by a given change in distending pressure
The change in distending pressure produced by a given change in volume
The speed at which air flows through the conducting airways
The force with which the lung returns to its resting volume
questions.why: Compliance is delta V divided by delta P, so it answers how much the lung inflates per unit of pressure applied, which is a measure of stretchability. The reversed ratio is elastance, the stiffness of the tissue. Airflow speed depends on airway resistance rather than tissue stretch, and the force of return to resting volume is elastic recoil.
questions.answerText: The change in lung volume produced by a given change in distending pressure

questions.q: What does elastic recoil of the lung describe?
options: The ease with which the lung can be inflated
The tendency of the stretched lung to return to its smaller resting volume
The resistance of the airways to airflow during expiration
The pressure needed to overcome the surface tension of the fluid in the trachea
questions.why: Elastic recoil is stored energy in stretched elastin and in the alveolar surface film that pulls the lung back down in volume, and it is what powers quiet expiration. Ease of inflation is compliance, the opposite property. Airway resistance is a separate flow property, and the surface tension that matters acts at the alveolar air liquid interface rather than in the trachea.
questions.answerText: The tendency of the stretched lung to return to its smaller resting volume

questions.q: Which expression correctly gives lung compliance?
options: Change in transpulmonary pressure divided by change in volume
Change in volume multiplied by change in transpulmonary pressure
Change in volume divided by change in transpulmonary pressure
Change in volume divided by change in airflow
questions.why: Compliance is volume gained per unit of pressure, written as delta V over delta P, and normal lung values are near 200 mL per cmH2O. Inverting the ratio gives elastance, which rises when compliance falls. Multiplying the two has no physiological meaning, and dividing volume by airflow gives a time, not a stretch property.
questions.answerText: Change in volume divided by change in transpulmonary pressure

questions.q: How are lung compliance and elastic recoil related?
options: They vary directly, so high compliance goes with high recoil
They are unrelated properties of lung tissue
They vary directly, so low compliance goes with low recoil
They vary inversely, so high compliance goes with low recoil
questions.why: A lung that stretches easily stores little elastic energy, so it also pulls back weakly, which is why the two properties move in opposite directions. A direct relationship would mean the easiest lung to inflate is also the hardest to keep inflated, which is not how elastic tissue behaves. The two are tightly linked rather than independent.
questions.answerText: They vary inversely, so high compliance goes with low recoil

questions.q: What does pulmonary fibrosis do to lung compliance?
options: It decreases compliance
It increases compliance
It leaves compliance unchanged
It increases compliance only during expiration
questions.why: Fibrosis lays down stiff collagen in the lung interstitium, so a given distending pressure produces a much smaller volume change and the lung becomes hard to inflate. Increased compliance is what happens in emphysema, where elastic tissue is destroyed instead of added. Compliance is not left untouched by scarring, and it does not change direction between phases of the breath.
questions.answerText: It decreases compliance

questions.q: What does pulmonary fibrosis do to elastic recoil?
options: It abolishes elastic recoil completely
It increases elastic recoil
It decreases elastic recoil
It leaves elastic recoil unchanged
questions.why: The stiff scarred lung pulls back harder toward its resting volume, so recoil is high, which is the necessary partner of the low compliance that fibrosis produces. Decreased or abolished recoil describes emphysema, where the elastic fibers themselves are broken down. Because compliance and recoil are inversely linked, recoil cannot stay unchanged while compliance falls.
questions.answerText: It increases elastic recoil

questions.q: What does emphysema do to lung compliance?
options: It decreases compliance
It leaves compliance unchanged
It increases compliance
It decreases compliance only during inspiration
questions.why: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and their elastin, so the remaining tissue offers little resistance to stretch and a small pressure produces a large volume change, making the lung floppy and easy to inflate. Decreased compliance belongs to fibrosis, where collagen makes the lung stiff. The change is structural and permanent rather than absent or phase dependent.
questions.answerText: It increases compliance

questions.q: What does emphysema do to elastic recoil?
options: It increases elastic recoil
It leaves elastic recoil unchanged
It increases elastic recoil only at high lung volumes
It decreases elastic recoil
questions.why: Elastase driven destruction of elastic fibers removes the springs that pull the lung back down, so recoil is lost and the lung tends to stay inflated, which is why these patients trap air. Increased recoil is the fibrosis pattern, paired with low compliance. Recoil cannot remain unchanged when compliance rises, since the two are inversely related.
questions.answerText: It decreases elastic recoil

questions.q: A lung takes in 500 mL when transpulmonary pressure rises by 2 cmH2O. What is its compliance?
options: 250 mL per cmH2O
1000 mL per cmH2O
0.004 mL per cmH2O
100 mL per cmH2O
questions.why: Compliance is 500 divided by 2, giving 250 mL per cmH2O, which is at the upper end of the normal adult range near 200. The value 1000 comes from multiplying the two numbers instead of dividing. The tiny value inverts the ratio into elastance units, and 100 would require a 5 cmH2O pressure change.
questions.answerText: 250 mL per cmH2O

questions.q: A patient needs a transpulmonary pressure change of 8 cmH2O to move 400 mL of air. What is the compliance and what does it indicate?
options: 3200 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally high and indicates a floppy lung
50 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally low and indicates a stiff lung
50 mL per cmH2O, which is normal for an adult
200 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally low and indicates a stiff lung
questions.why: Dividing 400 by 8 gives 50 mL per cmH2O, about a quarter of the normal 200, so this lung resists inflation and points toward a restrictive process such as fibrosis. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 3200 and the wrong conclusion. Fifty is well below normal rather than normal, and 200 is the normal figure rather than a low one.
questions.answerText: 50 mL per cmH2O, which is abnormally low and indicates a stiff lung

questions.q: Which patient must generate a larger inspiratory pressure to take in a 500 mL breath?
options: The patient with emphysema, because high compliance resists inflation
The patient with fibrosis, because low compliance resists inflation
The patient with emphysema, because low compliance resists inflation
Neither, because compliance affects only expiration
questions.why: Low compliance means each milliliter of inflation costs more pressure, so the fibrotic patient does far more inspiratory work for a normal sized breath. High compliance makes inflation easier, not harder, which is why the emphysema patient struggles on the way out rather than the way in. Emphysema raises compliance rather than lowering it, and compliance governs inflation directly.
questions.answerText: The patient with fibrosis, because low compliance resists inflation

questions.q: In a patient with emphysema, which phase of quiet breathing becomes difficult and why?
options: Inspiration, because the stiff lung resists stretching
Expiration, because the loss of elastic recoil removes the force that empties the lung
Inspiration, because elastic recoil pulls the lung closed during inflation
Expiration, because the elastic recoil is excessive and pulls the small airways closed
questions.why: Quiet expiration is passive and depends entirely on stored elastic energy, so when recoil is destroyed the lung cannot empty on its own and the patient must push air out actively. The emphysematous lung is floppy rather than stiff, so inspiration is easy. Excessive recoil is the fibrosis pattern and would speed emptying rather than slow it.
questions.answerText: Expiration, because the loss of elastic recoil removes the force that empties the lung

questions.q: Which two factors together determine lung compliance?
options: The diameter of the bronchi and the strength of the diaphragm
The thickness of the pleural fluid and the rate of blood flow
The elastic fibers of lung tissue and the surface tension of the alveolar fluid
The number of type I alveolar cells and the concentration of oxygen in alveolar gas
questions.why: Stretching the lung means stretching elastin and collagen and also enlarging the air liquid interface against surface tension, so both must be overcome and both set compliance. Bronchial diameter and muscle strength affect resistance and effort rather than tissue stretch. Pleural fluid volume and pulmonary blood flow do not set the stretchability of the parenchyma, and alveolar oxygen has no direct mechanical effect.
questions.answerText: The elastic fibers of lung tissue and the surface tension of the alveolar fluid

questions.q: A newborn produces almost no surfactant. What is the predicted effect on lung compliance?
options: Compliance rises, because there is less material lining the alveoli
Compliance is unchanged, because surfactant affects only airway resistance
Compliance rises, because surface tension helps the alveoli expand
Compliance falls, because unopposed surface tension resists inflation
questions.why: Surface tension is one of the two forces opposing inflation, so without surfactant to lower it each breath requires far more pressure and the lung behaves as if it were stiff. Removing surfactant does not make the lung easier to inflate, since the lining film is not what resists stretch. Surfactant acts on the alveolar surface rather than on airway caliber, and surface tension always opposes expansion.
questions.answerText: Compliance falls, because unopposed surface tension resists inflation

questions.q: A pressure volume curve for a diseased lung is much flatter than normal, so each pressure step adds little volume. Which pair of changes does this represent?
options: High compliance and low elastic recoil
Low compliance and low elastic recoil
Low compliance and high elastic recoil
High compliance and high elastic recoil
questions.why: A flat curve means a small delta V for a given delta P, which is low compliance by definition, and because the two properties are inversely related the recoil force must be high. High compliance would produce a steep curve instead. Low compliance with low recoil, or high compliance with high recoil, would break the inverse relationship between the two.
questions.answerText: Low compliance and high elastic recoil

questions.q: Patient A has a lung compliance of 350 mL per cmH2O and Patient B has 45 mL per cmH2O. Identify the likely disease in each and predict their elastic recoil.
options: A has fibrosis with high recoil and B has emphysema with low recoil
A has emphysema with low recoil and B has fibrosis with high recoil
A has emphysema with high recoil and B has fibrosis with low recoil
Both have fibrosis, but A is at an earlier stage than B
questions.why: Compliance well above the normal 200 means a floppy lung that has lost elastic tissue, which is emphysema, and the same loss means weak recoil, while a compliance of 45 means a stiff scarred lung that pulls back hard. Assigning fibrosis to the high compliance patient reverses the definition of compliance. Pairing emphysema with high recoil ignores that the two properties move in opposite directions.
questions.answerText: A has emphysema with low recoil and B has fibrosis with high recoil

questions.q: A patient with advanced pulmonary fibrosis is tested. Predict compliance, elastic recoil, and where the extra work of breathing falls.
options: Compliance is low, recoil is high, and the extra work falls on inspiration
Compliance is high, recoil is low, and the extra work falls on expiration
Compliance is low, recoil is low, and the extra work falls on expiration
Compliance is high, recoil is high, and the extra work is spread evenly
questions.why: Scar tissue makes the lung stiff, so it resists being stretched open and the inspiratory muscles must work much harder, while the strong recoil actually makes emptying easy and even fast. The high compliance and low recoil combination with expiratory difficulty describes emphysema, the opposite disease. Low compliance cannot coexist with low recoil, and neither can high compliance with high recoil.
questions.answerText: Compliance is low, recoil is high, and the extra work falls on inspiration

questions.q: In emphysema, the destruction of elastic tissue also removes the outward pull that surrounding alveoli exert on small airways. Trace the consequence during forced expiration.
options: Small airways are held open more firmly, so expiratory flow rises above normal
Small airways lose radial traction and collapse, so air is trapped and residual volume rises
Small airways stay unchanged, so expiratory flow is normal despite the tissue loss
Small airways narrow because of smooth muscle contraction, so residual volume falls instead of rising
questions.why: Bronchioles have no cartilage and depend on the surrounding elastic tissue to tether them open, so when that tissue is destroyed the rising pleural pressure of a forced expiration squeezes them shut and gas is trapped behind the closure. Losing tissue cannot hold airways open more firmly. The airways are directly affected by the parenchymal loss, and the problem is loss of tethering rather than smooth muscle contraction, with residual volume rising rather than falling.
questions.answerText: Small airways lose radial traction and collapse, so air is trapped and residual volume rises

questions.q: Two lungs are inflated in the laboratory. Lung X reaches 800 mL at 4 cmH2O of distending pressure, and Lung Y reaches 200 mL at the same pressure. Predict which one empties faster when the pressure is released, and why.
options: Lung X empties faster, because its higher compliance means stronger elastic recoil
Lung X empties faster, because it holds more air to push out
Lung Y empties faster, because its lower compliance means stronger elastic recoil
Both empty at the same rate, because recoil depends only on airway diameter
questions.why: Lung Y gains only 50 mL per cmH2O against Lung X at 200 mL per cmH2O, so Y is the stiff one, and stiffness means it stores more elastic energy and snaps back harder when released. Saying high compliance gives strong recoil reverses the inverse relationship between them. Holding more air does not by itself create a stronger restoring force, and recoil is a property of the tissue rather than of airway diameter.
questions.answerText: Lung Y empties faster, because its lower compliance means stronger elastic recoil

questions.q: Which cell secretes pulmonary surfactant?
options: The type I alveolar cell
The alveolar macrophage
The type II alveolar cell
The goblet cell of the bronchial lining
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal secretory cells that package surfactant into lamellar bodies and release it onto the alveolar surface. Type I cells form the thin diffusion surface but do not secrete. Macrophages clear debris from the alveolus, and goblet cells make mucus in the conducting airways, which is a different secretion entirely.
questions.answerText: The type II alveolar cell

questions.q: What kind of molecule is the main active component of surfactant?
options: A steroid
A polysaccharide
A nucleotide
A phospholipid
questions.why: Surfactant is mostly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, a phospholipid whose water loving head sits in the fluid film while its water fearing tails point into the air, which is exactly the arrangement that breaks up surface tension. A steroid such as cortisol can stimulate surfactant production but is not surfactant itself. Polysaccharides and nucleotides have no amphipathic structure suited to an air liquid interface.
questions.answerText: A phospholipid

questions.q: What does the law of Laplace state for a fluid lined sphere such as an alveolus?
options: Collapsing pressure equals twice the surface tension divided by the radius
Collapsing pressure equals twice the radius divided by the surface tension
Collapsing pressure equals surface tension multiplied by the radius
Collapsing pressure equals the radius divided by twice the surface tension
questions.why: The relationship P equals 2T over r means that for a fixed surface tension a smaller alveolus generates a larger inward pressure, which is why small alveoli are the ones at risk of collapsing. Putting the radius on top would predict that large alveoli collapse first, the opposite of what happens. The other two forms do not preserve the inverse dependence on radius.
questions.answerText: Collapsing pressure equals twice the surface tension divided by the radius

questions.q: What is the direct effect of surfactant on the alveolar fluid lining?
options: It raises surface tension
It lowers surface tension
It thickens the fluid layer
It removes the fluid layer entirely
questions.why: Surfactant molecules insert between water molecules at the air liquid interface and weaken their attraction to each other, which is what lowering surface tension means. Raising surface tension would make alveoli harder to keep open. Surfactant does not add bulk fluid, and the thin aqueous film must remain for gases to dissolve and diffuse.
questions.answerText: It lowers surface tension

questions.q: What effect does normal surfactant have on lung compliance?
options: It decreases compliance
It has no effect on compliance
It increases compliance
It increases compliance only during expiration
questions.why: Surface tension is one of the two forces the lung must overcome to inflate, so reducing it means less pressure is needed for a given volume change, which is higher compliance. Decreasing compliance is what happens when surfactant is missing. Compliance is affected throughout the breathing cycle rather than in one phase only.
questions.answerText: It increases compliance

questions.q: When during fetal development does surfactant production usually reach adequate levels?
options: During the first trimester
During the second trimester
Only after the first breath is taken
During the third trimester
questions.why: Type II cells begin secreting surfactant in the later weeks of gestation and reach reliably adequate amounts in the third trimester, which is why prematurity is the main risk factor for surfactant deficiency. The first and second trimesters are too early, as the alveoli themselves are still forming. Production begins before birth rather than being triggered by the first breath.
questions.answerText: During the third trimester

questions.q: What is the name of the condition caused by surfactant deficiency in a premature newborn?
options: Infant respiratory distress syndrome
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
questions.why: Infant respiratory distress syndrome is defined by insufficient surfactant, high surface tension, and widespread alveolar collapse in a baby born too early. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis are adult disorders of airway narrowing and interstitial scarring, neither caused by a lack of surfactant. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung injury that can follow prolonged ventilation, so it is a later complication rather than the initial deficiency.
questions.answerText: Infant respiratory distress syndrome

questions.q: What does surface tension at the alveolar air liquid interface tend to do?
options: Push the alveolar walls outward toward expansion
Pull the alveolar walls inward toward collapse
Hold the alveolar walls at a fixed diameter
Increase the rate of oxygen diffusion across the wall
questions.why: Water molecules at the surface attract one another strongly and pull the film into the smallest possible area, which for a sphere means shrinking it, so surface tension is always a collapsing force. It cannot push outward, since the attraction between water molecules is inward. It does not fix diameter, and it slows rather than aids gas movement by making the alveolus harder to keep open.
questions.answerText: Pull the alveolar walls inward toward collapse

questions.q: Two alveoli have the same surface tension, but one has half the radius of the other. How do their collapsing pressures compare?
options: The smaller alveolus has half the collapsing pressure
The smaller alveolus has twice the collapsing pressure
The smaller alveolus has four times the collapsing pressure
The two have equal collapsing pressures
questions.why: Laplace's law puts radius in the denominator, so halving the radius doubles the pressure when surface tension is held constant. Halving the pressure would require the radius to double instead. A fourfold change would happen only if pressure varied with the square of the radius, which it does not, and equal pressures would require equal radii.
questions.answerText: The smaller alveolus has twice the collapsing pressure

questions.q: How does surfactant physically lower surface tension?
options: It dissolves the water film completely so that no air liquid interface remains
It adds positive charge that repels the alveolar walls apart
Its molecules get between water molecules and weaken the hydrogen bonding at the surface
It stiffens the alveolar wall so it resists inward pull
questions.why: Surface tension comes from water molecules attracting each other, so inserting amphipathic phospholipids between them breaks up that cohesive network and the surface pulls inward much less strongly. The thin fluid film is not dissolved and must remain in place for gases to dissolve and cross. Surfactant does not work by electrostatic repulsion, and it acts on the liquid film rather than on the tissue of the wall.
questions.answerText: Its molecules get between water molecules and weaken the hydrogen bonding at the surface

questions.q: Why do small alveoli not simply empty into larger ones that share the same airway?
options: Small alveoli have thicker walls that resist emptying
Small alveoli are closed off by smooth muscle sphincters
Small alveoli have a higher surface tension of their own, which holds them open against the pressure
Surfactant is more concentrated in small alveoli, so it lowers their surface tension more
questions.why: As an alveolus shrinks the same surfactant molecules crowd into a smaller surface, so tension drops further, which offsets the small radius in Laplace's law and equalizes pressures across alveoli of different sizes. Alveolar walls are uniformly thin. There are no sphincters at the alveolar level, and a higher surface tension of their own would promote collapse rather than prevent it.
questions.answerText: Surfactant is more concentrated in small alveoli, so it lowers their surface tension more

questions.q: What happens to the work of breathing when surfactant is absent?
options: It increases, because much more pressure is needed to inflate each alveolus
It decreases, because the alveoli are already partly collapsed
It is unchanged, because tidal volume is set by the respiratory centers
It decreases, because surface tension helps pull air inward
questions.why: With surface tension unopposed, every breath must generate a large transpulmonary pressure just to reopen collapsed alveoli, so muscular work rises sharply and the infant tires. Partly collapsed alveoli make breathing harder, not easier, because they must be reinflated from nothing each time. Work depends on the mechanics of the lung, not only on the neural drive, and surface tension always opposes inflation.
questions.answerText: It increases, because much more pressure is needed to inflate each alveolus

questions.q: A premature infant receives exogenous surfactant into the airway. Predict the effect on surface tension and compliance.
options: Surface tension rises and compliance falls
Surface tension falls and compliance falls
Surface tension falls and compliance rises
Surface tension rises and compliance rises
questions.why: Replacing the missing phospholipid restores the low tension film, so the lung takes in more volume for the same pressure and becomes easier to inflate. Rising surface tension is what the treatment is designed to prevent. Falling tension cannot lower compliance, since tension is one of the forces opposing inflation, and tension and compliance move in opposite directions.
questions.answerText: Surface tension falls and compliance rises

questions.q: What happens to alveoli at the end of expiration when surfactant is missing?
options: They stay open but become overinflated
Many collapse completely and must be reopened on the next breath
They fill with surfactant from neighboring alveoli
They remain exactly at their end inspiratory volume
questions.why: End expiration is when alveolar radius is smallest, and Laplace's law makes the collapsing pressure highest at exactly that moment, so without surfactant the alveoli close and the next breath must generate a very high opening pressure. Overinflation is the opposite of what high surface tension causes. Surfactant does not migrate between alveoli to rescue them, and volume necessarily falls during expiration.
questions.answerText: Many collapse completely and must be reopened on the next breath

questions.q: An alveolus with a radius of 100 micrometers shrinks to a radius of 25 micrometers while surface tension stays constant. By what factor does the collapsing pressure change?
options: It decreases fourfold
It increases twofold
It increases sixteenfold
It increases fourfold
questions.why: Pressure varies as one over the radius, so cutting the radius to one quarter multiplies the pressure by four. A decrease would require the alveolus to enlarge instead. A twofold rise corresponds to halving the radius, and a sixteenfold change would need pressure to depend on radius to the fourth power, which is the rule for airway resistance rather than for surface tension.
questions.answerText: It increases fourfold

questions.q: An infant born at 27 weeks has rapid labored breathing and a stiff lung. Trace the chain from the missing molecule to the clinical picture.
options: Low surfactant raises surface tension, alveoli collapse, compliance falls, and the work of breathing rises
Low surfactant lowers surface tension, alveoli overinflate, compliance rises, and the work of breathing rises
Excess surfactant lowers surface tension, alveoli collapse, compliance falls, and the work of breathing rises
Low surfactant raises airway resistance, bronchioles constrict, and expiration becomes prolonged
questions.why: Every step follows from surface tension being unopposed: the alveoli close at end expiration, the lung becomes hard to inflate, and each breath demands a large pressure from small respiratory muscles. Missing surfactant cannot lower surface tension, since surfactant is what lowers it. There is no excess of surfactant here, and the primary defect is at the alveolar surface rather than in airway smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: Low surfactant raises surface tension, alveoli collapse, compliance falls, and the work of breathing rises

questions.q: Consider two connected alveoli of unequal size sharing one alveolar duct, with surfactant absent. Predict what happens and explain using Laplace's law.
options: Both stay the same size, because they share the same air pressure
The larger alveolus empties into the smaller one, because a bigger radius generates a greater inward collapsing pressure
The smaller alveolus empties into the larger one, because its higher collapsing pressure drives air toward the lower pressure sac
Both collapse simultaneously, because collapsing pressure is independent of radius
questions.why: With a fixed surface tension the smaller radius produces the greater inward pressure, so gas flows down that pressure gradient into the larger sac and the small one closes, which is exactly what surfactant normally prevents by lowering tension most in the smallest alveoli. Sharing a duct means sharing a connection, not sharing equal pressures. Larger radius means lower pressure, and collapsing pressure clearly does depend on radius.
questions.answerText: The smaller alveolus empties into the larger one, because its higher collapsing pressure drives air toward the lower pressure sac

questions.q: A mother in preterm labor is given a glucocorticoid, which accelerates fetal type II cell maturation. Predict the newborn's surface tension, compliance, and end expiratory alveolar stability.
options: Higher surface tension, lower compliance, and alveoli that collapse at end expiration
Lower surface tension, lower compliance, and alveoli that stay open at end expiration
Higher surface tension, higher compliance, and alveoli that collapse at end expiration
Lower surface tension, higher compliance, and alveoli that stay open at end expiration
questions.why: More mature type II cells make more surfactant, and each downstream effect follows: tension falls, the lung inflates more readily for a given pressure, and the smallest alveoli no longer close at the end of a breath. Higher surface tension describes the untreated premature lung. Falling tension cannot coexist with falling compliance, and stable alveoli cannot coexist with rising tension.
questions.answerText: Lower surface tension, higher compliance, and alveoli that stay open at end expiration

questions.q: In an infant with widespread alveolar collapse from surfactant deficiency, predict what happens to functional residual capacity and to arterial PO2.
options: Functional residual capacity rises and arterial PO2 falls
Functional residual capacity falls and arterial PO2 falls
Functional residual capacity falls and arterial PO2 rises
Both are unchanged because tidal volume is maintained
questions.why: Collapsed alveoli hold no gas, so the volume left in the lung at the end of a quiet breath shrinks, and because blood still perfuses those airless regions it leaves the lung without picking up oxygen, dropping arterial PO2. A rising functional residual capacity would require air trapping, which is the emphysema pattern rather than the collapse pattern. Arterial PO2 cannot rise when exchange surface is lost, and maintaining tidal volume does not restore the collapsed regions.
questions.answerText: Functional residual capacity falls and arterial PO2 falls

questions.q: What is the main determinant of airway resistance?
options: The radius of the airway
The length of the airway
The viscosity of the air
The total number of alveoli
questions.why: Resistance depends on radius raised to the fourth power, so even a small change in caliber overwhelms every other variable, which is why bronchodilation and bronchoconstriction matter so much. Airway length and gas viscosity are in the equation but barely change from moment to moment. Alveolar number affects gas exchange surface rather than resistance to flow.
questions.answerText: The radius of the airway

questions.q: According to Poiseuille's relationship, how does resistance depend on the radius of a tube?
options: Resistance is directly proportional to the radius
Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius
Resistance is inversely proportional to the radius
Resistance is directly proportional to the square of the radius
questions.why: The fourth power dependence means halving the radius multiplies resistance by sixteen, which explains why modest airway narrowing produces dramatic changes in the effort of breathing. A simple inverse relationship badly understates the effect. Direct proportionality would mean wider tubes resist flow more, which is backwards.
questions.answerText: Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius

questions.q: What does sympathetic stimulation do to bronchial smooth muscle?
options: It contracts the muscle and narrows the airway
It has no effect, since airways receive only parasympathetic fibers
It relaxes the muscle and dilates the airway
It thickens the airway wall by stimulating mucus glands
questions.why: Circulating epinephrine acting on beta 2 receptors relaxes airway smooth muscle, which widens the airways during exercise or stress when more airflow is needed. Contraction and narrowing is the parasympathetic effect. Airways are influenced by both divisions, and sympathetic activity reduces rather than increases airway secretions.
questions.answerText: It relaxes the muscle and dilates the airway

questions.q: What does parasympathetic stimulation through the vagus nerve do to the airways?
options: It causes bronchodilation
It has no effect on airway diameter
It causes bronchodilation and increased mucus clearance
It causes bronchoconstriction
questions.why: Acetylcholine released from vagal fibers acts on muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle and contracts it, narrowing the lumen and raising resistance. Bronchodilation is the sympathetic and epinephrine effect. The vagus definitely influences airway caliber, and it increases mucus secretion rather than clearance.
questions.answerText: It causes bronchoconstriction

questions.q: Where in the airway tree is total resistance to airflow greatest?
options: In the medium sized bronchi
In the terminal bronchioles
In the alveolar ducts
In the respiratory bronchioles
questions.why: Although each small bronchiole is narrow, there are so many of them in parallel that their combined cross sectional area is enormous, so most of the resistance sits in the medium bronchi where the airways are still relatively few. Assuming the smallest tube must have the highest resistance ignores how parallel pathways add. Alveolar ducts and respiratory bronchioles are the most numerous of all and contribute almost nothing to resistance.
questions.answerText: In the medium sized bronchi

questions.q: What effect does histamine released during an allergic reaction have on the airways?
options: It dilates bronchial smooth muscle
It constricts bronchial smooth muscle
It paralyzes the cilia of the airway lining
It destroys elastic fibers in the alveolar wall
questions.why: Histamine from mast cells contracts airway smooth muscle and also causes mucosal swelling, both of which narrow the lumen and raise resistance. Dilation would relieve rather than trigger an asthma attack. Ciliary paralysis is caused by tobacco smoke, and elastic fiber destruction is the mechanism of emphysema.
questions.answerText: It constricts bronchial smooth muscle

questions.q: Which expression gives airflow through the airways?
options: The pressure gradient multiplied by the resistance
The resistance divided by the pressure gradient
The pressure gradient divided by the resistance
The pressure gradient divided by lung compliance
questions.why: Flow equals delta P over R, the same form used for blood flow, so airflow rises with a bigger driving pressure and falls when airways narrow. Multiplying the two would predict that narrower airways carry more air. Dividing resistance by pressure inverts the relationship, and compliance describes tissue stretch rather than opposition to flow.
questions.answerText: The pressure gradient divided by the resistance

questions.q: What effect does an increase in carbon dioxide within a region of airway have on the local bronchioles?
options: It constricts them
It has no local effect
It constricts them only in the presence of histamine
It dilates them
questions.why: Local bronchiolar dilation in response to rising CO2 sends more ventilation to regions that are well perfused, which helps match airflow with blood flow. Constriction would send air away from the regions that need it most. The response is a direct local effect and does not require histamine.
questions.answerText: It dilates them

questions.q: An airway narrows so that its radius is halved. By what factor does its resistance change?
options: It increases twofold
It increases fourfold
It increases eightfold
It increases sixteenfold
questions.why: Resistance varies as one over the radius to the fourth power, and two raised to the fourth is sixteen, so halving the radius makes the airway sixteen times harder to move air through. A twofold rise assumes a simple inverse relationship. Fourfold assumes a square relationship, and eightfold assumes a cube relationship.
questions.answerText: It increases sixteenfold

questions.q: During an asthma attack the driving pressure stays the same while airway smooth muscle contracts. What happens to airflow?
options: It rises, because resistance rises
It falls, because resistance rises
It is unchanged, because the driving pressure did not change
It falls, because lung compliance falls
questions.why: Flow equals pressure divided by resistance, so with the numerator fixed and the denominator climbing steeply, airflow drops, which is why an asthmatic must work harder to move the same volume. Rising resistance can never raise flow. Flow depends on both terms rather than on driving pressure alone, and asthma is an airway caliber problem rather than a compliance problem.
questions.answerText: It falls, because resistance rises

questions.q: Thick mucus partly fills the lumen of a bronchus. How does this raise resistance?
options: It reduces the effective radius available for airflow
It increases the length of the airway
It lowers the compliance of the surrounding alveoli
It raises the viscosity of the inspired air
questions.why: Anything occupying the lumen leaves a narrower channel for air, and because resistance depends on radius to the fourth power even a modest layer of mucus has a large effect. Airway length is set by anatomy and is unchanged by secretions. Alveolar compliance is a tissue property, and mucus does not mix into the air to change its viscosity.
questions.answerText: It reduces the effective radius available for airflow

questions.q: A patient inhales a beta 2 adrenergic agonist. Predict the effect on airway radius and on airway resistance.
options: Radius decreases and resistance rises
Radius increases and resistance rises
Radius increases and resistance falls
Radius decreases and resistance falls
questions.why: Beta 2 receptors on airway smooth muscle relax it when stimulated, so the lumen widens and resistance drops steeply because of the fourth power relationship. Narrowing is what a muscarinic agonist or histamine would produce. Radius and resistance always move in opposite directions, so the two mismatched pairings cannot occur.
questions.answerText: Radius increases and resistance falls

questions.q: In a patient with narrowed airways, why is expiration usually more difficult than inspiration?
options: The expiratory muscles are inherently weaker than the inspiratory muscles of the chest wall
Rising pleural pressure during expiration compresses the airways and narrows them further
Air is denser during expiration because it is warmer
Airway smooth muscle contracts only during expiration
questions.why: During inspiration the falling pleural pressure pulls airways open, while during expiration the pressure around the airways rises and squeezes them, so an already narrowed airway can close off completely. Muscle strength is not the limiting factor here. Expired air is not usefully denser, and smooth muscle tone does not switch on and off with the breathing cycle.
questions.answerText: Rising pleural pressure during expiration compresses the airways and narrows them further

questions.q: Which change would produce the largest increase in airway resistance?
options: A doubling of the length of the airway
A twofold increase in the viscosity of the gas breathed
A reduction in airway radius from 4 mm to 2 mm
A doubling of the airflow rate through the airway
questions.why: Halving the radius multiplies resistance by sixteen, far more than the twofold changes produced by doubling either length or viscosity, both of which appear in the numerator to the first power. Airflow rate is the result of resistance rather than a determinant of it in this relationship.
questions.answerText: A reduction in airway radius from 4 mm to 2 mm

questions.q: During an asthma attack a patient has bronchial smooth muscle contraction, mucosal swelling, and mucus in the lumen at the same time. Predict airway resistance and the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity.
options: Resistance rises sharply and the ratio falls below normal
Resistance rises sharply and the ratio rises above normal
Resistance falls and the ratio falls below normal
Resistance rises sharply but the ratio stays normal
questions.why: All three processes shrink the lumen, so resistance climbs steeply, and because a high resistance slows the air leaving the chest, the volume exhaled in the first second drops more than the total exhaled volume, lowering the ratio. A rising ratio is the restrictive pattern seen when the lung is stiff rather than obstructed. Resistance cannot fall when the lumen is narrowed, and an obstructive process does not leave the ratio normal.
questions.answerText: Resistance rises sharply and the ratio falls below normal

questions.q: An airway radius is reduced to half its original value while the patient doubles the driving pressure. What happens to airflow compared with the original?
options: It rises to twice the original
It falls to one half of the original
It falls to one eighth of the original
It stays the same, since the two effects cancel
questions.why: Halving the radius raises resistance sixteenfold, and flow equals pressure over resistance, so doubling the pressure gives a flow of two divided by sixteen, which is one eighth. Flow cannot rise when resistance climbs sixteen times faster than the driving pressure. A halving would occur only if resistance had merely quadrupled, and cancellation would require resistance to change by only a factor of two.
questions.answerText: It falls to one eighth of the original

questions.q: A healthy person begins vigorous exercise. Trace the effect of sympathetic activation on airway caliber, resistance, and the airflow achievable per unit of effort.
options: Airways constrict, resistance rises, and less air moves for the same driving pressure
Airways dilate, resistance rises, and less air moves for the same driving pressure
Airways dilate, resistance is unchanged, and airflow depends only on muscle strength
Airways dilate, resistance falls, and more air moves for the same driving pressure
questions.why: Epinephrine acting on beta 2 receptors relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, and because resistance falls with the fourth power of the widening radius, the same respiratory effort now moves much more air, which is exactly what exercise demands. Constriction during exercise would work against the increased need for ventilation. Dilation must lower resistance, so the pairings with unchanged or rising resistance are internally inconsistent.
questions.answerText: Airways dilate, resistance falls, and more air moves for the same driving pressure

questions.q: In emphysema the elastic tissue that tethers small airways open has been destroyed. Predict how airway resistance compares between quiet inspiration and forced expiration in these patients.
options: Resistance is equally raised in both phases of the breath because the airway walls are permanently thickened and narrowed
Resistance is near normal on inspiration but rises sharply on forced expiration as untethered airways collapse
Resistance is raised on inspiration but normal on expiration because recoil is strong
Resistance is normal in both phases because emphysema affects only the alveoli
questions.why: Falling pleural pressure during inspiration still helps hold airways open, but during forced expiration the surrounding pressure rises and there is no longer any elastic tethering to resist it, so the small airways close and trap air. The airway walls themselves are not thickened in emphysema. Recoil is reduced rather than strong in this disease, and the alveolar destruction has direct consequences for the airways that run through that tissue.
questions.answerText: Resistance is near normal on inspiration but rises sharply on forced expiration as untethered airways collapse

questions.q: What is tidal volume?
options: The volume of air moved in or out during one quiet breath
The maximum volume that can be inhaled after a quiet inspiration
The volume remaining in the lung after a maximal expiration
The total volume the lung can hold at full inflation
questions.why: Tidal volume is the ordinary breath at rest, the amount that moves in and out without any extra effort. The extra volume available beyond a quiet inspiration is the inspiratory reserve volume. Air left after maximal expiration is residual volume, and full inflation defines total lung capacity.
questions.answerText: The volume of air moved in or out during one quiet breath

questions.q: What is the approximate tidal volume of a healthy adult at rest?
options: About 150 mL
About 500 mL
About 1200 mL
About 3000 mL
questions.why: A quiet breath moves roughly 500 mL, of which about 350 mL reaches the alveoli. The 150 mL figure is anatomic dead space, the part of that breath left in the conducting airways. About 1200 mL is close to residual volume, and 3000 mL is closer to the inspiratory reserve volume.
questions.answerText: About 500 mL

questions.q: What is the inspiratory reserve volume?
options: The air remaining after a maximal expiration
The extra air that can be exhaled beyond a normal tidal expiration
The extra air that can be inhaled beyond a normal tidal inspiration
The total air inhaled and exhaled in one minute
questions.why: Inspiratory reserve volume is the reserve available on top of a normal breath, roughly 3000 mL in an adult, and it is what a deep breath draws on. Air left after maximal expiration is residual volume. The extra air available on expiration is the expiratory reserve volume, and air moved per minute is minute ventilation.
questions.answerText: The extra air that can be inhaled beyond a normal tidal inspiration

questions.q: What is the expiratory reserve volume?
options: The air that enters the lung during a maximal inspiration
The air that cannot be exhaled from the lungs no matter how hard a person tries
