The air left in the lung at the end of a quiet expiration
The extra air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration
questions.why: After a quiet breath out, about 1200 mL can still be forced out with effort, and that reserve is the expiratory reserve volume. Air that cannot be exhaled at all is residual volume. The air present at the end of a quiet expiration is functional residual capacity, which is the expiratory reserve plus the residual volume.
questions.answerText: The extra air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal tidal expiration

questions.q: What is the residual volume?
options: The air remaining in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration
The air remaining in the lungs after a quiet expiration
The air remaining in the conducting airways after each breath
The air that can still be inhaled after a quiet inspiration
questions.why: Even after blowing out as hard as possible, roughly 1200 mL stays in the lung and keeps the alveoli from collapsing and gas exchange from stopping between breaths. Air present after a quiet expiration is functional residual capacity, a larger number. Air left in the conducting airways is anatomic dead space, and inhalable reserve is the inspiratory reserve volume.
questions.answerText: The air remaining in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration

questions.q: Which volumes add together to give vital capacity?
options: Tidal volume plus residual volume
Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume plus expiratory reserve volume
Inspiratory reserve volume plus residual volume
Expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume plus the anatomic dead space
questions.why: Vital capacity is all the air a person can move voluntarily, which is the ordinary breath plus both reserves, about 4700 mL in an adult. Residual volume cannot be exhaled, so it is never part of vital capacity. Expiratory reserve plus residual volume is functional residual capacity, and adding the anatomic dead space to that gives no meaningful quantity at all.
questions.answerText: Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume plus expiratory reserve volume

questions.q: How is total lung capacity defined?
options: Vital capacity plus tidal volume
Vital capacity minus residual volume
Vital capacity plus residual volume
Inspiratory capacity plus vital capacity
questions.why: Total lung capacity is every bit of air the lung holds at full inflation, so it is the volume a person can move plus the volume that always stays behind, about 5900 mL. Adding tidal volume double counts, since tidal volume is already inside vital capacity. Subtracting residual volume would give back vital capacity, and inspiratory capacity is also already contained within vital capacity.
questions.answerText: Vital capacity plus residual volume

questions.q: Which lung volume cannot be measured with a simple spirometer?
options: Tidal volume
Expiratory reserve volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
questions.why: A spirometer records only air that actually moves through it, and residual volume by definition never leaves the lung, so it must be obtained by helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography. Tidal volume and both reserve volumes are all exhaled or inhaled through the mouthpiece and are recorded directly.
questions.answerText: Residual volume

questions.q: A student has a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL, and an expiratory reserve volume of 1200 mL. What is the vital capacity?
questions.why: Vital capacity is 500 plus 3000 plus 1200, which is 4700 mL. Leaving out the tidal volume gives 4200. Leaving out the expiratory reserve gives 3500, and 5900 would be total lung capacity once a residual volume of 1200 mL is added.

questions.q: A patient has a vital capacity of 4700 mL and a residual volume of 1200 mL. What is the total lung capacity?
questions.why: Total lung capacity is vital capacity plus residual volume, so 4700 plus 1200 gives 5900 mL. Subtracting instead of adding gives 3500. Reporting 4700 ignores the residual volume entirely, and 6100 does not follow from these two numbers.

questions.q: A patient has an expiratory reserve volume of 1200 mL and a residual volume of 1300 mL. What is the functional residual capacity?
options: 100 mL
questions.why: Functional residual capacity is the air still in the lung at the end of a quiet expiration, which is the expiratory reserve plus the residual volume, so 1200 plus 1300 gives 2500 mL. Reporting 1300 counts only the residual volume and leaves out the reserve that can still be forced out. Subtracting gives 100, which would leave the lung nearly empty between breaths, and 3000 does not match either number.

questions.q: A person has a tidal volume of 500 mL and an inspiratory reserve volume of 3100 mL. What is the inspiratory capacity?
options: 500 mL
questions.why: Inspiratory capacity is the most that can be inhaled starting from the end of a quiet expiration, so it is the tidal volume plus the inspiratory reserve, giving 3600 mL. Subtracting gives 2600. Reporting either component alone leaves out the other half of the maneuver.

questions.q: A patient has a total lung capacity of 6000 mL and a vital capacity of 4500 mL. What is the residual volume?
questions.why: Residual volume is the part of total lung capacity that cannot be exhaled, so it is 6000 minus 4500, which is 1500 mL. Adding the two gives 10500, far beyond any human lung. The value 4500 is the vital capacity itself, and 3000 does not follow from the subtraction.

questions.q: On a spirogram, a subject breathes quietly and then, from the end of a quiet expiration, inhales as deeply as possible. Which value has been measured?
options: Vital capacity
Inspiratory capacity
Functional residual capacity
Inspiratory reserve volume
questions.why: Starting from the resting end expiratory level and filling the lung completely measures inspiratory capacity, which combines the tidal volume and the inspiratory reserve. Vital capacity would require a maximal expiration first. Functional residual capacity is the starting point rather than the excursion, and inspiratory reserve volume is measured from the top of a normal tidal inspiration instead.
questions.answerText: Inspiratory capacity

questions.q: A subject has a vital capacity of 4800 mL, a tidal volume of 500 mL, and an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL. What is the expiratory reserve volume?
options: 800 mL
questions.why: Vital capacity is the sum of the three moveable volumes, so subtracting both 500 and 3000 from 4800 leaves 1300 mL. Subtracting only the inspiratory reserve gives 1800 and forgets that the tidal volume is also part of the sum. The values 2500 and 800 do not satisfy the sum, since adding either to 3500 does not return the measured vital capacity.

questions.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis is tested. Predict what happens to total lung capacity, vital capacity, and residual volume.
options: Total lung capacity and vital capacity fall while residual volume rises
All three rise above predicted values
All three fall below predicted values
Total lung capacity is unchanged while vital capacity falls and residual volume rises
questions.why: Stiff scarred lungs cannot be stretched to a normal size, so every volume shrinks, which is the defining feature of a restrictive pattern. The pattern of falling capacities with a rising residual volume belongs to obstructive disease with air trapping. Rising volumes across the board would require a floppy overinflated lung, which fibrosis is not.
questions.answerText: All three fall below predicted values

questions.q: A patient with advanced emphysema is tested. Predict the changes in residual volume, functional residual capacity, and vital capacity.
options: Residual volume and functional residual capacity rise while vital capacity falls
All three fall together because the lung holds less air
Residual volume falls while functional residual capacity and vital capacity rise
Residual volume rises while functional residual capacity and vital capacity are unchanged
questions.why: Loss of elastic recoil and collapse of untethered small airways trap gas at the end of every expiration, so residual volume and the resting lung volume both climb, and because the lung is already near full, less of the total remains available to move, so vital capacity falls. A uniform fall in all three is the restrictive picture instead. Residual volume cannot fall when air is being trapped, and functional residual capacity must rise with it, since it contains the residual volume.
questions.answerText: Residual volume and functional residual capacity rise while vital capacity falls

questions.q: On a spirogram the pen rises steadily through several quiet breaths, then makes one very large upward excursion followed immediately by one very large downward excursion to the lowest point on the trace. Which measurement does the full excursion represent?
options: Total lung capacity
Functional residual capacity
Vital capacity
Inspiratory capacity
questions.why: A maximal inspiration followed by a maximal expiration moves every milliliter a person can voluntarily move, and that excursion is vital capacity. Total lung capacity cannot be traced this way because it includes residual volume, which never leaves the lung. Functional residual capacity is a resting level rather than an excursion, and inspiratory capacity covers only the upward half of the maneuver.
questions.answerText: Vital capacity

questions.q: A subject has a total lung capacity of 5800 mL, a functional residual capacity of 2400 mL, and an expiratory reserve volume of 1100 mL. Calculate the residual volume and then the vital capacity.
options: Residual volume 3500 mL and vital capacity 2300 mL
Residual volume 1100 mL and vital capacity 4700 mL
Residual volume 2400 mL and vital capacity 3400 mL
Residual volume 1300 mL and vital capacity 4500 mL
questions.why: Functional residual capacity is expiratory reserve plus residual volume, so residual volume is 2400 minus 1100, which is 1300 mL, and vital capacity is total lung capacity minus residual volume, so 5800 minus 1300 gives 4500 mL. Using the total lung capacity minus the functional residual capacity gives 3400, which is inspiratory capacity rather than vital capacity. Treating the expiratory reserve or the functional residual capacity as the residual volume skips the first subtraction.
questions.answerText: Residual volume 1300 mL and vital capacity 4500 mL

questions.q: What does forced expiratory volume in one second measure?
options: The volume of air blown out during the first second of a maximal forced expiration
The total volume blown out during one maximal forced expiration from full inflation
The volume inhaled during the first second of a maximal inspiration
The volume of air moved during one quiet breath
questions.why: This value captures how fast air can leave the chest, which is why it is sensitive to anything that narrows the airways. The total volume blown out over the whole maneuver is forced vital capacity. Measuring inspiration would not test expiratory airflow, and a quiet breath is tidal volume.
questions.answerText: The volume of air blown out during the first second of a maximal forced expiration

questions.q: What does forced vital capacity measure?
options: The volume exhaled in the first second of a forced expiration
The total volume exhaled as forcefully and completely as possible after a maximal inspiration
The volume remaining in the lung after a forced expiration
The volume of air exhaled per minute at rest
questions.why: Forced vital capacity is the whole amount a person can move out in one maximal effort, so it reflects how much lung is available rather than how quickly it empties. The first second alone is forced expiratory volume in one second. Air left behind is residual volume, and air moved per minute is minute ventilation.
questions.answerText: The total volume exhaled as forcefully and completely as possible after a maximal inspiration

questions.q: What is the approximate normal value for the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity in a healthy young adult?
options: About 0.40
About 0.60
About 0.80
About 1.00
questions.why: A healthy adult blows out roughly 80 percent of the whole forced vital capacity in the first second, which is why values below about 0.70 are treated as abnormal. Ratios of 0.40 and 0.60 indicate obstruction. A ratio of 1.00 would mean the entire capacity left the lung within one second, which does not occur in normal lungs.
questions.answerText: About 0.80

questions.q: What happens to the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity in obstructive lung disease?
options: It rises above normal
It stays exactly normal
It falls below normal
It first rises and then falls
questions.why: Narrowed airways slow the exit of air, so the volume delivered in the first second drops much more than the total volume does, and the ratio falls, typically under 0.70. A rising ratio is the restrictive pattern. A normal ratio means airflow is not limited, which is the opposite of obstruction.
questions.answerText: It falls below normal

questions.q: What happens to the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity in restrictive lung disease?
options: It falls well below 0.70
It falls to about half of normal
It becomes impossible to calculate
It is preserved or even higher than normal
questions.why: Restriction shrinks both the volume exhaled in the first second and the total forced vital capacity by similar proportions, and the strong elastic recoil of a stiff lung actually speeds emptying, so the ratio holds up or rises. A ratio below 0.70 defines obstruction rather than restriction. Both values are still measurable, so the ratio can always be calculated.
questions.answerText: It is preserved or even higher than normal

questions.q: Which disease produces an obstructive spirometry pattern?
options: Asthma
Pulmonary fibrosis
Severe scoliosis of the thoracic spine
Muscular dystrophy affecting the diaphragm
questions.why: Asthma narrows the airways, which limits how fast air can leave and lowers the ratio, the definition of an obstructive pattern. Pulmonary fibrosis stiffens lung tissue and produces restriction. Scoliosis and diaphragmatic weakness restrict how much the chest can expand, so they also give restrictive patterns rather than obstructive ones.
questions.answerText: Asthma

questions.q: Which disease produces a restrictive spirometry pattern?
options: Chronic bronchitis
Pulmonary fibrosis
Emphysema
Asthma
questions.why: Fibrosis fills the interstitium with stiff collagen, so the lung cannot expand normally and all volumes fall while airflow stays proportionally well preserved. Chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and asthma all narrow or collapse airways and give obstructive patterns with a reduced ratio.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary fibrosis

questions.q: What happens to total lung capacity in restrictive lung disease?
options: It increases
It stays normal while only airflow falls
It decreases
It increases early and decreases only in late disease
questions.why: Restriction means the lung cannot be filled to a normal size, so total lung capacity is reduced, and this is the measurement that confirms restriction when the ratio is normal. An increased total lung capacity is seen in emphysema because of air trapping. A normal total lung capacity with reduced airflow describes obstruction instead.
questions.answerText: It decreases

questions.q: A patient has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 1.8 L and a forced vital capacity of 3.0 L. Calculate the ratio and classify the pattern.
options: 0.60, a restrictive pattern
1.67, an obstructive pattern
0.60, an obstructive pattern
0.60, a normal result
questions.why: Dividing 1.8 by 3.0 gives 0.60, well under the 0.70 threshold, so airflow is limited and the pattern is obstructive. Restriction would show a preserved or raised ratio. The value 1.67 comes from inverting the fraction, and 0.60 is clearly below the normal range rather than within it.
questions.answerText: 0.60, an obstructive pattern

questions.q: A patient has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 2.4 L and a forced vital capacity of 3.0 L, but the predicted forced vital capacity for this patient is 4.8 L. Classify the pattern.
options: Obstructive, because the measured forced vital capacity is far below the predicted value for this patient
Restrictive, because the ratio is 0.80 while the forced vital capacity is far below predicted
Normal, because the ratio of 0.80 is within the normal range
Obstructive, because the ratio of 0.80 is at the lower limit of normal
questions.why: The ratio of 2.4 to 3.0 is 0.80, so airflow is not limited, but the lung is only holding about 62 percent of the predicted volume, which is the signature of restriction. A reduced volume alone does not make a result obstructive, since obstruction is defined by the ratio. Calling the result normal ignores that the measured capacity is only about two thirds of predicted.
questions.answerText: Restrictive, because the ratio is 0.80 while the forced vital capacity is far below predicted

questions.q: A patient has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 3.2 L and a forced vital capacity of 4.0 L. What is the ratio?
questions.why: Dividing 3.2 by 4.0 gives 0.80, a normal ratio showing that airflow is not limited. The value 1.25 inverts the fraction. The value 0.64 would come from a forced expiratory volume of 2.56 L, and 0.32 does not follow from these numbers.

questions.q: Predict the spirometry ratio in a patient with advanced emphysema.
options: The ratio is raised, because elastic recoil is increased
The ratio is normal, because emphysema affects only gas exchange
The ratio is reduced, because airflow is limited more than lung volume
The ratio is reduced, because total lung capacity is decreased
questions.why: Emphysema destroys the elastic tissue that tethers small airways open, so they collapse during forced expiration and the first second delivers much less air than it should, dropping the ratio. Elastic recoil in emphysema is reduced, not increased. The disease clearly affects mechanics as well as exchange, and total lung capacity actually rises because of air trapping.
questions.answerText: The ratio is reduced, because airflow is limited more than lung volume

questions.q: Predict the spirometry ratio in a patient with pulmonary fibrosis.
options: The ratio is reduced, while both measured volumes are reduced
The ratio is preserved or raised, while both measured volumes are raised
The ratio is reduced, while both measured volumes are raised
The ratio is preserved or raised, while both measured volumes are reduced
questions.why: Fibrosis shrinks the lung, so the forced expiratory volume in one second and the forced vital capacity both fall, but the stiff lung recoils hard and empties quickly, so the fraction delivered in the first second holds up or improves. A reduced ratio would indicate obstruction. Raised volumes do not occur in a lung that cannot expand normally.
questions.answerText: The ratio is preserved or raised, while both measured volumes are reduced

questions.q: Why does airway obstruction lower the ratio rather than lowering both values equally?
options: Narrowed airways slow the flow rate, so the first second is affected far more than the eventual total
Narrowed airways reduce total lung capacity, so the forced vital capacity falls first
Narrowed airways prevent full inspiration, so the maneuver cannot be completed
Narrowed airways also stiffen the surrounding lung tissue, so both measured values fall in equal proportion
questions.why: Given enough time an obstructed patient can still empty most of the lung, so the total exhaled volume is relatively preserved while the rate of emptying is not, which is exactly why the ratio is the diagnostic number. Obstruction does not primarily reduce lung size, and total lung capacity is often increased instead. Inspiration is generally easier than expiration in obstruction, and airway narrowing does not stiffen the parenchyma.
questions.answerText: Narrowed airways slow the flow rate, so the first second is affected far more than the eventual total

questions.q: Why does a restrictive process leave the ratio intact?
options: The forced vital capacity is unchanged in restriction, so only the one second volume falls and the ratio drops
Both the one second volume and the total capacity fall together, and strong recoil keeps flow rates high
Airway radius increases to compensate for the smaller lung
The measurement is taken over a longer interval in restrictive disease
questions.why: Restriction reduces the size of the lung without narrowing the airways, so the numerator and denominator shrink together and the stiff tissue actually pushes air out quickly, holding the ratio at or above normal. The forced vital capacity is definitely reduced in restriction rather than unchanged, so the numerator is not the only value that falls. Airway radius does not enlarge to compensate, and the one second interval is the same for every patient.
questions.answerText: Both the one second volume and the total capacity fall together, and strong recoil keeps flow rates high

questions.q: Patient A has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 1.6 L and a forced vital capacity of 4.0 L. Classify the pattern and predict this patient's lung compliance and elastic recoil.
options: Restrictive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
Obstructive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
Obstructive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
Restrictive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
questions.why: The ratio is 1.6 divided by 4.0, or 0.40, far below 0.70, so this is obstruction, and when the cause is emphysema the destroyed elastic tissue leaves a lung that inflates easily but recoils weakly. Restriction would show a preserved ratio with reduced volumes. Low compliance with high recoil is the fibrosis pairing, and it does not belong to an obstructive result of this kind.
questions.answerText: Obstructive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil

questions.q: Patient B has a forced expiratory volume in one second of 2.1 L, a forced vital capacity of 2.5 L, and a total lung capacity of 4.0 L against a predicted 6.0 L. Classify the pattern and predict compliance and recoil.
options: Obstructive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
Restrictive, with high compliance and low elastic recoil
Obstructive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
Restrictive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil
questions.why: The ratio is 2.1 divided by 2.5, which is 0.84, above normal, while the total lung capacity is only two thirds of predicted, so this is restriction, and a lung that cannot be filled is stiff, meaning low compliance and correspondingly strong recoil. An obstructive label would require a ratio below 0.70. High compliance with low recoil describes emphysema, the opposite mechanical picture.
questions.answerText: Restrictive, with low compliance and high elastic recoil

questions.q: A spirometry report shows a forced vital capacity that is 60 percent of predicted and a ratio of 0.85. Working back from the result, what does this say about the lung?
options: The lung is stiffer than normal and cannot be inflated to a normal size, but its airways are not narrowed
The airways are narrowed and the lung tissue itself is normal
Both the airways and the lung tissue are normal, so the effort was poor
The lung is floppier than normal and traps air behind small airways that collapse during forced expiration
questions.why: A high ratio with a small capacity means air leaves quickly but there was not much to start with, which points to reduced expansion of stiff tissue rather than to any flow limitation. Narrowed airways would drag the ratio down instead of pushing it up. Poor effort tends to reduce both values without raising the ratio, and a floppy air trapping lung produces a low ratio with a raised total lung capacity.
questions.answerText: The lung is stiffer than normal and cannot be inflated to a normal size, but its airways are not narrowed

questions.q: A patient with a baseline ratio of 0.55 inhales a bronchodilator, and the forced expiratory volume in one second rises by 18 percent while the forced vital capacity changes little. What does this response indicate about the obstruction?
options: The obstruction is entirely due to permanent destruction of alveolar walls
A large part of the obstruction is reversible airway smooth muscle contraction
The result should be reclassified as a restrictive pattern
The lung tissue has become more compliant within minutes
questions.why: A bronchodilator acts on smooth muscle, so a marked jump in the one second volume shows that much of the narrowing was muscular tone rather than fixed structural change, which is characteristic of asthma. Destroyed alveolar walls cannot be reopened by a drug, so that would give little or no improvement. The ratio remains below normal, so the pattern is still obstructive, and tissue compliance does not change in minutes.
questions.answerText: A large part of the obstruction is reversible airway smooth muscle contraction

questions.q: How is minute ventilation calculated?
options: Tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency
Tidal volume minus dead space, multiplied by breathing frequency
Vital capacity multiplied by breathing frequency
Tidal volume divided by breathing frequency
questions.why: Minute ventilation is simply all the air moved in and out per minute, so it is the size of each breath times how many breaths occur. Subtracting dead space first gives alveolar ventilation, a smaller and more meaningful number. Vital capacity is a maximal effort rather than a resting breath, and dividing would not give a volume per minute.
questions.answerText: Tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency

questions.q: How is alveolar ventilation calculated?
options: Tidal volume multiplied by the breathing frequency in breaths per minute
Tidal volume minus dead space volume, multiplied by breathing frequency
Minute ventilation multiplied by dead space volume
Dead space volume multiplied by breathing frequency
questions.why: Only the part of each breath that gets past the conducting airways can exchange gas, so dead space must be subtracted from every breath before multiplying by rate. Tidal volume times frequency gives minute ventilation, which overstates useful ventilation. Dead space times frequency gives dead space ventilation, the wasted portion.
questions.answerText: Tidal volume minus dead space volume, multiplied by breathing frequency

questions.q: What is the approximate anatomic dead space volume in a healthy adult?
options: About 350 mL
About 500 mL
About 150 mL
About 50 mL
questions.why: The conducting airways hold roughly 150 mL, so a 500 mL breath delivers only about 350 mL of fresh air to the alveoli. The 350 mL figure is that useful portion rather than the dead space itself. About 500 mL is the whole tidal volume, and 50 mL is far too small for the entire airway tree.
questions.answerText: About 150 mL

questions.q: What is anatomic dead space?
options: The volume of alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused
The volume of air left in the lung after maximal expiration
The volume of alveoli that are perfused but not ventilated
The volume of the conducting airways, where no gas exchange occurs
questions.why: Anatomic dead space is a structural volume, the air sitting in the nose, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles where there is no exchange surface. Ventilated but unperfused alveoli make up alveolar dead space, a functional rather than anatomic category. Air left after maximal expiration is residual volume, and perfused but unventilated alveoli form a shunt.
questions.answerText: The volume of the conducting airways, where no gas exchange occurs

questions.q: What is alveolar dead space?
options: Alveoli that receive air but receive little or no blood flow
Alveoli that receive blood but receive no air
The air in the trachea and bronchi at the end of a breath
Alveoli that have collapsed and hold no air
questions.why: An alveolus with air but no capillary blood flow cannot exchange anything, so its ventilation is wasted just as thoroughly as air sitting in the trachea. Alveoli with blood but no air are a shunt, the opposite mismatch. Air in the trachea and bronchi is anatomic dead space, and collapsed alveoli are atelectatic rather than dead space.
questions.answerText: Alveoli that receive air but receive little or no blood flow

questions.q: What is physiologic dead space?
options: Anatomic dead space minus alveolar dead space
Anatomic dead space plus alveolar dead space
Alveolar dead space minus anatomic dead space
Tidal volume minus anatomic dead space
questions.why: Physiologic dead space is the total wasted ventilation from both sources, and in a healthy person it is nearly equal to the anatomic dead space because alveolar dead space is very small. The subtractions do not describe any real quantity. Tidal volume minus anatomic dead space is the useful fresh air per breath, the opposite of wasted volume.
questions.answerText: Anatomic dead space plus alveolar dead space

questions.q: What is a typical resting breathing frequency for a healthy adult?
options: About 4 breaths per minute
About 12 breaths per minute
About 30 breaths per minute
About 60 breaths per minute
questions.why: Twelve breaths of about 500 mL give the familiar resting minute ventilation of 6 L/min. Four breaths per minute would be severe hypoventilation. Thirty breaths per minute is the rapid shallow pattern of distress, and 60 is a newborn rate rather than an adult one.
questions.answerText: About 12 breaths per minute

questions.q: Which measure best predicts how well the blood is oxygenated and cleared of carbon dioxide?
options: Minute ventilation
Tidal volume alone
Alveolar ventilation
Breathing frequency alone
questions.why: Only air that reaches exchange surface can change blood gases, so alveolar ventilation is the number that tracks arterial PCO2. Minute ventilation can look completely normal while alveolar ventilation is dangerously low. Tidal volume and frequency each tell only half the story, since the same minute ventilation can come from very different combinations.
questions.answerText: Alveolar ventilation

questions.q: A person breathes 500 mL fourteen times per minute. What is the minute ventilation?
options: 514 mL/min
4900 mL/min
6000 mL/min
7000 mL/min
questions.why: Minute ventilation is 500 times 14, which is 7000 mL/min or 7 L/min. Adding the two numbers gives 514, which is not a rate. The value 4900 would be the alveolar ventilation once a 150 mL dead space is subtracted, and 6000 corresponds to twelve breaths rather than fourteen.
questions.answerText: 7000 mL/min

questions.q: A person breathes 500 mL twelve times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
options: 4200 mL/min
6000 mL/min
1800 mL/min
5850 mL/min
questions.why: Each breath delivers 500 minus 150, or 350 mL, and twelve of those give 4200 mL/min. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation, which ignores dead space. The value 1800 is the dead space ventilation, and 5850 comes from subtracting the dead space only once instead of from every breath.
questions.answerText: 4200 mL/min

questions.q: A patient breathes 400 mL fifteen times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
options: 6000 mL/min
3750 mL/min
2250 mL/min
5850 mL/min
questions.why: Fresh air per breath is 400 minus 150, or 250 mL, and multiplying by 15 gives 3750 mL/min. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation before dead space is removed. The value 2250 is dead space ventilation, and 5850 subtracts the dead space only once from the whole minute.
questions.answerText: 3750 mL/min

questions.q: A patient has a minute ventilation of 6 L/min at a rate of 12 breaths per minute. What is the tidal volume?
options: 72 mL
350 mL
500 mL
720 mL
questions.why: Rearranging minute ventilation as tidal volume times frequency gives 6000 divided by 12, which is 500 mL. The value 72 comes from dividing the wrong way. The value 350 is the fresh air per breath after a 150 mL dead space is subtracted, not the tidal volume itself.
questions.answerText: 500 mL

questions.q: A patient breathes 300 mL twenty times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
options: 6000 mL/min
4500 mL/min
3000 mL/min
1500 mL/min
questions.why: Only 150 mL of each 300 mL breath gets past the dead space, and 150 times 20 gives 3000 mL/min, half of the alveolar ventilation a normal pattern would provide at the same minute ventilation. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation. The other values do not follow from this tidal volume and rate.
questions.answerText: 3000 mL/min

questions.q: A patient breathes 750 mL eight times per minute with a dead space of 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
options: 1200 mL/min
6000 mL/min
5850 mL/min
4800 mL/min
questions.why: Fresh air per breath is 750 minus 150, or 600 mL, and 600 times 8 gives 4800 mL/min. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation, and 1200 is the dead space ventilation. The value 5850 wrongly subtracts a single 150 mL from the minute total instead of from each breath.
questions.answerText: 4800 mL/min

questions.q: A swimmer breathes through a snorkel that adds 200 mL of dead space, breathing 500 mL twelve times per minute. What is the alveolar ventilation?
options: 1800 mL/min
4200 mL/min
6000 mL/min
3600 mL/min
questions.why: Total dead space becomes 150 plus 200, or 350 mL, so each breath delivers only 150 mL and twelve breaths give 1800 mL/min, far below the normal 4200. The value 4200 ignores the added tubing. The value 6000 is the minute ventilation, which the snorkel does not change at all, which is exactly why minute ventilation is a misleading number here.
questions.answerText: 1800 mL/min

questions.q: Person A breathes 1000 mL six times per minute and Person B breathes 250 mL twenty four times per minute. Dead space is 150 mL in both. Compare their minute and alveolar ventilations.
options: Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, but alveolar ventilation is 5100 mL/min in A and 2400 mL/min in B
Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, and alveolar ventilation is also equal in both
Minute ventilation is higher in B, and alveolar ventilation is also higher in B
Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, but alveolar ventilation is 2400 mL/min in A and 5100 mL/min in B
questions.why: Both move 6 L/min, but A wastes 150 mL only six times while B wastes it twenty four times, so A delivers 850 times 6 equals 5100 mL/min and B delivers 100 times 24 equals 2400 mL/min. Equal alveolar ventilations would require equal dead space fractions, which deep and shallow breathing do not have. Minute ventilation is identical rather than higher in B, and reversing the two values contradicts the arithmetic.
questions.answerText: Minute ventilation is 6000 mL/min in both, but alveolar ventilation is 5100 mL/min in A and 2400 mL/min in B

questions.q: A patient in distress breathes 200 mL thirty times per minute with a 150 mL dead space. Calculate alveolar ventilation and predict arterial PCO2.
options: Alveolar ventilation is 6000 mL/min and arterial PCO2 falls
Alveolar ventilation is 1500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 falls
Alveolar ventilation is 1500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 rises
Alveolar ventilation is 4500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 stays normal
questions.why: Only 50 mL of each breath clears the dead space, so 50 times 30 gives 1500 mL/min, roughly a third of normal, and since carbon dioxide removal depends on alveolar ventilation, PCO2 climbs even though minute ventilation is a normal looking 6000 mL/min. Reporting 6000 as alveolar ventilation confuses the two measures. Falling PCO2 would require hyperventilation at the alveolar level, which is the opposite of what is happening here.
questions.answerText: Alveolar ventilation is 1500 mL/min and arterial PCO2 rises

questions.q: A clot blocks blood flow to a region of lung while that region keeps receiving air. Predict the effect on physiologic dead space and on alveolar ventilation at unchanged minute ventilation.
options: Physiologic dead space falls and effective alveolar ventilation rises
Physiologic dead space rises and effective alveolar ventilation falls
Physiologic dead space is unchanged because the airways are normal
Physiologic dead space rises and effective alveolar ventilation rises to compensate
questions.why: Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused add alveolar dead space to the anatomic dead space, so more of every breath is wasted and less of the same minute ventilation actually exchanges gas. Dead space cannot fall when a perfusion defect appears. Physiologic dead space includes both anatomic and alveolar components, so normal airways do not keep it unchanged, and effective alveolar ventilation cannot rise while the wasted fraction grows.
questions.answerText: Physiologic dead space rises and effective alveolar ventilation falls

questions.q: A patient has a minute ventilation of 8 L/min at 32 breaths per minute, yet arterial PCO2 is rising. Dead space is 150 mL. Work out why.
options: Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 3200 mL/min despite the high minute ventilation
Tidal volume is 500 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 11200 mL/min and the rise must come from another cause
Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 8000 mL/min and dead space is irrelevant
Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 4800 mL/min, which is normal
questions.why: Dividing 8000 by 32 gives a tidal volume of 250 mL, and subtracting the 150 mL dead space leaves 100 mL per breath, so alveolar ventilation is 100 times 32, or 3200 mL/min, well below the normal 4200. A tidal volume of 500 mL would require a minute ventilation of 16 L/min at this rate. Alveolar ventilation can never equal minute ventilation while dead space exists, and 4800 does not match the arithmetic.
questions.answerText: Tidal volume is only 250 mL, so alveolar ventilation is 3200 mL/min despite the high minute ventilation

questions.q: What does a spirometer record?
options: The volume of air moved into and out of the lungs over time
The pressure inside the pleural cavity during each breath
The percentage of oxygen in the exhaled air
The rate of blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries
questions.why: A spirometer measures moving volume against time, which is why every value it reports is either a volume or a flow derived from one. Pleural pressure requires an esophageal balloon or a direct measurement, not a mouthpiece. Exhaled gas fractions come from a gas analyzer, and pulmonary blood flow is not measured by this instrument at all.
questions.answerText: The volume of air moved into and out of the lungs over time

questions.q: What do the two axes of a standard spirogram show?
options: Pressure on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis
Volume on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis
Flow on the vertical axis and pressure on the horizontal axis
Time on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis
questions.why: Reading volume against time lets you see both how much air moved and how quickly, which is what makes the one second measurement possible. A pressure volume plot is used to study compliance, not to record a breathing trace. Flow against volume gives the flow volume loop, a different display, and swapping the axes is simply not the convention.
questions.answerText: Volume on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis

questions.q: Which value cannot be obtained from a spirogram alone?
options: Vital capacity
Tidal volume
Residual volume
Expiratory reserve volume
questions.why: The spirometer only sees air that passes the mouthpiece, and residual volume never leaves the lung, so it and every capacity containing it must be measured by another method. Vital capacity, tidal volume, and expiratory reserve volume are all exhaled through the instrument and are read directly from the trace.
questions.answerText: Residual volume

questions.q: Which capacities can be calculated directly from a spirogram?
options: Functional residual capacity and total lung capacity
Total lung capacity and vital capacity
Functional residual capacity and inspiratory capacity
Vital capacity and inspiratory capacity
questions.why: Both of these are built only from volumes that move through the mouthpiece, so they can be read straight off the trace. Functional residual capacity and total lung capacity each contain residual volume, which the spirometer cannot see, so neither can be obtained without a dilution or plethysmography technique.
questions.answerText: Vital capacity and inspiratory capacity

questions.q: Which subject characteristics are used to calculate predicted lung volumes?
options: Height, age, and sex
Blood pressure, pulse, and body temperature
Resting breathing rate and tidal volume
Hemoglobin concentration and arterial PO2
questions.why: Lung size scales with body size and declines with age, and reference equations use height, age, and sex to give the value a healthy person of that description should reach. Vital signs describe cardiovascular state rather than lung size. Breathing pattern is a result rather than a predictor, and blood measurements report gas transport rather than lung volume.
questions.answerText: Height, age, and sex

questions.q: How is percent predicted calculated for a lung volume?
options: Predicted value divided by measured value, multiplied by 100
Measured value divided by predicted value, multiplied by 100
Measured value minus predicted value, divided by 100
Measured value plus predicted value, divided by 2
questions.why: Percent predicted expresses the measured result as a fraction of what was expected, so the measured value goes on top and the result is a straightforward percentage. Inverting the fraction would make a small lung look large. Subtracting gives a raw difference in liters rather than a percentage, and averaging the two numbers has no interpretive meaning.
questions.answerText: Measured value divided by predicted value, multiplied by 100

questions.q: Why is a nose clip used during spirometry?
options: To slow the rate of breathing during the maneuver
To prevent the subject from smelling the equipment
To prevent air escaping through the nose instead of the mouthpiece
To keep the upper airway humidified during a forced expiratory maneuver
questions.why: The spirometer can only measure what goes through it, so any air lost through the nose makes every recorded volume too small. The clip does not change breathing rate, which the subject controls. Smell is irrelevant to the measurement, and humidification of the upper airway happens regardless of the clip.
questions.answerText: To prevent air escaping through the nose instead of the mouthpiece

questions.q: Which maneuver measures vital capacity?
options: A single quiet breath in and out
A maximal inspiration held for ten seconds
A maximal expiration followed by a period of quiet tidal breathing
A maximal inspiration followed immediately by a maximal expiration
questions.why: Vital capacity is the largest volume a person can move voluntarily, so the lung must be filled completely and then emptied completely in one continuous effort. A quiet breath gives only the tidal volume. Holding a breath records no volume change, and a maximal expiration alone leaves out the inspiratory half of the excursion.
questions.answerText: A maximal inspiration followed immediately by a maximal expiration

questions.q: A student measures a vital capacity of 3.6 L against a predicted value of 4.5 L. What is the percent predicted?
options: 80 percent
125 percent
90 percent
20 percent
questions.why: Dividing 3.6 by 4.5 gives 0.80, so the student reached 80 percent of the predicted value. Inverting the fraction gives 125 percent and would suggest a larger than expected lung. The value 20 percent is the shortfall rather than the result, and 90 percent does not follow from these numbers.
questions.answerText: 80 percent

questions.q: A student measures a forced expiratory volume in one second of 2.0 L against a predicted 3.2 L. What is the percent predicted?
options: 160 percent
62.5 percent
37.5 percent
64 percent
questions.why: Dividing 2.0 by 3.2 gives 0.625, so the measured value is 62.5 percent of predicted. The value 160 percent comes from inverting the fraction. The value 37.5 percent is the shortfall from predicted rather than the percent achieved, and 64 percent does not match the division.
questions.answerText: 62.5 percent

questions.q: A lab group needs to determine total lung capacity, but the spirometer cannot supply it. Which approach is required?
options: Repeating the vital capacity maneuver with greater effort
Adding the tidal volume to the vital capacity
A helium dilution or nitrogen washout test to find residual volume first
Measuring the forced expiratory volume in one second and doubling it
questions.why: Total lung capacity contains residual volume, so the missing piece must be found by a method that measures gas still inside the lung, and then it is added to the vital capacity. Greater effort cannot expel air that is trapped by definition. Adding tidal volume double counts, since it is already inside vital capacity, and doubling a one second volume has no physiological basis.
questions.answerText: A helium dilution or nitrogen washout test to find residual volume first

questions.q: On a recorded spirogram, from which point does the expiratory reserve volume excursion begin?
options: From the peak of a maximal inspiration
From the lowest point of a maximal expiration
From the peak of a quiet inspiration
From the resting level at the end of a quiet expiration
questions.why: Expiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be forced out after an ordinary breath has already been let go, so the trace must start at the resting end expiratory level and go down from there. Starting at maximal inspiration would trace the vital capacity instead. The lowest point of the trace is the end of that excursion, and starting from a quiet inspiration would include the tidal volume.
questions.answerText: From the resting level at the end of a quiet expiration

questions.q: A student stops exhaling early during the vital capacity maneuver. What is the effect on the recorded value?
options: Vital capacity is underestimated
Vital capacity is overestimated
Vital capacity is unaffected because the maneuver is standardized
Vital capacity is unaffected but residual volume appears larger
questions.why: The instrument records only the air that actually passed the mouthpiece, so stopping short leaves part of the expiratory reserve volume in the lung and the number comes out too small. It cannot be overestimated, since no extra air was moved. Standardizing the instructions does not guarantee full effort, and residual volume is not recorded by a spirometer in the first place.
questions.answerText: Vital capacity is underestimated

questions.q: Two healthy students of the same age and sex are tested, one 150 cm tall and one 190 cm tall. How should their predicted vital capacities compare?
options: The shorter student has the larger predicted vital capacity
The taller student has the larger predicted vital capacity
Both have the same predicted vital capacity, since age and sex match
Predicted values cannot be compared between two people
questions.why: Reference equations scale strongly with height because a taller thorax houses larger lungs, so the 190 cm student is expected to move considerably more air. The relationship runs with height rather than against it. Age and sex are only two of the three inputs, and comparing predicted values across subjects is exactly what reference equations are for.
questions.answerText: The taller student has the larger predicted vital capacity

questions.q: A student records a vital capacity that is 105 percent of predicted. How should this result be interpreted?
options: As evidence of emphysema, since the lung is holding more air than the reference equation expects
As a measurement error, since values above 100 percent are impossible
As a normal result, since predicted values describe an average rather than a ceiling
As evidence of restriction, since the value differs from predicted
questions.why: Predicted equations give the center of a healthy range, so results modestly above or below 100 percent are ordinary, and roughly 80 to 120 percent is generally treated as normal. Emphysema raises total lung capacity through trapping but lowers vital capacity. Values above predicted are entirely possible, and restriction would show a value well below predicted rather than above it.
questions.answerText: As a normal result, since predicted values describe an average rather than a ceiling

questions.q: From a spirogram a student reads a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 2900 mL, and an expiratory reserve volume of 1300 mL, with a predicted vital capacity of 5000 mL. Calculate the vital capacity and the percent predicted.
options: Vital capacity 4700 mL, which is 94 percent of predicted
Vital capacity 4700 mL, which is 106 percent of predicted
Vital capacity 3400 mL, which is 68 percent of predicted
Vital capacity 4200 mL, which is 84 percent of predicted
questions.why: Adding 500 plus 2900 plus 1300 gives 4700 mL, and 4700 divided by 5000 is 0.94, a normal result. The figure 106 percent comes from inverting the fraction. A vital capacity of 3400 leaves out the inspiratory reserve or the tidal volume, and 4200 omits the tidal volume from the sum.
questions.answerText: Vital capacity 4700 mL, which is 94 percent of predicted

questions.q: A student records a vital capacity of 3.2 L against a predicted 4.6 L, with a ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity of 0.85. Interpret the pair of findings.
options: An obstructive pattern, since the measured vital capacity is well below the predicted value
A restrictive pattern, since volume is markedly reduced while airflow is well preserved
A normal result, since the ratio is above 0.80
An obstructive pattern, since the ratio is above 0.80
questions.why: The measured vital capacity is about 70 percent of predicted, which is a real reduction, yet the high ratio shows air is leaving quickly, and that combination defines restriction. A reduced volume by itself does not indicate obstruction, which is defined by a low ratio. Calling the result normal ignores how far the volume falls short, and a high ratio is the opposite of the obstructive finding.
questions.answerText: A restrictive pattern, since volume is markedly reduced while airflow is well preserved

questions.q: A student records a vital capacity of 4.6 L against a predicted 4.7 L, but a ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity of 0.62. Interpret the pair of findings.
options: A normal result, since the vital capacity is 98 percent of predicted
A restrictive pattern, since the ratio is below 0.70
An obstructive pattern, since airflow is limited even though lung volume is normal
A measurement error, since a normal lung volume cannot occur together with a low ratio
questions.why: Obstruction is defined by how fast air leaves, not by how much the lung holds, so a normal capacity with a ratio of 0.62 is exactly the early obstructive picture seen in asthma. A normal volume alone does not clear the result, since the ratio is the diagnostic number. A low ratio never indicates restriction, and this combination is common in practice rather than impossible.
questions.answerText: An obstructive pattern, since airflow is limited even though lung volume is normal

questions.q: Two students of identical height obtain very different results, and the one with the lower values had a poor seal around the mouthpiece. Predict how the leak affected the recorded volumes and the calculated percent predicted.
options: All recorded volumes are too high, so every percent predicted value is falsely raised
Only the forced expiratory volume in one second is affected, so the ratio falls
All recorded volumes are too low, so every percent predicted value is falsely reduced
The volumes are unaffected because the predicted values correct for technique
questions.why: Air escaping around the lips never reaches the sensor, so every volume the instrument sees is smaller than the volume the lung actually moved, and dividing those small numbers by unchanged predicted values makes the student look falsely restricted. A leak cannot add volume to the record. It affects both the one second volume and the total similarly rather than only one, and predicted equations depend on body size and cannot correct for a technical fault.
questions.answerText: All recorded volumes are too low, so every percent predicted value is falsely reduced

questions.q: Dalton's law says the partial pressure of a gas in a mixture equals what?
options: Its solubility in water times the total pressure
Its molecular weight divided by the total pressure
Its diffusion coefficient times the total pressure
Its fractional concentration times the total pressure
questions.why: Each gas in a mixture exerts pressure in proportion to how much of the mixture it makes up, so partial pressure is the fraction of that gas times the total pressure of the mixture. Solubility governs how much gas dissolves in a liquid once it contacts blood, which is Henry's law, not the pressure the gas exerts in air. Molecular weight and the diffusion coefficient set how fast a gas crosses a membrane, not the partial pressure it starts with.
questions.answerText: Its fractional concentration times the total pressure

questions.q: What is the total atmospheric pressure at sea level?
options: 860 mmHg
473 mmHg
760 mmHg
660 mmHg
questions.why: Sea level barometric pressure is 760 mmHg, and every partial pressure calculation in respiratory physiology starts from that number. 660 and 860 mmHg are not standard values and would give wrong inspired oxygen figures. 473 mmHg is roughly the pressure at the summit of Mount Everest, which is why oxygen is so scarce there.
questions.answerText: 760 mmHg

questions.q: What percentage of dry atmospheric air is oxygen?
options: About 16 percent
About 40 percent
About 78 percent
About 21 percent
questions.why: Dry air is about 21 percent oxygen, and that fraction stays the same at every altitude even though the total pressure falls. About 16 percent is the oxygen content of expired air, after the alveoli have taken some up. About 40 percent is a common supplemental oxygen setting, not room air, and about 78 percent is the nitrogen fraction of the atmosphere.
questions.answerText: About 21 percent

questions.q: At body temperature, what partial pressure does water vapor exert in fully humidified airway gas?
options: 40 mmHg
104 mmHg
5 mmHg
47 mmHg
questions.why: Gas is saturated with water vapor by the time it reaches the alveoli, and at 37 C that vapor exerts 47 mmHg, which must be subtracted from barometric pressure before applying the oxygen fraction. 40 mmHg is alveolar PCO2, a different gas entirely. 104 mmHg is alveolar PO2, and 5 mmHg is roughly the carbon dioxide gradient across the respiratory membrane.
questions.answerText: 47 mmHg

questions.q: What is the normal partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air?
options: About 104 mmHg
About 150 mmHg
About 40 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
questions.why: Alveolar PO2 sits near 104 mmHg because inspired gas is diluted by carbon dioxide entering the alveolus and by water vapor, and because oxygen is continuously removed by blood. About 150 mmHg is humidified inspired air before that dilution occurs. About 40 mmHg is mixed venous PO2, and about 60 mmHg is the point where the oxyhemoglobin curve starts to fall steeply.
questions.answerText: About 104 mmHg

questions.q: What is the normal partial pressure of carbon dioxide in alveolar air?
options: 40 mmHg
45 mmHg
24 mmHg
104 mmHg
questions.why: Alveolar PCO2 is held near 40 mmHg by alveolar ventilation, and arterial PCO2 tracks it closely because equilibration is essentially complete. 45 mmHg is mixed venous PCO2, the value before blood reaches the lung. 24 mmHg is a plasma bicarbonate concentration in mEq/L, not a partial pressure, and 104 mmHg is alveolar PO2.
questions.answerText: 40 mmHg

questions.q: What is the normal partial pressure of oxygen in systemic arterial blood?
options: About 75 mmHg
About 100 mmHg
About 120 mmHg
About 40 mmHg
questions.why: Arterial PO2 runs about 100 mmHg, just under alveolar PO2 because a small amount of unoxygenated blood drains into the pulmonary veins. About 120 mmHg exceeds alveolar PO2, which is impossible when blood equilibrates with alveolar gas. About 40 mmHg is mixed venous PO2, and about 75 mmHg would be a clearly hypoxemic value rather than a normal one.
questions.answerText: About 100 mmHg

questions.q: What are the normal partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide in mixed venous blood?
options: PO2 100 mmHg and PCO2 40 mmHg
PO2 60 mmHg and PCO2 50 mmHg
PO2 40 mmHg and PCO2 45 mmHg
PO2 45 mmHg and PCO2 40 mmHg
questions.why: Blood returning from the tissues has given up oxygen and picked up carbon dioxide, so PO2 has dropped to about 40 mmHg while PCO2 has risen to about 45 mmHg. Reversing the two numbers is the common slip, and it hides the real pattern, which is that oxygen falls a long way across a capillary while carbon dioxide rises only about 5 mmHg. PO2 100 with PCO2 40 describes arterial blood, and 60 with 50 matches neither arterial nor venous blood.
questions.answerText: PO2 40 mmHg and PCO2 45 mmHg

questions.q: Dry room air at sea level is 21 percent oxygen and the barometric pressure is 760 mmHg. What is the PO2 of that air?
options: 104 mmHg
100 mmHg
160 mmHg
150 mmHg
questions.why: Dalton's law gives 0.21 times 760, which is about 160 mmHg for dry air that has not yet been humidified. 150 mmHg is the answer after subtracting the 47 mmHg of water vapor added in the airways. 104 mmHg is alveolar PO2 after carbon dioxide dilution and oxygen uptake, and 100 mmHg is arterial PO2.
questions.answerText: 160 mmHg

questions.q: Inspired air is fully humidified in the conducting airways at sea level. What is the PO2 of tracheal gas?
options: About 113 mmHg
About 104 mmHg
About 150 mmHg
About 160 mmHg
questions.why: Water vapor takes up 47 mmHg of the 760 mmHg, leaving 713 mmHg of dry gas pressure, and 0.21 times 713 is about 150 mmHg. About 160 mmHg ignores humidification and applies to dry atmospheric air. About 113 mmHg would result from subtracting water vapor twice, and about 104 mmHg is alveolar gas, which has also been diluted by carbon dioxide.
questions.answerText: About 150 mmHg

questions.q: A climber reaches an altitude where barometric pressure is 380 mmHg. What is the PO2 of the dry air she breathes?
options: 70 mmHg
40 mmHg
80 mmHg
160 mmHg
questions.why: The oxygen fraction stays at 21 percent at every altitude, so only total pressure changes: 0.21 times 380 is about 80 mmHg. 160 mmHg is the sea level value and would only apply if pressure had not fallen. 70 mmHg is the humidified value after subtracting 47 mmHg of water vapor, and 40 mmHg is mixed venous PO2, not an inspired value.
questions.answerText: 80 mmHg

questions.q: A patient breathes 50 percent oxygen at sea level. What is the PO2 of the humidified inspired gas reaching the alveoli?
options: About 357 mmHg
About 380 mmHg
About 150 mmHg
About 713 mmHg
questions.why: Subtract water vapor first, giving 760 minus 47 equals 713 mmHg, then take half of that for the 50 percent oxygen fraction, which is about 357 mmHg. About 380 mmHg comes from taking half of 760 without correcting for humidification. About 150 mmHg is room air humidified, and 713 mmHg is the dry gas pressure, which would only be the PO2 if the patient breathed 100 percent oxygen.
questions.answerText: About 357 mmHg

questions.q: Why is arterial PO2 slightly lower than alveolar PO2 in a healthy person?
options: Hemoglobin cannot become more than 90 percent saturated in the lung
A small amount of unoxygenated venous blood drains into the pulmonary veins
Oxygen is consumed by the walls of the pulmonary capillaries themselves
The respiratory membrane is slightly too thick for complete equilibration
questions.why: Bronchial and thebesian veins add a small volume of deoxygenated blood downstream of the alveoli, so the blood that reaches the systemic arteries is very slightly diluted, giving a normal gradient of a few mmHg. Capillary wall metabolism is far too small to explain the difference. In a healthy lung the membrane is thin enough that equilibration is complete well before the end of the capillary, and hemoglobin does reach roughly 98 percent saturation in arterial blood.
questions.answerText: A small amount of unoxygenated venous blood drains into the pulmonary veins

questions.q: What is the partial pressure gradient driving carbon dioxide from pulmonary capillary blood into the alveolus?
options: About 5 mmHg
About 45 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
About 20 mmHg
questions.why: Mixed venous PCO2 is 45 mmHg and alveolar PCO2 is 40 mmHg, so the gradient is only about 5 mmHg, and carbon dioxide still moves fast enough because it is roughly twenty times more soluble than oxygen. About 45 mmHg is the venous value itself, not a difference. About 60 mmHg is the oxygen gradient at the lung, and about 20 mmHg is not a gradient found at the respiratory membrane.
questions.answerText: About 5 mmHg

questions.q: What is the partial pressure gradient driving oxygen from systemic capillary blood into resting tissue?
options: About 40 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
About 100 mmHg
About 5 mmHg
questions.why: Arterial blood arrives at 100 mmHg and resting tissue PO2 is about 40 mmHg, so the gradient is roughly 60 mmHg, which is what drives oxygen out of the capillary. About 100 mmHg is arterial PO2 itself, which would only be the gradient if tissue PO2 were zero. About 5 mmHg is the carbon dioxide gradient at the lung, and about 40 mmHg is tissue PO2, again a value rather than a difference.
questions.answerText: About 60 mmHg

questions.q: A sedated patient hypoventilates until alveolar PCO2 reaches 60 mmHg while breathing room air at sea level. Using a respiratory exchange ratio of 0.8, what is the approximate alveolar PO2?
options: About 40 mmHg
About 75 mmHg
About 90 mmHg
About 110 mmHg
questions.why: Humidified inspired PO2 is about 150 mmHg, and the alveolar gas equation subtracts PCO2 divided by 0.8, so 150 minus 75 gives roughly 75 mmHg. About 90 mmHg would follow if carbon dioxide were subtracted one for one, which understates its dilution effect. About 110 mmHg is higher than normal alveolar PO2 and cannot occur when carbon dioxide is accumulating, and about 40 mmHg would be a near lethal alveolar value not produced by this degree of hypoventilation.
questions.answerText: About 75 mmHg

questions.q: A climber at a barometric pressure of 380 mmHg hyperventilates until alveolar PCO2 falls to 20 mmHg. Using a respiratory exchange ratio of 0.8, what is her approximate alveolar PO2?
options: About 80 mmHg
About 45 mmHg
About 70 mmHg
About 25 mmHg
questions.why: Humidified inspired PO2 at this pressure is (380 minus 47) times 0.21, about 70 mmHg, and subtracting 20 divided by 0.8 leaves roughly 45 mmHg. About 70 mmHg is the inspired value before any carbon dioxide dilution. About 25 mmHg subtracts the inspired value from the carbon dioxide term in the wrong direction, and about 80 mmHg ignores humidification and the carbon dioxide correction together.
questions.answerText: About 45 mmHg

questions.q: Alveolar air at sea level contains oxygen at 104 mmHg, carbon dioxide at 40 mmHg, and water vapor at 47 mmHg. What partial pressure does nitrogen exert?
options: About 569 mmHg
About 616 mmHg
About 713 mmHg
About 600 mmHg
questions.why: The partial pressures of all gases present must sum to the total pressure, so nitrogen is 760 minus the sum of 104, 40, and 47, which is about 569 mmHg. About 616 mmHg leaves out the water vapor term. About 713 mmHg is the total dry gas pressure, which still includes oxygen and carbon dioxide, and about 600 mmHg does not follow from these numbers.
questions.answerText: About 569 mmHg

questions.q: During heavy exercise, mixed venous PO2 falls from 40 mmHg to 20 mmHg while alveolar PO2 stays near 104 mmHg. What happens to oxygen uptake in the lung, and why?
options: It falls, because blood arrives with too little oxygen to be loaded efficiently
It is unchanged, because alveolar PO2 sets oxygen uptake all by itself
It falls, because faster blood flow leaves no time for any transfer
It rises, because the gradient across the respiratory membrane is larger
questions.why: Blood arriving at the lung with a lower PO2 widens the gradient from about 64 mmHg to about 84 mmHg, and a bigger driving force moves more oxygen per unit time, which is exactly what exercise requires. Blood arriving with less oxygen loads more, not less, since the deficit is what gets filled. Alveolar PO2 is only one end of the gradient, so it cannot set uptake alone, and although transit time does shorten in exercise, equilibration still completes in a healthy lung because capillary recruitment adds surface area.
questions.answerText: It rises, because the gradient across the respiratory membrane is larger

questions.q: What supplies the driving force for a gas to diffuse across the respiratory membrane?
options: The hydrostatic pressure difference across the capillary wall
The partial pressure difference for that gas across the membrane
The total barometric pressure on the two sides of the membrane
The concentration of hemoglobin in the pulmonary capillary
questions.why: Gases diffuse down their own partial pressure gradients, so only the difference in that gas between alveolus and blood drives net transfer. Total barometric pressure is the same on both sides and creates no gradient for any single gas. Hemoglobin keeps the gradient from collapsing by removing dissolved oxygen, but it is not the driving force itself, and hydrostatic pressure drives bulk fluid movement, which is filtration rather than diffusion.
questions.answerText: The partial pressure difference for that gas across the membrane

questions.q: If the surface area available for gas exchange doubles and nothing else changes, what happens to the rate of diffusion?
options: It is unchanged
It falls to one quarter
It doubles
It halves
questions.why: Diffusion rate is directly proportional to surface area, so doubling the area doubles the number of molecules crossing per unit time. Halving would be the effect of doubling membrane thickness, since thickness is in the denominator. Nothing about area leaves the rate unchanged, and a fall to one quarter does not match any single change in the diffusion relationship.
questions.answerText: It doubles

questions.q: How does diffusion rate across the respiratory membrane change as the membrane gets thicker?
options: It rises, because rate is directly proportional to thickness
It is unaffected, because thickness only changes the time required
It falls, but only when the gas is carbon dioxide
It falls, because rate is inversely proportional to thickness
questions.why: Thickness sits in the denominator of the diffusion relationship, so any added distance, whether from fluid or scar tissue, slows transfer for every gas. Rate rising with thickness reverses the relationship. Thickness does change the time required, but that is exactly why it lowers the rate, and it slows oxygen more than carbon dioxide rather than affecting carbon dioxide alone.
questions.answerText: It falls, because rate is inversely proportional to thickness

questions.q: Carbon dioxide diffuses across the respiratory membrane about twenty times faster than oxygen. What accounts for that?
options: Carbon dioxide is far more soluble in the membrane and in plasma
Carbon dioxide molecules are much smaller than oxygen molecules
Carbon dioxide has a much larger partial pressure gradient
Carbon dioxide is carried by a membrane transport protein
questions.why: Solubility is part of the diffusion coefficient, and carbon dioxide is roughly twenty four times more soluble than oxygen in the fluid lining and in plasma, which more than makes up for its slightly larger molecular weight. Carbon dioxide is in fact the larger molecule, so size works against it. Its gradient is much smaller, about 5 mmHg against 60 mmHg for oxygen, and it crosses by simple diffusion with no carrier protein involved.
questions.answerText: Carbon dioxide is far more soluble in the membrane and in plasma

questions.q: About how thick is the respiratory membrane in a healthy lung?
options: About 0.5 millimeters
About 0.5 micrometers
About 5 micrometers
About 50 micrometers
questions.why: The alveolar epithelium, the fused basement membranes, and the capillary endothelium together span roughly half a micrometer, which is thin enough for equilibration in a fraction of the capillary transit time. About 5 micrometers is closer to the diameter of a capillary lumen. About 50 micrometers and 0.5 millimeters are hundreds of times too thick and would make gas exchange impossible.
questions.answerText: About 0.5 micrometers

questions.q: About how much total alveolar surface area is available for gas exchange in a healthy adult?
options: About 70 square meters
About 7 square meters
About 700 square meters
About 0.7 square meters
questions.why: Roughly 300 million alveoli give a combined surface of about 70 square meters, close to the floor area of a small apartment, which is why a small membrane thickness plus a huge area moves so much gas. About 7 square meters is nearer to the surface area of the skin and far too small. About 700 square meters and 0.7 square meters are off by an order of magnitude in either direction.
questions.answerText: About 70 square meters

questions.q: At rest, how long does a red blood cell take to equilibrate with alveolar gas compared with its time in the pulmonary capillary?
options: Equilibration takes the entire transit time with no reserve
About 0.25 seconds to equilibrate out of about 0.75 seconds of transit
About 0.75 seconds to equilibrate out of about 0.25 seconds of transit
About 0.75 seconds to equilibrate out of about 3 seconds of transit
questions.why: Equilibration is complete in roughly a third of the transit time, and that spare two thirds is the reserve that lets healthy people exercise without desaturating. Equilibration cannot take longer than the transit and still produce normal arterial blood, so the reversed version is impossible. Transit time is about 0.75 seconds at rest rather than 3 seconds, and if equilibration used the whole transit there would be no reserve at all, which is what happens in disease.
questions.answerText: About 0.25 seconds to equilibrate out of about 0.75 seconds of transit

questions.q: Emphysema reduces gas transfer mainly through which change to the respiratory membrane?
options: Accumulation of fluid in the alveolar space
A fall in the partial pressure of inspired oxygen
Loss of alveolar surface area as alveolar walls are destroyed
Thickening of the membrane by collagen deposited in the alveolar wall
questions.why: Emphysema destroys alveolar septa, so many small alveoli merge into fewer large ones and the total surface area collapses, cutting the area term in the diffusion relationship. Collagen deposition and membrane thickening describe pulmonary fibrosis. Fluid in the alveolar space describes pulmonary edema, and inspired PO2 depends on barometric pressure and oxygen fraction, neither of which the disease changes.
questions.answerText: Loss of alveolar surface area as alveolar walls are destroyed

questions.q: Left heart failure raises pulmonary capillary pressure and fluid accumulates in the interstitium and alveoli. Which diffusion term changes, and in which direction?
options: The partial pressure gradient increases, so the rate of transfer rises
The diffusion coefficient increases, so the rate of transfer rises
Diffusion distance increases, so the rate of transfer falls
Surface area increases, so the rate of transfer rises
questions.why: Fluid inserts an extra layer between alveolar gas and blood, lengthening the path each molecule must cross, and since distance is in the denominator the transfer rate falls. Surface area is not increased by edema, and flooded alveoli actually take area out of service. The alveolar to capillary gradient is set by ventilation and blood flow, not by the fluid layer, and the diffusion coefficient is a property of the gas and the tissue, not something edema raises.
questions.answerText: Diffusion distance increases, so the rate of transfer falls

questions.q: In pulmonary fibrosis, collagen is deposited in the alveolar walls. What is the immediate effect on gas transfer?
options: Transfer rises because the stiffer wall holds alveoli open
Transfer is unchanged because the gradient is unchanged
Transfer falls because the diffusion distance is longer
Transfer falls because the alveolar PO2 has dropped
questions.why: Scarring thickens the barrier between alveolar gas and capillary blood, and a longer path means fewer molecules cross per second. Alveolar PO2 is determined by ventilation and inspired gas, so it is not lowered by the scarring itself. Stiffer walls do resist collapse, but they also resist inflation and do nothing to speed diffusion, and an unchanged gradient does not rescue transfer when the distance term has grown.
questions.answerText: Transfer falls because the diffusion distance is longer

questions.q: A patient has one lung removed. What happens to the maximum rate at which oxygen can cross the respiratory membrane?
options: It rises, because all blood flow now passes through one lung
It falls, because roughly half the exchange surface area is gone
It falls, because the remaining membrane becomes thicker
It is unchanged, because the gradient is what sets transfer
questions.why: Removing a lung removes about half the alveolar surface, and since diffusion is proportional to area the ceiling on transfer drops, which typically shows up as breathlessness on exertion rather than at rest. The remaining membrane does not thicken as a result of the surgery. The gradient is one term among several and cannot compensate for lost area, and directing all blood flow through one lung shortens transit time, which hurts rather than helps.
questions.answerText: It falls, because roughly half the exchange surface area is gone

questions.q: During exercise, previously closed pulmonary capillaries open and partly filled ones distend. What does this do to diffusing capacity?
options: It raises it, because the respiratory membrane becomes thinner
It lowers it, because blood transit time is shortened
It leaves it unchanged, because the number of alveoli is fixed
It raises it, because the surface area for exchange increases
questions.why: Recruitment and distension put more capillary surface in contact with alveolar gas, and more area means more molecules crossing per second, which is why diffusing capacity roughly triples in heavy exercise. Membrane thickness is not reduced by recruitment. Transit time does shorten in exercise, but that is a separate effect that only matters once diffusion is already impaired, and the fixed number of alveoli does not fix the amount of capillary surface in use.
questions.answerText: It raises it, because the surface area for exchange increases

questions.q: In mild thickening of the respiratory membrane, why does arterial PO2 fall before arterial PCO2 rises?
options: Carbon dioxide is far more soluble, so it still crosses adequately
Carbon dioxide is produced more slowly than oxygen is consumed
Carbon dioxide is carried mostly by hemoglobin, so it bypasses the membrane
Carbon dioxide has a much larger gradient, so it is unaffected
questions.why: A thicker barrier slows both gases, but carbon dioxide starts with a roughly twentyfold advantage in diffusion rate from its solubility, so it keeps up long after oxygen transfer has begun to fail. Production and consumption rates are close to each other and are not the reason. Carbon dioxide bound to hemoglobin must still leave the red cell and cross the same membrane, and its gradient is much smaller than the oxygen gradient rather than larger.
questions.answerText: Carbon dioxide is far more soluble, so it still crosses adequately

questions.q: A disease process doubles the thickness of the respiratory membrane with no other change. What happens to the rate of oxygen diffusion?
options: It falls to about one quarter
It falls by about 20 percent
It doubles
It falls to about half
questions.why: Rate is inversely proportional to thickness, so doubling the distance halves the transfer rate for a given gradient. A fall to one quarter would require the rate to vary with the square of thickness, which it does not. A 20 percent fall understates the effect of doubling, and the rate cannot rise when the barrier has grown.
questions.answerText: It falls to about half

questions.q: Which gas transfer is described as perfusion limited in a healthy lung, meaning uptake depends on blood flow rather than on the membrane?
options: Oxygen, because the healthy membrane is too thick for full equilibration
Nitrogen, because it is inert and is not carried by hemoglobin
Oxygen, because blood equilibrates with alveolar gas before the capillary ends
Carbon monoxide, because hemoglobin binds it so tightly that its pressure never rises
questions.why: Oxygen reaches equilibrium in about a third of the transit time, so the only way to move more oxygen is to send more blood past the alveoli, which is the definition of perfusion limitation. Carbon monoxide is the classic diffusion limited gas, because hemoglobin binds it so avidly that its partial pressure in blood never rises to meet the alveolar value. Oxygen is not limited by the healthy membrane, and nitrogen is inert and near equilibrium already.
questions.answerText: Oxygen, because blood equilibrates with alveolar gas before the capillary ends

questions.q: A patient with early pulmonary fibrosis has a normal arterial PO2 at rest but desaturates during a brisk walk. What explains the pattern?
options: Exercise lowers alveolar PO2, so the gradient across the thickened membrane disappears
Exercise thickens the membrane further by driving fluid into the alveolar walls
Exercise raises hemoglobin affinity for oxygen, so less is loaded
Exercise shortens capillary transit time, so the thickened membrane cannot finish equilibration
questions.why: At rest the diffusion reserve covers the extra distance, but exercise raises cardiac output and cuts transit time, and a slowed membrane can no longer finish loading before the red cell leaves the capillary. Alveolar PO2 does not fall in exercise, since ventilation rises in step with metabolism. The membrane does not thicken acutely with walking, and exercise shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve right, lowering affinity rather than raising it.
questions.answerText: Exercise shortens capillary transit time, so the thickened membrane cannot finish equilibration

questions.q: A patient with advanced emphysema has both destroyed alveolar walls and lost elastic recoil. Predict the effect on diffusing capacity and on arterial PO2.
options: Diffusing capacity falls from lost surface area, and arterial PO2 falls
