Diffusing capacity falls from a thicker membrane, and arterial PO2 falls
Diffusing capacity is preserved, and arterial PO2 falls only from airway obstruction
Diffusing capacity rises with the larger air spaces, and arterial PO2 is normal
questions.why: Alveolar septa carry both the exchange surface and the capillary bed, so their destruction lowers the area term directly, and with less surface and worse ventilation matching the arterial PO2 falls. The membrane in emphysema is not thickened, which is what separates it from fibrosis. Diffusing capacity is measurably reduced rather than preserved, and larger air spaces mean less surface, not more, because surface area falls as the spaces coalesce.
questions.answerText: Diffusing capacity falls from lost surface area, and arterial PO2 falls

questions.q: A patient in acute pulmonary edema has an arterial PO2 of 55 mmHg and an arterial PCO2 of 32 mmHg. Why is the carbon dioxide low rather than high?
options: Carbon dioxide production falls when tissue oxygen delivery is reduced
Hypoxemia drives an increase in ventilation, and carbon dioxide is blown off
Fluid in the alveoli traps oxygen but allows carbon dioxide to be absorbed by plasma
Edema selectively thickens the membrane on the alveolar side for oxygen only
questions.why: Low arterial PO2 stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors, ventilation rises, and because carbon dioxide crosses even a thickened membrane easily, the increased ventilation drives its partial pressure below normal while oxygen stays low. Alveolar fluid slows both gases and does not selectively trap oxygen. A membrane cannot be thickened for one gas and not the other, and carbon dioxide production does not fall enough to explain the value.
questions.answerText: Hypoxemia drives an increase in ventilation, and carbon dioxide is blown off

questions.q: A person with a thickened respiratory membrane travels to an altitude where alveolar PO2 is 60 mmHg. Why is she far more hypoxemic there than a healthy companion?
options: The smaller gradient and the longer diffusion distance both slow transfer, with no reserve left
Altitude raises the oxygen fraction of the air, which her thickened membrane cannot make use of
Altitude thickens the respiratory membrane further in everyone who ascends
Her hemoglobin cannot bind oxygen at a reduced barometric pressure
questions.why: Transfer depends on the gradient divided by the distance, so a lower alveolar PO2 shrinks the numerator at the same time her disease has enlarged the denominator, and with no diffusion reserve left equilibration fails. The oxygen fraction of air stays at 21 percent at every altitude, so it is total pressure that falls. Altitude does not thicken the membrane, and hemoglobin binds oxygen normally at any barometric pressure as long as PO2 is adequate.
questions.answerText: The smaller gradient and the longer diffusion distance both slow transfer, with no reserve left

questions.q: What is the normal overall ventilation perfusion ratio for the whole lung?
options: About 3.0
About 0.8
About 1.5
About 0.2
questions.why: Alveolar ventilation of roughly 4 L/min divided by pulmonary blood flow of roughly 5 L/min gives about 0.8 for the lung as a whole. About 1.5 is higher than any whole lung average and describes an overventilated region. About 0.2 describes a poorly ventilated region close to shunt, and about 3.0 is the ratio at the apex of an upright lung, not the average.
questions.answerText: About 0.8

questions.q: In the ventilation perfusion ratio, what does the ventilation term actually refer to?
options: Alveolar ventilation, the fresh gas reaching exchange surfaces
Total minute ventilation, including gas in the conducting airways
Tidal volume measured at the mouth
The respiratory rate in breaths per minute
questions.why: Only gas that reaches perfused alveoli can participate in exchange, so the ratio uses alveolar ventilation, which is minute ventilation minus the dead space contribution. Total minute ventilation includes air that never reaches an alveolus and would overstate the ratio. Tidal volume and respiratory rate are the two components of minute ventilation, and neither is the ventilation term on its own.
questions.answerText: Alveolar ventilation, the fresh gas reaching exchange surfaces

questions.q: How do pulmonary arterioles respond when the alveolar PO2 in their region falls?
options: They constrict, but only when arterial PCO2 also rises
They do not respond, because the response is confined to bronchioles
They constrict, diverting blood toward better ventilated regions
They dilate, increasing blood flow to the hypoxic region
questions.why: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction moves blood away from an alveolus that has little oxygen to offer and toward alveoli that are well ventilated, which protects arterial PO2. Dilating in response to hypoxia is the systemic pattern and would send more blood past useless alveoli. The response works on alveolar PO2 directly and does not require a change in PCO2, and bronchioles respond as well but the vascular response is real and central.
questions.answerText: They constrict, diverting blood toward better ventilated regions

questions.q: How does the pulmonary vascular response to low PO2 compare with the systemic vascular response?
options: It is opposite: pulmonary vessels dilate while systemic vessels constrict
It is opposite: pulmonary vessels constrict while systemic vessels dilate
It is the same: both constrict to conserve oxygen
It is the same: both dilate to restore flow
questions.why: A hypoxic systemic tissue needs more blood, so its arterioles dilate, while a hypoxic alveolus has no oxygen to give, so its arterioles constrict and send blood elsewhere. Both constricting would starve hypoxic tissues throughout the body. Both dilating would waste pulmonary blood flow on unventilated alveoli, and the reversed version has the pulmonary and systemic behaviors swapped.
questions.answerText: It is opposite: pulmonary vessels constrict while systemic vessels dilate

questions.q: In an upright person at rest, how does the ventilation perfusion ratio at the apex compare with the base?
options: Equal throughout, because gravity affects both equally
Higher at the base, because the base receives the most ventilation
Higher at the apex, because blood flow falls more than ventilation does
Lower at the apex, because ventilation falls more than blood flow does
questions.why: Gravity reduces both ventilation and perfusion toward the top of the lung, but perfusion falls far more steeply, so the apex ends up overventilated relative to its blood flow with a ratio near 3. The reversed version describes the base, where the ratio is closer to 0.6. Gravity does not affect the two equally, and although the base does receive more ventilation than the apex, it receives proportionally even more blood flow.
questions.answerText: Higher at the apex, because blood flow falls more than ventilation does

questions.q: What is the ventilation perfusion ratio of a true shunt?
options: Zero, because the region is perfused but not ventilated
Infinite, because the region is ventilated but not perfused
About 0.8, the same as the normal lung average
About 3.0, the value found at the lung apex
questions.why: A shunt unit receives blood but no fresh gas, so the ventilation term is zero and the blood leaving it has the composition of mixed venous blood. An infinite ratio describes alveolar dead space, the opposite problem. A ratio of 0.8 is normal matching, and 3.0 is a high but finite apex value, not a shunt.
questions.answerText: Zero, because the region is perfused but not ventilated

questions.q: What is alveolar dead space?
options: Alveoli that are perfused but not ventilated
The volume of the conducting airways
Alveoli that are collapsed and receive neither gas nor blood
Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused
questions.why: Alveolar dead space is fresh gas delivered to alveoli with no blood flow to receive it, so the gas is wasted and the ratio approaches infinity. Perfused but unventilated alveoli are shunt, the mirror image. The conducting airway volume is anatomic dead space, which is normal, and collapsed alveoli that receive neither gas nor blood are neither category since they take no ventilation to waste.
questions.answerText: Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused

questions.q: How do bronchioles respond when the carbon dioxide level in the air they supply falls?
options: They constrict, reducing wasted ventilation to that region
They dilate, sending more air to that region
They constrict, but only if alveolar PO2 also falls
They do not respond, because airway tone is set only by the vagus nerve
questions.why: Low local PCO2 signals that a region is receiving more gas than its blood flow can use, so bronchiolar constriction steers air toward better perfused regions. Dilating would send even more air to a region already overventilated. The airway response tracks local PCO2 rather than requiring a fall in PO2, and although vagal tone contributes to overall airway caliber, local carbon dioxide adjusts individual regions.
questions.answerText: They constrict, reducing wasted ventilation to that region

questions.q: A mucus plug blocks the bronchiole supplying one small region of lung, while blood flow continues. What happens to the ventilation perfusion ratio and to the blood leaving that region?
options: The ratio rises toward infinity, and blood leaves with an alveolar composition
The ratio falls toward zero, and blood leaves fully oxygenated
The ratio is unchanged, because blood flow is unchanged
The ratio falls toward zero, and blood leaves with a mixed venous composition
questions.why: Blocking ventilation with perfusion intact drives the ratio toward zero, and since no fresh gas arrives the blood picks up nothing and leaves with roughly the PO2 and PCO2 it arrived with. A ratio rising toward infinity describes an occluded vessel, not an occluded airway. Blood cannot leave fully oxygenated with no gas supply, and the ratio must change when only one of its two terms is cut off.
questions.answerText: The ratio falls toward zero, and blood leaves with a mixed venous composition

questions.q: A pulmonary embolus blocks blood flow to a lung segment while ventilation continues. What happens to the gas composition inside those alveoli?
options: PO2 rises toward the inspired value and PCO2 falls toward zero
PO2 falls toward mixed venous values and PCO2 rises
PO2 and PCO2 both stay at their normal alveolar values
PO2 rises and PCO2 rises, because gas is trapped in the segment
questions.why: With no blood arriving, nothing removes oxygen and nothing delivers carbon dioxide, so the alveolar gas drifts toward the composition of humidified inspired air. Falling PO2 with rising PCO2 is what happens when ventilation stops instead, not perfusion. Normal alveolar values require normal blood flow to set them, and carbon dioxide cannot rise when its only source, the blood, has been cut off.
questions.answerText: PO2 rises toward the inspired value and PCO2 falls toward zero

questions.q: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction responds to a blocked airway in one small region. What is the benefit to the rest of the lung?
options: Blood is redirected to ventilated alveoli, so arterial PO2 is better preserved
Ventilation is redirected to the blocked region, reopening the airway
Pulmonary artery pressure falls, reducing right ventricular work
Carbon dioxide removal from the blocked region improves
questions.why: Constricting the vessels supplying an unventilated region shunts less venous blood past useless alveoli, so a greater share of cardiac output goes where gas exchange can happen and arterial PO2 stays higher. Vasoconstriction acts on vessels and cannot redirect air or clear an airway. Regional constriction raises rather than lowers pulmonary resistance, and no gas exchange of any kind improves in a region with no ventilation.
questions.answerText: Blood is redirected to ventilated alveoli, so arterial PO2 is better preserved

questions.q: A person living at high altitude has low alveolar PO2 throughout both lungs. What is the consequence of hypoxic vasoconstriction under these conditions?
options: Blood is redirected toward the better ventilated apex of each lung
Pulmonary vascular resistance falls as more vessels are recruited
Arterial PO2 returns to sea level values within a few days
Widespread vasoconstriction raises pulmonary artery pressure
questions.why: The response is useful when it is local, because there is somewhere better to send the blood, but when every alveolus is hypoxic every vessel constricts and the result is pulmonary hypertension and increased right ventricular work. There is no better ventilated region to receive redirected flow when the hypoxia is global. Resistance rises rather than falls, and acclimatization improves oxygen delivery through ventilation and 2,3 BPG changes without restoring sea level arterial PO2.
questions.answerText: Widespread vasoconstriction raises pulmonary artery pressure

questions.q: Blood leaving the base of an upright lung has a slightly lower PO2 than blood leaving the apex. Why?
options: The base receives less blood flow, so less oxygen can be picked up
The base has a lower ventilation perfusion ratio, so its blood is less fully oxygenated
The base has a higher ventilation perfusion ratio, so much of its fresh gas is wasted
The base has a thicker respiratory membrane because gravity pools fluid there
questions.why: Perfusion at the base outstrips ventilation, giving a ratio near 0.6, and a unit with relatively too much blood for its gas supply cannot fully oxygenate all of it. A high ratio describes the apex, where blood leaves with a slightly higher PO2. Gravity redistributes blood and gas but does not thicken the membrane, and the base receives more blood flow, not less.
questions.answerText: The base has a lower ventilation perfusion ratio, so its blood is less fully oxygenated

questions.q: Local carbon dioxide accumulates in a region whose blood flow has increased relative to its ventilation. What is the airway response and its purpose?
options: Bronchodilation, which lowers pulmonary vascular resistance in that region
No airway response, because airways respond only to oxygen
Bronchodilation, which increases ventilation to match the increased perfusion
Bronchoconstriction, which limits ventilation to a poorly perfused region
questions.why: A rise in local PCO2 signals that blood flow has outrun gas delivery, and dilating the bronchiole brings more fresh gas to the region so the two match again. Bronchoconstriction is the response to low PCO2, in a region that is overventilated. Airway caliber does not set pulmonary vascular resistance directly, and airways do respond, tracking carbon dioxide rather than oxygen.
questions.answerText: Bronchodilation, which increases ventilation to match the increased perfusion

questions.q: A patient has lobar pneumonia with one lobe completely filled with exudate but still perfused. He remains hypoxemic even on a high inspired oxygen fraction. Explain the sequence.
options: The exudate raises the diffusion distance so much that no lobe can equilibrate
The lobe behaves as a shunt, and blood shunted through it never meets the enriched gas
The lobe behaves as dead space, so the added oxygen is wasted on unperfused alveoli
The added oxygen abolishes hypoxic vasoconstriction, so blood floods the healthy lobes
questions.why: Fluid filled but perfused alveoli give a ventilation perfusion ratio of zero, and shunted blood never meets alveolar gas, so raising the oxygen in gas the blood never touches adds only a little dissolved oxygen to the rest. Dead space is the opposite problem, ventilation without perfusion, and it does not cause this pattern of refractory hypoxemia. Oxygen can blunt hypoxic vasoconstriction in ventilated regions, but that would improve rather than explain the hypoxemia, and the healthy lobes have a normal membrane and equilibrate fine.
questions.answerText: The lobe behaves as a shunt, and blood shunted through it never meets the enriched gas

questions.q: A patient with a large pulmonary embolus has a sudden fall in end tidal carbon dioxide even though her arterial PCO2 is near normal. Trace why.
options: Cardiac output falls abruptly, so less carbon dioxide is produced by the tissues
The embolus raises pulmonary artery pressure, which drives carbon dioxide back into the blood
The embolized region is ventilated but unperfused, so it exhales gas with almost no carbon dioxide in it
The embolized region is perfused but unventilated, so carbon dioxide accumulates there and never reaches the mouth
questions.why: Gas from an unperfused region has never met blood, so it contains almost no carbon dioxide, and mixing it with normal gas from the rest of the lung lowers the exhaled value while increased ventilation keeps the arterial value near normal. A perfused but unventilated region is a shunt, which is not what an embolus produces. Tissue carbon dioxide production is set by metabolism rather than by cardiac output over these minutes, and pressure changes in the artery do not reverse the direction of carbon dioxide diffusion.
questions.answerText: The embolized region is ventilated but unperfused, so it exhales gas with almost no carbon dioxide in it

questions.q: A drug that dilates pulmonary vessels is given to a patient who has one poorly ventilated lung region. Predict what happens to arterial PO2 and why.
options: It is unchanged, because arterial PO2 depends only on alveolar PO2
It falls, because the drug blunts hypoxic vasoconstriction and perfuses the bad region more
It rises, because more blood now reaches all alveoli including the poorly ventilated ones
It rises, because dilated vessels lengthen capillary transit time everywhere
questions.why: Hypoxic vasoconstriction had been steering blood away from the bad region, and a vasodilator releases that protection, so a larger share of cardiac output passes alveoli that cannot oxygenate it and arterial PO2 falls. Sending more blood to a poorly ventilated region adds poorly oxygenated blood to the arterial pool rather than improving it. Transit time changes are trivial next to the mismatch effect, and arterial PO2 depends on how blood flow is distributed among alveoli, not on alveolar PO2 alone.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the drug blunts hypoxic vasoconstriction and perfuses the bad region more

questions.q: A person aspirates a foreign body that occludes the left main bronchus. Two minutes later, what has happened to blood flow through the left lung and to the mixed arterial PO2?
options: Left lung blood flow rises to compensate for the block, and arterial PO2 is preserved
Left lung blood flow is unchanged, and arterial PO2 falls to mixed venous levels
Left lung blood flow falls sharply, and arterial PO2 returns fully to normal
Left lung blood flow falls from hypoxic vasoconstriction, and arterial PO2 falls only partway
questions.why: Alveolar PO2 in the unventilated lung collapses, its vessels constrict, and much of the cardiac output is diverted to the right lung, so the shunt fraction is smaller than it would otherwise be and arterial PO2 falls only partway. Blood flow rising to a lung with no ventilation would worsen the shunt. Flow is not left unchanged, since the vascular response is prompt, and the response is incomplete, so arterial PO2 does not return all the way to normal.
questions.answerText: Left lung blood flow falls from hypoxic vasoconstriction, and arterial PO2 falls only partway

questions.q: How many oxygen molecules can one hemoglobin molecule carry when fully saturated?
options: Two
One
Eight
Four
questions.why: Hemoglobin has four globin chains, each with one heme group holding one iron atom, and each iron binds one oxygen molecule, so four is the maximum. Two and one understate the number of heme groups. Eight would be the number of oxygen atoms rather than molecules, which is a common way to double count.
questions.answerText: Four

questions.q: What does cooperative binding mean in hemoglobin?
options: Oxygen binding requires a second hemoglobin molecule to be present
Binding one oxygen raises the affinity of the remaining sites
Binding one oxygen lowers the affinity of the remaining sites
All four sites must fill at the same instant
questions.why: The first oxygen shifts hemoglobin toward its relaxed conformation, and each subsequent oxygen binds more readily than the last, which is what bends the curve into its sigmoid shape. Falling affinity with successive binding would give a curve that flattens early rather than steepening. The sites fill in sequence rather than simultaneously, and one hemoglobin binds oxygen without needing a partner molecule.
questions.answerText: Binding one oxygen raises the affinity of the remaining sites

questions.q: About what fraction of the oxygen in arterial blood is carried bound to hemoglobin rather than dissolved in plasma?
options: About 98 percent
About 70 percent
About 50 percent
About 25 percent
questions.why: Oxygen is poorly soluble, so only about 1.5 percent travels dissolved and roughly 98 percent rides on hemoglobin, which is why anemia lowers oxygen delivery so sharply. About 70 percent resembles the bicarbonate share of carbon dioxide transport, not oxygen. About 50 percent and about 25 percent both overstate the dissolved fraction by a wide margin.
questions.answerText: About 98 percent

questions.q: What is the normal P50 of adult hemoglobin?
options: About 27 mmHg
About 40 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
About 100 mmHg
questions.why: P50 is the PO2 at which hemoglobin is half saturated, and for normal adult blood that is about 27 mmHg, which is why the steep part of the curve sits in the tissue range. About 40 mmHg is mixed venous PO2, where saturation is already 75 percent. About 60 mmHg is where the curve begins to flatten near 90 percent saturation, and about 100 mmHg is arterial PO2 with saturation near 98 percent.
questions.answerText: About 27 mmHg

questions.q: At an arterial PO2 of 100 mmHg, what is the approximate saturation of hemoglobin?
options: About 85 percent
About 98 percent
About 90 percent
About 75 percent
questions.why: Arterial blood at 100 mmHg sits on the flat upper plateau of the curve with saturation close to 98 percent, essentially fully loaded. About 90 percent corresponds to a PO2 near 60 mmHg. About 75 percent corresponds to a PO2 of 40 mmHg, which is mixed venous blood, and about 85 percent falls between those two points.
questions.answerText: About 98 percent

questions.q: At a PO2 of 40 mmHg, the value in mixed venous blood, what is the approximate saturation of hemoglobin?
options: About 75 percent
About 50 percent
About 90 percent
About 98 percent
questions.why: Mixed venous blood is about 75 percent saturated, which means resting tissues have extracted only about a quarter of the oxygen carried and the rest is held in reserve. About 50 percent corresponds to the P50 near 27 mmHg. About 90 percent corresponds to a PO2 of 60 mmHg, and about 98 percent is arterial blood at 100 mmHg.
questions.answerText: About 75 percent

questions.q: Over which range of PO2 is the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve relatively flat?
options: Between about 20 and 40 mmHg
Below about 20 mmHg
Between about 10 and 27 mmHg
Above about 60 mmHg
questions.why: Above roughly 60 mmHg the curve plateaus, so large falls in alveolar PO2 cost only a few percent of saturation, which is the safety margin for loading. Between 20 and 40 mmHg the curve is at its steepest, which is what makes unloading efficient. Below 20 mmHg and between 10 and 27 mmHg the curve is also steep, not flat.
questions.answerText: Above about 60 mmHg

questions.q: Over which range of PO2 does the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve fall most steeply?
options: Above about 100 mmHg
Between about 100 and 150 mmHg
Between about 20 and 40 mmHg
Between about 60 and 100 mmHg
questions.why: The steep segment sits between about 20 and 40 mmHg, which is exactly the PO2 range found in tissues, so a small further drop in tissue PO2 releases a large amount of oxygen. Between 60 and 100 mmHg the curve is already flattening. Above 100 mmHg the curve is essentially horizontal, and between 100 and 150 mmHg additional PO2 adds almost no bound oxygen at all.
questions.answerText: Between about 20 and 40 mmHg

questions.q: Alveolar PO2 falls from 100 mmHg to 80 mmHg in a person with otherwise normal lungs. What happens to arterial oxygen saturation?
options: It does not change at all, because saturation is fixed above 60 mmHg
It falls only slightly, from about 98 percent to about 95 percent
It falls sharply, from about 98 percent to about 75 percent
It falls to about 50 percent, since PO2 dropped by a fifth
questions.why: Both values lie on the flat upper part of the curve, so a 20 mmHg fall costs only about three percentage points of saturation, and this is the physiological advantage of the plateau. A drop to 75 percent would require PO2 to reach 40 mmHg. Saturation does not fall in proportion to PO2 because the relationship is sigmoid rather than linear, and it is very insensitive above 60 mmHg but not literally fixed.
questions.answerText: It falls only slightly, from about 98 percent to about 95 percent

questions.q: In an exercising muscle, tissue PO2 falls from 40 mmHg to 20 mmHg. What happens to hemoglobin saturation in that capillary?
options: It falls only slightly, from about 75 percent to about 70 percent
It falls from about 98 percent to about 90 percent
It stays near 75 percent, because saturation is set in the lung
It falls steeply, from about 75 percent to about 35 percent
questions.why: This 20 mmHg drop happens on the steep part of the curve, so it releases roughly 40 percent of the carried oxygen, which is the physiological advantage of the steep portion. A small fall of five points would be typical of the plateau, not the steep region. Falling from 98 to 90 percent describes a change occurring at much higher PO2, and saturation is set by the local PO2 that blood encounters, not fixed at its lung value.
questions.answerText: It falls steeply, from about 75 percent to about 35 percent

questions.q: At rest, arterial blood is about 98 percent saturated and mixed venous blood is about 75 percent saturated. What fraction of the carried oxygen do tissues extract?
options: About 75 percent
About 5 percent
About 25 percent
About 50 percent
questions.why: The difference between 98 and 75 percent is roughly a quarter of the oxygen carried, so resting extraction is about 25 percent and the remaining 75 percent is a reserve that exercise can draw on. About 50 percent and about 75 percent extraction occur only in heavily exercising muscle. About 5 percent would leave venous blood nearly as saturated as arterial blood, which is not the case.
questions.answerText: About 25 percent

questions.q: Why does cooperative binding produce a sigmoid curve rather than a straight line?
options: Affinity rises as sites fill, so the curve steepens then flattens as sites run out
Affinity is constant, so the curve rises evenly until saturation is reached
Affinity falls as sites fill, so the curve rises quickly then levels off early
Affinity depends on plasma pH alone, which changes along the capillary
questions.why: Each bound oxygen makes the next one bind more easily, which accelerates loading through the middle of the range, and the curve then flattens simply because few empty sites remain. Constant affinity would give the hyperbolic curve of myoglobin, not a sigmoid. Falling affinity would flatten the curve early at low PO2, and pH modifies affinity but does not create the sigmoid shape.
questions.answerText: Affinity rises as sites fill, so the curve steepens then flattens as sites run out

questions.q: A climber has an arterial PO2 of 60 mmHg. What is her approximate arterial oxygen saturation?
options: About 60 percent
About 98 percent
About 90 percent
About 75 percent
questions.why: A PO2 of 60 mmHg sits at the shoulder where the curve begins to steepen, and saturation is still about 90 percent, which is why moderate hypoxemia is tolerated surprisingly well. About 75 percent corresponds to 40 mmHg. About 60 percent would require a PO2 near 30 mmHg, and about 98 percent requires a PO2 near 100 mmHg.
questions.answerText: About 90 percent

questions.q: How much oxygen is carried dissolved in 100 mL of arterial plasma at a PO2 of 100 mmHg?
options: About 15 mL
About 0.3 mL
About 3 mL
About 20 mL
questions.why: Dissolved oxygen is only 0.003 mL per 100 mL of blood for each mmHg, so 100 mmHg gives about 0.3 mL, a trivial amount next to the roughly 20 mL bound to hemoglobin. About 3 mL is ten times too high. About 20 mL is total arterial content including hemoglobin bound oxygen, and about 15 mL is closer to normal venous content.
questions.answerText: About 0.3 mL

questions.q: Myoglobin in muscle has a hyperbolic oxygen curve lying well to the left of hemoglobin's. What does that let it do?
options: Carry four oxygen molecules per protein like hemoglobin does
Buffer hydrogen ions produced during muscle contraction
Take oxygen from blood at low PO2 and hold it until PO2 falls very low
Release oxygen to blood whenever capillary PO2 falls below 40 mmHg
questions.why: Higher affinity means myoglobin loads at the low PO2 of muscle cytoplasm and only gives oxygen up when PO2 falls near zero, making it a local store for the start of contraction. It takes oxygen from blood rather than giving it back at 40 mmHg, since its affinity is greater than hemoglobin's. Myoglobin has a single heme and carries one oxygen, and hydrogen ion buffering in blood is a job of hemoglobin, not myoglobin.
questions.answerText: Take oxygen from blood at low PO2 and hold it until PO2 falls very low

questions.q: During heavy exercise, capillary PO2 in working muscle falls from 40 mmHg to 20 mmHg while arterial saturation stays near 98 percent. Trace the effect on oxygen extraction and explain what makes it possible.
options: Extraction falls, because less oxygen reaches a muscle with such a low PO2
Extraction is unchanged, because arterial saturation did not change and venous saturation follows it
Extraction rises from about 25 percent to well over 60 percent, because tissue PO2 is now on the steep part of the curve
Extraction rises only slightly, because saturation changes little for a 20 mmHg drop
questions.why: Venous saturation drops from about 75 percent to about 35 percent, so the arterial to venous difference widens from roughly 23 points to roughly 63 points, and the steep segment of the curve is what converts a modest fall in PO2 into a large release of oxygen. A 20 mmHg drop matters little only when it happens on the plateau, above 60 mmHg. Low tissue PO2 is the signal that draws oxygen out rather than a barrier to it, and extraction depends on the arterial to venous difference, not on the arterial value alone.
questions.answerText: Extraction rises from about 25 percent to well over 60 percent, because tissue PO2 is now on the steep part of the curve

questions.q: A visitor at high altitude has an arterial PO2 of 55 mmHg with normal hemoglobin. Predict her arterial saturation and the effect on her arterial oxygen content compared with sea level.
options: Saturation is about 88 percent, so content falls by roughly a tenth
Saturation is about 55 percent, so content falls by nearly half
Saturation is about 98 percent, so content is unchanged
Saturation is about 75 percent, so content falls by about a quarter
questions.why: A PO2 of 55 mmHg sits just below the shoulder of the curve at roughly 88 percent saturation, and since content is set almost entirely by saturation times hemoglobin, it falls by about the same proportion, near 10 percent. Saturation does not equal PO2 as a percentage, which is the trap in the second option. A saturation of 98 percent belongs to a PO2 near 100 mmHg, and 75 percent belongs to a PO2 of 40 mmHg.
questions.answerText: Saturation is about 88 percent, so content falls by roughly a tenth

questions.q: An engineered hemoglobin loses cooperativity, so its curve is hyperbolic with a very high affinity at low PO2. Predict what happens to loading in the lung and unloading at the tissue.
options: Loading in the lung fails, but unloading at the tissue is normal
Both loading and unloading improve, because affinity is higher throughout
Both loading and unloading fail, because the protein can no longer bind oxygen
Loading in the lung is still complete, but unloading at the tissue is badly impaired
questions.why: High affinity means the molecule fills easily at alveolar PO2, but a hyperbolic curve stays near saturation across the tissue PO2 range, so very little oxygen comes off where it is needed. Loading is the easy step for a high affinity carrier, so it does not fail. Higher affinity helps loading and hurts unloading, which is why it cannot improve both, and the protein still binds oxygen perfectly well, which is precisely the problem.
questions.answerText: Loading in the lung is still complete, but unloading at the tissue is badly impaired

questions.q: Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3 BPG poorly, so its curve lies to the left of the maternal curve. Trace what this means for oxygen transfer at the placenta.
options: The leftward position matters only after birth, when fetal hemoglobin is replaced
At any placental PO2 fetal blood is more saturated, so oxygen moves from mother to fetus
At any placental PO2 fetal blood is less saturated, so oxygen moves from fetus to mother
Fetal blood is more saturated but cannot unload in fetal tissues at all
questions.why: A left shifted curve means that at the low PO2 of placental blood the fetal molecule holds more oxygen than the maternal one, so oxygen diffuses down its partial pressure gradient into fetal blood and is then bound more tightly there. Less saturated fetal blood would send oxygen the wrong way and could not support a fetus. Fetal tissues run at a very low PO2, which is low enough for fetal hemoglobin to unload, and the advantage operates before birth rather than after it.
questions.answerText: At any placental PO2 fetal blood is more saturated, so oxygen moves from mother to fetus

questions.q: A rise in PCO2 shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction?
options: It does not move the curve
To the right
To the left
Downward without a horizontal shift
questions.why: Carbon dioxide lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, both directly and through the hydrogen ions it generates, and lower affinity is drawn as a rightward shift. A leftward shift is what falling carbon dioxide produces. The curve shifts sideways rather than dropping vertically, since the maximum saturation is unchanged, and carbon dioxide is one of the four classic modifiers rather than a neutral factor.
questions.answerText: To the right

questions.q: A fall in blood pH shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction?
options: To the right
To the left
To the right only if temperature also falls
It does not move the curve
questions.why: A lower pH means more hydrogen ions, which bind hemoglobin and stabilize the form that holds oxygen loosely, so the curve moves right and oxygen comes off more readily. A leftward shift follows a rise in pH, that is alkalosis. Acidosis shifts the curve right on its own without needing a temperature change, and pH is one of the strongest modifiers rather than a neutral one.
questions.answerText: To the right

questions.q: A rise in body temperature shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction?
options: To the right
To the left
To the left in muscle and to the right in lung
It does not move the curve
questions.why: Heat destabilizes the oxygen hemoglobin bond, so warming lowers affinity and shifts the curve right, which helps a working or febrile tissue extract more oxygen. A leftward shift follows cooling. Temperature acts the same way wherever the blood is, so it does not shift in opposite directions in different tissues, and it is a genuine modifier of the curve.
questions.answerText: To the right

questions.q: A rise in red cell 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve in which direction?
options: To the right for the first two binding sites only
It does not move the curve
To the right
To the left
questions.why: 2,3 BPG binds in the central cavity of deoxygenated hemoglobin and holds it in the low affinity form, so more of it shifts the whole curve right and improves unloading. A leftward shift follows depletion of 2,3 BPG, as happens in stored blood. The molecule acts on the whole tetramer rather than on selected sites, and it is one of the four classic modifiers.
questions.answerText: To the right

questions.q: A rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve reflects what change in hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen?
options: Increased number of binding sites
Decreased affinity
Increased affinity
Decreased maximum carrying capacity
questions.why: Shifting right means a higher PO2 is needed to reach any given saturation, which is another way of saying hemoglobin holds oxygen less tightly. Increased affinity produces a leftward shift instead. Carrying capacity depends on how much hemoglobin is present rather than on affinity, and the four binding sites per molecule do not change in number.
questions.answerText: Decreased affinity

questions.q: What happens to P50 when the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right?
options: P50 falls below the normal 27 mmHg
P50 stays at 27 mmHg because it is a fixed property
P50 rises only if hemoglobin concentration also rises
P50 rises above the normal 27 mmHg
questions.why: P50 is the PO2 giving 50 percent saturation, and with lower affinity a higher PO2 is required, so a rightward shift raises P50. A falling P50 marks a leftward shift and tighter binding. P50 is not fixed, since it is exactly the number used to report shifts, and it is independent of how much hemoglobin is present.
questions.answerText: P50 rises above the normal 27 mmHg

questions.q: What does a rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve mean for oxygen delivery to tissue?
options: Delivery is unchanged, since arterial saturation is unchanged
More oxygen is released to tissue at a given tissue PO2
Less oxygen is released to tissue at a given tissue PO2
More oxygen is loaded in the lung and none is released
questions.why: Lower affinity means hemoglobin gives up oxygen more readily, so at any tissue PO2 saturation is lower and more oxygen has been handed over. Less release is the consequence of a leftward shift. A rightward shift slightly reduces loading rather than increasing it, and delivery to tissue depends on how much is unloaded, not on arterial saturation alone.
questions.answerText: More oxygen is released to tissue at a given tissue PO2

questions.q: Where is 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate produced?
options: In the liver, and carried to red cells in plasma
In the kidney, alongside erythropoietin
In the lung, by type II alveolar cells
In the red blood cell, as a side branch of glycolysis
questions.why: Red cells have no mitochondria and rely on glycolysis, and a branch of that pathway generates 2,3 BPG right where it is needed, inside the cell with the hemoglobin. The liver does not export it to red cells. The kidney makes erythropoietin, which controls red cell number rather than oxygen affinity, and type II alveolar cells make surfactant.
questions.answerText: In the red blood cell, as a side branch of glycolysis

questions.q: Working skeletal muscle is warm, has a high PCO2, and has a low pH. Which way does the local oxyhemoglobin curve shift, and what is the result?
options: Right, so more oxygen is unloaded where it is needed
Left, so more oxygen is held until the blood reaches the lung
Right, so less oxygen is unloaded and venous saturation rises
Left, so oxygen unloading increases at low tissue PO2
questions.why: All three conditions lower affinity and all three point the same way, which is why exercising tissue is so effective at extracting oxygen. A leftward shift would hold oxygen on the molecule and worsen delivery to a tissue that needs it. A rightward shift increases unloading and lowers venous saturation rather than raising it, and left shifts reduce rather than increase unloading.
questions.answerText: Right, so more oxygen is unloaded where it is needed

questions.q: A person hyperventilates during a panic attack and develops a respiratory alkalosis with a low PCO2. What happens to the oxyhemoglobin curve?
options: It does not shift, because her arterial PO2 is normal or slightly high
It shifts left, so oxygen is held more tightly and less is unloaded
It shifts right, so more oxygen is unloaded to tissue despite the alkalosis
It shifts left, so more oxygen is unloaded at any tissue PO2
questions.why: Both the low carbon dioxide and the high pH raise hemoglobin's affinity, so the curve moves left and tissues extract less oxygen at any given PO2. A rightward shift would require rising carbon dioxide or falling pH, the opposite of what hyperventilation does. A leftward shift means tighter binding, so it cannot increase unloading, and the curve responds to pH and carbon dioxide regardless of whether arterial PO2 is normal.
questions.answerText: It shifts left, so oxygen is held more tightly and less is unloaded

questions.q: Blood stored for several weeks loses most of its 2,3 BPG. What happens to its oxyhemoglobin curve and to its ability to release oxygen?
options: The curve is unchanged, because hemoglobin itself is intact
The curve shifts left, and the blood releases oxygen less readily
The curve shifts right, and the blood releases oxygen more readily
The curve shifts left, and the blood releases oxygen more readily
questions.why: 2,3 BPG is what holds hemoglobin in its low affinity state, so losing it raises affinity, shifts the curve left, and makes the transfused cells poor at handing oxygen over until they regenerate the compound. A rightward shift would require more 2,3 BPG rather than less. A leftward shift always means tighter binding and less release, and intact hemoglobin still changes affinity when its regulator is gone.
questions.answerText: The curve shifts left, and the blood releases oxygen less readily

questions.q: After several days at high altitude, red cell 2,3 BPG concentration rises. What is the effect on the oxyhemoglobin curve and why is it useful?
options: A rightward shift, which raises arterial saturation back toward sea level values
A leftward shift, which raises P50 and thereby improves tissue delivery
A rightward shift, which helps unload oxygen at the tissue despite low saturation
A leftward shift, which helps load oxygen in the lung despite low alveolar PO2
questions.why: More 2,3 BPG lowers affinity and moves the curve right, so even though arterial blood carries less oxygen the tissues can strip a larger fraction of it. A leftward shift would help loading slightly but would make the more urgent problem, unloading, worse. A rightward shift does not raise arterial saturation and in fact lowers it a little, and a leftward shift lowers P50 rather than raising it.
questions.answerText: A rightward shift, which helps unload oxygen at the tissue despite low saturation

questions.q: A patient is deliberately cooled to 30 C during surgery. What happens to the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?
options: It shifts left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly
It shifts right, so hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily
It shifts left, so P50 rises above normal
It flattens, so maximum saturation falls
questions.why: Cooling strengthens the oxygen hemoglobin bond, raising affinity and moving the curve left, which reduces unloading, though tissue oxygen demand is also much lower at that temperature. A rightward shift would follow fever rather than cooling. A leftward shift lowers P50, so pairing left with a rising P50 is contradictory, and temperature moves the curve sideways rather than lowering its plateau.
questions.answerText: It shifts left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly

questions.q: A leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve has what combined effect on loading in the lung and unloading at the tissue?
options: Loading is impaired and unloading is slightly favored
Both loading and unloading are impaired
Both loading and unloading are favored
Loading is slightly favored and unloading is impaired
questions.why: Higher affinity means hemoglobin picks oxygen up more eagerly and lets go of it more reluctantly, so the lung end benefits a little and the tissue end suffers. The reversed version describes a rightward shift. A shift cannot impair both ends, since affinity acts in opposite directions at the two ends, and for the same reason it cannot favor both.
questions.answerText: Loading is slightly favored and unloading is impaired

questions.q: Why does a rightward shift of the curve cost very little oxygen loading in the lung?
options: Hemoglobin ignores pH and carbon dioxide while it is in the pulmonary capillary
The lung generates enough 2,3 BPG of its own to cancel out the shift
Alveolar PO2 sits on the flat part of the curve, where a shift changes saturation little
Alveolar PO2 sits on the steep part of the curve, where a change in affinity has no effect
questions.why: At a PO2 near 100 mmHg the curve is nearly horizontal, so even a shifted curve is still close to full saturation there, while the tissue end sits on the steep segment where the same shift produces a large gain in unloading. The plateau, not the steep part, is what makes loading insensitive. Hemoglobin responds to pH and carbon dioxide everywhere, and 2,3 BPG is made in red cells rather than in the lung.
questions.answerText: Alveolar PO2 sits on the flat part of the curve, where a shift changes saturation little

questions.q: A sprinter's quadriceps reaches 40 C with a local pH of 7.15 and a PCO2 of 60 mmHg. Predict what happens to P50 in that muscle and to the fraction of oxygen extracted.
options: P50 rises well above 27 mmHg and extraction decreases
P50 is unchanged because the three factors cancel one another
P50 rises well above 27 mmHg and extraction increases sharply
P50 falls well below 27 mmHg and extraction increases sharply
questions.why: Heat, acidosis, and a high carbon dioxide all push the curve the same direction, to the right, so P50 climbs and the muscle strips a much larger share of the oxygen delivered. A falling P50 marks a leftward shift, which is the opposite of what these conditions produce. A rightward shift always improves extraction rather than reducing it, and the three factors reinforce each other rather than canceling.
questions.answerText: P50 rises well above 27 mmHg and extraction increases sharply

questions.q: A septic patient has a temperature of 40 C and a lactic acidosis with a pH of 7.20. Her arterial saturation is 96 percent. Explain what her curve is doing at the tissue and at the lung.
options: It is shifted right, which greatly improves tissue unloading and costs little loading in the lung
It is shifted right, which impairs unloading at the tissue and impairs loading in the lung
It is shifted left, which improves unloading at the tissue and impairs loading in the lung
It is shifted left at the tissue and right in the lung, because pH differs in the two places
questions.why: Fever and acidosis both lower affinity, so the curve is shifted right, and because the lung end sits on the plateau the near normal arterial saturation is preserved while the steep tissue end gives up far more oxygen. A rightward shift improves rather than impairs unloading, which is the whole point of the shift. A leftward shift would tighten binding and reduce unloading, and although pH does differ slightly between arterial and venous blood, the systemic acidosis shifts the curve everywhere.
questions.answerText: It is shifted right, which greatly improves tissue unloading and costs little loading in the lung

questions.q: A patient receives several units of blood stored for four weeks. His arterial saturation reads 99 percent, yet lactate is rising. Work back to what the stored cells are doing.
options: Their curve is right shifted from 2,3 BPG depletion, so they cannot load in the lung
Their hemoglobin has been denatured, so total carrying capacity has fallen
Their oxygen content is low, which is why saturation reads high
Their curve is left shifted from 2,3 BPG depletion, so they load fully but unload poorly
questions.why: Depleted cells bind oxygen tightly, so saturation measured in arterial blood looks excellent while the tissue end of the curve gives up very little, and anaerobic metabolism produces lactate despite the reassuring number. Depletion shifts the curve left rather than right, since 2,3 BPG is what lowers affinity. Hemoglobin is not denatured in stored blood, and a high saturation with normal hemoglobin means content is adequate, so content is not the failing step.
questions.answerText: Their curve is left shifted from 2,3 BPG depletion, so they load fully but unload poorly

questions.q: A newcomer to high altitude has a respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation and, after several days, an increased red cell 2,3 BPG. What is the net effect on the position of her oxyhemoglobin curve?
options: Both changes push the curve right, so affinity falls sharply
The alkalosis pushes right and the 2,3 BPG pulls left, so the net is a marked leftward shift
The alkalosis pulls left and the 2,3 BPG pushes right, so the net position is near normal
Both changes pull the curve left, so affinity rises sharply
questions.why: A high pH raises affinity and moves the curve left, while a rise in 2,3 BPG lowers affinity and moves it right, and the two roughly offset so the net curve sits near its usual position. The two changes act in opposite directions, so neither the both left nor the both right option is correct. The last option has the two effects assigned backwards, since alkalosis is always a leftward influence and 2,3 BPG is always a rightward one.
questions.answerText: The alkalosis pulls left and the 2,3 BPG pushes right, so the net position is near normal

questions.q: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
options: As carbaminohemoglobin bound to hemoglobin
As carbon dioxide dissolved in plasma
As carbonic acid circulating in plasma
As bicarbonate ion dissolved in plasma
questions.why: About 70 percent of carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate, produced inside the red cell and then exported to plasma, which is why the blood's carbon dioxide store is also its main pH buffer. Carbaminohemoglobin accounts for roughly 23 percent, and dissolved carbon dioxide for about 7 percent. Carbonic acid is only a fleeting intermediate and is present in negligible amounts.
questions.answerText: As bicarbonate ion dissolved in plasma

questions.q: About what percentage of carbon dioxide is carried as bicarbonate?
options: About 70 percent
About 23 percent
About 7 percent
About 45 percent
questions.why: Roughly 70 percent is converted to bicarbonate inside red cells by carbonic anhydrase and then exported to plasma. About 23 percent is the carbamino fraction bound to hemoglobin. About 7 percent is the dissolved fraction, and about 45 percent does not correspond to any of the three transport forms.
questions.answerText: About 70 percent

questions.q: About what percentage of carbon dioxide is carried bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin?
options: About 23 percent
About 70 percent
About 7 percent
About 50 percent
questions.why: Roughly 23 percent binds directly to hemoglobin, making it the second largest transport form. About 70 percent is the bicarbonate share, the largest. About 7 percent is dissolved carbon dioxide, and about 50 percent overstates the carbamino share by more than double.
questions.answerText: About 23 percent

questions.q: About what percentage of carbon dioxide is carried simply dissolved in plasma?
options: About 30 percent
About 7 percent
About 23 percent
About 1.5 percent
questions.why: About 7 percent travels dissolved, which is a larger share than for oxygen because carbon dioxide is far more soluble, and it is this fraction that a blood gas analyzer reports as PCO2. About 23 percent is the carbamino share. About 1.5 percent is the dissolved share of oxygen, not carbon dioxide, and about 30 percent is too high for the dissolved form.
questions.answerText: About 7 percent

questions.q: Which enzyme converts carbon dioxide and water into carbonic acid, and where is it concentrated?
options: Carbonic anhydrase, inside the red blood cell
Carbonic anhydrase, in the plasma
Carboxypeptidase, inside the red blood cell
Carbonic anhydrase, on the alveolar epithelial surface
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase sits in high concentration inside red cells, which is why bicarbonate formation happens there rather than in plasma and why the chloride shift is needed to move the product out. Plasma has almost no carbonic anhydrase, so the uncatalyzed reaction there is far too slow to matter. Carboxypeptidase is a digestive protease with no role in gas transport, and the alveolar surface is not where the reaction is catalyzed.
questions.answerText: Carbonic anhydrase, inside the red blood cell

questions.q: Where on the hemoglobin molecule does carbon dioxide bind?
options: On the porphyrin ring surrounding the iron
On terminal amine groups of the globin chains
On the iron atom in the center of each heme group
On the same site that binds 2,3 BPG
questions.why: Carbon dioxide forms carbamino compounds with amine groups on the globin protein, which is why it can be carried at the same time as oxygen rather than competing for the same site. The heme iron binds oxygen and carbon monoxide, not carbon dioxide. The 2,3 BPG site is the central cavity of the tetramer, and the porphyrin ring holds the iron rather than binding gases itself.
questions.answerText: On terminal amine groups of the globin chains

questions.q: During the chloride shift in a systemic capillary, which ion moves into the red blood cell?
options: Chloride
Bicarbonate
Sodium
Potassium
questions.why: Bicarbonate made inside the cell leaves for the plasma, and chloride moves in to take its place so the cell does not build up a net charge. Bicarbonate moves in the opposite direction, out of the cell, in a systemic capillary. Sodium and potassium are not exchanged by this transporter and are not part of the shift.
questions.answerText: Chloride

questions.q: Which membrane protein carries out the chloride shift?
options: Aquaporin 1, which allows water to follow the ions
A voltage gated chloride channel opened by depolarization
The band 3 anion exchanger, which swaps bicarbonate for chloride
The Na+/K+ ATPase, which swaps sodium for potassium
questions.why: Band 3 is an antiporter that trades one bicarbonate out for one chloride in, moving the product of the reaction into plasma without charge imbalance. The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains cation gradients and has nothing to do with bicarbonate. Aquaporin 1 does let water follow, but it moves water rather than performing the anion exchange, and red cells do not depolarize to open voltage gated channels.
questions.answerText: The band 3 anion exchanger, which swaps bicarbonate for chloride

questions.q: Hemoglobin buffers the hydrogen ions released when bicarbonate forms inside the red cell. What would happen to bicarbonate production if it did not?
options: It would be unchanged, because carbonic anhydrase is not affected by pH
It would stop entirely, because hemoglobin is the source of the bicarbonate
It would slow, because accumulating hydrogen ion would stall the reaction
It would speed up, because free hydrogen ion drives the reaction forward
questions.why: Carbonic acid dissociates into bicarbonate and hydrogen ion, so letting hydrogen ion pile up pushes the equilibrium backwards and shuts the pathway down, which is why an on site buffer matters so much. Free hydrogen ion is a product, not a driver, so more of it slows rather than speeds the reaction. Enzyme activity and equilibrium position both depend on pH, and the bicarbonate comes from carbon dioxide and water rather than from hemoglobin.
questions.answerText: It would slow, because accumulating hydrogen ion would stall the reaction

questions.q: Carbon dioxide diffuses from a metabolically active tissue into a red blood cell. What is the next step?
options: It is converted straight to bicarbonate without an intermediate
Carbonic anhydrase combines it with water to form carbonic acid
It binds directly to the heme iron in place of oxygen
It is pumped into the plasma by band 3
questions.why: Inside the cell the enzyme catalyzes the hydration of carbon dioxide to carbonic acid, which then dissociates almost instantly into hydrogen ion and bicarbonate. Carbon dioxide does not bind heme iron, since it uses globin amine groups instead. Band 3 exports bicarbonate rather than carbon dioxide, and the carbonic acid intermediate does exist even though it is short lived.
questions.answerText: Carbonic anhydrase combines it with water to form carbonic acid

questions.q: In a systemic capillary, which way does bicarbonate move across the red cell membrane, and why?
options: Into the cell, because the plasma bicarbonate concentration is rising faster
Out of the cell, because an ATPase is actively pumping chloride into the cell
It does not move, because bicarbonate cannot cross the cell membrane at all
Out of the cell, because bicarbonate is accumulating inside the cell
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase produces bicarbonate inside the cell, its concentration rises above the plasma value, and band 3 lets it move down that gradient into plasma while chloride comes in. Bicarbonate moves into the cell at the lung, where the reaction runs in reverse. The exchange is passive and driven by gradients rather than by ATP, and bicarbonate crosses readily through the anion exchanger.
questions.answerText: Out of the cell, because bicarbonate is accumulating inside the cell

questions.q: Why does a red blood cell swell slightly as it passes through a systemic capillary?
options: Hemoglobin unfolds when it releases oxygen, taking up more volume
Chloride entering during the chloride shift raises intracellular osmolarity, and water follows
Bicarbonate accumulating inside the cell raises intracellular osmolarity, and water follows
Carbon dioxide is a large molecule and physically occupies more space
questions.why: Chloride enters to replace exported bicarbonate, but the hydrogen ions from the same reaction stay behind bound to hemoglobin, so the cell gains solute overall and water follows it in, which is why venous hematocrit runs slightly higher than arterial. Bicarbonate is leaving rather than accumulating, so it cannot be the osmotic cause. Dissolved carbon dioxide contributes negligible volume, and hemoglobin changes conformation without a meaningful change in cell volume.
questions.answerText: Chloride entering during the chloride shift raises intracellular osmolarity, and water follows

questions.q: In a pulmonary capillary, which way does chloride move across the red cell membrane?
options: Into the cell, as bicarbonate continues to move out toward the plasma
Out of the cell, as bicarbonate also moves out into the plasma
Chloride does not move at the lung, only in the systemic capillary
Out of the cell, as bicarbonate moves in to be reconverted to carbon dioxide
questions.why: At the lung the whole sequence runs backwards: bicarbonate re-enters the red cell, combines with hydrogen ion, and is converted back to carbon dioxide for exhalation, so chloride must leave in exchange. Chloride entering with bicarbonate leaving is the systemic capillary pattern. Band 3 is an exchanger, so the two anions cannot both move the same way, and the reverse chloride shift is a real and necessary step at the lung.
questions.answerText: Out of the cell, as bicarbonate moves in to be reconverted to carbon dioxide

questions.q: A drug inhibits carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells. What happens to carbon dioxide carriage?
options: Carbon dioxide binds hemoglobin instead, so total carriage is unchanged
Less carbon dioxide can be converted to bicarbonate, so tissue and venous PCO2 rise
More carbon dioxide is converted to bicarbonate, so venous PCO2 falls
Carbon dioxide carriage is unaffected, because most of it is carried dissolved
questions.why: Blocking the enzyme cripples the pathway that handles about 70 percent of carbon dioxide transport, so the gas backs up as dissolved carbon dioxide and its partial pressure in tissue and venous blood climbs. Inhibiting an enzyme reduces rather than increases the reaction it catalyzes. Only about 7 percent is carried dissolved, so that route cannot absorb the load, and the carbamino route can take up only a small part of the shortfall.
questions.answerText: Less carbon dioxide can be converted to bicarbonate, so tissue and venous PCO2 rise

questions.q: Which form of carbon dioxide does a blood gas analyzer actually report when it gives a PCO2?
options: The bicarbonate concentration converted into pressure units
The carbamino bound fraction only
Only the dissolved carbon dioxide
The total of all three transport forms
questions.why: Partial pressure describes gas molecules in solution exerting pressure, so PCO2 reflects only the dissolved fraction, and the far larger bicarbonate and carbamino pools are invisible to that measurement. Total carbon dioxide content is a separate quantity reported in mL/dL or mmol/L. Bicarbonate is reported as its own concentration, and the carbamino fraction is not measured directly at all.
questions.answerText: Only the dissolved carbon dioxide

questions.q: Trace one carbon dioxide molecule that enters a systemic capillary and is carried as bicarbonate. What is the correct sequence?
options: It binds hemoglobin at a heme site, is released as bicarbonate, and then diffuses into the plasma
It enters the red cell, binds 2,3 BPG, and is carried in the central cavity
It enters the red cell, is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase, and its bicarbonate leaves in exchange for chloride
It is hydrated in the plasma, and the bicarbonate it forms then enters the red cell in exchange for chloride
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase is inside the red cell, so the gas must enter first, and only after the reaction and dissociation does the bicarbonate exit through band 3 with chloride coming in. Plasma has too little carbonic anhydrase for the reaction to run there at any useful speed. Hemoglobin binding is the separate carbamino route and does not produce bicarbonate, and 2,3 BPG occupies the central cavity to modify oxygen affinity rather than to carry carbon dioxide.
questions.answerText: It enters the red cell, is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase, and its bicarbonate leaves in exchange for chloride

questions.q: A red cell has a genetic defect that leaves band 3 non functional. Predict what happens to carbon dioxide carriage in a systemic capillary.
options: Bicarbonate accumulates inside the cell, the reaction slows, and less is loaded
Bicarbonate accumulates in plasma, so carriage is increased
Carbon dioxide carriage is unaffected, because carbonic anhydrase is still working
Carbon dioxide is carried entirely as carbaminohemoglobin instead, with no net loss
questions.why: Without an exit route the product builds up inside the cell, and by mass action a piled up product slows the reaction that makes it, so the main carriage pathway stalls. Bicarbonate cannot accumulate in plasma when the only transporter that puts it there is broken. An intact enzyme is not enough if the product cannot leave, and the carbamino route handles only about 23 percent normally and cannot expand to cover the rest.
questions.answerText: Bicarbonate accumulates inside the cell, the reaction slows, and less is loaded

questions.q: A patient hypoventilates for several minutes. Predict what happens to the three forms of carbon dioxide in blood and to arterial pH.
options: All three forms fall, and pH rises toward alkalosis
Bicarbonate rises while the dissolved and carbamino forms fall, and pH is unchanged
All three forms rise, and pH falls as more hydrogen ion is generated
Only the dissolved form rises, and pH is unchanged because bicarbonate buffers it
questions.why: Retained carbon dioxide raises the dissolved fraction first, and since that fraction feeds both the carbonic anhydrase reaction and carbamino binding, all three pools rise together while the added hydrogen ion drives pH down into a respiratory acidosis. Bicarbonate rises rather than staying put, but it is generated together with hydrogen ion so it cannot prevent the pH fall. All three forms falling describes hyperventilation, and the forms move together rather than in opposite directions.
questions.answerText: All three forms rise, and pH falls as more hydrogen ion is generated

questions.q: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is present in the blood. Explain the consequence at the tissue and then at the lung.
options: More bicarbonate forms at the tissue, and at the lung the extra bicarbonate is exhaled as carbon dioxide
Loading at the tissue is normal, but at the lung the carbon dioxide cannot be released from hemoglobin
Loading at the tissue fails, but exhalation at the lung is normal because the dissolved fraction is enough
Less bicarbonate forms at the tissue, so less is loaded, and at the lung less is reconverted, so less is exhaled
questions.why: The same enzyme runs the reaction in both directions, so inhibition slows bicarbonate formation in the tissue capillary and slows its reconversion to carbon dioxide in the pulmonary capillary, leaving carbon dioxide to accumulate in the body. Inhibiting the enzyme cannot increase the reaction. The blocked step is the bicarbonate reaction rather than carbamino release from hemoglobin, and the dissolved fraction is only about 7 percent of normal carriage, far too little to sustain exhalation on its own.
questions.answerText: Less bicarbonate forms at the tissue, so less is loaded, and at the lung less is reconverted, so less is exhaled

questions.q: What does the Bohr effect describe?
options: A rise in carbon dioxide or hydrogen ion lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
A fall in oxygen saturation raises hemoglobin's ability to carry carbon dioxide
A rise in temperature raises hemoglobin's affinity for carbon dioxide
A rise in 2,3 BPG raises hemoglobin's affinity for hydrogen ion
questions.why: The Bohr effect is carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion acting on the oxygen binding of hemoglobin, lowering affinity and shifting the curve right so more oxygen is released where metabolism is high. Deoxygenation raising carbon dioxide carriage is the Haldane effect, the mirror image. Temperature does shift the oxygen curve, but that is not what the Bohr effect names, and 2,3 BPG acts on oxygen affinity rather than on hydrogen ion binding.
questions.answerText: A rise in carbon dioxide or hydrogen ion lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen

questions.q: What does the Haldane effect describe?
options: A fall in pH raises the amount of dissolved carbon dioxide in plasma
Deoxygenated hemoglobin carries more carbon dioxide than oxygenated hemoglobin
A rise in carbon dioxide lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly than oxygenated hemoglobin
questions.why: The Haldane effect is about carbon dioxide carriage: giving up oxygen converts hemoglobin into a better hydrogen ion buffer and a better carbamino former, so it picks up more carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide lowering oxygen affinity is the Bohr effect, which runs the other way. Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds oxygen less tightly, not more, and dissolved carbon dioxide depends on PCO2 and solubility rather than on pH.
questions.answerText: Deoxygenated hemoglobin carries more carbon dioxide than oxygenated hemoglobin

questions.q: The Bohr effect acts on which property of hemoglobin?
options: Its rate of synthesis in the bone marrow
Its affinity for oxygen
Its affinity for carbon dioxide
Its total oxygen carrying capacity
questions.why: The Bohr effect changes how tightly hemoglobin holds oxygen, which is why it is drawn as a shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. Affinity for carbon dioxide is what the Haldane effect changes. Carrying capacity depends on how much hemoglobin is present, not on affinity, and synthesis in the marrow is regulated by erythropoietin over days.
questions.answerText: Its affinity for oxygen

questions.q: The Haldane effect acts on which property of hemoglobin?
options: Its ability to carry carbon dioxide and to buffer acid
Its ability to bind oxygen at the iron of the heme group
Its ability to bind 2,3 BPG in its own central cavity
Its ability to release iron for recycling
questions.why: The Haldane effect describes how the oxygenation state of hemoglobin sets how much carbon dioxide it can carry, both as carbamino compounds and indirectly through buffering the hydrogen ion from bicarbonate formation. Oxygen binding at the heme iron is what the Bohr effect modulates. 2,3 BPG binding is a separate regulator of oxygen affinity, and iron recycling happens when the cell is broken down, not during gas transport.
questions.answerText: Its ability to carry carbon dioxide and to buffer acid

questions.q: At a systemic capillary, the Bohr effect shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve in which direction?
options: To the right
To the left
To the right only during exercise
It does not shift the curve
questions.why: Tissue carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion lower affinity, so the curve shifts right and hemoglobin releases more oxygen exactly where metabolism is producing those signals. A leftward shift would hold oxygen on and defeat the purpose. The effect operates at rest as well as in exercise, just more strongly in exercise, and a shift is precisely what the Bohr effect produces.
questions.answerText: To the right

questions.q: Why does deoxygenated hemoglobin carry more carbon dioxide than oxygenated hemoglobin?
options: It is a better hydrogen ion buffer and forms carbamino compounds more readily
It has empty heme sites where carbon dioxide can bind instead of oxygen
It contains more 2,3 BPG, which carries carbon dioxide in the central cavity
It is more permeable, so carbon dioxide diffuses into it faster
questions.why: Releasing oxygen changes hemoglobin's conformation so that its amine groups accept carbon dioxide more readily and its histidine residues take up hydrogen ion more readily, and both changes let the red cell absorb more carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide binds globin amine groups rather than the heme iron, so empty heme sites are not the mechanism. 2,3 BPG modifies oxygen affinity and does not carry carbon dioxide, and hemoglobin is a protein rather than a membrane with permeability.
questions.answerText: It is a better hydrogen ion buffer and forms carbamino compounds more readily

questions.q: Where in the circulation is the Bohr effect most useful?
options: In the pulmonary capillaries, where oxygen is loaded
In the large systemic arteries, where pressure is highest
In the pulmonary veins, where blood returns to the heart
In the systemic capillaries of metabolically active tissue
questions.why: Active tissue produces the carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion that trigger the effect, and it is exactly where extra oxygen release is needed, so the signal and the benefit coincide. In the pulmonary capillary the situation reverses, and the loss of carbon dioxide helps loading instead. Large arteries and pulmonary veins are conduits where no gas exchange with tissue takes place.
questions.answerText: In the systemic capillaries of metabolically active tissue

questions.q: At the lung, what does the Haldane effect do?
options: Hydrogen ion binding to hemoglobin promotes the release of oxygen
Oxygen binding to hemoglobin promotes carbon dioxide release
Carbon dioxide release from plasma promotes the binding of oxygen
Oxygen binding promotes further loading of carbon dioxide onto hemoglobin
questions.why: As hemoglobin takes on oxygen it becomes a poorer carbon dioxide carrier and a poorer buffer, so it dumps carbamino carbon dioxide and releases hydrogen ion that combines with bicarbonate to regenerate carbon dioxide for exhalation. Carbon dioxide loss promoting oxygen binding is the Bohr effect running in reverse at the lung, which is a real effect but a different one. Loading more carbon dioxide at the lung would be backwards, and hydrogen ion promoting oxygen release is again the Bohr effect.
questions.answerText: Oxygen binding to hemoglobin promotes carbon dioxide release

questions.q: Exercising muscle produces lactic acid, and local pH falls. Which effect is at work, and what is the result?
options: The Bohr effect, so hemoglobin picks up more carbon dioxide from the muscle
The Haldane effect, so hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly
The Bohr effect, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen to the muscle
The Haldane effect, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen to the muscle
questions.why: Hydrogen ion acting on oxygen affinity is the Bohr effect by definition, and the lowered affinity means more oxygen is unloaded in the muscle that generated the acid. The Haldane effect concerns carbon dioxide carriage rather than oxygen release. Extra carbon dioxide pickup driven by deoxygenation is the Haldane effect, not the Bohr effect, and acidosis loosens rather than tightens oxygen binding.
questions.answerText: The Bohr effect, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen to the muscle

questions.q: In the pulmonary capillary, hemoglobin becomes saturated with oxygen and immediately gives up carbon dioxide. Which effect explains the carbon dioxide release?
options: The Haldane effect, because alveolar PCO2 is lower than blood PCO2
The Bohr effect, because alveolar PO2 is higher than blood PO2
The Haldane effect, because oxygenated hemoglobin is a poorer carbon dioxide carrier
The Bohr effect, because oxygenated hemoglobin is a poorer carbon dioxide carrier
questions.why: The change in carbon dioxide carriage caused by a change in oxygenation state is the Haldane effect, and it makes carbon dioxide unloading at the lung considerably faster than diffusion gradients alone would allow. The Bohr effect names carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion acting on oxygen, so it cannot be the label here. The alveolar to blood PCO2 gradient is real but is simple diffusion rather than the Haldane effect, and the PO2 gradient is what drives oxygen loading.
questions.answerText: The Haldane effect, because oxygenated hemoglobin is a poorer carbon dioxide carrier

questions.q: A rise in tissue PCO2 increases the amount of oxygen released from hemoglobin. Classify this observation.
options: Haldane effect
Chloride shift
Cooperative binding
Bohr effect
questions.why: Carbon dioxide acting on oxygen affinity is the Bohr effect, whichever of the two signals, carbon dioxide or hydrogen ion, is named. The Haldane effect would be the reverse arrangement, oxygen state acting on carbon dioxide carriage. The chloride shift moves bicarbonate out of the red cell and does not itself change oxygen release, and cooperative binding is the interaction among the four heme sites that shapes the curve.
questions.answerText: Bohr effect

questions.q: Deoxygenated blood in a systemic capillary takes up more carbon dioxide than fully oxygenated blood would at the same PCO2. Classify this observation.
options: Reverse chloride shift
Increased 2,3 BPG binding
Haldane effect
Bohr effect
questions.why: The oxygenation state of hemoglobin setting its carbon dioxide capacity is the Haldane effect, and it is why the carbon dioxide dissociation curve for venous blood lies above the arterial one. The Bohr effect goes the other way, with carbon dioxide acting on oxygen. The reverse chloride shift is the lung end of bicarbonate handling, and 2,3 BPG changes oxygen affinity rather than carbon dioxide carriage.
questions.answerText: Haldane effect

questions.q: Suppose a modified hemoglobin has no Bohr effect but is otherwise normal. Predict the effect on oxygen delivery to exercising muscle.
options: Delivery falls, because loading in the lung would now be incomplete
Delivery falls, because the curve no longer shifts right where acid accumulates
Delivery rises, because oxygen is no longer driven off before reaching the muscle
Delivery is unchanged, because arterial saturation is unchanged
questions.why: Without the Bohr effect the local carbon dioxide and acid of working muscle no longer lower affinity, so hemoglobin holds onto oxygen and extraction falls at exactly the moment demand is highest. Oxygen is not lost prematurely, since the shift only takes effect where carbon dioxide and acid are high. Arterial saturation is unchanged in both cases, which is why it cannot be what determines delivery, and loading in the lung would if anything be slightly easier.
questions.answerText: Delivery falls, because the curve no longer shifts right where acid accumulates

questions.q: At the same PCO2 of 45 mmHg, venous blood holds more total carbon dioxide than arterial blood does. What accounts for the difference?
options: The Bohr effect, since venous blood has a slightly lower pH
The slightly higher hematocrit of venous blood
The larger dissolved carbon dioxide fraction in venous plasma
The Haldane effect, since venous hemoglobin is deoxygenated
questions.why: Venous hemoglobin has given up oxygen and is therefore a better carbon dioxide carrier and buffer, so at any given PCO2 it holds more total carbon dioxide, which is drawn as a higher carbon dioxide dissociation curve. The Bohr effect describes the pH change acting on oxygen, not on carbon dioxide content. Venous hematocrit is only trivially higher, and at the same PCO2 the dissolved fraction is by definition the same in both.
questions.answerText: The Haldane effect, since venous hemoglobin is deoxygenated

questions.q: Trace what happens at a systemic capillary in exercising muscle when both effects operate together.
options: Oxygen comes off first for reasons unrelated to carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide is then carried entirely as bicarbonate in plasma
Carbon dioxide binds the heme sites, displacing oxygen, and hemoglobin then carries carbon dioxide instead of oxygen
Acid raises oxygen affinity so oxygen is retained, and carbon dioxide is carried dissolved instead
Carbon dioxide and acid lower oxygen affinity so oxygen comes off, and the resulting deoxygenated hemoglobin then takes up more carbon dioxide
questions.why: The two effects are a coupled loop: the Bohr effect uses tissue carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion to drive oxygen off, and the Haldane effect uses the resulting deoxygenated hemoglobin to soak up more carbon dioxide, so each gas helps move the other. Bicarbonate carries most carbon dioxide, but its formation inside the red cell still depends on hemoglobin buffering the hydrogen ion. Carbon dioxide binds globin amine groups rather than competing for heme iron, and acid lowers rather than raises oxygen affinity.
questions.answerText: Carbon dioxide and acid lower oxygen affinity so oxygen comes off, and the resulting deoxygenated hemoglobin then takes up more carbon dioxide

questions.q: Trace what happens in a pulmonary capillary when both effects operate together.
options: Oxygen binding raises carbon dioxide carriage, and the rising carbon dioxide then improves loading further
Both effects are switched off at the lung, so exchange depends only on the partial pressure gradients
